follow.why: Osteoblasts lay down matrix around themselves until they are trapped in a lacuna; they then become osteocytes. Osteoclasts form by fusion of blood-forming cells and do not become osteocytes, and osteogenic cells divide on bone surfaces, not in lacunae.

labels.name: Osteoblast
labels.fn: A bone-building cell on the bone surface. It secretes the organic part of the matrix (osteoid) and helps it mineralize; when it is walled in by its own matrix it becomes an osteocyte.

labels.name: Osteogenic cell
labels.fn: A flat stem cell in the inner periosteum and the endosteum. It is the only bone cell that divides; its daughters become osteoblasts.

labels.name: Osteoclast
labels.fn: A very large cell with many nuclei on the bone surface. It dissolves the mineral and digests the collagen of bone, breaking bone down (resorption).

follow.q: An osteoclast is large and has many nuclei. Why?
options: It divides its nucleus without dividing
It forms by fusion of several cells
It grows from an osteogenic cell over years
follow.why: Osteoclasts form when several precursor cells from the blood-forming lineage fuse, so one cell carries many nuclei. It does not arise from the osteogenic cell line, which makes osteoblasts, and it does not engulf cells.

labels.name: Spongy bone
labels.fn: Bone built as a lattice of thin struts (trabeculae) instead of solid layers. It fills the ends of long bones, where it is light but strong along the lines of stress.

labels.name: Compact bone
labels.fn: The dense, solid bone that forms the wall of the shaft and the outer shell of every bone. It is made of tightly packed osteons.

labels.name: Trabeculae
labels.fn: The thin struts and plates of bone that make up spongy bone. They line up along the lines of stress, and the spaces between them hold red marrow.

follow.q: Why does spongy bone have no osteons or central canals?
options: Its cells need no oxygen to survive
It has no living cells in its matrix
Its trabeculae are thin, near marrow spaces
Its trabeculae are made of hyaline cartilage
follow.why: Each trabecula is thin enough that osteocytes are supplied by diffusion through canaliculi from the marrow spaces around it, so no central canal is needed. Spongy bone is living bone tissue with osteocytes, not cartilage.

labels.name: Lacuna
labels.fn: A small cavity in the bone matrix that holds one osteocyte. Lacunae sit between the lamellae.

labels.name: Osteocyte
labels.fn: A mature bone cell in its lacuna. It maintains the matrix around it and passes signals and nutrients to its neighbors through canaliculi.

labels.name: Osteoclast
labels.fn: A large cell with many nuclei on the surface of a trabecula. It breaks down (resorbs) bone, working with osteoblasts to reshape the struts.

labels.name: Osteoblasts aligned along trabeculae of new bone
labels.fn: Bone-building cells lined up along the surface of a trabecula. They lay down new matrix, which thickens the strut.

labels.name: Canaliculi openings on surface
labels.fn: The tiny openings of canaliculi on the surface of a trabecula. Through them, osteocytes inside the strut exchange nutrients and wastes with the marrow space.

labels.name: Endosteum
labels.fn: The thin cell layer covering the surfaces of the trabeculae. It holds osteogenic cells, osteoblasts and osteoclasts.

labels.name: Lamellae
labels.fn: The thin layers of matrix that build up a trabecula, laid down one on top of another.

labels.name: Canaliculi
labels.fn: Tiny channels in the matrix that link lacunae with each other and with the bone surface. The arms of osteocytes run through them, carrying nutrients, wastes and signals.

follow.q: An osteocyte is walled in by hard matrix. How does it get nutrients?
options: Through blood vessels inside its lacuna
By dissolving the matrix around it
By diffusion straight through the hard mineral
Through canaliculi linking it to other cells
follow.why: Osteocyte arms run through canaliculi and join at gap junctions, so nutrients and signals pass from cell to cell out to the nearest vessel or marrow space. There is no vessel in a lacuna, the mineral blocks diffusion, and osteocytes do not dissolve their own walls to feed.

labels.name: Lamellae
labels.fn: Thin layers of mineralized matrix. Their collagen fibers run in a different direction in each layer, which helps bone resist twisting.

labels.name: Compact bone
labels.fn: The dense, solid bone that forms the outer plates of this flat bone. Its tightly packed osteons resist bending and twisting.

labels.name: Periosteum
labels.fn: The two-layer membrane covering the outer surfaces of the bone, anchoring tendons and carrying vessels and nerves into the bone.

labels.name: Spongy bone (diploë)
labels.fn: The layer of spongy bone sandwiched between the two plates of compact bone in a flat skull bone, called the diploë. Its lattice of trabeculae makes the bone light, and its spaces hold red marrow.

follow.q: What fills the spaces between the trabeculae of the diploë?
follow.why: The spaces in spongy bone of flat bones hold red marrow, which makes blood cells. Yellow marrow fills the shaft of adult long bones, osteons are the units of compact bone, and articular cartilage only caps joint surfaces.

sets.title: Epiphyseal plate zones and bone formation

labels.name: Reserve zone
labels.fn: The zone of the epiphyseal plate nearest the epiphysis: small, scattered chondrocytes that rarely divide. It anchors the plate to the epiphysis, whose vessels feed the plate.

follow.q: A growth-plate injury kills the cells nearest the epiphysis. Why can this stop growth at that plate?
options: It removes the zone where bone replaces cartilage
It removes the cells that supply the dividing zone
It blocks the nutrient artery of the shaft
It destroys the calcified matrix that is later turned into bone
follow.why: The reserve and proliferative zones supply the new chondrocytes that lengthen the plate; lose them and the plate stops adding cartilage. Bone forms on the diaphysis side, which is not where the injury is, and the nutrient artery supplies the shaft, not the plate.

labels.name: Proliferative zone
labels.fn: The zone where chondrocytes divide rapidly and stack in columns like piles of coins. The new cells push the epiphysis away from the diaphysis; this is where most length comes from.

follow.q: In which zone do chondrocytes divide to add length?
follow.why: Rapid division in stacks happens in the proliferative zone. Reserve-zone cells rarely divide, calcified-matrix cells are dying, and the zone of ossification is where bone replaces the cartilage.

labels.name: Calcified matrix
labels.fn: The zone where the matrix around the enlarged chondrocytes calcifies. Cut off from diffusion, the chondrocytes die, leaving columns of calcified cartilage.

labels.name: Primary spongiosa
labels.fn: The first spongy bone laid down on the calcified cartilage columns just below the plate; it still has cartilage at its core.

labels.name: Zone of ossification
labels.fn: The region below the plate, on the diaphysis side, where capillaries and osteogenic cells invade the empty spaces and osteoblasts lay bone on the calcified cartilage columns.

labels.name: Metaphysis
labels.fn: The flared region between the diaphysis and the epiphysis. In a growing bone it holds the epiphyseal plate and the new bone forming below it.

labels.name: Secondary spongiosa
labels.fn: Deeper, older spongy bone below the primary spongiosa, where osteoclasts have cleared the cartilage cores and the trabeculae have been rebuilt.

labels.name: Epiphysis
labels.fn: The rounded end of the long bone, filled with spongy bone and red marrow. In a child it is separated from the metaphysis by the epiphyseal plate.

labels.name: Metaphysis
labels.fn: The flared region where the shaft widens toward the epiphysis. The epiphyseal plate lies in it in a growing bone.

labels.name: Epiphyseal line
labels.fn: A thin line of bone where the epiphyseal plate used to be. It forms when growth in length ends and bone replaces the last of the plate’s cartilage.

labels.name: Diaphysis
labels.fn: The shaft of the long bone, between the two metaphyses. It grows in width by appositional growth under the periosteum.

labels.name: Epiphyseal plate (growth plate)
labels.fn: The disc of hyaline cartilage between the epiphysis and the diaphysis of a growing long bone. Its chondrocytes keep dividing while bone replaces cartilage on the diaphysis side, so the bone gets longer.

follow.q: Why can a bone no longer grow in length once the epiphyseal plate has become an epiphyseal line?
options: The periosteum has stopped making cells
The medullary cavity has filled with red marrow
The osteoclasts in the shaft have died
Bone has replaced all the plate’s cartilage
follow.why: Growth in length needs dividing cartilage in the plate. When the chondrocytes stop dividing and bone replaces the last of the cartilage, only a bony line remains. The periosteum still adds width, and marrow and osteoclasts do not set length.

labels.name: Metaphysis
labels.fn: The flared region where the shaft widens toward the lower epiphysis; it holds the lower epiphyseal plate in a growing bone.

labels.name: Epiphysis
labels.fn: The rounded lower end of the long bone, filled with spongy bone and red marrow and separated from the metaphysis by an epiphyseal plate while the bone grows.

labels.name: Perichondrium
labels.fn: The dense connective tissue sheath around the cartilage model. When blood vessels invade it, its cells become osteoblasts and it becomes the periosteum.

labels.name: Primary ossification center
labels.fn: The first site of bone formation in the cartilage model, in the middle of the diaphysis. A nutrient artery brings in osteogenic cells, and osteoblasts lay spongy bone on the remains of calcified cartilage.

follow.q: What arrives with the nutrient artery to start the primary ossification center?
options: Mesenchymal cells from the overlying skin
follow.why: The invading artery carries osteogenic cells, which become osteoblasts, and the precursors of osteoclasts. Chondrocytes are what is being replaced, and marrow and mesenchyme do not come from those places.

labels.name: Hyaline cartilage
labels.fn: The cartilage that forms the model of the future long bone. Bone later replaces it everywhere except the articular cartilage and the epiphyseal plate.

labels.name: Calcified matrix
labels.fn: Cartilage matrix in the middle of the model that has taken up calcium salts. It blocks diffusion, so the chondrocytes in it die and leave cavities.

labels.name: Periosteum
labels.fn: The former perichondrium, now with blood vessels. Its osteoblasts lay a collar of compact bone around the middle of the shaft.

labels.name: Uncalcified matrix
labels.fn: Cartilage matrix that has not yet calcified, at the ends of the model. Nutrients still diffuse through it, so its chondrocytes stay alive.

labels.name: Uncalcified matrix
labels.fn: Living hyaline cartilage still filling the bone end before a secondary ossification center forms in it.

labels.name: Nutrient artery
labels.fn: The artery that grows into the middle of the cartilage model through the bone collar, bringing the cells that form the primary ossification center.

labels.name: Spongy bone
labels.fn: The first bone laid down at the primary ossification center, on the remains of calcified cartilage.

labels.name: Calcified matrix
labels.fn: Calcified cartilage matrix at the edge of the growing bone end, where chondrocytes die and bone will replace the cartilage.

labels.name: Periosteum
labels.fn: The membrane covering the shaft. Osteoblasts in it keep adding compact bone to the outside of the shaft, widening it.

labels.name: Medullary cavity
labels.fn: The space in the middle of the shaft, opened as osteoclasts break down the first spongy bone there.

labels.name: Artery and vein
labels.fn: Vessels entering the shaft; they carry nutrients, osteogenic cells and osteoclast precursors to the forming bone.

labels.name: Secondary ossification center
labels.fn: A site of bone formation in an epiphysis, forming around birth or after. Vessels enter the bone end and spongy bone replaces the cartilage there, leaving cartilage only on the joint surface and at the epiphyseal plate.

labels.name: Articular cartilage
labels.fn: Hyaline cartilage left on the joint surface of the bone end after ossification. It stays cartilage for life.

labels.name: Artery and vein
labels.fn: Vessels growing into the cartilage of the bone end; they bring the cells that start the secondary ossification center.

labels.name: Uncalcified matrix
labels.fn: Cartilage in the bone end that has not calcified; part of it will remain as the epiphyseal plate.

labels.name: Spongy bone
labels.fn: Spongy bone filling the epiphysis after the secondary ossification center has replaced the cartilage there. Its spaces hold red marrow.

labels.name: Epiphyseal plate
labels.fn: The disc of cartilage left between the epiphysis and the diaphysis. It keeps lengthening the bone until growth ends.

labels.name: Artery and vein
labels.fn: Vessels supplying the shaft of the developing bone with nutrients and bone-forming cells.

labels.name: Mesenchymal cells
labels.fn: Unspecialized embryonic connective tissue cells. In intramembranous ossification they cluster and turn directly into osteogenic cells and osteoblasts.

labels.name: Osteoid
labels.fn: Freshly secreted, not yet mineralized matrix around the trapped cells.

labels.name: Collagen fibers
labels.fn: Protein fibers of the surrounding embryonic connective tissue, in which the bone begins to form.

labels.name: Osteoblast
labels.fn: A bone-building cell lining the edge of the new bone, adding more matrix.

labels.name: Ossification center
labels.fn: The cluster of cells where bone first forms. Here mesenchymal cells become osteoblasts, which begin laying down matrix.

follow.q: In intramembranous ossification, what does bone form in?
options: A blood clot at the site
follow.why: Intramembranous bone forms directly in mesenchyme with no cartilage stage, as in the flat bones of the skull. A cartilage model belongs to endochondral ossification, and clots and marrow are not where bone first forms.

labels.name: Osteocyte
labels.fn: An osteoblast that has walled itself in with matrix and now sits in a lacuna, maintaining the new bone.

labels.name: New bone matrix
labels.fn: Osteoid that has mineralized with calcium salts, forming hard new bone.

labels.name: Osteoid
labels.fn: The unmineralized organic matrix, mostly collagen, that osteoblasts secrete. Calcium salts later deposit in it to harden it.

labels.name: Osteoblast
labels.fn: A bone-building cell. In the ossification center it secretes osteoid around itself.

labels.name: Mesenchyme forms the periosteum
labels.fn: Mesenchyme that condenses on the surface of the new bone and becomes the periosteum.

labels.name: Fibrous periosteum
labels.fn: The outer fibrous layer of the periosteum that has formed from the surface mesenchyme.

labels.name: Osteoblast
labels.fn: Bone-building cells under the periosteum, laying down compact bone on the surface.

labels.name: Compact bone
labels.fn: The layer of compact bone laid down on the surface, under the periosteum, replacing the outer spongy bone.

labels.name: Trabeculae
labels.fn: Struts of new bone that grow and join into a network, forming spongy bone around blood vessels.

labels.name: Spongy bone
labels.fn: The spongy bone left in the middle of a flat bone, between the compact plates; its spaces hold red marrow.

labels.name: Blood vessel
labels.fn: A blood vessel trapped between the growing trabeculae; its tissue later becomes red marrow.

labels.name: Coracoclavicular ligament
labels.fn: A strong band from the coracoid process of the scapula up to the underside of the clavicle. It anchors the clavicle to the scapula and keeps the scapula from dropping away from the clavicle.

labels.name: Costoclavicular ligament
labels.fn: A short band from the first rib and its costal cartilage to the underside of the sternal end of the clavicle. It holds the inner end of the clavicle down near the sternum.

labels.name: Clavicle
labels.fn: The S-shaped collarbone running from the manubrium of the sternum out to the acromion of the scapula. It acts as a strut that holds the shoulder out to the side and passes force from the upper limb to the axial skeleton.

labels.name: Clavicle
labels.fn: The S-shaped collarbone running from the manubrium of the sternum out to the acromion of the scapula. It acts as a strut that holds the shoulder out to the side and passes force from the upper limb to the axial skeleton.

labels.name: Scapula
labels.fn: The flat, triangular shoulder blade on the back of the upper ribs. It is held in place mainly by muscles, and its glenoid cavity is the socket for the head of the humerus.

labels.name: Scapula
labels.fn: The flat, triangular shoulder blade on the back of the upper ribs. It is held in place mainly by muscles, and its glenoid cavity is the socket for the head of the humerus.

labels.name: Rib
labels.fn: One of the curved bones of the thoracic cage. The scapula lies against the back of the upper ribs, gliding over them as the shoulder moves.

labels.name: Vertebrae
labels.fn: The bones of the vertebral column. The medial border of each scapula lies a few centimeters out from the thoracic vertebrae.

labels.name: Acromial end
labels.fn: The flattened lateral end of the clavicle, which meets the acromion of the scapula at the tip of the shoulder.

labels.name: Sternal end
labels.fn: The rounded medial end of the clavicle, which meets the manubrium of the sternum. It is the only place the upper limb joins the axial skeleton bone to bone.

labels.name: Pectoral girdle
labels.fn: The clavicle and scapula of one side. The girdle attaches the upper limb to the axial skeleton, and its only bony link to the trunk is the clavicle meeting the sternum, which leaves the shoulder free to move widely.

labels.name: Clavicle
labels.fn: The S-shaped collarbone running from the manubrium of the sternum out to the acromion of the scapula. It acts as a strut that holds the shoulder out to the side and passes force from the upper limb to the axial skeleton.

labels.name: Scapula
labels.fn: The flat, triangular shoulder blade on the back of the upper ribs. It is held in place mainly by muscles, and its glenoid cavity is the socket for the head of the humerus.

labels.name: Acromion
labels.fn: The flat end of the spine of the scapula, forming the bony tip of the shoulder. It meets the acromial end of the clavicle.

follow.q: A fall onto the outstretched hand pushes force up the arm. Which bone carries that force from the scapula to the axial skeleton?
follow.why: The scapula has no bony link to the trunk of its own. Force passes from the acromion to the clavicle and along it to the sternum, which is why the clavicle is one of the most often broken bones.

labels.name: Acromion
labels.fn: The flat end of the spine of the scapula, forming the bony tip of the shoulder. It meets the acromial end of the clavicle.

labels.name: Suprascapular notch
labels.fn: A small notch in the superior border of the scapula, just medial to the coracoid process. A nerve passes through it on its way to muscles on the back of the scapula.

labels.name: Suprascapular notch
labels.fn: A small notch in the superior border of the scapula, just medial to the coracoid process. A nerve passes through it on its way to muscles on the back of the scapula.

labels.name: Superior border
labels.fn: The short upper edge of the scapula, running from the superior angle out to the coracoid process.

labels.name: Coracoid process
labels.fn: The hook-shaped projection on the front of the scapula, below the lateral end of the clavicle. Muscles of the chest and arm and the coracoclavicular ligament attach to it.

follow.q: Which part of the scapula projects forward and can be felt below the lateral clavicle?
follow.why: The coracoid process curves forward under the clavicle, so it can be pressed just below the clavicle's outer third. The spine and borders lie on the back of the scapula, and the inferior angle points down.

labels.name: Coracoid process
labels.fn: The hook-shaped projection on the front of the scapula, below the lateral end of the clavicle. Muscles of the chest and arm and the coracoclavicular ligament attach to it.

labels.name: Superior angle
labels.fn: The upper medial corner of the scapula, where the superior border meets the medial border. It sits at about the level of the second rib.

labels.name: Supraspinous fossa
labels.fn: The shallow hollow on the back of the scapula above the spine. A muscle that helps lift the arm to the side fills it.

labels.name: Glenoid cavity
labels.fn: The shallow socket at the lateral angle of the scapula where the head of the humerus sits. Its shallowness lets the arm move in every direction but makes the shoulder less stable.

follow.q: Why can the arm move through a wider range at the shoulder than the thigh can at the hip?
options: Its socket, the glenoid cavity, is small and shallow
The head of the humerus is much larger than the head of the femur
The scapula is fused firmly to the ribs, giving a steady base
The shoulder is held together by bone rather than by muscles
follow.why: The head of the humerus sits against a small, shallow glenoid cavity, so little bone blocks its motion. The acetabulum of the hip is a deep cup that holds most of the head of the femur, trading range for stability.

labels.name: Glenoid cavity
labels.fn: The shallow socket at the lateral angle of the scapula where the head of the humerus sits. Its shallowness lets the arm move in every direction but makes the shoulder less stable.

labels.name: Spine
labels.fn: The ridge of bone running across the back of the scapula. It divides the back into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and ends laterally as the acromion.

labels.name: Infraspinous fossa
labels.fn: The broad hollow on the back of the scapula below the spine. A muscle that turns the arm outward fills it.

labels.name: Subscapular fossa
labels.fn: The broad, slightly hollow front surface of the scapula, facing the ribs. A muscle that turns the arm inward fills it.

labels.name: Lateral border
labels.fn: The thick outer edge of the scapula, running from the glenoid cavity down to the inferior angle, toward the armpit.

labels.name: Lateral border
labels.fn: The thick outer edge of the scapula, running from the glenoid cavity down to the inferior angle, toward the armpit.

labels.name: Medial border
labels.fn: The long inner edge of the scapula, running parallel to the vertebral column. Muscles from the vertebrae attach along it and move the scapula.

labels.name: Inferior angle
labels.fn: The lowest point of the scapula, where the medial and lateral borders meet. It lies at about the level of the seventh rib and is a landmark for counting ribs on the back.

labels.name: Humerus
labels.fn: The single bone of the arm, from the shoulder to the elbow. Its head fits the glenoid cavity above, and its lower end meets the radius and ulna.

labels.name: Anatomical neck
labels.fn: The slight groove circling the head of the humerus, marking where the head's smooth surface ends. It lies just outside the head's smooth surface, above the tubercles.

labels.name: Greater tubercle
labels.fn: The large bump on the lateral side of the upper humerus. Several muscles from the scapula that stabilize the shoulder attach to it.

follow.q: On the upper humerus, where is the greater tubercle compared with the lesser tubercle?
options: Lateral to it, across a groove
Medial to it, on the front of the humerus
Directly above it, on top of the head
Below it, at the lower end near the elbow
follow.why: The greater tubercle sits on the outer side of the upper humerus and the smaller lesser tubercle on the front, with the intertubercular groove running between them.

labels.name: Greater tubercle
labels.fn: The large bump on the lateral side of the upper humerus. Several muscles from the scapula that stabilize the shoulder attach to it.

labels.name: Head
labels.fn: The rounded upper end of the humerus, which fits the glenoid cavity of the scapula. It faces up, in and back.

labels.name: Lesser tubercle
labels.fn: The smaller bump on the front of the upper humerus, medial to the greater tubercle. A muscle from the front of the scapula attaches to it.

labels.name: Surgical neck
labels.fn: The narrowed part of the humerus just below the tubercles, where the head joins the shaft. It is the most common place the upper humerus breaks.

follow.q: An older adult falls and breaks the upper humerus. Which region is most likely to break, and why?
options: The surgical neck, where the wide upper end narrows
The anatomical neck, which is the thinnest part of the whole bone
The capitulum, which carries the most weight in the arm
The deltoid tuberosity, which has no compact bone at all
follow.why: The surgical neck is where the wide upper end tapers into the narrower shaft, so bending forces concentrate there. That is why it is named for how often surgeons repair it.

labels.name: Deltoid tuberosity
labels.fn: A roughened area on the lateral side of the shaft of the humerus, about halfway down. The large muscle that caps the shoulder attaches here.

labels.name: Body (shaft)
labels.fn: The shaft (diaphysis) of the long bone: a tube of compact bone around the medullary cavity, carrying the bone's length between its two ends.

labels.name: Lateral supracondylar ridge
labels.fn: A sharp ridge on the lateral side of the lower humerus, running up from the lateral epicondyle. Forearm muscles attach along it.

labels.name: Olecranon fossa
labels.fn: The deep hollow on the back of the lower humerus. The olecranon of the ulna fits into it when the elbow is straightened, which stops the elbow bending backward.

follow.q: What stops the elbow from bending backward when the arm is straightened?
options: The olecranon fitting into the olecranon fossa
The head of the radius locking into the radial fossa
The capitulum fitting into the trochlear notch of the ulna
The coronoid process pressing on the lateral epicondyle
follow.why: As the elbow straightens, the olecranon swings up into the olecranon fossa on the back of the humerus. Bone meets bone there, so the forearm cannot go past straight.

labels.name: Lateral epicondyle
labels.fn: The smaller bump on the lateral side of the lower humerus, above the capitulum. Muscles that straighten the wrist and fingers attach to it.

labels.name: Radial fossa
labels.fn: A small hollow on the front of the lower humerus, above the capitulum. The head of the radius slides into it when the elbow is fully bent.

labels.name: Coronoid fossa
labels.fn: A hollow on the front of the lower humerus, above the trochlea. The coronoid process of the ulna fits into it when the elbow is fully bent.

labels.name: Olecranon of ulna
labels.fn: The large hooked upper end of the ulna, forming the point of the elbow. It fits the olecranon fossa of the humerus when the elbow is straight, and the muscle that straightens the elbow attaches to it.

labels.name: Capitulum
labels.fn: The rounded knob on the lateral side of the lower humerus. The head of the radius presses against it.

labels.name: Medial epicondyle
labels.fn: The large bump on the medial side of the lower humerus. Muscles that bend the wrist and fingers attach to it, and a nerve runs just behind it (the "funny bone").

labels.name: Head of radius
labels.fn: The disc-shaped upper end of the radius. Its top presses against the capitulum of the humerus and its rim turns against the radial notch of the ulna, letting the radius spin when the palm turns.

labels.name: Head of radius
labels.fn: The disc-shaped upper end of the radius. Its top presses against the capitulum of the humerus and its rim turns against the radial notch of the ulna, letting the radius spin when the palm turns.

labels.name: Trochlea
labels.fn: The spool-shaped surface on the medial side of the lower humerus. The trochlear notch of the ulna wraps around it, so the elbow bends in one plane like a hinge.

labels.name: Coronoid process of ulna
labels.fn: The lip on the front of the upper ulna, forming the lower edge of the trochlear notch. It fits the coronoid fossa of the humerus when the elbow is fully bent.

labels.name: Radial notch of the ulna
labels.fn: A small curved facet on the lateral side of the upper ulna, beside the trochlear notch. The rim of the head of the radius turns against it.

labels.name: Head of radius
labels.fn: The disc-shaped upper end of the radius. Its top presses against the capitulum of the humerus and its rim turns against the radial notch of the ulna, letting the radius spin when the palm turns.

labels.name: Head of radius
labels.fn: The disc-shaped upper end of the radius. Its top presses against the capitulum of the humerus and its rim turns against the radial notch of the ulna, letting the radius spin when the palm turns.

labels.name: Neck of radius
labels.fn: The narrow part of the radius just below its head, joining the head to the shaft.

labels.name: Neck of radius
labels.fn: The narrow part of the radius just below its head, joining the head to the shaft.

labels.name: Radial tuberosity
labels.fn: A rough bump on the medial side of the radius just below its neck. The main muscle on the front of the arm attaches here and pulls on it to bend the elbow.

follow.q: Which bone does the radial tuberosity belong to, and on which forearm bone does the thumb side lie?
options: The radius, the forearm bone on the thumb side
The ulna, the forearm bone on the thumb side
The radius, the forearm bone on the little-finger side
The humerus, above both forearm bones
follow.why: The radial tuberosity is a bump on the upper radius. In anatomical position the radius lies on the lateral, thumb side of the forearm and the ulna on the medial, little-finger side.

labels.name: Olecranon process
labels.fn: The large hooked upper end of the ulna, forming the point of the elbow. It fits the olecranon fossa of the humerus when the elbow straightens.

labels.name: Trochlear notch
labels.fn: The large C-shaped notch at the upper end of the ulna, between the olecranon and the coronoid process. It wraps around the trochlea of the humerus, so the elbow bends like a hinge.

follow.q: Which surfaces meet to form the main hinge of the elbow?
options: The trochlear notch of the ulna and the trochlea
The head of the radius and the olecranon fossa of the humerus
The styloid process of the ulna and the capitulum of the humerus
The radial notch of the ulna and the coronoid fossa of the humerus
follow.why: The C-shaped trochlear notch grips the spool-shaped trochlea, allowing movement in one plane only. The radius meets the capitulum beside it but carries less of the hinge.

labels.name: Coronoid process
labels.fn: The lip on the front of the upper ulna, forming the lower edge of the trochlear notch. It fits the coronoid fossa of the humerus when the elbow is fully bent.

labels.name: Ulna
labels.fn: The forearm bone on the little-finger (medial) side. It is large at the elbow, where it grips the humerus, and small at the wrist.

labels.name: Radius
labels.fn: The forearm bone on the thumb (lateral) side. It is small at the elbow and wide at the wrist, where it carries most of the load from the hand.

labels.name: Radius
labels.fn: The forearm bone on the thumb (lateral) side. It is small at the elbow and wide at the wrist, where it carries most of the load from the hand.

labels.name: Ulnar notch of the radius
labels.fn: A shallow notch on the medial side of the lower radius. The head of the ulna sits in it, so the radius can swing around the ulna when the palm turns.

labels.name: Head of ulna
labels.fn: The small rounded lower end of the ulna, near the wrist on the little-finger side. It sits in the ulnar notch of the radius.

labels.name: Styloid process of ulna
labels.fn: The small pointed projection at the lower end of the ulna, on the little-finger side of the wrist. A ligament of the wrist attaches to it.

labels.name: Styloid process of radius
labels.fn: The pointed projection at the lower end of the radius on the thumb side of the wrist. It reaches further down than the styloid process of the ulna.

follow.q: Which styloid process reaches further toward the hand?
options: The styloid process of the radius
The styloid process of the ulna
They end at exactly the same level
follow.why: The radial styloid extends about a centimeter lower than the ulnar styloid. Clinicians compare the two to spot a shortened radius after a wrist break.

labels.name: Carpals
labels.fn: The eight small wrist bones, set in two rows of four between the radius and the metacarpals.

labels.name: Metacarpals
labels.fn: The five long bones of the palm, numbered 1 (thumb) to 5 (little finger). Their heads form the knuckles.

labels.name: Phalanges
labels.fn: The finger bones: two in the thumb (proximal and distal) and three in each finger (proximal, middle and distal), fourteen in each hand.

labels.name: Middle finger
labels.fn: Digit 3, the longest finger. Like the other fingers it has three phalanges.

labels.name: Index finger
labels.fn: Digit 2, next to the thumb. It has three phalanges.

labels.name: Ring finger
labels.fn: Digit 4, between the middle and little fingers. It has three phalanges.

labels.name: Little finger
labels.fn: Digit 5, on the medial (ulnar) side of the hand. It has three phalanges.

labels.name: Distal
labels.fn: The distal phalanx, the bone at the tip of the digit, farthest from the palm.

labels.name: Middle
labels.fn: The middle phalanx, between the proximal and distal phalanges of a finger. The thumb has none.

labels.name: Proximal
labels.fn: The proximal phalanx, the first bone of the digit beyond the metacarpal and the longest of its phalanges.

labels.name: Phalanges
labels.fn: The finger bones: two in the thumb (proximal and distal) and three in each finger (proximal, middle and distal), fourteen in each hand.

labels.name: Thumb (pollex)
labels.fn: Digit 1, the pollex. It has only two phalanges, proximal and distal, and its metacarpal sits at an angle to the others so the thumb can reach across the palm.

labels.name: Distal
labels.fn: The distal phalanx, the bone at the tip of the digit, farthest from the palm.

labels.name: Proximal
labels.fn: The proximal phalanx, the first bone of the digit beyond the metacarpal and the longest of its phalanges.

labels.name: Head
labels.fn: The rounded distal end of the bone, which meets the next bone toward the fingertip.

labels.name: Shaft
labels.fn: The long middle part of the bone, between its base and its head.

labels.name: Base
labels.fn: The wider proximal end of the bone, which meets the bone before it.

labels.name: Head
labels.fn: The rounded distal end of the bone, which meets the next bone toward the fingertip.

labels.name: Shaft
labels.fn: The long middle part of the bone, between its base and its head.

labels.name: Base
labels.fn: The wider proximal end of the bone, which meets the bone before it.

labels.name: Metacarpals (1–5)
labels.fn: The five long bones of the palm, numbered 1 (thumb) to 5 (little finger). Their heads form the knuckles.

labels.name: Trapezium
labels.fn: The carpal bone at the thumb end of the distal row. The base of the first metacarpal sits on its saddle-shaped surface, which lets the thumb swing across the palm.

follow.q: A student mixes up the trapezium and the trapezoid. Which one sits at the base of the thumb?
options: Neither; the thumb sits on the scaphoid
follow.why: The trapezium carries the first metacarpal (the thumb), and the trapezoid, beside it, carries the second metacarpal. A memory aid: "trapeziUM goes with the thUMb."

labels.name: Trapezoid
labels.fn: The small wedge-shaped carpal bone in the distal row between the trapezium and the capitate. The second metacarpal (index finger) sits on it.

labels.name: Scaphoid
labels.fn: The boat-shaped carpal bone at the thumb end of the proximal row, meeting the radius. It is the most often broken carpal bone, usually in a fall onto the outstretched hand.

follow.q: After a fall on the outstretched hand, a person has pain on the thumb side of the wrist just past the end of the radius. Which carpal bone is most likely broken?
follow.why: The scaphoid sits on the thumb side of the proximal row, right against the radius, so it takes the force of the fall. The pisiform, hamate and triquetrum lie on the little-finger side.

labels.name: Hamate
labels.fn: The carpal bone at the little-finger end of the distal row, with a hook that projects toward the palm. It forms part of the wall of the carpal tunnel.

labels.name: Capitate
labels.fn: The largest carpal bone, in the middle of the distal row. The third metacarpal (middle finger) sits on it.

labels.name: Pisiform
labels.fn: The small pea-shaped carpal bone on the palm side of the triquetrum, at the little-finger end of the proximal row. A tendon of the wrist runs into it.

labels.name: Triquetrum
labels.fn: The pyramid-shaped carpal bone of the proximal row, between the lunate and the pisiform on the little-finger side.

labels.name: Lunate
labels.fn: The moon-shaped carpal bone in the middle of the proximal row, between the scaphoid and the triquetrum. It meets the radius.

labels.name: Trapezium
labels.fn: The carpal bone at the thumb end of the distal row. The base of the first metacarpal sits on its saddle-shaped surface, which lets the thumb swing across the palm.

labels.name: Trapezoid
labels.fn: The small wedge-shaped carpal bone in the distal row between the trapezium and the capitate. The second metacarpal (index finger) sits on it.

labels.name: Scaphoid
labels.fn: The boat-shaped carpal bone at the thumb end of the proximal row, meeting the radius. It is the most often broken carpal bone, usually in a fall onto the outstretched hand.

labels.name: Ulna
labels.fn: The forearm bone on the little-finger (medial) side. It is large at the elbow, where it grips the humerus, and small at the wrist.

labels.name: Radius
labels.fn: The forearm bone on the thumb (lateral) side. It is small at the elbow and wide at the wrist, where it carries most of the load from the hand.

shown.why: A group heading over the thumb's Distal and Proximal labels; it points to no structure of its own.
A group heading over the carpal bone labels below it; it points to no structure of its own.
A group heading over the carpal bone labels below it; it points to no structure of its own.
A group heading over the carpal bone labels below it; it points to no structure of its own.

labels.name: Carpal tunnel
labels.fn: The passage on the palm side of the wrist, with the carpal bones as its floor and walls and the flexor retinaculum as its roof. Tendons of the finger muscles and a nerve pass through it.

follow.q: Swelling inside the carpal tunnel causes tingling in the fingers. What does the swelling press on?
options: The nerve that runs through the tunnel
The lower ends of the radius and the ulna
The bases of the five metacarpals in the palm
The skin and fat over the back of the wrist
follow.why: The tunnel is rigid: bone on three sides and the tough flexor retinaculum on top. Swollen tendons have nowhere to expand except against the nerve that shares the tunnel, which makes the fingers tingle and feel numb.

labels.name: Muscle tendons
labels.fn: The tendons of the forearm muscles that bend the fingers. They pass through the carpal tunnel on their way to the fingers.

labels.name: Hamate
labels.fn: The carpal bone at the little-finger end of the distal row, with a hook that projects toward the palm. It forms part of the wall of the carpal tunnel.

labels.name: Trapezium
labels.fn: The carpal bone at the thumb end of the distal row. The base of the first metacarpal sits on its saddle-shaped surface, which lets the thumb swing across the palm.

labels.name: Trapezoid
labels.fn: The small wedge-shaped carpal bone in the distal row between the trapezium and the capitate. The second metacarpal (index finger) sits on it.

labels.name: Capitate
labels.fn: The largest carpal bone, in the middle of the distal row. The third metacarpal (middle finger) sits on it.

labels.name: Flexor retinaculum
labels.fn: The tough band of connective tissue across the palm side of the wrist, from the hamate and pisiform to the scaphoid and trapezium. It forms the roof of the carpal tunnel and holds the tendons in place.

labels.name: Nerve
labels.fn: The nerve that passes through the carpal tunnel with the tendons. It supplies sensation to the thumb side of the palm and fingers, so pressure in the tunnel causes tingling there.

shown.why: A group heading over the carpal bone labels below it; it points to no structure of its own.

labels.name: Hip bone
labels.fn: The large bone forming each side of the pelvic girdle, made of the ilium, ischium and pubis fused together. It meets the sacrum at the back and the other hip bone at the front.

labels.name: Sacral promontory
labels.fn: The forward-projecting upper edge of the body of the first sacral vertebra. It forms the back of the pelvic brim.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone of five fused vertebrae at the back of the pelvis. It sits wedged between the two hip bones and passes the weight of the upper body to them.

labels.name: Pelvic brim
labels.fn: The rim running from the sacral promontory around to the pubic symphysis. It divides the greater pelvis above from the lesser pelvis below and outlines the pelvic inlet.

follow.q: What does the pelvic brim separate?
options: The greater pelvis above from the lesser pelvis below
The ilium above from the ischium and pubis below
The left hip bone from the right hip bone at the front
The sacrum above from the coccyx below it at the back
follow.why: The brim is the ring around the pelvic inlet. Above it, the flared iliac bones form the greater pelvis; below it, the bony ring of the lesser pelvis surrounds the pelvic cavity.

labels.name: Acetabulum
labels.fn: The deep cup-shaped socket on the outer side of the hip bone, where the ilium, ischium and pubis meet. The head of the femur fits into it.

follow.q: Why is the hip more stable than the shoulder?
options: The acetabulum is a deep cup around most of the femoral head
The femur has no neck, so its head sits directly on the shaft
The acetabulum is shallower than the glenoid cavity of the scapula
The hip bone and the femur are fused together in the adult
follow.why: The deep acetabulum wraps around the head of the femur, so bone holds it in place. The shoulder's shallow glenoid cavity allows more movement but holds the humerus less securely.

labels.name: Coccyx
labels.fn: The small tailbone of three to five fused vertebrae below the sacrum.

labels.name: Obturator foramen
labels.fn: The large oval opening in the hip bone below the acetabulum, framed by the pubis and ischium. A sheet of connective tissue covers most of it, leaving a gap for vessels and a nerve to reach the thigh.

labels.name: Pubic symphysis
labels.fn: The pad of fibrocartilage joining the two pubic bones at the front midline of the pelvis. It allows only a little movement.

labels.name: Ischial tuberosity
labels.fn: The thick, rough bump at the bottom of the ischium. It carries the body's weight when sitting, and muscles on the back of the thigh attach to it.

follow.q: Which part of the hip bone takes your weight when you sit upright?
follow.why: The ischial tuberosities are the thick lower ends of the ischia, the "sitting bones." The iliac crest and the spines lie high on the ilium, and the pubic tubercle is at the front.

labels.name: Ilium
labels.fn: The large, fan-shaped upper part of the hip bone. It forms the upper part of the acetabulum and meets the sacrum at the back.

labels.name: Iliac fossa
labels.fn: The broad, shallow hollow on the inner surface of the ilium. A large muscle that bends the hip fills it.

labels.name: Iliac crest
labels.fn: The curved upper edge of the ilium, felt at the top of the hip. It runs from the anterior superior iliac spine to the posterior superior iliac spine.

follow.q: A clinician finds the top of the iliac crests to locate a level of the lower back. Where does the iliac crest run?
options: Along the upper edge of the ilium, front to back
Along the lower edge of the ischium, down to the tuberosity
Across the front of the pubis, from one side to the other
Around the rim of the acetabulum on the outer side of the bone
follow.why: The iliac crest is the curved upper border of the ilium. A line joining the tops of both crests crosses the lumbar vertebrae, a common landmark on the back.

labels.name: Anterior superior iliac spine
labels.fn: The rounded bony point at the front end of the iliac crest, easily felt at the front of the hip. It is a common landmark for measuring the lower limb.

labels.name: Posterior superior iliac spine
labels.fn: The bony point at the back end of the iliac crest. It lies under the small dimples of the lower back, over the sacrum.

labels.name: Posterior superior iliac spine
labels.fn: The bony point at the back end of the iliac crest. It lies under the small dimples of the lower back, over the sacrum.

labels.name: Anterior inferior iliac spine
labels.fn: A bony point on the front of the ilium below the anterior superior iliac spine, just above the acetabulum. A thigh muscle attaches to it.

labels.name: Posterior inferior iliac spine
labels.fn: A bony point on the back of the ilium below the posterior superior iliac spine, at the top of the greater sciatic notch.

labels.name: Posterior inferior iliac spine
labels.fn: A bony point on the back of the ilium below the posterior superior iliac spine, at the top of the greater sciatic notch.

labels.name: Acetabulum
labels.fn: The deep cup-shaped socket on the outer side of the hip bone, where the ilium, ischium and pubis meet. The head of the femur fits into it.

labels.name: Auricular surface
labels.fn: The ear-shaped rough area on the inner side of the ilium where it meets the sacrum.

labels.name: Greater sciatic notch
labels.fn: The large notch on the back edge of the hip bone, below the posterior inferior iliac spine. Ligaments turn it into the greater sciatic foramen, through which a large nerve and vessels leave the pelvis.

labels.name: Greater sciatic notch
labels.fn: The large notch on the back edge of the hip bone, below the posterior inferior iliac spine. Ligaments turn it into the greater sciatic foramen, through which a large nerve and vessels leave the pelvis.

labels.name: Arcuate line
labels.fn: The curved ridge on the inner surface of the ilium, below the iliac fossa. It forms part of the pelvic brim.

labels.name: Ischial body
labels.fn: The thick main part of the ischium, forming the lower back part of the acetabulum.

labels.name: Ischial spine
labels.fn: The pointed projection on the back of the ischium, between the greater and lesser sciatic notches. The sacrospinous ligament attaches to it.

labels.name: Ischial spine
labels.fn: The pointed projection on the back of the ischium, between the greater and lesser sciatic notches. The sacrospinous ligament attaches to it.

labels.name: Pubic tubercle
labels.fn: A small bump on the upper edge of the pubis, near the midline. A ligament running from the anterior superior iliac spine attaches to it.

labels.name: Lesser sciatic notch
labels.fn: The smaller notch on the back edge of the ischium, below the ischial spine. Ligaments turn it into the lesser sciatic foramen.

labels.name: Lesser sciatic notch
labels.fn: The smaller notch on the back edge of the ischium, below the ischial spine. Ligaments turn it into the lesser sciatic foramen.

labels.name: Pubic body
labels.fn: The thickened medial part of the pubis, near the midline. Its inner surface meets the other pubis at the pubic symphysis.

labels.name: Pubis
labels.fn: The front part of the hip bone. It forms the front of the acetabulum and meets the other pubis at the pubic symphysis.

labels.name: Obturator foramen
labels.fn: The large oval opening in the hip bone below the acetabulum, framed by the pubis and ischium. A sheet of connective tissue covers most of it, leaving a gap for vessels and a nerve to reach the thigh.

labels.name: Obturator foramen
labels.fn: The large oval opening in the hip bone below the acetabulum, framed by the pubis and ischium. A sheet of connective tissue covers most of it, leaving a gap for vessels and a nerve to reach the thigh.

labels.name: Articular surface of pubis (at pubic symphysis)
labels.fn: The oval surface on the medial side of the pubic body that meets the other pubis through the pad of fibrocartilage of the pubic symphysis.

labels.name: Ischium
labels.fn: The lower back part of the hip bone. It forms the back of the acetabulum and ends below in the ischial tuberosity.

labels.name: Ischium
labels.fn: The lower back part of the hip bone. It forms the back of the acetabulum and ends below in the ischial tuberosity.

labels.name: Ischial tuberosity
labels.fn: The thick, rough bump at the bottom of the ischium. It carries the body's weight when sitting, and muscles on the back of the thigh attach to it.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone of five fused vertebrae at the back of the pelvis. It sits wedged between the two hip bones and passes the weight of the upper body to them.

labels.name: Posterior superior iliac spine
labels.fn: The bony point at the back end of the iliac crest. It lies under the small dimples of the lower back, over the sacrum.

labels.name: Posterior sacroiliac ligament
labels.fn: Strong bands on the back of the pelvis from the sacrum to the ilium. They bind the sacrum between the hip bones so the weight of the body does not push it down and forward.

labels.name: Ilium
labels.fn: The large, fan-shaped upper part of the hip bone. It forms the upper part of the acetabulum and meets the sacrum at the back.

labels.name: Greater sciatic foramen
labels.fn: The large opening formed where the sacrospinous ligament closes off the greater sciatic notch. The largest nerve of the body and vessels pass through it from the pelvis to the buttock.

labels.name: Sacrospinous ligament
labels.fn: A ligament from the side of the sacrum and coccyx to the ischial spine. It separates the greater sciatic foramen above from the lesser sciatic foramen below.

labels.name: Sacrospinous ligament
labels.fn: A ligament from the side of the sacrum and coccyx to the ischial spine. It separates the greater sciatic foramen above from the lesser sciatic foramen below.

labels.name: Ischial spine
labels.fn: The pointed projection on the back of the ischium, between the greater and lesser sciatic notches. The sacrospinous ligament attaches to it.

labels.name: Pubis
labels.fn: The front part of the hip bone. It forms the front of the acetabulum and meets the other pubis at the pubic symphysis.

labels.name: Lesser sciatic foramen
labels.fn: The smaller opening, below the sacrospinous ligament, formed where the sacrotuberous ligament closes off the lesser sciatic notch.

labels.name: Ischium
labels.fn: The lower back part of the hip bone. It forms the back of the acetabulum and ends below in the ischial tuberosity.

labels.name: Sacrotuberous ligament
labels.fn: A long ligament from the sacrum and the posterior iliac spines to the ischial tuberosity. With the sacrospinous ligament it keeps the lower sacrum from tipping upward under the body's weight.

follow.q: Which two openings do the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments create from the notches of the hip bone?
options: The greater and lesser sciatic foramina
The obturator foramen and the pelvic inlet
The pelvic inlet and the pelvic outlet
The acetabulum and the obturator foramen
follow.why: The ligaments bridge the greater and lesser sciatic notches on the back of the hip bone, closing each into a foramen. The obturator foramen is a hole in the bone itself, framed by the pubis and ischium.

labels.name: Ischial tuberosity
labels.fn: The thick, rough bump at the bottom of the ischium. It carries the body's weight when sitting, and muscles on the back of the thigh attach to it.

labels.name: Subpubic angle
labels.fn: The angle formed below the pubic symphysis by the inferior pubic rami of the two sides. It is wider (80 degrees or more) in the female pelvis and narrower (under 70 degrees) in the male pelvis.

follow.q: A pelvis has a wide subpubic angle, a round pelvic inlet and a short, wide sacrum. It most likely belongs to which person?
options: A female, whose pelvis is adapted for childbirth
A male, whose pelvis is built for heavier bones
A child of either sex, before the hip bone fuses
An adult of either sex; the shape does not differ
follow.why: The female pelvis is wider and shallower, with a subpubic angle of 80 degrees or more and a rounder inlet, giving a larger passage for the baby's head. The male pelvis is narrower, with a subpubic angle under 70 degrees.

labels.name: Obturator foramen
labels.fn: The large oval opening in the hip bone below the acetabulum, framed by the pubis and ischium. A sheet of connective tissue covers most of it, leaving a gap for vessels and a nerve to reach the thigh.

labels.name: Hip bone
labels.fn: The large bone forming each side of the pelvic girdle, made of the ilium, ischium and pubis fused together. It meets the sacrum at the back and the other hip bone at the front.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone of five fused vertebrae at the back of the pelvis. It sits wedged between the two hip bones and passes the weight of the upper body to them.

labels.name: Pelvic brim
labels.fn: The rim running from the sacral promontory around to the pubic symphysis. It divides the greater pelvis above from the lesser pelvis below and outlines the pelvic inlet.

labels.name: Subpubic angle
labels.fn: The angle formed below the pubic symphysis by the inferior pubic rami of the two sides. It is wider (80 degrees or more) in the female pelvis and narrower (under 70 degrees) in the male pelvis.

labels.name: Hip bone
labels.fn: The large bone forming each side of the pelvic girdle, made of the ilium, ischium and pubis fused together. It meets the sacrum at the back and the other hip bone at the front.

labels.name: Femur
labels.fn: The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone of the body. Its head fits the acetabulum at the hip and its condyles rest on the tibia at the knee.

labels.name: Greater trochanter
labels.fn: The large bump on the lateral side of the upper femur, felt at the side of the hip. Strong muscles of the buttock attach to it.

follow.q: Which bony landmark can be felt on the side of the hip, a hand's width below the iliac crest?
options: The greater trochanter of the femur
The lesser trochanter on the inner femur
The ischial spine of the hip bone
The pubic tubercle near the midline
follow.why: The greater trochanter projects outward at the top of the femur, just under the skin at the side of the hip. The lesser trochanter faces inward and backward and lies deep.

labels.name: Greater trochanter
labels.fn: The large bump on the lateral side of the upper femur, felt at the side of the hip. Strong muscles of the buttock attach to it.

labels.name: Head
labels.fn: The ball-shaped upper end of the femur, which sits deep in the acetabulum of the hip bone.

labels.name: Neck
labels.fn: The narrow part of the femur joining the head to the shaft at an angle. It is the usual site of a "broken hip" in older adults with thinned bone.

follow.q: A "broken hip" in an older adult is most often a break of which part?
options: The crest along the top of the ilium
The linea aspera on the back of the shaft
The medial condyle at the knee
follow.why: The femoral neck is a narrow bridge of bone set at an angle between the head and shaft, so weight bends it. As bone thins with age, a simple fall can snap it.

labels.name: Gluteal tuberosity
labels.fn: A roughened ridge on the back of the upper shaft of the femur, below the greater trochanter. The large muscle of the buttock attaches here.

labels.name: Intertrochanteric line
labels.fn: A ridge on the front of the femur running between the greater and lesser trochanters, where the neck meets the shaft. The strong capsule of the hip attaches along it.

labels.name: Intertrochanteric crest
labels.fn: The raised ridge on the back of the femur joining the greater and lesser trochanters.

labels.name: Lesser trochanter
labels.fn: The smaller bump on the back and medial side of the upper femur, below the neck. The strong muscle that bends the hip attaches to it.

labels.name: Linea aspera
labels.fn: The long rough ridge running down the back of the shaft of the femur. Many thigh muscles attach along it.

labels.name: Body (shaft)
labels.fn: The shaft (diaphysis) of the long bone: a tube of compact bone around the medullary cavity, carrying the bone's length between its two ends.

labels.name: Adductor tubercle
labels.fn: A small bump on the upper edge of the medial epicondyle of the femur, where a muscle that pulls the thigh inward attaches.

labels.name: Lateral epicondyle
labels.fn: The smaller bump on the lateral side of the lower end of the bone, above the condyle. Muscles and ligaments of the joint below attach to it.

labels.name: Lateral epicondyle
labels.fn: The smaller bump on the lateral side of the lower end of the bone, above the condyle. Muscles and ligaments of the joint below attach to it.

labels.name: Medial epicondyle
labels.fn: The larger bump on the medial side of the lower end of the bone. Muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Intercondylar fossa
labels.fn: The deep notch between the medial and lateral condyles on the back of the lower femur. Ligaments inside the knee attach within it.

labels.name: Patella
labels.fn: The kneecap, a sesamoid bone that forms inside the tendon of the large muscle on the front of the thigh. It protects the knee and gives that tendon more leverage.

follow.q: Why is the patella called a sesamoid bone?
options: It is shaped like a sesame seed and has no function
It is part of the femur
It forms from cartilage in the skull
follow.why: Sesamoid bones develop inside tendons where they pass over a joint. The patella, the largest one, sits in the tendon of the front thigh muscle and holds it away from the knee, which increases its leverage.

labels.name: Lateral condyle
labels.fn: The rounded lateral knob at the lower end of the femur, which rests on the lateral condyle of the tibia at the knee.

labels.name: Medial condyle
labels.fn: The rounded medial knob at the lower end of the femur, which rests on the medial condyle of the tibia at the knee.

labels.name: Fibula
labels.fn: The thin bone on the lateral side of the leg. It carries little of the body's weight; it anchors muscles and forms the outer side of the ankle.

labels.name: Fibula
labels.fn: The thin bone on the lateral side of the leg. It carries little of the body's weight; it anchors muscles and forms the outer side of the ankle.

labels.name: Tibia
labels.fn: The shinbone, the large weight-bearing bone on the medial side of the leg. Its upper end carries the femur at the knee and its lower end sits on the talus at the ankle.

follow.q: Which bone of the leg carries almost all of the body's weight?
follow.why: The femur passes weight to the tibia at the knee, and the tibia passes it to the talus at the ankle. The fibula does not reach the knee and carries little weight; it mainly anchors muscles and steadies the ankle.

labels.name: Lateral condyle
labels.fn: The lateral side of the wide upper end of the tibia. The lateral condyle of the femur rests on its upper surface, and the head of the fibula meets its underside.

labels.name: Articular surface of medial condyle
accept: articular surface of the medial condyle
labels.fn: The smooth, slightly hollow upper surface of the medial condyle of the tibia, on which the medial condyle of the femur rests.

labels.name: Articular surface of lateral condyle
accept: articular surface of the lateral condyle
labels.fn: The smooth upper surface of the lateral condyle of the tibia, on which the lateral condyle of the femur rests.

labels.name: Head of fibula
labels.fn: The knob-shaped upper end of the fibula, which meets the underside of the lateral condyle of the tibia just below the knee.

labels.name: Medial condyle
labels.fn: The medial side of the wide upper end of the tibia. Its upper surface carries the medial condyle of the femur.

labels.name: Tibial tuberosity
labels.fn: The rough bump on the front of the upper tibia, below the condyles. The patellar ligament from the kneecap attaches here, so the front thigh muscle pulls on it to straighten the knee.

follow.q: The large muscle on the front of the thigh straightens the knee. Where does its pull finally reach the tibia?
options: The tibial tuberosity, below the kneecap
The medial malleolus at the inner ankle
The head of the fibula on the outer side of the knee
The soleal line on the back of the upper tibia
follow.why: The muscle's tendon wraps the patella, and the patellar ligament runs on from the patella to the tibial tuberosity. Pulling on the tuberosity swings the leg forward.

labels.name: Anterior border
labels.fn: The sharp ridge down the front of the tibia, the shin, which lies just under the skin.

labels.name: Soleal line
labels.fn: An oblique ridge on the back of the upper tibia, where a calf muscle attaches.

labels.name: Fibula
labels.fn: The thin bone on the lateral side of the leg. It carries little of the body's weight; it anchors muscles and forms the outer side of the ankle.

labels.name: Fibula
labels.fn: The thin bone on the lateral side of the leg. It carries little of the body's weight; it anchors muscles and forms the outer side of the ankle.

labels.name: Tibia
labels.fn: The shinbone, the large weight-bearing bone on the medial side of the leg. Its upper end carries the femur at the knee and its lower end sits on the talus at the ankle.

labels.name: Medial malleolus
labels.fn: The bony bump on the inner side of the ankle, formed by the lower end of the tibia. It steadies the talus from the medial side.

labels.name: Lateral malleolus
labels.fn: The bony bump on the outer side of the ankle, formed by the lower end of the fibula. It reaches lower than the medial malleolus and steadies the talus from the lateral side.

follow.q: Which bone forms the bump on the outer side of the ankle?
follow.why: The lateral malleolus is the lower end of the fibula. The medial malleolus, on the inner side, belongs to the tibia; between them they hold the talus like a clamp.

labels.name: Lateral malleolus
labels.fn: The bony bump on the outer side of the ankle, formed by the lower end of the fibula. It reaches lower than the medial malleolus and steadies the talus from the lateral side.

labels.name: Articular surface
accept: inferior articular surface of the tibia
labels.fn: The smooth lower surface of the tibia that sits on the trochlea of the talus at the ankle.

labels.name: Tarsals
labels.fn: The seven bones of the back of the foot and ankle: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms.

labels.name: Metatarsals
labels.fn: The five long bones of the middle of the foot, numbered 1 (great toe) to 5 (little toe). Their heads form the ball of the foot.

labels.name: Phalanges
labels.fn: The toe bones: two in the great toe and three in each of the other toes, fourteen in each foot, arranged like those of the hand.

labels.name: Navicular
labels.fn: The boat-shaped tarsal bone on the medial side of the foot, between the talus behind and the three cuneiforms in front.

follow.q: Which tarsal bone lies between the head of the talus and the three cuneiforms?
follow.why: On the medial side of the foot the order runs talus, navicular, then the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms. The cuboid sits on the lateral side, in front of the calcaneus.

labels.name: Talus
labels.fn: The tarsal bone at the top of the foot that meets the tibia and fibula at the ankle. It passes the body's weight from the tibia down to the calcaneus and forward to the navicular.

labels.name: Facet for medial malleolus
labels.fn: The smooth surface on the medial side of the talus that meets the medial malleolus of the tibia.

labels.name: Intermediate cuneiform
labels.fn: The smallest of the three cuneiforms, a wedge-shaped tarsal bone between the medial and lateral cuneiforms. The second metatarsal meets it.

labels.name: Sustentaculum tali (talar shelf)
labels.fn: The shelf of bone on the medial side of the calcaneus that supports part of the talus above it.

labels.name: First metatarsal
labels.fn: The short, thick metatarsal of the great toe. Its head carries a large share of the body's weight when pushing off the ground.

labels.name: Calcaneus
labels.fn: The heel bone, the largest tarsal bone. It carries the body's weight from the talus to the ground, and the large tendon of the calf muscles attaches to its back.

follow.q: Which bone of the foot touches the ground at the heel and carries the weight passed down from the talus?
follow.why: The talus sits on top of the calcaneus, and the calcaneus rests on the ground behind the arch. The navicular, cuboid and cuneiforms lie in front, in the arch of the foot.

labels.name: Medial cuneiform
labels.fn: The largest cuneiform, the wedge-shaped tarsal bone on the medial side of the foot. The first metatarsal meets it.

labels.name: Calcaneal tuberosity
labels.fn: The rough back and lower part of the calcaneus that forms the heel. The large tendon of the calf attaches to it, and it touches the ground in standing.

labels.name: Distal
labels.fn: The distal phalanx of the great toe, the bone at its tip.

labels.name: Proximal phalanges
labels.fn: The first row of toe bones, beyond the metatarsals. Each toe has one.

labels.name: Distal phalange
labels.fn: The distal phalanx, the bone at the tip of the toe.

labels.name: Middle phalange
labels.fn: The middle phalanx of a toe, between the proximal and distal phalanges. The great toe has none.

labels.name: Proximal phalange
labels.fn: The proximal phalanx of a toe, the first toe bone beyond the metatarsal.

labels.name: Medial cuneiform
labels.fn: The largest cuneiform, the wedge-shaped tarsal bone on the medial side of the foot. The first metatarsal meets it.

labels.name: Intermediate cuneiform
labels.fn: The smallest of the three cuneiforms, a wedge-shaped tarsal bone between the medial and lateral cuneiforms. The second metatarsal meets it.

labels.name: Lateral cuneiform
labels.fn: The wedge-shaped tarsal bone between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid. The third metatarsal meets it.

labels.name: Cuboid
labels.fn: The cube-shaped tarsal bone on the lateral side of the foot, in front of the calcaneus. The fourth and fifth metatarsals meet it.

labels.name: Navicular
labels.fn: The boat-shaped tarsal bone on the medial side of the foot, between the talus behind and the three cuneiforms in front.

labels.name: Talus
labels.fn: The tarsal bone at the top of the foot that meets the tibia and fibula at the ankle. It passes the body's weight from the tibia down to the calcaneus and forward to the navicular.

labels.name: Trochlea of talus
labels.fn: The rounded upper surface of the talus, which fits under the lower end of the tibia at the ankle so the foot tilts up and down.

labels.name: Calcaneus
labels.fn: The heel bone, the largest tarsal bone. It carries the body's weight from the talus to the ground, and the large tendon of the calf muscles attaches to its back.

labels.name: Facet for lateral malleolus
labels.fn: The smooth surface on the lateral side of the talus that meets the lateral malleolus of the fibula.

labels.name: Navicular
labels.fn: The boat-shaped tarsal bone on the medial side of the foot, between the talus behind and the three cuneiforms in front.

labels.name: Intermediate cuneiform
labels.fn: The smallest of the three cuneiforms, a wedge-shaped tarsal bone between the medial and lateral cuneiforms. The second metatarsal meets it.

labels.name: Lateral cuneiform
labels.fn: The wedge-shaped tarsal bone between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid. The third metatarsal meets it.

labels.name: Talus
labels.fn: The tarsal bone at the top of the foot that meets the tibia and fibula at the ankle. It passes the body's weight from the tibia down to the calcaneus and forward to the navicular.

labels.name: Calcaneus
labels.fn: The heel bone, the largest tarsal bone. It carries the body's weight from the talus to the ground, and the large tendon of the calf muscles attaches to its back.

labels.name: Cuboid
labels.fn: The cube-shaped tarsal bone on the lateral side of the foot, in front of the calcaneus. The fourth and fifth metatarsals meet it.

labels.name: Fifth metatarsal
labels.fn: The metatarsal of the little toe, on the lateral edge of the foot. Its base has a bump that can be felt halfway along the outer edge of the foot.

sets.title: Skull: anterior, lateral and inferior views

labels.name: Coronal suture
labels.fn: The wavy seam that runs across the top of the skull from side to side, joining the frontal bone in front to the two parietal bones behind it.

labels.name: Frontal bone
labels.fn: The single bone of the forehead. It forms the front of the brain case, the roofs of the orbits and the ridges above the eyes, and holds the frontal sinuses.

labels.name: Glabella
labels.fn: The smooth, slightly raised area of the frontal bone between the eyebrows, just above the root of the nose.

labels.name: Parietal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of large, curved plates that form most of the top and upper sides of the brain case. The two meet each other along the sagittal suture on the midline.

labels.name: Supraorbital foramen
labels.fn: A small hole (sometimes an open notch) in the upper rim of each orbit. It lets a nerve and vessels pass up to the skin of the forehead.

labels.name: Supraorbital margin
labels.fn: The thick, curved upper rim of the orbit, formed by the frontal bone. It shields the eye from above.

labels.name: Orbit
labels.fn: The bony socket that holds the eye. Seven bones help build its walls: the frontal, sphenoid, ethmoid, lacrimal, zygomatic, maxilla and palatine bones.

labels.name: Sphenoid bone
labels.fn: A single butterfly-shaped cranial bone that runs across the middle of the skull base and joins with every other cranial bone. Its center holds the sella turcica and the sphenoid sinus.

labels.name: Optic canal
labels.fn: A round opening at the back of the orbit, through the sphenoid bone. The nerve for vision and an artery to the eye pass through it.

labels.name: Temporal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of cranial bones that form the lower sides and part of the base of the skull. Each holds the ear canal, the mastoid process, the styloid process and the socket where the mandible hinges.

labels.name: Superior orbital fissure
labels.fn: A slit between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone, at the back of the orbit. Nerves that move the eye and give sensation to the forehead pass through it.

labels.name: Ethmoid bone
labels.fn: A light, spongy cranial bone between the orbits. It forms the roof and upper walls of the inside of the nose and the upper part of the bony wall between its two sides, and it holds the ethmoid air cells.

labels.name: Lacrimal bone
labels.fn: The smallest facial bone, a thin plate in the inner wall of each orbit. It carries a groove for the tear sac, which drains tears toward the nose.

labels.name: Nasal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of small, flat facial bones that form the bony bridge of the nose. The lower, flexible part of the nose is cartilage.

labels.name: Inferior orbital fissure
labels.fn: A long slit in the floor of the orbit, between the maxilla and the greater wing of the sphenoid bone. Nerves and vessels pass through it to the face below the eye.

labels.name: Palatine bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of L-shaped facial bones at the back of the nose and mouth. Their horizontal plates form the back part of the bony roof of the mouth.

labels.name: Zygomatic bone
labels.fn: The cheekbone. It forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the outer wall and floor of the orbit, and its temporal process joins the zygomatic arch.

labels.name: Perpendicular plate of ethmoid bone
accept: perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone
labels.fn: A thin vertical plate of the ethmoid bone that hangs down in the midline. It forms the upper part of the bony wall that divides the inside of the nose into left and right sides, with the vomer below it.

labels.name: Infraorbital foramen
labels.fn: A hole in the maxilla just below each orbit. A nerve and vessels pass through it to the skin of the cheek, upper lip and side of the nose.

labels.name: Vomer bone
labels.fn: A thin, flat facial bone in the midline of the nose. It forms the lower back part of the bony wall that divides the inside of the nose, below the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone.

labels.name: Middle nasal concha
labels.fn: A thin, curled shelf of the ethmoid bone that sticks out from the side wall of the inside of the nose. The conchae make incoming air swirl so it is warmed, moistened and cleaned.

labels.name: Inferior nasal concha
labels.fn: The largest nasal concha, a separate curled facial bone on the lower side wall of the inside of the nose. Like the others, it makes incoming air swirl over the moist lining.

labels.name: Maxilla
labels.fn: The upper jaw bone, formed by two maxillae fused in the midline. It holds the upper teeth, forms most of the bony roof of the mouth and the floor of the orbit, and holds the large maxillary sinus.

labels.name: Alveolar process of mandible
labels.fn: The upper ridge of the mandible that holds the sockets for the lower teeth.

labels.name: Alveolar process of maxilla
labels.fn: The lower ridge of the maxilla that holds the sockets for the upper teeth.

labels.name: Mental foramen
labels.fn: A hole on the front of the mandible, one on each side of the chin below the lower teeth. A nerve and vessels pass through it to the skin of the chin and lower lip.

labels.name: Mandible
labels.fn: The lower jaw, the only skull bone that moves freely. It holds the lower teeth and hinges on the temporal bones for chewing and speaking.

labels.name: Zygomatic arch
labels.fn: The bony bridge on the side of the face, formed by the zygomatic process of the temporal bone meeting the temporal process of the zygomatic bone. It is easy to feel in front of the ear.

labels.name: Pterion
labels.fn: The small H-shaped area on the side of the skull where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet. The bone is thin here, and an artery runs just inside it, so a blow at this spot can cause dangerous bleeding.

follow.q: Why is a blow to the pterion especially dangerous?
options: Thin bone lies over an artery there
The spinal cord lies directly beneath this spot
It is the point where the lower jaw hinges
It covers the largest of the paranasal sinuses
follow.why: Four bones meet at the pterion and the bone is thin, with an artery running on its inner surface; a fracture can tear that artery and cause dangerous bleeding inside the skull. The spinal cord begins below the skull base, the jaw hinges at the mandibular fossa, and the maxillary sinus is in the face.

labels.name: Coronal suture
labels.fn: The wavy seam that runs across the top of the skull from side to side, joining the frontal bone in front to the two parietal bones behind it.

labels.name: Parietal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of large, curved plates that form most of the top and upper sides of the brain case. The two meet each other along the sagittal suture on the midline.

labels.name: Frontal bone
labels.fn: The single bone of the forehead. It forms the front of the brain case, the roofs of the orbits and the ridges above the eyes, and holds the frontal sinuses.

labels.name: Greater wing of sphenoid bone
labels.fn: The part of the sphenoid bone that shows on the side of the skull, in front of the temporal bone. It also forms part of the back wall of the orbit and the floor of the brain case.

labels.name: Squamous suture
labels.fn: The curved seam on the side of the skull where the squamous (flat) part of the temporal bone overlaps the parietal bone.

labels.name: Ethmoid bone
labels.fn: A light, spongy cranial bone between the orbits. It forms the roof and upper walls of the inside of the nose and the upper part of the bony wall between its two sides, and it holds the ethmoid air cells.

labels.name: Temporal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of cranial bones that form the lower sides and part of the base of the skull. Each holds the ear canal, the mastoid process, the styloid process and the socket where the mandible hinges.

labels.name: Squamous temporal
accept: squamous part of the temporal bone
labels.fn: The thin, flat upper part of the temporal bone, which forms part of the side wall of the brain case.

labels.name: Lacrimal bone
labels.fn: The smallest facial bone, a thin plate in the inner wall of each orbit. It carries a groove for the tear sac, which drains tears toward the nose.

labels.name: Lacrimal fossa
labels.fn: A shallow groove in the inner wall of the orbit, made by the lacrimal bone and the maxilla. It holds the tear sac, which drains tears toward the nose.

labels.name: Zygomatic process
accept: zygomatic process of the temporal bone
labels.fn: A bar of the temporal bone that projects forward from above the ear canal. It meets the temporal process of the zygomatic bone to form the zygomatic arch.

labels.name: Nasal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of small, flat facial bones that form the bony bridge of the nose. The lower, flexible part of the nose is cartilage.

labels.name: External acoustic meatus
labels.fn: The ear canal opening in the temporal bone. Sound travels through it toward the eardrum.

labels.name: Zygomatic bone
labels.fn: The cheekbone. It forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the outer wall and floor of the orbit, and its temporal process joins the zygomatic arch.

labels.name: Lambdoid suture
labels.fn: The seam at the back of the skull where the two parietal bones meet the occipital bone. It is shaped like the Greek letter lambda.

labels.name: Temporal process
accept: temporal process of the zygomatic bone
labels.fn: The backward-pointing bar of the zygomatic bone. It meets the zygomatic process of the temporal bone to form the zygomatic arch.

labels.name: Mastoid portion
accept: mastoid part of the temporal bone
labels.fn: The rear, lower part of the temporal bone, behind the ear canal. It ends in the mastoid process and is filled with small air spaces.

labels.name: Styloid process
labels.fn: A thin, pointed spike of the temporal bone that projects down below the ear. Several small muscles and ligaments of the tongue and neck attach to it.

labels.name: Maxilla
labels.fn: The upper jaw bone, formed by two maxillae fused in the midline. It holds the upper teeth, forms most of the bony roof of the mouth and the floor of the orbit, and holds the large maxillary sinus.

labels.name: Mastoid process
labels.fn: The rounded bump of the temporal bone you can feel just behind the ear. Muscles of the neck attach to it, and inside it holds small air spaces.

labels.name: Articular tubercle
labels.fn: A rounded ridge of the temporal bone just in front of the mandibular fossa. When the mouth opens wide, the head of the mandible slides forward onto it.

labels.name: Occipital bone
