labels.fn: The cranial bone that forms the back and much of the base of the skull. It surrounds the foramen magnum and carries the occipital condyles.

labels.name: Mandibular fossa
labels.fn: A smooth hollow on the underside of the temporal bone, in front of the ear canal. The head of the mandible sits in it, forming the jaw hinge.

labels.name: Mandible
labels.fn: The lower jaw, the only skull bone that moves freely. It holds the lower teeth and hinges on the temporal bones for chewing and speaking.

labels.name: Mental protuberance of mandible
labels.fn: The bony point of the chin, on the front of the mandible in the midline.

labels.name: Vomer
labels.fn: A thin, flat facial bone in the midline of the nose. It forms the lower back part of the bony wall that divides the inside of the nose, below the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone.

labels.name: Palatine process
labels.fn: A flat shelf of each maxilla that meets its partner in the midline. Together they form the front two thirds of the bony roof of the mouth.

labels.name: Zygomatic bone
labels.fn: The cheekbone. It forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the outer wall and floor of the orbit, and its temporal process joins the zygomatic arch.

labels.name: Palatine bone (horizontal plate)
accept: horizontal plate of the palatine bone
labels.fn: The horizontal plate of the palatine bone forms the back part of the bony roof of the mouth, behind the palatine processes of the maxillae. A small part of each palatine bone also reaches up into the orbit.

labels.name: Zygomatic arch
labels.fn: The bony bridge on the side of the face, formed by the zygomatic process of the temporal bone meeting the temporal process of the zygomatic bone. It is easy to feel in front of the ear.

labels.name: Articular tubercle
labels.fn: A rounded ridge of the temporal bone just in front of the mandibular fossa. When the mouth opens wide, the head of the mandible slides forward onto it.

labels.name: Sphenoid bone
labels.fn: A single butterfly-shaped cranial bone that runs across the middle of the skull base and joins with every other cranial bone. Its center holds the sella turcica and the sphenoid sinus.

labels.name: Foramen spinosum
labels.fn: A small round hole in the sphenoid bone, just behind the larger oval opening. An artery passes through it to supply the coverings of the brain.

labels.name: Mandibular fossa
labels.fn: A smooth hollow on the underside of the temporal bone, in front of the ear canal. The head of the mandible sits in it, forming the jaw hinge.

labels.name: Foramen lacerum
labels.fn: A jagged opening at the skull base between the sphenoid, temporal and occipital bones. In life it is mostly closed by cartilage.

labels.name: External auditory meatus
labels.fn: The ear canal opening in the temporal bone (also called the external acoustic meatus). Sound travels through it toward the eardrum.

labels.name: Jugular foramen
labels.fn: A large, irregular opening between the temporal and occipital bones, beside the foramen magnum. The main vein that drains blood from the brain leaves through it, along with several nerves.

labels.name: Mastoid process
labels.fn: The rounded bump of the temporal bone you can feel just behind the ear. Muscles of the neck attach to it, and inside it holds small air spaces.

labels.name: Occipital condyle
labels.fn: One of a pair of smooth, oval knobs on the occipital bone on either side of the foramen magnum. They rest on the first vertebra of the neck, letting you nod your head.

follow.q: The occipital condyles rest on which bone?
options: The second vertebra of the neck
The first vertebra of the neck
follow.why: The occipital condyles sit in cupped facets on the first vertebra of the neck; rocking there lets you nod. The second vertebra lies below the first, the mandible hinges on the temporal bone, and the hyoid touches no bone at all.

labels.name: Styloid process
labels.fn: A thin, pointed spike of the temporal bone that projects down below the ear. Several small muscles and ligaments of the tongue and neck attach to it.

labels.name: Temporal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of cranial bones that form the lower sides and part of the base of the skull. Each holds the ear canal, the mastoid process, the styloid process and the socket where the mandible hinges.

labels.name: Stylomastoid foramen
labels.fn: A small hole between the styloid and mastoid processes of the temporal bone. The nerve that moves the muscles of the face leaves the skull through it.

labels.name: Foramen magnum
labels.fn: The large hole in the occipital bone at the base of the skull. The lowest part of the brain passes through it and continues as the spinal cord.

follow.q: What passes through the foramen magnum?
options: The nerve that carries vision to the brain
The lowest part of the brain
The nerve fibers that carry smell
The main vein that drains the brain
follow.why: The foramen magnum is the large hole in the occipital bone where the lowest part of the brain continues down as the spinal cord. The nerve for vision uses the optic canal, the smell fibers pass through the cribriform plate, and the main draining vein leaves through the jugular foramen.

labels.name: Entrance to carotid canal
accept: external opening of the carotid canal
labels.fn: The opening on the underside of the temporal bone where the carotid canal begins. A major artery to the brain enters the skull here and runs forward through the canal.

labels.name: Occipital bone
labels.fn: The cranial bone that forms the back and much of the base of the skull. It surrounds the foramen magnum and carries the occipital condyles.

labels.name: Superior nuchal line
labels.fn: A curved ridge on the outer surface of the occipital bone, running sideways from the external occipital protuberance. Neck and back muscles attach along it.

labels.name: External occipital protuberance
labels.fn: The bump in the midline on the back of the skull, on the occipital bone. A ligament along the back of the neck and muscles of the neck attach to it.

labels.name: Frontal bone
labels.fn: The single bone of the forehead. It forms the front of the brain case, the roofs of the orbits and the ridges above the eyes, and holds the frontal sinuses.

labels.name: Crista galli
labels.fn: A small upward ridge of the ethmoid bone in the midline of the anterior cranial fossa. A fold of the brain's outer covering anchors to it.

labels.name: Cribriform plate
accept: cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
labels.fn: The flat, sieve-like part of the ethmoid bone on each side of the crista galli. Nerve fibers for smell pass through its tiny holes from the nose to the brain.

follow.q: A fracture of the cribriform plate would most likely affect which sense?
follow.why: Nerve fibers for smell pass from the nose to the brain through the tiny holes in the cribriform plate, so a fracture there can tear them. Hearing nerves use the internal acoustic meatus, the vision nerve uses the optic canal, and taste nerves do not pass through the cribriform plate.

labels.name: Superior orbital fissure
labels.fn: A slit between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone, at the back of the orbit. Nerves that move the eye and give sensation to the forehead pass through it.

labels.name: Lesser wing
accept: lesser wing of the sphenoid bone
labels.fn: The smaller, upper wing of the sphenoid bone. It forms the back edge of the anterior cranial fossa and part of the roof of the orbit.

labels.name: Sella turcica
labels.fn: The saddle-shaped bony formation on the top of the sphenoid bone, in the middle cranial fossa. Its seat, the hypophyseal fossa, holds a small gland that hangs below the brain.

labels.name: Hypophyseal fossa
labels.fn: The deep seat of the sella turcica on the sphenoid bone. A small gland that hangs from the underside of the brain sits in this hollow.

labels.name: Foramen rotundum
labels.fn: A round hole in the sphenoid bone just below the superior orbital fissure. It carries a nerve branch that gives sensation to the upper jaw and cheek.

labels.name: Foramen lacerum and exit of carotid canal
labels.fn: The jagged foramen lacerum, where the carotid canal opens into the brain case. The artery that ran through the canal enters the brain case here; the foramen lacerum itself is mostly closed by cartilage in life.

labels.name: Foramen spinosum
labels.fn: A small round hole in the sphenoid bone, just behind the larger oval opening. An artery passes through it to supply the coverings of the brain.

labels.name: Internal acoustic meatus
labels.fn: An opening on the inner surface of the petrous part of the temporal bone. The nerves for hearing, balance and facial movement pass through it.

labels.name: Temporal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of cranial bones that form the lower sides and part of the base of the skull. Each holds the ear canal, the mastoid process, the styloid process and the socket where the mandible hinges.

labels.name: Hypoglossal canal
labels.fn: A small tunnel through the occipital bone just above each occipital condyle. The nerve that moves the tongue passes through it.

labels.name: Petrous portion (petrous ridge)
accept: petrous part of the temporal bone
labels.fn: The dense, ridge-shaped part of the temporal bone in the floor of the brain case. It houses the organs of hearing and balance and separates the middle from the posterior cranial fossa.

labels.name: Foramen magnum
labels.fn: The large hole in the occipital bone at the base of the skull. The lowest part of the brain passes through it and continues as the spinal cord.

labels.name: Jugular foramen
labels.fn: A large, irregular opening between the temporal and occipital bones, beside the foramen magnum. The main vein that drains blood from the brain leaves through it, along with several nerves.

labels.name: Occipital bone
labels.fn: The cranial bone that forms the back and much of the base of the skull. It surrounds the foramen magnum and carries the occipital condyles.

labels.name: Parietal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of large, curved plates that form most of the top and upper sides of the brain case. The two meet each other along the sagittal suture on the midline.

hints.why: A heading ("Maxilla:") over the palatine process label; it names the bone the answer belongs to.
A heading ("Ethmoid bone:") over the crista galli and cribriform plate labels; it gives away which bone they belong to.
A heading ("Sphenoid bone:") over the lesser wing and sella turcica labels; it gives away which bone they belong to.

labels.name: Hypophyseal fossa
labels.fn: The deep seat of the sella turcica on the sphenoid bone. A small gland that hangs from the underside of the brain sits in this hollow.

labels.name: Crista galli
labels.fn: A small upward ridge of the ethmoid bone in the midline of the anterior cranial fossa. A fold of the brain's outer covering anchors to it.

labels.name: Parietal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of large, curved plates that form most of the top and upper sides of the brain case. The two meet each other along the sagittal suture on the midline.

labels.name: Frontal sinus
labels.fn: An air-filled space inside the frontal bone above the eyes. Like the other paranasal sinuses, it is lined with mucous membrane, drains into the nose and makes the skull lighter.

labels.name: Cribriform plate
accept: cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
labels.fn: The flat, sieve-like part of the ethmoid bone on each side of the crista galli. Nerve fibers for smell pass through its tiny holes from the nose to the brain.

labels.name: Perpendicular plate
accept: perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone
labels.fn: The thin vertical plate of the ethmoid bone, seen here from the side. It forms the upper part of the bony wall that divides the inside of the nose into left and right sides, with the vomer below it.

labels.name: Nasal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of small, flat facial bones that form the bony bridge of the nose. The lower, flexible part of the nose is cartilage.

labels.name: Temporal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of cranial bones that form the lower sides and part of the base of the skull. Each holds the ear canal, the mastoid process, the styloid process and the socket where the mandible hinges.

labels.name: Sphenoid bone
labels.fn: A single butterfly-shaped cranial bone that runs across the middle of the skull base and joins with every other cranial bone. Its center holds the sella turcica and the sphenoid sinus.

labels.name: Internal acoustic meatus
labels.fn: An opening on the inner surface of the petrous part of the temporal bone. The nerves for hearing, balance and facial movement pass through it.

labels.name: Sphenoid sinus
labels.fn: An air-filled space inside the body of the sphenoid bone, just below the sella turcica. It drains into the back of the nose.

labels.name: Hypoglossal canal
labels.fn: A small tunnel through the occipital bone just above each occipital condyle. The nerve that moves the tongue passes through it.

labels.name: Inferior nasal concha
labels.fn: The largest nasal concha, a separate curled facial bone on the lower side wall of the inside of the nose. Like the others, it makes incoming air swirl over the moist lining.

labels.name: Occipital bone
labels.fn: The cranial bone that forms the back and much of the base of the skull. It surrounds the foramen magnum and carries the occipital condyles.

labels.name: Vomer
labels.fn: A thin, flat facial bone in the midline of the nose. It forms the lower back part of the bony wall that divides the inside of the nose, below the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid bone.

labels.name: Styloid process
labels.fn: A thin, pointed spike of the temporal bone that projects down below the ear. Several small muscles and ligaments of the tongue and neck attach to it.

labels.name: Maxilla
labels.fn: The upper jaw bone, formed by two maxillae fused in the midline. It holds the upper teeth, forms most of the bony roof of the mouth and the floor of the orbit, and holds the large maxillary sinus.

labels.name: Palatine bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of L-shaped facial bones at the back of the nose and mouth. Their horizontal plates form the back part of the bony roof of the mouth.

labels.name: Mylohyoid line
labels.fn: A ridge on the inner surface of the mandible where the muscle forming the floor of the mouth attaches.

labels.name: Mandibular foramen
labels.fn: A hole on the inner surface of each side of the mandible. The nerve and vessels to the lower teeth enter the bone here; dentists inject anesthetic near it.

labels.name: Mandible
labels.fn: The lower jaw, the only skull bone that moves freely. It holds the lower teeth and hinges on the temporal bones for chewing and speaking.

labels.name: Lingula
labels.fn: A small tongue-shaped flap of bone at the edge of the mandibular foramen, on the inner surface of the mandible. A ligament from the skull base attaches to it.

labels.name: Hyoid bone
labels.fn: A U-shaped bone in the upper neck that touches no other bone. Muscles and ligaments hold it in place, and it supports the tongue and helps with swallowing.

hints.why: A heading ("Sella turcica:") over the hypophyseal fossa label, with no leader line of its own; it gives that answer away.

labels.name: Frontal sinus
labels.fn: An air-filled space inside the frontal bone above the eyes. Like the other paranasal sinuses, it is lined with mucous membrane, drains into the nose and makes the skull lighter.

labels.name: Sphenoid sinus
labels.fn: An air-filled space inside the body of the sphenoid bone, just below the sella turcica. It drains into the back of the nose.

labels.name: Ethmoid air cells
labels.fn: Many small air spaces inside the ethmoid bone, between the orbits. They drain into the side walls of the inside of the nose.

labels.name: Maxillary sinus
labels.fn: The largest paranasal sinus, an air-filled space in each maxilla below the orbit. Its roots lie close to the upper back teeth, so a sinus infection can feel like toothache.

follow.q: A patient with a maxillary sinus infection complains of pain in the upper back teeth. Why?
options: The sinus drains straight into the mouth
Those tooth roots lie just under the sinus
The sinus sits inside the mandible, next to them
Those teeth are held in the palatine bone
follow.why: The maxillary sinus sits in the maxilla just above the roots of the upper back teeth, so swelling there presses on the same nerves. The sinus drains into the nose, not the mouth; it is in the maxilla, not the mandible; and the upper teeth sit in the alveolar process of the maxilla.

labels.name: Frontal suture
labels.fn: The seam between the two halves of the frontal bone in a newborn. It usually closes and disappears in the first year or two.

labels.name: Frontal bone
labels.fn: The single bone of the forehead. It forms the front of the brain case, the roofs of the orbits and the ridges above the eyes, and holds the frontal sinuses.

labels.name: Anterior fontanelle
labels.fn: The largest soft spot on a newborn skull, a diamond-shaped area of membrane where the frontal and two parietal bones meet. It lets the skull flex during birth and grow with the brain, and it closes by about 18 to 24 months.

follow.q: Why does a newborn skull have fontanelles?
options: They let the skull flex at birth and grow later
They drain excess fluid away from the brain
They mark where all skull bones fuse into one
They hold the air-filled paranasal sinuses
follow.why: Fontanelles are areas of membrane between the skull bones that have not yet turned to bone. They let the plates shift during birth and leave room for the fast-growing brain. They do not drain fluid, the bones join at sutures rather than into one piece, and the sinuses are inside the facial and cranial bones.

labels.name: Ossification center
labels.fn: The spot in the middle of a newborn's flat skull bone where bone formation began. Bone spreads outward from it through the membrane, so it is the thickest point of the young bone.

labels.name: Parietal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of large, curved plates that form most of the top and upper sides of the brain case. The two meet each other along the sagittal suture on the midline.

labels.name: Posterior fontanelle
labels.fn: The small, triangular soft spot at the back of a newborn skull, where the two parietal bones meet the occipital bone. It closes within the first two to three months.

labels.name: Occipital bone
labels.fn: The cranial bone that forms the back and much of the base of the skull. It surrounds the foramen magnum and carries the occipital condyles.

labels.name: Parietal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of large, curved plates that form most of the top and upper sides of the brain case. The two meet each other along the sagittal suture on the midline.

labels.name: Frontal bone
labels.fn: The single bone of the forehead. It forms the front of the brain case, the roofs of the orbits and the ridges above the eyes, and holds the frontal sinuses.

labels.name: Ossification center
labels.fn: The spot in the middle of a newborn's flat skull bone where bone formation began. Bone spreads outward from it through the membrane, so it is the thickest point of the young bone.

labels.name: Posterior fontanelle
labels.fn: The small, triangular soft spot at the back of a newborn skull, where the two parietal bones meet the occipital bone. It closes within the first two to three months.

labels.name: Sphenoidal fontanelle
labels.fn: A soft spot on the side of a newborn skull, where the frontal, parietal, sphenoid and temporal bones meet. It closes early in infancy, leaving the pterion.

labels.name: Mastoid fontanelle
labels.fn: A soft spot at the back of the side of a newborn skull, where the parietal, occipital and temporal bones meet. It closes during the first year or so.

labels.name: Occipital bone
labels.fn: The cranial bone that forms the back and much of the base of the skull. It surrounds the foramen magnum and carries the occipital condyles.

labels.name: Temporal bone (squamous portion)
accept: squamous part of the temporal bone
labels.fn: The flat upper part of the newborn's temporal bone, on the side of the skull. It meets the parietal bone at the squamous suture.

labels.name: Cervical vertebrae
labels.fn: The seven vertebrae of the neck, C1 to C7. They are the smallest vertebrae and each has a hole in each transverse process.

labels.name: Cervical curve
labels.fn: The forward (anterior) bend of the neck region. It is a secondary curve that forms in infancy once the baby holds up its head.

follow.q: Which spinal curves are secondary curves that form after birth?
follow.why: The cervical curve forms when an infant holds up its head and the lumbar curve when a child stands and walks. The thoracic and sacrococcygeal curves are primary curves, already present before birth.

labels.name: Thoracic vertebrae
labels.fn: The twelve vertebrae of the chest region, T1 to T12. Each carries facets where ribs attach. (The figure misprints "vertebrae".)

labels.name: Thoracic curve
labels.fn: The backward (posterior) bend of the chest region. It is a primary curve, present before birth.

labels.name: Intervertebral disc
labels.fn: A pad of fibrocartilage between the bodies of two neighboring vertebrae. It absorbs shock and lets the column bend, and together the discs make up about a quarter of the column's length.

labels.name: Lumbar vertebrae
labels.fn: The five vertebrae of the lower back, L1 to L5. They have the largest, thickest bodies because they carry the most body weight.

follow.q: Why do lumbar vertebrae have the largest bodies?
options: They protect the heart and lungs
They carry the lowest pairs of ribs
They pivot to turn the head
follow.why: Weight builds up down the column, so the lumbar bodies, which carry the whole trunk above them, are the biggest. They do not protect the heart or carry ribs (that is the thoracic region), and head movement happens at the top of the neck.

labels.name: Lumbar curve
labels.fn: The forward (anterior) bend of the lower back. It is a secondary curve that forms when a child begins to stand and walk.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone at the base of the column, formed by five sacral vertebrae that fuse in the late teens and twenties. It joins the hip bones on each side.

labels.name: Fused vertebrae of sacrum and coccyx
labels.fn: The lowest part of the column is made of vertebrae that fuse together: five form the sacrum and three to five small ones form the coccyx.

labels.name: Coccyx
labels.fn: The tailbone: three to five small vertebrae fused together below the sacrum. Several ligaments and muscles attach to it.

labels.name: Sacrococcygeal curve
labels.fn: The backward (posterior) bend formed by the sacrum and coccyx. Like the thoracic curve, it is a primary curve present before birth.

labels.name: Scoliosis
labels.fn: An abnormal sideways (lateral) bend of the vertebral column, usually in the thoracic region. It is often first noticed in adolescence.

labels.name: Kyphosis
labels.fn: An exaggerated backward bend of the thoracic region that gives a hunched back. It is common in older adults with weakened vertebrae.

labels.name: Lordosis
labels.fn: An exaggerated forward bend of the lumbar region (swayback). It can appear temporarily in late pregnancy or with extra weight in the belly.

labels.name: Spinal cord
labels.fn: The column of nerve tissue that runs down from the brain inside the vertebral foramen. The vertebrae stacked around it protect it.

labels.name: Spinal cord
labels.fn: The column of nerve tissue that runs down from the brain inside the vertebral foramen. The vertebrae stacked around it protect it.

labels.name: Spinous process
labels.fn: The single process that points backward from the junction of the two laminae. It is the bump you feel down the middle of the back, and muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Transverse process
labels.fn: The process that sticks out sideways from each side of the vertebral arch, where the pedicle meets the lamina. Back muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Facet of superior articular process
accept: facet of the superior articular process
labels.fn: The smooth surface on top of the superior articular process. It meets the inferior articular process of the vertebra above, guiding how the two vertebrae move against each other.

labels.name: Vertebral foramen
labels.fn: The large opening enclosed by the vertebral body in front and the vertebral arch behind. Stacked together, the foramina form the vertebral canal that holds the spinal cord.

follow.q: What do the vertebral foramina form when the vertebrae are stacked?
options: The intervertebral foramina on each side
The transverse foramina of the neck
The sacral hiatus at the lower end
follow.why: Lined up, the vertebral foramina make one long vertebral canal that houses the spinal cord. Intervertebral foramina are the side gaps between vertebrae, transverse foramina are in cervical transverse processes, and the sacral hiatus is only the lower end of the sacral canal.

labels.name: Intervetebral disc
labels.fn: A pad of fibrocartilage between the bodies of two neighboring vertebrae (the label misspells "intervertebral"). It absorbs shock and lets the column bend.

labels.name: Facet for head of rib
accept: facet for the head of the rib
labels.fn: A smooth pit on the side of a thoracic vertebral body where the end of a rib meets it. Only thoracic vertebrae have these costal facets.

labels.name: Facet of superior articular process
accept: facet of the superior articular process
labels.fn: The smooth surface on top of the superior articular process. It meets the inferior articular process of the vertebra above, guiding how the two vertebrae move against each other.

labels.name: Lamina
labels.fn: One of a pair of flat plates that form the back part of the vertebral arch. The two laminae meet in the midline at the spinous process.

labels.name: Pedicle
labels.fn: One of a pair of short, thick pillars that join the vertebral body to the rest of the arch. Notches above and below the pedicles form the intervertebral foramina.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The vertebral body: the thick, drum-shaped front part of a vertebra that carries body weight. Intervertebral discs sit between neighboring bodies.

labels.name: Inferior articular process
labels.fn: The process that projects downward from the vertebral arch. Its facet meets the superior articular process of the vertebra below.

labels.name: Facet for head of rib
accept: facet for the head of the rib
labels.fn: A smooth pit on the side of a thoracic vertebral body where the end of a rib meets it. Only thoracic vertebrae have these costal facets.

labels.name: Spinous process
labels.fn: The single process that points backward from the junction of the two laminae. It is the bump you feel down the middle of the back, and muscles and ligaments attach to it.

hints.why: A heading ("Vertebral arch:") over the lamina and pedicle labels, with no leader line of its own; it gives away what they are parts of.

labels.name: Vertebral body
labels.fn: The thick, drum-shaped front part of a vertebra that carries body weight. Intervertebral discs sit between neighboring bodies.

labels.name: Intervertebral foramen
labels.fn: The opening on each side between two neighboring vertebrae, formed by notches in their pedicles. The nerves that branch off the spinal cord leave the vertebral canal through it.

labels.name: Anulus fibrosus
labels.fn: The tough outer ring of the intervertebral disc, made of layers of fibrocartilage. It holds the soft center in place and anchors the disc to the vertebral bodies.

labels.name: Nucleus pulposus
labels.fn: The soft, gel-like center of the intervertebral disc. It absorbs shock and spreads pressure; if it pushes through a tear in the outer ring, the result is a herniated disc.

follow.q: In a herniated disc, what happens?
options: A vertebral body cracks under a heavy load
The soft center bulges through a torn outer ring
The disc hardens and slowly turns to bone
follow.why: A herniated disc is the gel-like nucleus pulposus bulging through a weakened or torn anulus fibrosus, where it can press on nearby nerves. A cracked body is a fracture, spinous processes do not fuse in this condition, and discs do not turn to bone.

labels.name: Dens of axis
labels.fn: The tooth-like peg that projects upward from the body of the axis (C2). It sits inside the ring of the atlas and acts as the pivot the atlas turns around when you shake your head "no".

follow.q: Which movement depends on the dens of the axis?
options: Nodding the head up and down, "yes"
follow.why: The atlas and skull rotate around the dens, which is what turns the head side to side. Nodding happens between the occipital condyles and the atlas, bending forward happens along the whole column, and the jaw opens at the temporal bone.

labels.name: Transverse ligament
labels.fn: A strong band that stretches across the ring of the atlas, holding the dens against the anterior arch. It keeps the dens from pressing back on the spinal cord.

labels.name: Spinous process (bifid)
labels.fn: The spinous process of a typical cervical vertebra (C3 to C6) is short and split into two tips (bifid). Muscles of the neck and the nuchal ligament attach to it.

labels.name: C1 (atlas)
labels.fn: The atlas, the first cervical vertebra. It is a ring with no body and no spinous process; its superior facets hold the occipital condyles of the skull, letting you nod.

labels.name: Vertebral foramen
labels.fn: The large opening enclosed by the vertebral body in front and the vertebral arch behind. Stacked together, the foramina form the vertebral canal that holds the spinal cord.

labels.name: C2 (axis)
labels.fn: The axis, the second cervical vertebra. Its dens projects up into the atlas as the pivot for turning the head.

labels.name: Lamina
labels.fn: One of a pair of flat plates that form the back part of the vertebral arch. The two laminae meet in the midline at the spinous process.

labels.name: Pedicle
labels.fn: One of a pair of short, thick pillars that join the vertebral body to the rest of the arch. Notches above and below the pedicles form the intervertebral foramina.

labels.name: C3
labels.fn: The third cervical vertebra, the first typical one: a small body, a bifid spinous process and a transverse foramen on each side.

labels.name: Inferior articular process
labels.fn: The process that projects downward from the vertebral arch. Its facet meets the superior articular process of the vertebra below.

labels.name: Superior articular process
labels.fn: The process that projects upward from the vertebral arch. Its facet meets the inferior articular process of the vertebra above.

labels.name: Bifid spinous process
labels.fn: A short spinous process split into two tips, typical of cervical vertebrae C3 to C6.

labels.name: Transverse process
labels.fn: The process that sticks out sideways from each side of the vertebral arch, where the pedicle meets the lamina. Back muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Transverse process
labels.fn: The process that sticks out sideways from each side of the vertebral arch, where the pedicle meets the lamina. Back muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Transverse foramen
labels.fn: A hole through each transverse process of a cervical vertebra; only cervical vertebrae have them. Arteries that help supply the brain run up through them.

follow.q: Which feature marks a vertebra as cervical?
options: A smooth costal facet on each side of its body
A transverse foramen on each side
A large, heavy body built to carry weight
Fusion with the vertebrae above and below
follow.why: Only cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina, which carry arteries up toward the brain. Costal facets mark thoracic vertebrae, the largest bodies are lumbar, and fused vertebrae form the sacrum and coccyx.

labels.name: C7 (vertebra prominens)
labels.fn: C7, the vertebra prominens: the last cervical vertebra, whose long, single spinous process is the easy-to-feel bump at the base of the neck.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The vertebral body: the thick, drum-shaped front part of a vertebra that carries body weight. Intervertebral discs sit between neighboring bodies.

labels.name: Dens
labels.fn: The tooth-like peg that projects upward from the axis (C2). It is the pivot the atlas and skull rotate around, held in place by the transverse ligament.

labels.name: Anterior arch
labels.fn: The short front part of the atlas ring. The dens sits against its inner surface.

labels.name: Superior articular facet
labels.fn: A large, cupped facet on the top of the atlas where an occipital condyle of the skull rests. This pairing lets you nod your head "yes".

labels.name: Transverse process
labels.fn: The process that sticks out sideways from each side of the vertebral arch, where the pedicle meets the lamina. Back muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Transverse foramen
labels.fn: A hole through each transverse process of a cervical vertebra; only cervical vertebrae have them. Arteries that help supply the brain run up through them.

labels.name: Ligament
labels.fn: The transverse ligament of the atlas, a strong band across the ring that holds the dens against the anterior arch and away from the spinal cord.

labels.name: Posterior arch
labels.fn: The back part of the atlas ring. The atlas has no spinous process, only a small bump on this arch.

labels.name: Dens
labels.fn: The tooth-like peg that projects upward from the axis (C2). It is the pivot the atlas and skull rotate around, held in place by the transverse ligament.

labels.name: Superior articular facet
labels.fn: A broad facet on the top of the axis, beside the dens. It meets the atlas above and lets the atlas rotate on the axis.

labels.name: Transverse process
labels.fn: The process that sticks out sideways from each side of the vertebral arch, where the pedicle meets the lamina. Back muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Transverse foramen
labels.fn: A hole through each transverse process of a cervical vertebra; only cervical vertebrae have them. Arteries that help supply the brain run up through them.

labels.name: Lamina
labels.fn: One of a pair of flat plates that form the back part of the vertebral arch. The two laminae meet in the midline at the spinous process.

labels.name: Spinous process
labels.fn: The single process that points backward from the junction of the two laminae. It is the bump you feel down the middle of the back, and muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Dens
labels.fn: The tooth-like peg that projects upward from the axis (C2). It is the pivot the atlas and skull rotate around, held in place by the transverse ligament.

labels.name: Transverse process
labels.fn: The process that sticks out sideways from each side of the vertebral arch, where the pedicle meets the lamina. Back muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Inferior articular process
labels.fn: The process that projects downward from the vertebral arch. Its facet meets the superior articular process of the vertebra below.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The vertebral body: the thick, drum-shaped front part of a vertebra that carries body weight. Intervertebral discs sit between neighboring bodies.

labels.name: Superior articular facets
labels.fn: The smooth surfaces on top of the superior articular processes. In the thoracic region they face backward, and they meet the inferior articular facets of the vertebra above.

labels.name: Articular facet for tubercle of rib
accept: facet for the tubercle of the rib
labels.fn: A smooth facet on the tip of a thoracic transverse process. A knob on the back of a rib meets it, steadying the rib.

labels.name: Transverse process
labels.fn: The process that sticks out sideways from each side of the vertebral arch, where the pedicle meets the lamina. Back muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Pedicle
labels.fn: One of a pair of short, thick pillars that join the vertebral body to the rest of the arch. Notches above and below the pedicles form the intervertebral foramina.

labels.name: Intervertebral disc
labels.fn: A pad of fibrocartilage between the bodies of two neighboring vertebrae. It absorbs shock and lets the column bend, and together the discs make up about a quarter of the column's length.

labels.name: Lamina
labels.fn: One of a pair of flat plates that form the back part of the vertebral arch. The two laminae meet in the midline at the spinous process.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The vertebral body: the thick, drum-shaped front part of a vertebra that carries body weight. Intervertebral discs sit between neighboring bodies.

labels.name: Spinous process
labels.fn: The single process that points backward from the junction of the two laminae. It is the bump you feel down the middle of the back, and muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Superior costal facet
labels.fn: A smooth half-pit on the upper edge of a thoracic vertebral body. Together with the inferior costal facet of the vertebra above, it forms the socket where the end of a rib meets the column.

labels.name: Inferior costal facet
labels.fn: A smooth half-pit on the lower edge of a thoracic vertebral body. With the superior costal facet of the vertebra below, it forms the socket for the end of a rib.

labels.name: Inferior articular facets
labels.fn: The smooth surfaces on the inferior articular processes. They meet the superior articular facets of the vertebra below and guide how the two move.

labels.name: Superior articular process
labels.fn: The process that projects upward from the vertebral arch. Its facet meets the inferior articular process of the vertebra above.

labels.name: Transverse process
labels.fn: The process that sticks out sideways from each side of the vertebral arch, where the pedicle meets the lamina. Back muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The vertebral body: the thick, drum-shaped front part of a vertebra that carries body weight. Intervertebral discs sit between neighboring bodies.

labels.name: Inferior articular process
labels.fn: The process that projects downward from the vertebral arch. Its facet meets the superior articular process of the vertebra below.

labels.name: Spinous process
labels.fn: The single process that points backward from the junction of the two laminae. It is the bump you feel down the middle of the back, and muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Intervertebral disc
labels.fn: A pad of fibrocartilage between the bodies of two neighboring vertebrae. It absorbs shock and lets the column bend, and together the discs make up about a quarter of the column's length.

labels.name: Inferior articular process
labels.fn: The process that projects downward from the vertebral arch. Its facet meets the superior articular process of the vertebra below.

labels.name: Sacral promontory
labels.fn: The forward-jutting upper edge of the body of the first sacral vertebra. It is a landmark for the back edge of the opening into the true pelvis.

labels.name: Body of first sacral vertebra
accept: body of the first sacral vertebra
labels.fn: The large body at the top of the sacrum. It carries the weight of the whole column above and meets L5 through an intervertebral disc.

labels.name: Transverse ridges (sites of vertebral fusion)
labels.fn: Horizontal lines across the front of the sacrum that mark where the bodies of the five sacral vertebrae fused together.

labels.name: Anterior sacral foramina
labels.fn: Four pairs of holes on the front of the sacrum. Branches of the nerves in the sacral canal pass through them to the front.

labels.name: Apex
labels.fn: The narrow lower tip of the sacrum, where it meets the coccyx.

labels.name: Coccyx
labels.fn: The tailbone: three to five small vertebrae fused together below the sacrum. Several ligaments and muscles attach to it.

labels.name: Sacral canal
labels.fn: The tunnel through the sacrum, continuing the vertebral canal. It holds the lowest nerve roots that run down from the spinal cord.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The body of the first sacral vertebra, seen from behind. It is the top of the sacrum, which meets L5 through an intervertebral disc.

labels.name: Facet of superior articular process
accept: facet of the superior articular process
labels.fn: The smooth surface on top of the superior articular process. It meets the inferior articular process of the vertebra above, guiding how the two vertebrae move against each other.

labels.name: Auricular surface
labels.fn: The ear-shaped rough area on each side of the sacrum. It meets the hip bone, where the weight of the upper body passes into the pelvis.

labels.name: Median sacral crest
labels.fn: A ridge down the midline of the back of the sacrum, formed by the fused spinous processes of the sacral vertebrae.

labels.name: Lateral sacral crest
labels.fn: A ridge on each side of the back of the sacrum, formed by the fused transverse processes of the sacral vertebrae.

labels.name: Posterior sacral foramina
labels.fn: Four pairs of holes on the back of the sacrum. Small nerve branches pass through them to the skin and muscles of the lower back and buttock.

labels.name: Sacral hiatus
labels.fn: The opening at the lower end of the sacral canal, where the laminae of the last sacral vertebrae failed to fuse. Anesthetic can be injected here into the canal.

labels.name: Coccyx
labels.fn: The tailbone: three to five small vertebrae fused together below the sacrum. Several ligaments and muscles attach to it.

labels.name: External occipital protuberance
labels.fn: The bump in the midline on the back of the skull, on the occipital bone. The nuchal ligament attaches to it and runs down from here to C7.

labels.name: Nuchal ligament
labels.fn: A thick, elastic band along the back of the neck from the external occipital protuberance to the spinous process of C7. It helps hold the head up and anchors muscles of the neck.

labels.name: Spinous process of T1 vertebra
labels.fn: The spinous process of the first thoracic vertebra, just below the vertebra prominens. Below the neck, the supraspinous ligament runs along these tips.

labels.name: Anterior longitudinal ligament
labels.fn: A broad band running down the front of the vertebral bodies from the skull to the sacrum. It limits backward bending of the column.

labels.name: Supraspinous ligament
labels.fn: A ligament that joins the tips of the spinous processes from C7 down to the sacrum. It limits forward bending of the column.

labels.name: Jugular notch
labels.fn: The shallow dip in the top edge of the manubrium, between the ends of the collarbones. You can feel it at the base of the front of the neck.

labels.name: Clavicular notch
labels.fn: A shallow notch on each upper corner of the manubrium where the collarbone meets the sternum.

labels.name: Manubrium
labels.fn: The wide top piece of the sternum. It meets the collarbones and the first pair of ribs, and joins the body of the sternum at the sternal angle.

labels.name: Sternal angle
labels.fn: The slight ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum. The second ribs attach here, so it is the starting point for counting ribs.

follow.q: A nurse feels for the sternal angle to count ribs. Which rib attaches there?
follow.why: The second rib's costal cartilage meets the sternum at the sternal angle, the ridge between manubrium and body, so it is where counting starts. The first rib sits higher on the manubrium, the seventh lower on the body, and the twelfth does not reach the sternum.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The long middle part of the sternum. Costal cartilages of ribs 2 through 7 attach along its edges.

labels.name: Xiphoid process
labels.fn: The small, pointed lower tip of the sternum. It is cartilage in young people and hardens into bone with age; hand position in CPR stays above it.

follow.q: Why do CPR instructions keep the hands above the xiphoid process?
options: It is too thick and rigid to compress
It can snap off and injure organs below
It anchors the first pair of ribs to the sternum
It is the only part of the sternum made of bone
follow.why: The xiphoid is a small tip that can snap off under force and be driven into the liver or other organs below. It is thin, not thick; the first ribs attach to the manubrium; and the rest of the sternum is bone too.

labels.name: Clavicular notch
labels.fn: A shallow notch on each upper corner of the manubrium where the collarbone meets the sternum.

labels.name: Jugular notch
labels.fn: The shallow dip in the top edge of the manubrium, between the ends of the collarbones. You can feel it at the base of the front of the neck.

labels.name: Manubrium
labels.fn: The wide top piece of the sternum. It meets the collarbones and the first pair of ribs, and joins the body of the sternum at the sternal angle.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The long middle part of the sternum. Costal cartilages of ribs 2 through 7 attach along its edges.

labels.name: Sternal angle
labels.fn: The slight ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum. The second ribs attach here, so it is the starting point for counting ribs.

labels.name: Xiphoid process
labels.fn: The small, pointed lower tip of the sternum. It is cartilage in young people and hardens into bone with age; hand position in CPR stays above it.

labels.name: Costal cartilages
labels.fn: Bars of hyaline cartilage that join the front ends of the ribs to the sternum, directly or through the cartilage above. Their flexibility lets the chest wall move with breathing.

follow.q: What lets the thoracic cage expand when you breathe in?
options: The ribs themselves are made of soft cartilage
Flexible cartilage joins ribs to the sternum
The sternum splits apart down the middle
The thoracic vertebrae slide apart from each other
follow.why: The bars of hyaline cartilage between the ribs and sternum bend, so the ribs can swing up and out. The ribs themselves are bone, the sternum is one bone, and the vertebrae stay in place.

labels.name: Intercostal space
labels.fn: The gap between two neighboring ribs. It is filled with muscles and carries nerves and vessels that run along the lower edge of each rib.

hints.why: A heading ("Sternum:") over the manubrium, body and xiphoid process labels, with no leader line of its own.

labels.name: Superior costal facet
labels.fn: A smooth half-pit on the upper edge of a thoracic vertebral body. Together with the inferior costal facet of the vertebra above, it forms the socket where the end of a rib meets the column.

labels.name: Superior articular facets
labels.fn: The smooth surfaces on top of the superior articular processes. In the thoracic region they face backward, and they meet the inferior articular facets of the vertebra above.

labels.name: Body of vertebra
labels.fn: The vertebral body of a thoracic vertebra. The end of a rib meets the sides of neighboring bodies at their costal facets.

labels.name: Facet for tubercle of rib
accept: facet for the tubercle of the rib
labels.fn: The smooth facet on the tip of a thoracic transverse process where the tubercle of the rib rests.

labels.name: Head of rib
labels.fn: The back end of the rib, which meets the costal facets on the bodies of two neighboring thoracic vertebrae and the disc between them.

follow.q: The head of a typical rib meets which structures?
options: The transverse process of a single vertebra
Facets on two neighboring vertebral bodies
The edge of the sternum through cartilage
The spinous process of the vertebra above
follow.why: The head of a typical rib fits into a socket formed by the inferior costal facet of the vertebra above and the superior costal facet of the one below. The tubercle, not the head, meets the transverse process; the front end reaches the sternum through costal cartilage; and no rib meets a spinous process.

labels.name: Intervertebral disc
labels.fn: A pad of fibrocartilage between the bodies of two neighboring vertebrae. It absorbs shock and lets the column bend, and together the discs make up about a quarter of the column's length.

labels.name: Tranverse processes
labels.fn: The transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae (the label misspells "transverse"). The tubercle of each rib rests on the tip of one.

labels.name: Neck of rib
labels.fn: The short narrow part of the rib between the head and the tubercle.

labels.name: Body of vertebra
labels.fn: The vertebral body of a thoracic vertebra. The end of a rib meets the sides of neighboring bodies at their costal facets.

labels.name: Spinous process
labels.fn: The single process that points backward from the junction of the two laminae. It is the bump you feel down the middle of the back, and muscles and ligaments attach to it.

labels.name: Tubercle of rib
labels.fn: A small knob on the back of the rib, just past the neck. It meets the facet on the transverse process of a thoracic vertebra.

labels.name: Inferior costal facet
labels.fn: A smooth half-pit on the lower edge of a thoracic vertebral body. With the superior costal facet of the vertebra below, it forms the socket for the end of a rib.

labels.name: Angle of rib
labels.fn: The point on the rib's shaft where it bends most sharply forward, a little beyond the tubercle. It is the weakest part of the rib and a common place for fractures.

labels.name: Skull
labels.fn: The bones of the head: the cranial bones that enclose the brain and the facial bones that frame the face.

labels.name: Cranial portion
labels.fn: The part of the skull that encloses and protects the brain, made of eight cranial bones.

labels.name: Facial portion
labels.fn: The front part of the skull that frames the face, made of fourteen facial bones including the jaws, cheekbones and nasal bones.

labels.name: Pectoral (shoulder) girdle
labels.fn: The clavicle and scapula on each side. They attach the upper limb to the axial skeleton.

labels.name: Clavicle
labels.fn: The collarbone, a long S-shaped bone that runs across the top of the chest from the manubrium to the shoulder.

labels.name: Scapula
labels.fn: The shoulder blade, a flat triangular bone on the back of the chest wall.

labels.name: Thoracic cage
labels.fn: The ribs, costal cartilages, sternum and thoracic vertebrae. The cage protects the heart and lungs and moves with breathing.

labels.name: Sternum
labels.fn: The breastbone: a flat bone in the midline of the chest made of the manubrium, body and xiphoid process.

labels.name: Ribs
labels.fn: The twelve pairs of curved bones of the chest wall. All attach to thoracic vertebrae behind; most reach the sternum in front through costal cartilages.

labels.name: Upper limb
labels.fn: The arm, forearm, wrist and hand, with 30 bones on each side: humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges.

labels.name: Vertebral column
labels.fn: The backbone: 24 separate vertebrae plus the sacrum and coccyx. It supports the head and trunk and surrounds the spinal cord.

labels.name: Vertebral column
labels.fn: The backbone: 24 separate vertebrae plus the sacrum and coccyx. It supports the head and trunk and surrounds the spinal cord.

labels.name: Humerus
labels.fn: The single long bone of the arm, from shoulder to elbow.

labels.name: Ulna
labels.fn: The forearm bone on the little-finger side. Its upper end forms the main hinge of the elbow with the humerus.

labels.name: Pelvic girdle (hip bones)
labels.fn: The two hip bones. They attach the lower limbs to the axial skeleton at the sacrum and carry the weight of the upper body to the legs.

follow.q: What is the job of the pelvic girdle?
options: It surrounds and protects the lungs
It joins the legs to the axial skeleton
It lets the skull turn on the neck
It holds the upper limbs to the trunk
follow.why: The two hip bones meet the sacrum behind and hold the femurs, so the weight of the trunk passes through them to the legs. The ribs protect the lungs, and the pectoral girdle holds the upper limbs.

labels.name: Pelvic girdle (hip bones)
labels.fn: The two hip bones. They attach the lower limbs to the axial skeleton at the sacrum and carry the weight of the upper body to the legs.

labels.name: Radius
labels.fn: The forearm bone on the thumb side. Its lower end forms most of the wrist joint and turns around the ulna to rotate the forearm.

labels.name: Carpals
labels.fn: The eight small wrist bones, in two rows of four.

labels.name: Metacarpals
labels.fn: The five bones of the palm, one behind each finger.

labels.name: Phalanges
labels.fn: The finger bones: 14 in each hand, two in the thumb and three in each other finger.

labels.name: Lower limb
labels.fn: The thigh, leg, ankle and foot, with 30 bones on each side: femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsals, metatarsals and phalanges.

labels.name: Femur
labels.fn: The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. Its head fits into the hip socket and its lower end forms the knee with the tibia.

follow.q: Which is the longest and strongest bone of the body?
follow.why: The femur, the thigh bone, is the longest and strongest. The tibia is the main weight-bearing bone below the knee, the humerus is the arm bone, and the fibula is thin and carries little weight.

labels.name: Patella
labels.fn: The kneecap, a sesamoid bone inside the tendon of the front thigh muscles. It protects the knee and improves the pull of those muscles.

labels.name: Tibia
labels.fn: The shinbone, the larger, weight-bearing bone of the leg on the big-toe side.

labels.name: Fibula
labels.fn: The thin bone on the outer side of the leg. It carries little weight but anchors muscles and forms the outer ankle bump.

labels.name: Tarsals
labels.fn: The seven bones of the ankle and back of the foot, including the heel bone (calcaneus) and the talus.

labels.name: Metatarsals
labels.fn: The five long bones of the middle of the foot, one behind each toe.

labels.name: Phalanges
labels.fn: The toe bones: 14 in each foot, two in the big toe and three in each other toe.

labels.name: Axial skeleton
labels.fn: The 80 bones along the body's central axis: skull, hyoid, the six tiny bones inside the ears, vertebral column and thoracic cage. It protects the brain, spinal cord and chest organs.

follow.q: Which bones belong to the axial skeleton?
options: Skull, vertebral column and thoracic cage
Pectoral girdle, clavicles and both upper limbs
Pelvic girdle, hip bones and both lower limbs
Only the skull and the facial bones
follow.why: The axial skeleton runs along the body's central axis: skull, vertebral column, thoracic cage (plus the hyoid and the tiny bones inside the ears). The girdles and limbs make up the appendicular skeleton.

labels.name: Appendicular skeleton
labels.fn: The 126 bones of the limbs and the girdles that attach them to the axial skeleton. It is built mainly for movement.

labels.name: Bone
labels.fn: The rigid bone on one side of the joint. At a synovial joint the two bone ends do not touch directly: each is capped with articular cartilage and separated by the joint cavity.

labels.name: Articular capsule
labels.fn: The sleeve of connective tissue that encloses a synovial joint and joins its bones. Its outer fibrous membrane holds the bones together, and its inner synovial membrane lines the joint cavity and makes synovial fluid.

labels.name: Synovial membrane (inner)
labels.fn: The thin inner layer of the articular capsule. It lines the joint cavity (but not the articular cartilage) and makes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint and feeds the cartilage.

labels.name: Fibrous membrane (outer)
accept: fibrous layer of the articular capsule
labels.fn: The tough outer layer of the articular capsule, made of dense connective tissue. It attaches to both bones and holds them together; thickened bands of it form ligaments.

labels.name: Joint cavity containing synovial fluid
labels.fn: The narrow space between the bones of a synovial joint, the feature that defines a synovial joint. It holds a thin film of slippery synovial fluid that cuts friction and feeds the articular cartilage.

follow.q: Which feature is found in every synovial joint but in no fibrous or cartilaginous joint?
options: A joint cavity between the bones
Hyaline cartilage joining the bones end to end
Dense connective tissue binding the bones together
A fibrocartilage pad joining the two bones
follow.why: A synovial joint is defined by the fluid-filled joint cavity that separates its bones. Fibrous joints bind bones with dense connective tissue, and cartilaginous joints join them with hyaline cartilage or a fibrocartilage pad, with no space between.

labels.name: Articular cartilage
labels.fn: The smooth layer of hyaline cartilage that caps the bone ends inside a synovial joint. It has no blood vessels; it lowers friction and absorbs compression as the bones move.

follow.q: Articular cartilage has no blood vessels. Where do its cells get their nutrients?
options: From synovial fluid in the joint cavity
From blood vessels running through it
From yellow bone marrow in the shaft
follow.why: Nutrients diffuse into articular cartilage from the synovial fluid that bathes it, helped by the squeezing and release of the cartilage as the joint moves. The cartilage has no vessels of its own, the fibrous membrane lies outside the cavity, and marrow in the shaft is sealed off by bone.

labels.name: Bone
labels.fn: The bone on the other side of the joint. Its end is also capped with articular cartilage, and the articular capsule attaches around it, sealing the joint cavity.

labels.name: Ball-and-socket joint (hip joint)
labels.fn: A rounded head fits into a cup-shaped socket, as at the hip and the shoulder. It moves around all three axes (multiaxial), so it is the most freely movable joint type.

labels.name: Pivot joint (between C1 and C2 vertebrae)
labels.fn: A rounded bone surface or peg turns inside a ring made of bone and ligament, allowing turning around one axis (uniaxial). Between C1 and C2 the dens of the axis turns inside the ring of the atlas as you shake your head.

labels.name: Hinge joint (elbow)
labels.fn: A rounded surface fits into a trough-shaped one, so the joint only bends and straightens in one plane (uniaxial), like a door hinge. The elbow, the knee and the joints between finger bones are hinges.

follow.q: A joint lets its bones bend and straighten in only one plane, like a door. Which type of synovial joint is it?
follow.why: A hinge joint fits a rounded surface into a trough, which allows movement in one plane only (uniaxial). A saddle joint moves in two planes, a ball-and-socket joint in all three, and a plane joint only glides a little.

labels.name: Condyloid joint (between radius and carpal bones of wrist)
labels.fn: An oval, shallow knob fits into an oval depression, allowing movement in two planes (biaxial) but no turning. The joint between the radius and the carpal bones at the wrist is condyloid.

labels.name: Plane joint (between tarsal bones)
labels.fn: Two flat or slightly curved surfaces slide over each other, allowing small gliding movements. The joints between the tarsal bones, and between the carpal bones, are plane joints.

labels.name: Saddle joint (between trapezium carpal bone and 1st metacarpal bone)
labels.fn: Each surface is saddle-shaped, curving up one way and down the other, so the two bones interlock and move in two planes (biaxial). The joint between the trapezium and the first metacarpal lets the thumb swing across the palm.

labels.name: Normal hip joint
labels.fn: A healthy hip joint: smooth articular cartilage of even thickness covers the head of the femur and the socket, and a clear joint space separates the two bones.

labels.name: Decreased joint space
labels.fn: In osteoarthritis the articular cartilage wears thin, so the gap between the bone ends narrows. On an X-ray this narrowed joint space is a key sign of cartilage loss.

labels.name: Exposed bone
labels.fn: Where the articular cartilage has worn through, bone grinds on bone. The exposed bone surfaces thicken and can grow spurs, causing pain and stiffness.

labels.name: Worn cartilage
labels.fn: In osteoarthritis the articular cartilage breaks down with years of load, becoming rough, cracked and thin. It has no blood vessels, so it repairs poorly.

follow.q: Why does worn articular cartilage in osteoarthritis heal so poorly?
options: It is replaced every few days
It is made of bone tissue
follow.why: Articular cartilage has no blood supply, so few repair cells and nutrients reach damaged areas, and lost cartilage is not rebuilt. It is not bone, it is not quickly replaced, and synovial fluid feeds cartilage rather than dissolving it.

labels.name: Articular disc
labels.fn: A pad of fibrocartilage inside the temporomandibular joint that splits the joint cavity into upper and lower spaces. It helps the bone surfaces fit and cushions the joint as you chew.

labels.name: Mandibular fossa
labels.fn: The depression in the temporal bone that holds the mandibular condyle, forming the upper surface of the temporomandibular joint.

labels.name: Superior joint cavity
labels.fn: The fluid-filled space above the articular disc, between the disc and the temporal bone. Gliding of the disc and condyle forward, as when you open wide or jut the jaw, happens mainly here.

labels.name: Inferior joint cavity
labels.fn: The fluid-filled space below the articular disc, between the disc and the mandibular condyle. The hinge-like swing of opening and closing the mouth happens mainly here.

labels.name: Mandibular condyle
labels.fn: The rounded knob at the back of the upper end of the mandible. It sits in the mandibular fossa, with the articular disc between them, forming the temporomandibular joint.

labels.name: Articular tubercle
labels.fn: The rounded ridge of the temporal bone just in front of the mandibular fossa. When you open your mouth wide, the condyle and disc glide forward onto it.

labels.name: Articular capsule
labels.fn: The loose connective tissue capsule that encloses the temporomandibular joint, attaching to the temporal bone above and the neck of the mandible below.

labels.name: Clavicle
labels.fn: The collarbone. Its outer end meets the acromion of the scapula at the acromioclavicular joint, holding the shoulder out to the side.

labels.name: Acromioclavicular ligament
labels.fn: The band of connective tissue across the top of the acromioclavicular joint, binding the clavicle to the acromion of the scapula.

labels.name: Acromion of scapula
labels.fn: The flat bony tip of the scapula at the top of the shoulder. It forms a roof over the glenohumeral joint and meets the clavicle.

labels.name: Coracoacromial ligament
labels.fn: A ligament from the coracoid process to the acromion of the scapula. Together they form an arch over the head of the humerus that blocks it from dislocating upward.

labels.name: Glenoid labrum
labels.fn: A ring of fibrocartilage around the rim of the glenoid cavity. It deepens the shallow socket so the head of the humerus sits more securely.

follow.q: Why does the shoulder dislocate more often than the hip?
options: A shallow socket and a loose capsule
It has no articular capsule at all
It is a hinge joint rather than a ball-and-socket joint
Its bone ends carry no articular cartilage
follow.why: The glenoid cavity is small and shallow even with its labrum, and the shoulder's capsule is loose, so the head of the humerus is held mostly by surrounding tendons and muscles. That buys a wide range of motion at the cost of stability. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint with a capsule and articular cartilage, like the hip; the hip is simply deeper and more tightly bound.

labels.name: Subacromial bursa
labels.fn: A fluid-filled sac between the acromion and the tendons that cross the top of the shoulder joint. It lets those tendons slide under the bony roof with little friction.

labels.name: Glenoid cavity
labels.fn: The shallow socket on the side of the scapula that receives the head of the humerus. It is much smaller than the head, which lets the shoulder move freely but makes it less stable.

labels.name: Articular capsule
labels.fn: The loose capsule surrounding the glenohumeral joint. Its slack allows the shoulder's wide range of motion, so the joint relies on the surrounding tendons and muscles for stability.

labels.name: Scapula
labels.fn: The shoulder blade. Its glenoid cavity forms the socket of the shoulder (glenohumeral) joint, and its acromion forms the roof above it.

labels.name: Tendon sheath
labels.fn: A tube of synovial membrane wrapped around a tendon where it rubs on bone. Fluid inside lets the tendon glide; here it surrounds the tendon running in the groove on the front of the humerus.

labels.name: Articular cartilage
labels.fn: The smooth layer of hyaline cartilage that caps the bone ends inside a synovial joint. It has no blood vessels; it lowers friction and absorbs compression as the bones move.

labels.name: Synovial membrane
labels.fn: The thin inner layer of the articular capsule. It lines the joint cavity (but not the articular cartilage) and makes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint and feeds the cartilage.

labels.name: Fibrous membrane
labels.fn: The tough outer layer of the articular capsule, made of dense connective tissue. It attaches to both bones and holds them together; thickened bands of it form ligaments.

labels.name: Head of humerus
labels.fn: The smooth, rounded upper end of the humerus. It is the ball of the shoulder's ball-and-socket joint, resting against the glenoid cavity.

labels.name: Humerus
labels.fn: The bone of the arm. Its rounded head forms the shoulder joint above, and its lower end (trochlea and capitulum) forms the elbow joint below.

hints.why: A heading over the two capsule layers listed under it, not a pointer to one structure; it would give those layers away.

labels.name: Humerus
labels.fn: The bone of the arm. Its rounded head forms the shoulder joint above, and its lower end (trochlea and capitulum) forms the elbow joint below.

labels.name: Fat pad
labels.fn: A pad of fat inside the elbow's articular capsule but outside its synovial membrane. It fills space and cushions the joint as the bones move.

labels.name: Bursa
labels.fn: A small flattened sac of synovial membrane holding a little fluid. It sits where a tendon or skin rubs over bone and reduces the friction between them.

labels.name: Trochlea
labels.fn: The spool-shaped part of the lower humerus that fits into the trochlear notch of the ulna, forming the hinge of the elbow (the humeroulnar joint).

labels.name: Articular cartilage of the trochlear notch
labels.fn: Hyaline cartilage lining the trochlear notch of the ulna, where it glides against the trochlea of the humerus.

labels.name: Olecranon bursa
labels.fn: A subcutaneous bursa between the skin and the olecranon at the point of the elbow. It lets the skin slide over the bone; leaning on the elbow for long periods can inflame it.

labels.name: Articular capsule
labels.fn: The sleeve of connective tissue that encloses a synovial joint and joins its bones. Its outer fibrous membrane holds the bones together, and its inner synovial membrane lines the joint cavity and makes synovial fluid.

labels.name: Synovial membrane
labels.fn: The thin inner layer of the articular capsule. It lines the joint cavity (but not the articular cartilage) and makes synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint and feeds the cartilage.

labels.name: Synovial cavity
labels.fn: The narrow space between the bones of a synovial joint, the feature that defines a synovial joint. It holds a thin film of slippery synovial fluid that cuts friction and feeds the articular cartilage.

labels.name: Articular cartilage of trochlea
labels.fn: Hyaline cartilage covering the trochlea of the humerus, where it glides in the trochlear notch of the ulna.

labels.name: Ulna
labels.fn: The medial forearm bone. Its trochlear notch grips the trochlea of the humerus, forming the hinge of the elbow (the humeroulnar joint).

labels.name: Coronoid process
labels.fn: The projection on the front of the ulna at the lower lip of the trochlear notch. It helps keep the trochlea of the humerus seated in the notch.

labels.name: Humerus
labels.fn: The bone of the arm. Its rounded head forms the shoulder joint above, and its lower end (trochlea and capitulum) forms the elbow joint below.

labels.name: Lateral epicondyle
labels.fn: The bony bump on the outer side of the lower humerus. The radial collateral ligament attaches here.

labels.name: Radius
labels.fn: The lateral forearm bone. Its disc-shaped head is held against the ulna by the annular ligament and turns inside that ring.

labels.name: Annular ligament
labels.fn: A ring-shaped ligament that wraps around the head of the radius and holds it against the ulna at the proximal radioulnar joint, while letting the head turn.

labels.name: Articular capsule
labels.fn: The articular capsule of the elbow, which encloses the humeroulnar, humeroradial and proximal radioulnar joints in one joint cavity.

labels.name: Radial collateral ligament
labels.fn: The ligament on the outer side of the elbow, from the lateral epicondyle of the humerus to the annular ligament. It keeps the elbow from bending sideways toward the inside.

labels.name: Ulna
labels.fn: The medial forearm bone. Its trochlear notch grips the trochlea of the humerus, forming the hinge of the elbow (the humeroulnar joint).

labels.name: Olecranon process
labels.fn: The large hook at the upper end of the ulna that forms the point of the elbow. It fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus when the arm is straight, stopping it there.

labels.name: Articular capsule
labels.fn: The articular capsule of the elbow, which encloses the humeroulnar, humeroradial and proximal radioulnar joints in one joint cavity.

labels.name: Annular ligament
labels.fn: A ring-shaped ligament that wraps around the head of the radius and holds it against the ulna at the proximal radioulnar joint, while letting the head turn.

labels.name: Radius
labels.fn: The lateral forearm bone. Its disc-shaped head is held against the ulna by the annular ligament and turns inside that ring.

labels.name: Ulnar collateral ligament
labels.fn: The strong triangular ligament on the inner side of the elbow, from the medial epicondyle of the humerus to the ulna. It resists forces that would bend the elbow open on the inner side, as in throwing.

labels.name: Ulna
labels.fn: The medial forearm bone. Its trochlear notch grips the trochlea of the humerus, forming the hinge of the elbow (the humeroulnar joint).

labels.name: Coronoid process
labels.fn: The projection on the front of the ulna at the lower lip of the trochlear notch. It helps keep the trochlea of the humerus seated in the notch.

labels.name: Articular cartilage
labels.fn: The smooth layer of hyaline cartilage that caps the bone ends inside a synovial joint. It has no blood vessels; it lowers friction and absorbs compression as the bones move.

labels.name: Acetabular labrum
labels.fn: A lip of fibrocartilage on the rim of the acetabulum. It deepens the socket and grips the head of the femur, adding to the hip's stability.

labels.name: Coxal (hip) bone
labels.fn: The hip bone, formed by the fused ilium, ischium and pubis. Its acetabulum forms the deep socket of the hip joint.

labels.name: Ligament of the head of the femur
labels.fn: A small ligament inside the hip joint, from the acetabulum to the head of the femur. It adds little strength, but it carries a small blood vessel to the head of the femur.

labels.name: Femur
labels.fn: The thigh bone. Its rounded head fits deep in the acetabulum at the hip, and its two condyles rest on the tibia at the knee.

labels.name: Synovial cavity
labels.fn: The narrow space between the bones of a synovial joint, the feature that defines a synovial joint. It holds a thin film of slippery synovial fluid that cuts friction and feeds the articular cartilage.

labels.name: Articular capsule
labels.fn: The thick, strong capsule of the hip joint, reinforced by the iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments. It is much tighter than the shoulder's capsule, trading range of motion for stability.

labels.name: Anterior inferior iliac spine
labels.fn: A bony knob on the front of the ilium, just above the acetabulum. The iliofemoral ligament attaches just below it.

labels.name: Iliofemoral ligament
labels.fn: A strong Y-shaped ligament on the front of the hip, from the ilium to the femur, and the strongest ligament of the hip. It tightens when you stand upright, stopping the thigh from swinging too far back.

labels.name: Greater trochanter
labels.fn: The large bony projection on the upper, outer femur, below the neck. Parts of the hip's capsule ligaments and several thigh muscles attach here.

labels.name: Pubofemoral ligament
labels.fn: The ligament on the front and lower side of the hip joint, from the pubis to the femur. It keeps the thigh from swinging too far out to the side.

labels.name: Ischium
labels.fn: The lower, back part of the hip bone, the part you sit on. The ischiofemoral ligament runs from it to the femur.

labels.name: Iliofemoral ligament
labels.fn: A strong Y-shaped ligament on the front of the hip, from the ilium to the femur, and the strongest ligament of the hip. It tightens when you stand upright, stopping the thigh from swinging too far back.

labels.name: Greater trochanter of femur
labels.fn: The large bony projection on the upper, outer femur, below the neck. Parts of the hip's capsule ligaments and several thigh muscles attach here.

labels.name: Ischiofemoral ligament
labels.fn: The ligament on the back of the hip joint, spiraling from the ischium to the femur. It tightens to stop the thigh turning too far inward.

labels.name: Tibia
labels.fn: The shin bone. Its lower end, including the medial malleolus, forms the roof and inner wall of the ankle (talocrural) joint over the talus.

labels.name: Fibula
labels.fn: The slender lateral bone of the leg. Its lower end, the lateral malleolus, forms the outer wall of the ankle joint.

labels.name: Medial malleolus
labels.fn: The bony bump on the inner side of the ankle, at the lower end of the tibia. It forms the inner wall of the ankle joint and anchors the deltoid ligament.

labels.name: Deltoid ligament
accept: medial collateral ligament of the ankle
labels.fn: The strong fan-shaped ligament on the inner side of the ankle, from the medial malleolus to the talus, calcaneus and navicular. It resists the foot rolling outward.

labels.name: Subtalar joint
labels.fn: The joint between the talus and the calcaneus, just below the ankle joint. Its gliding lets the sole of the foot tilt inward and outward.

labels.name: Fibula
labels.fn: The slender lateral bone of the leg. Its lower end, the lateral malleolus, forms the outer wall of the ankle joint and anchors the ligaments on the outer side of the ankle.

labels.name: Tibia
labels.fn: The shin bone. Its lower end forms the roof of the ankle (talocrural) joint and is bound to the fibula by the inferior tibiofibular ligaments.

labels.name: Posterior and anterior inferior tibiofibular ligaments
labels.fn: Ligaments that bind the lower ends of the tibia and fibula together at the distal tibiofibular joint, keeping the ankle's bony socket snug around the talus.

labels.name: Interosseous membrane
labels.fn: The sheet of dense connective tissue joining the shafts of the tibia and fibula along their length, a syndesmosis. It holds the two bones together.

labels.name: Anterior talofibular ligament
labels.fn: A ligament on the outer side of the ankle, from the lateral malleolus of the fibula forward to the talus. It is the ligament most often torn in an ankle sprain when the foot rolls inward.

follow.q: A runner lands on the edge of the foot and the sole rolls inward. Which ligament is most likely torn?
options: Ligament of the head of the femur
follow.why: Rolling the sole inward stretches the outer side of the ankle, and the anterior talofibular ligament there is the weakest and first to tear. The deltoid ligament is on the inner side and is very strong, the interosseous membrane joins the tibia and fibula higher up, and the ligament of the head of the femur is inside the hip.

labels.name: Calcaneofibular ligament
labels.fn: A ligament on the outer side of the ankle, from the lateral malleolus down and back to the calcaneus. It is the second ligament torn in a severe rolled ankle.

labels.name: Subtalar joint
labels.fn: The joint between the talus and the calcaneus, just below the ankle joint. Its gliding lets the sole of the foot tilt inward and outward.

labels.name: Femur
labels.fn: The thigh bone. Its rounded head fits deep in the acetabulum at the hip, and its two condyles rest on the tibia at the knee.

labels.name: Suprapatellar bursa
labels.fn: The bursa above the patella, between the femur and the large tendon on the front of the thigh. It opens into the knee's joint cavity and lets the tendon glide over the femur.

labels.name: Posterior cruciate ligament
labels.fn: An intracapsular ligament that runs from the back of the tibia up and forward to the femur, crossing the anterior cruciate ligament. It stops the tibia from sliding backward under the femur.

labels.name: Patella
labels.fn: The kneecap, a sesamoid bone inside the tendon on the front of the knee. It protects the front of the joint and gives that tendon a better angle to pull on the tibia.

labels.name: Prepatellar bursa
labels.fn: A subcutaneous bursa between the skin and the patella. It lets the skin slide over the kneecap; kneeling a lot can inflame it.

follow.q: What does a bursa such as the prepatellar bursa do?
options: Holds the patella to the tibia
follow.why: A bursa is a small fluid-filled sac of synovial membrane placed where skin, tendon or ligament rubs over bone, so the surfaces slide with little friction. The patellar ligament holds the patella to the tibia, cartilage cells make articular cartilage, and the anterior cruciate ligament stops the tibia sliding forward.

labels.name: Synovial cavity
labels.fn: The knee's joint cavity, filled with synovial fluid, between the femur, tibia and patella. The fluid lubricates the joint and feeds its articular cartilage.

labels.name: Anterior cruciate ligament
labels.fn: An intracapsular ligament that runs from the front of the tibia up and back to the femur. It stops the tibia from sliding forward under the femur and is the knee ligament most often torn in sports.

labels.name: Infrapatellar fat pad
labels.fn: A pad of fat below the patella, behind the patellar ligament. It fills space inside the capsule and cushions the front of the knee as it moves.

labels.name: Infrapatellar bursa
labels.fn: A bursa below the patella, between the patellar ligament and the tibia. It reduces friction where the ligament passes over bone.

labels.name: Tibia
labels.fn: The shin bone. Its broad, flat condyles form the lower surface of the knee joint, topped by the menisci.

labels.name: Patellar ligament
labels.fn: The strong band from the lower edge of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It carries on the pull of the thigh's large front tendon to the tibia.

labels.name: Femur
labels.fn: The thigh bone. Its rounded head fits deep in the acetabulum at the hip, and its two condyles rest on the tibia at the knee.

labels.name: Articular capsule
