labels.fn: The knee's articular capsule, which encloses the joint between femur, tibia and patella. It is thin at the front, where the patella and its tendon and ligament take its place.

labels.name: Posterior cruciate ligament
labels.fn: An intracapsular ligament that runs from the back of the tibia up and forward to the femur, crossing the anterior cruciate ligament. It stops the tibia from sliding backward under the femur.

labels.name: Lateral meniscus
labels.fn: A C-shaped pad of fibrocartilage on the lateral condyle of the tibia. It deepens the flat tibial surface to fit the rounded femur and absorbs shock.

labels.name: Anterior cruciate ligament
labels.fn: An intracapsular ligament that runs from the front of the tibia up and back to the femur. It stops the tibia from sliding forward under the femur and is the knee ligament most often torn in sports.

follow.q: The anterior cruciate ligament stops which movement of the tibia relative to the femur?
follow.why: The ACL runs from the front of the tibia up and back to the femur, so it goes tight when the tibia slides forward under the femur. The posterior cruciate ligament stops backward sliding, and the collateral ligaments on the sides resist tilting.

labels.name: Tibia
labels.fn: The shin bone. Its broad, flat condyles form the lower surface of the knee joint, topped by the menisci.

labels.name: Suprapatellar bursa
labels.fn: The bursa above the patella, between the femur and the large tendon on the front of the thigh. It opens into the knee's joint cavity and lets the tendon glide over the femur.

labels.name: Patella
labels.fn: The kneecap, a sesamoid bone inside the tendon on the front of the knee. It protects the front of the joint and gives that tendon a better angle to pull on the tibia.

labels.name: Prepatellar bursa
labels.fn: A subcutaneous bursa between the skin and the patella. It lets the skin slide over the kneecap; kneeling a lot can inflame it.

labels.name: Synovial cavity
labels.fn: The knee's joint cavity, filled with synovial fluid, between the femur, tibia and patella. The fluid lubricates the joint and feeds its articular cartilage.

labels.name: Lateral meniscus
labels.fn: A C-shaped pad of fibrocartilage on the lateral condyle of the tibia. It deepens the flat tibial surface to fit the rounded femur and absorbs shock.

labels.name: Infrapatellar fat pad
labels.fn: A pad of fat below the patella, behind the patellar ligament. It fills space inside the capsule and cushions the front of the knee as it moves.

labels.name: Infrapatellar bursa
labels.fn: A bursa below the patella, between the patellar ligament and the tibia. It reduces friction where the ligament passes over bone.

labels.name: Patellar ligament
labels.fn: The strong band from the lower edge of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It carries on the pull of the thigh's large front tendon to the tibia.

labels.name: Anterior cruciate ligament
labels.fn: An intracapsular ligament that runs from the front of the tibia up and back to the femur. It stops the tibia from sliding forward under the femur and is the knee ligament most often torn in sports.

labels.name: Articular cartilage on lateral tibial condyle
accept: articular cartilage of lateral tibial condyle
labels.fn: Hyaline cartilage covering the lateral condyle of the tibia, where the femur bears on it, partly under the lateral meniscus.

labels.name: Articular cartilage on medial tibial condyle
accept: articular cartilage of medial tibial condyle
labels.fn: Hyaline cartilage covering the medial condyle of the tibia, where the femur bears on it, partly under the medial meniscus.

labels.name: Medial meniscus
labels.fn: A C-shaped pad of fibrocartilage on the medial condyle of the tibia. It deepens the tibial surface and absorbs shock, and because it is attached to the tibial collateral ligament it is often torn along with it.

follow.q: Why is the medial meniscus torn more often than the lateral meniscus?
options: It is attached to the tibial collateral ligament
It is made of hyaline cartilage, which is brittle
It lies outside the joint, unprotected by the capsule
It carries no weight at all
follow.why: The medial meniscus is anchored to the tibial collateral ligament, so it cannot shift out of the way and is pulled on when that ligament is stressed. Both menisci are fibrocartilage inside the capsule, and both carry weight between femur and tibia.

labels.name: Lateral meniscus
labels.fn: A C-shaped pad of fibrocartilage on the lateral condyle of the tibia. It deepens the flat tibial surface to fit the rounded femur and absorbs shock.

labels.name: Posterior cruciate ligament
labels.fn: An intracapsular ligament that runs from the back of the tibia up and forward to the femur, crossing the anterior cruciate ligament. It stops the tibia from sliding backward under the femur.

labels.name: Patella
labels.fn: The kneecap, a sesamoid bone inside the tendon on the front of the knee. It protects the front of the joint and gives that tendon a better angle to pull on the tibia.

labels.name: Medial patellar retinaculum
labels.fn: A strip of connective tissue from the inner edge of the patella to the femur and tibia. With the lateral retinaculum it holds the patella in its groove on the femur.

labels.name: Lateral patellar retinaculum
labels.fn: A strip of connective tissue from the outer edge of the patella to the femur and tibia. With the medial retinaculum it holds the patella in its groove on the femur.

labels.name: Tibial collateral ligament
labels.fn: The broad extrinsic ligament on the inner side of the knee, from the femur to the tibia. It resists a blow to the outer knee that would bend the joint inward, and it is attached to the medial meniscus.

labels.name: Fibular collateral ligament
labels.fn: The cord-like extrinsic ligament on the outer side of the knee, from the femur to the head of the fibula. It resists forces that would bend the knee outward.

labels.name: Patellar ligament
labels.fn: The strong band from the lower edge of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It carries on the pull of the thigh's large front tendon to the tibia.

labels.name: Fibula
labels.fn: The slender lateral bone of the leg. It is not part of the knee joint itself, but its head anchors the fibular collateral ligament.

labels.name: Tibia
labels.fn: The shin bone. Its broad, flat condyles form the lower surface of the knee joint, topped by the menisci.

labels.name: Torn tibial (medial) collateral ligament
labels.fn: A blow to the outer side of the knee bends the joint inward and stretches the tibial collateral ligament on the inner side until it tears. This ligament normally holds the inner side of the knee together.

follow.q: A blow strikes the outer side of the knee. Why is the tibial collateral ligament, on the inner side, the one that tears?
options: The inner side is stretched as the knee bends inward
The blow crushes the inner side against the other knee
The inner ligament is much thinner than the outer one
Only the inner side of the knee has a ligament
follow.why: Pushing the knee inward from the outside opens the inner side of the joint, putting the tibial collateral ligament under tension until it tears. The outer side is compressed, not stretched. The knee has a collateral ligament on each side, and the tibial one is broad, not thin.

labels.name: Medial meniscus
labels.fn: Because the medial meniscus is attached to the tibial collateral ligament, the same blow to the outer knee often tears it along with that ligament.

labels.name: Torn anterior cruciate ligament
labels.fn: The same blow can also tear the anterior cruciate ligament, which normally stops the tibia sliding forward under the femur. The torn ACL, torn tibial collateral ligament and torn medial meniscus together are a classic combined knee injury.

labels.name: Flexion
labels.fn: Flexion is a movement in the sagittal plane that decreases the angle between bones. At the shoulder it swings the arm forward and up.

labels.name: Extension
labels.fn: Extension is the sagittal-plane movement that increases the angle between bones, the reverse of flexion. At the shoulder it swings the arm back down and behind the body.

labels.name: Flexion
labels.fn: Flexion at the knee bends the leg, bringing the heel toward the buttock and closing the angle between the leg and the thigh.

labels.name: Extension
labels.fn: Extension is the movement in the sagittal plane that increases the angle between bones, straightening a joint; it is the reverse of flexion and returns a part toward anatomical position.

labels.name: Extension
labels.fn: Extension of the neck lifts the head back up from a forward bend, returning it toward anatomical position.

labels.name: Extension
labels.fn: Tilting the head back past anatomical position is extension carried beyond the anatomical position, called hyperextension.

labels.name: Flexion
labels.fn: Flexion of the neck bends the head forward, bringing the chin toward the chest.

labels.name: Extension
labels.fn: Extension of the vertebral column straightens the trunk back up from a forward bend.

labels.name: Extension
labels.fn: Bending the trunk backward past upright is extension carried beyond anatomical position, called hyperextension.

labels.name: Flexion
labels.fn: Flexion of the vertebral column bends the trunk forward, as in touching your toes.

labels.name: Abduction
labels.fn: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline of the body in the frontal plane, like raising the arm out to the side.

follow.q: Raising your arm straight out to the side from anatomical position happens in which plane?
follow.why: Abduction and adduction swing a limb away from or toward the midline, which is movement in the frontal (coronal) plane. Flexion and extension happen in the sagittal plane, and rotation turns a part in the transverse plane.

labels.name: Adduction
labels.fn: Adduction moves a limb toward the midline of the body, like bringing the raised arm back down to your side.

labels.name: Circumduction
labels.fn: Circumduction moves the end of a limb in a circle so the whole limb traces a cone: flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence. It needs a biaxial or multiaxial joint such as the shoulder.

follow.q: Which of these joints can perform circumduction?
options: Pivot joint between C1 and C2
follow.why: Circumduction strings together movement in two planes, so it needs a joint that moves around at least two axes, such as the ball-and-socket shoulder or hip. A pivot joint only turns around one axis, a hinge only bends and straightens, and a plane joint only glides a little.

labels.name: Rotation
labels.fn: Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis. Shaking your head no turns the atlas around the dens of the axis at the pivot joint between C1 and C2.

labels.name: Lateral rotation
labels.fn: Lateral (external) rotation turns the front of a limb away from the midline, around the limb's own long axis.

follow.q: Standing in anatomical position, you turn your right thigh so the kneecap points outward. What is this movement?
follow.why: Turning the thigh around its own long axis so its front faces away from the midline is lateral rotation. Medial rotation turns it inward, abduction swings the whole limb out to the side without turning it, and eversion tilts the sole of the foot.

labels.name: Medial rotation
labels.fn: Medial (internal) rotation turns the front of a limb toward the midline, around the limb's own long axis.

labels.name: Supination (radius and ulna are parallel)
labels.fn: Supination turns the forearm so the palm faces forward (as in anatomical position) or up. The radius and ulna lie parallel.

follow.q: In which forearm position do the radius and ulna lie parallel?
follow.why: In supination the palm faces forward and the radius lies beside the ulna. Pronation crosses the radius over the ulna, opposition is a thumb movement, and circumduction is a circling movement of a whole limb.

labels.name: Pronation (Radius rotates over ulna)
labels.fn: Pronation turns the forearm so the palm faces back or down. The head of the radius turns in the annular ligament, and the radius crosses over the ulna.

labels.name: Dorsiflexion
labels.fn: Dorsiflexion at the ankle lifts the top of the foot toward the shin, as when you walk on your heels.

follow.q: You walk on your heels with your toes lifted off the floor. Which ankle movement holds the front of your feet up?
follow.why: Lifting the top of the foot toward the shin is dorsiflexion. Plantar flexion points the toes down (standing on tiptoe), and inversion and eversion tilt the sole inward and outward.

labels.name: Plantar flexion
labels.fn: Plantar flexion at the ankle points the toes down and lifts the heel, as when you stand on tiptoe.

labels.name: Inversion
labels.fn: Inversion tilts the sole of the foot inward, toward the midline, mostly at the subtalar and other tarsal joints.

labels.name: Eversion
labels.fn: Eversion tilts the sole of the foot outward, away from the midline, mostly at the subtalar and other tarsal joints.

labels.name: Retraction of mandible
labels.fn: Retraction pulls the mandible straight back, the reverse of protraction, gliding at the temporomandibular joints.

labels.name: Protraction of mandible
labels.fn: Protraction moves the mandible straight forward, jutting the chin out, a gliding movement at the temporomandibular joints.

labels.name: Elevation of mandible
labels.fn: Elevation lifts the mandible, closing the mouth, as when you bite.

labels.name: Depression of mandible
labels.fn: Depression lowers the mandible, opening the mouth.

labels.name: Opposition
labels.fn: Opposition brings the thumb across the palm to touch the fingertips, using the saddle joint at the base of the thumb. It lets you pinch and grip.

hints.why: A letter on the arrow standing for pronation; it would give the movement away.
A letter on the arrow standing for supination; it would give the movement away.

labels.name: Skeletal muscle
labels.fn: A whole skeletal muscle, an organ built from many bundles of muscle fibers plus connective tissue, blood vessels and nerves. Its connective tissue wrappings merge into the tendon that pulls on bone.

labels.name: Epimysium
labels.fn: The dense irregular connective tissue sheath around the whole muscle. It holds the muscle together, separates it from its neighbors, and continues into the tendon so the pull of the fibers reaches the bone.

follow.q: A surgeon repairing a torn muscle stitches the tough outer sheath that is continuous with the tendon. Which layer is being stitched?
follow.why: The epimysium is the dense irregular connective tissue around the whole muscle, and it blends into the tendon. The perimysium and endomysium are deeper, around fascicles and single fibers, and a myofibril is inside a fiber.

labels.name: Perimysium
labels.fn: The middle connective tissue layer, wrapping each fascicle (bundle of fibers). It carries the blood vessels and nerves into the muscle and lets fascicles slide a little past one another.

follow.q: Which connective tissue layer wraps each bundle of muscle fibers?
follow.why: The perimysium surrounds each fascicle. The epimysium wraps the whole muscle, the endomysium wraps each single fiber, the sarcolemma is the fiber's own plasma membrane and the sarcoplasmic reticulum is inside the fiber.

labels.name: Muscle fascicle
labels.fn: A bundle of muscle fibers wrapped in perimysium. Fascicles are the "grain" you see in a cut of meat.

labels.name: Endomysium
labels.fn: The thin layer of areolar connective tissue and reticular fibers around each individual muscle fiber. It holds the capillaries and nerve branches that serve that one fiber.

labels.name: Muscle fiber
labels.fn: One skeletal muscle cell: long, cylindrical, striated and multinucleated, formed when many embryonic cells fused. It runs much of the length of its fascicle.

follow.q: Why does one skeletal muscle fiber have many nuclei?
options: It copies its nucleus many times without dividing as it grows
It formed by the fusion of many embryonic cells
It takes up nuclei from the surrounding connective tissue
Each myofibril carries its own nucleus
follow.why: Each skeletal muscle fiber forms when many embryonic cells fuse, and each contributes a nucleus. The nuclei sit just under the sarcolemma; myofibrils have none of their own.

labels.name: Sarcolemma
accept: plasma membrane of the muscle fiber
labels.fn: The plasma membrane of a muscle fiber. Like any excitable membrane it holds a resting membrane potential and carries action potentials along the fiber.

labels.name: Myofibril
labels.fn: A long rod of contractile proteins packed inside the fiber, running its whole length. Each is a chain of sarcomeres; together the myofibrils fill most of the fiber.

labels.name: Sarcolemma
labels.fn: The muscle fiber's plasma membrane. At intervals it dips inward as T tubules, so a signal on the surface can reach deep into the fiber.

labels.name: Sarcoplasmic reticulum
labels.fn: The muscle fiber's specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a network of tubes wrapped around each myofibril. It stores calcium ions and releases them into the sarcoplasm.

labels.name: Terminal cisternae
labels.fn: The enlarged ends of the sarcoplasmic reticulum on either side of a T tubule. They hold the largest calcium store, right where the signal arrives.

labels.name: T-tubule
labels.fn: A transverse tubule: an inward fold of the sarcolemma that runs across the fiber between the terminal cisternae. It carries the electrical signal from the surface into the fiber's interior.

follow.q: What would a fiber with no T tubules have trouble doing?
options: Storing calcium ions for release into the sarcoplasm
Carrying the surface signal deep into the fiber
Anchoring thin filaments at the ends of the sarcomere
follow.why: T tubules are inward folds of the sarcolemma that bring the action potential into the fiber's interior, next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium storage is the sarcoplasmic reticulum's job, mitochondria make ATP and Z discs anchor thin filaments.

labels.name: Triad
labels.fn: One T tubule with the two terminal cisternae that flank it. This is where the electrical signal in the T tubule is passed to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

follow.q: A triad is made of which structures?
options: Two T tubules on either side of one terminal cisterna
One T tubule and two terminal cisternae
A Z disc with the two I bands that flank it
follow.why: Each T tubule is flanked by a terminal cisterna of the sarcoplasmic reticulum on either side, giving three structures in a row.

labels.name: Muscle fiber
labels.fn: One skeletal muscle cell: long, cylindrical, striated and multinucleated. Its striations come from the lined-up sarcomeres of its myofibrils.

labels.name: Nucleus
labels.fn: One of the many nuclei of a skeletal muscle fiber, pressed just under the sarcolemma at the edge of the cell because myofibrils fill the middle.

labels.name: Mitochondrion
labels.fn: Mitochondria sit between the myofibrils and make ATP by aerobic respiration, the fuel the contractile proteins use.

follow.q: Muscle fibers are packed with mitochondria between their myofibrils. What does that placement suggest?
options: Contractile proteins use a lot of ATP
Mitochondria store the fiber's calcium ions
Mitochondria anchor the thick and thin filaments
They are what make the striations visible
follow.why: Mitochondria make ATP by aerobic respiration, and placing them right beside the myofibrils puts the fuel next to the proteins that spend it. Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and striations come from the filament bands.

labels.name: Sarcolemma
labels.fn: The plasma membrane of the muscle fiber, which carries action potentials along the fiber and into its T tubules.

labels.name: Light I band
labels.fn: The light stripe on the fiber's surface: the I bands of all the myofibrils lined up, where only thin filaments lie.

labels.name: Myofibril
labels.fn: A long rod of contractile proteins running the length of the fiber, built from sarcomeres placed end to end.

labels.name: Dark A band
labels.fn: The dark stripe on the fiber's surface: the A bands of all the myofibrils lined up, the region that holds the thick filaments.

labels.name: Sarcoplasmic reticulum
labels.fn: The network of smooth endoplasmic reticulum that wraps each myofibril. It stores calcium ions and releases them when the fiber is stimulated.

labels.name: Sarcomere
labels.fn: The repeating unit of a myofibril, from one Z disc to the next. It is the smallest unit that contracts, and its bands give the fiber its striations.

follow.q: A sarcomere is the region between which two structures?
options: The two ends of a thick filament
follow.why: A sarcomere runs from one Z disc to the next, with the M line in its center. The A band and H zone lie inside one sarcomere, and a thick filament spans only the A band.

labels.name: Thin (actin) filament
labels.fn: The thinner filaments, made mostly of actin with the regulatory proteins troponin and tropomyosin. They are anchored at the Z discs and reach toward the center of the sarcomere.

labels.name: Thick (myosin) filament
labels.fn: The thicker filaments, made of myosin, anchored at the M line in the center of the sarcomere. Their myosin heads reach out toward the thin filaments.

labels.name: H zone
labels.fn: The central part of the A band where there are thick filaments but no overlapping thin filaments, so it looks lighter than the rest of the A band.

labels.name: Z disc
labels.fn: The protein disc that marks each end of a sarcomere and anchors the thin filaments.

labels.name: Z disc
labels.fn: The protein disc that marks each end of a sarcomere and anchors the thin filaments.

labels.name: I band
labels.fn: The light band on either side of a Z disc, where there are thin filaments but no thick filaments. Each I band is shared by two neighboring sarcomeres.

follow.q: Why does the I band look light?
options: It contains thin filaments but no thick filaments
It contains only thick filaments, which let light through
It holds no filaments at all, only sarcoplasm
It is where the fiber's many nuclei are lined up
follow.why: The I band holds only the thin actin filaments, which let more light through. The dark A band is where the thick myosin filaments lie.

labels.name: A band
labels.fn: The dark band in the middle of the sarcomere that spans the full length of the thick filaments, including where they overlap thin filaments.

labels.name: I band
labels.fn: The light band on either side of a Z disc, where there are thin filaments but no thick filaments. Each I band is shared by two neighboring sarcomeres.

labels.name: M line
labels.fn: The line in the middle of the sarcomere where proteins hold the thick filaments together at their centers.

labels.name: Sarcomere
labels.fn: The repeating contractile unit of a myofibril, running from one Z line to the next.

labels.name: H zone
labels.fn: The central region of the A band that holds thick filaments only, with no overlapping thin filaments.

follow.q: Which part of the sarcomere contains thick filaments but no thin filaments?
follow.why: The H zone is the central part of the A band where thick filaments are not overlapped by thin ones. The rest of the A band has both, and the I band has only thin filaments.

labels.name: M line
labels.fn: The line in the center of the sarcomere where the thick filaments are anchored to one another.

labels.name: Z line
labels.fn: The Z line (Z disc) at each end of the sarcomere, where the thin filaments of neighboring sarcomeres are anchored.

labels.name: Z line
labels.fn: The Z line (Z disc) at each end of the sarcomere, where the thin filaments of neighboring sarcomeres are anchored.

labels.name: Lighter I band
labels.fn: The light band at each end of the sarcomere, containing thin filaments only.

labels.name: Darker A band
labels.fn: The dark band in the middle of the sarcomere, as long as the thick filaments.

labels.name: Lighter I band
labels.fn: The light band at each end of the sarcomere, containing thin filaments only.

labels.name: Portion of a thick filament
labels.fn: A thick filament: a bundle of myosin molecules whose tails form the shaft and whose heads stick out toward the surrounding thin filaments.

labels.name: Portion of a thin filament
labels.fn: A thin filament: two twisted strands of actin with tropomyosin lying along the groove and troponin attached at intervals.

labels.name: Troponin
labels.fn: A small protein complex on the thin filament that binds calcium ions and is attached to tropomyosin. It is the switch that lets tropomyosin move.

labels.name: Actin
labels.fn: The main protein of the thin filament. Each actin subunit has a binding site that a myosin head can attach to.

labels.name: Tropomyosin
labels.fn: A long, thread-like protein that lies along the groove of the actin strand. In a resting muscle it covers the myosin-binding sites on actin.

follow.q: In a resting muscle fiber, what keeps myosin heads from binding actin?
options: Troponin covers the myosin heads until ATP arrives
Tropomyosin covers the binding sites on actin
The M line holds the heads back against the shaft
The Z disc blocks them from reaching the thin filaments
follow.why: Tropomyosin lies along the actin strand over the myosin-binding sites. Troponin holds tropomyosin in place; it does not cover the heads. The M line and Z discs anchor filaments.

labels.name: Head
labels.fn: A myosin head, one of many sticking out from the thick filament. Heads bind actin and split ATP.

labels.name: Actin-binding sites
labels.fn: The spots on each myosin head that attach to the binding sites on actin in the thin filament.

labels.name: Binding site for myosin
labels.fn: The site on each actin subunit where a myosin head can attach. At rest tropomyosin lies over these sites.

labels.name: Actin subunits
labels.fn: The bead-like actin molecules strung together into the thin filament, each carrying one myosin-binding site.

labels.name: ATP-binding site
labels.fn: The pocket on the myosin head that binds ATP and splits it (it acts as an ATPase), supplying the energy the head uses.

follow.q: The myosin head has an ATP-binding site. What does the head do with ATP?
options: Stores it for later release into the sarcoplasm
Splits it and uses the energy to move
Passes it on to the thin filament
Uses it to build new actin subunits
follow.why: The myosin head acts as an ATPase: it splits ATP into ADP and phosphate and uses the released energy to change shape. It does not store ATP or hand it to actin.

labels.name: Tail
labels.fn: The long tail of a myosin molecule. Tails bundle together to form the shaft of the thick filament.

labels.name: Heads
labels.fn: The two heads of one myosin molecule. Each carries an actin-binding site and an ATP-binding site.

labels.name: Myosin molecule
labels.fn: One myosin protein: two twisted tails ending in two heads joined by a flexible hinge. Hundreds of them make one thick filament.

labels.name: Flexible hinge region
labels.fn: The flexible neck between the myosin tail and heads, which lets the heads swing and change angle.

labels.name: Axon terminal
labels.fn: The branching end of the motor neuron's axon as it reaches the muscle. Each branch ends on one muscle fiber.

labels.name: Synaptic end bulb at the neuromuscular junction
labels.fn: The swollen tip of an axon terminal branch that sits in a shallow groove on the muscle fiber at the neuromuscular junction. It holds the vesicles of acetylcholine.

labels.name: Sarcolemma
labels.fn: The muscle fiber's plasma membrane. At the neuromuscular junction it forms the motor end plate.

labels.name: Myofibril of muscle fiber
labels.fn: A contractile rod inside the muscle fiber; the fiber the motor neuron controls is packed with them.

labels.name: Sarcoplasm
labels.fn: The cytoplasm of the muscle fiber, filling the space around the myofibrils.

labels.name: Synaptic end bulb
labels.fn: The swollen tip of an axon terminal branch that sits in a shallow groove on the muscle fiber at the neuromuscular junction. It holds the vesicles of acetylcholine.

labels.name: Synaptic vesicle containing ACh
labels.fn: A small membrane sac in the synaptic end bulb, filled with acetylcholine and waiting to be released.

follow.q: What triggers synaptic vesicles to release acetylcholine?
options: Calcium ions entering the end bulb
Sodium ions leaving the muscle fiber through its receptors
ACh binding the receptors of the end plate
The muscle fiber contracting and pulling on the axon
follow.why: When the action potential reaches the end bulb, voltage-gated calcium channels open and calcium ions flow in, making the vesicles fuse with the membrane. The end plate events come after release.

labels.name: Nerve impulse (action potential)
labels.fn: The action potential traveling down the motor neuron's axon. When it reaches the synaptic end bulb, calcium ions flow in and trigger release of acetylcholine.

labels.name: Sarcolemma
labels.fn: The muscle fiber's plasma membrane. At the neuromuscular junction it forms the motor end plate.

labels.name: Synaptic cleft
labels.fn: The narrow gap between the synaptic end bulb and the motor end plate. Acetylcholine diffuses across it, and acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks it down.

follow.q: A nerve agent blocks the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft. What happens at the end plate?
options: ACh is never released from the synaptic vesicles
ACh lingers, so stimulation lasts too long
The receptors are destroyed by the extra acetylcholine
The end plate stops responding the moment ACh arrives
follow.why: Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft normally clears ACh within milliseconds. When it is blocked, ACh stays in the cleft and keeps opening receptors, so the fiber is stimulated for too long. Release and the receptors themselves are not directly affected.

labels.name: Motor end-plate
labels.fn: The folded region of sarcolemma under the synaptic end bulb, packed with acetylcholine receptors. The folds add surface for more receptors.

follow.q: Why is the sarcolemma folded at the motor end plate?
options: To store acetylcholine until the next action potential
To hold more receptors in a small area
To make ATP for the synaptic end bulb
To slow the diffusion of ACh across the cleft
follow.why: The folds add membrane area, so more acetylcholine receptors fit under the synaptic end bulb and the fiber reliably responds. The fiber does not store ACh or supply ATP to the neuron.

labels.name: ACh
labels.fn: Acetylcholine (ACh), the neurotransmitter motor neurons release onto skeletal muscle. It diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors on the motor end plate.

labels.name: Synaptic vesicle
labels.fn: A small membrane sac in the synaptic end bulb, filled with acetylcholine and waiting to be released.

labels.name: Synaptic cleft
labels.fn: The narrow gap between the synaptic end bulb and the motor end plate. Acetylcholine diffuses across it, and acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks it down.

labels.name: ACh receptor
labels.fn: A nicotinic acetylcholine receptor: a ligand-gated channel in the motor end plate. When ACh binds, it opens and lets sodium ions rush in, depolarizing the end plate.

follow.q: What kind of channel is the acetylcholine receptor on the motor end plate?
options: A voltage-gated potassium channel that repolarizes the membrane
A ligand-gated channel that lets sodium ions in
A pump that moves sodium out using ATP
A gap junction linking the fiber to the neuron
follow.why: The receptor opens when its ligand, ACh, binds, and sodium ions rush in to depolarize the end plate. It is not opened by voltage, is not a pump and does not join the neuron and fiber.

labels.name: Motor end-plate
labels.fn: The folded region of sarcolemma under the synaptic end bulb, packed with acetylcholine receptors. The folds add surface for more receptors.

shown.why: A printed description of a step (release by exocytosis), not a structure to name.
A printed description of a step (ACh opening the receptor channel), not a structure to name.

labels.name: Muscle fiber
labels.fn: One skeletal muscle cell: long, cylindrical, striated and multinucleated. Its striations come from the lined-up sarcomeres of its myofibrils.

follow.q: Which combination identifies skeletal muscle?
options: Striated, short and branched, with one central nucleus
Not striated, spindle shaped, with one central nucleus
Not striated, branched, with many nuclei at the edge
follow.why: Skeletal fibers are long, cylindrical and striated with many nuclei at the edge. Striated, branched fibers with one central nucleus are cardiac; spindle-shaped, nonstriated cells are smooth muscle.

labels.name: Nucleus
labels.fn: One of the many nuclei of a skeletal muscle fiber, pressed just under the sarcolemma at the edge of the cell because myofibrils fill the middle.

labels.name: Mitochondrion
labels.fn: Mitochondria sit between the myofibrils and make ATP by aerobic respiration, the fuel the contractile proteins use.

labels.name: Sarcolemma
labels.fn: The plasma membrane of the muscle fiber, which carries action potentials along the fiber and into its T tubules.

labels.name: Light I band
labels.fn: The light stripe on the fiber's surface: the I bands of all the myofibrils lined up, where only thin filaments lie.

labels.name: Myofibril
labels.fn: A long rod of contractile proteins running the length of the fiber, built from sarcomeres placed end to end.

labels.name: Dark A band
labels.fn: The dark stripe on the fiber's surface: the A bands of all the myofibrils lined up, the region that holds the thick filaments.

labels.name: Sarcoplasmic reticulum
labels.fn: The network of smooth endoplasmic reticulum that wraps each myofibril. It stores calcium ions and releases them when the fiber is stimulated.

labels.name: Sarcomere
labels.fn: The repeating unit of a myofibril, from one Z disc to the next. It is the smallest unit that contracts, and its bands give the fiber its striations.

labels.name: Thin (actin) filament
labels.fn: The thinner filaments, made mostly of actin with the regulatory proteins troponin and tropomyosin. They are anchored at the Z discs and reach toward the center of the sarcomere.

labels.name: Thick (myosin) filament
labels.fn: The thicker filaments, made of myosin, anchored at the M line in the center of the sarcomere. Their myosin heads reach out toward the thin filaments.

labels.name: H zone
labels.fn: The central part of the A band where there are thick filaments but no overlapping thin filaments, so it looks lighter than the rest of the A band.

labels.name: Z disc
labels.fn: The protein disc that marks each end of a sarcomere and anchors the thin filaments.

labels.name: Z disc
labels.fn: The protein disc that marks each end of a sarcomere and anchors the thin filaments.

labels.name: I band
labels.fn: The light band on either side of a Z disc, where there are thin filaments but no thick filaments. Each I band is shared by two neighboring sarcomeres.

labels.name: A band
labels.fn: The dark band in the middle of the sarcomere that spans the full length of the thick filaments, including where they overlap thin filaments.

labels.name: I band
labels.fn: The light band on either side of a Z disc, where there are thin filaments but no thick filaments. Each I band is shared by two neighboring sarcomeres.

labels.name: M line
labels.fn: The line in the middle of the sarcomere where proteins hold the thick filaments together at their centers.

labels.name: Intercalated discs
labels.fn: The dark lines where cardiac muscle fibers join end to end. Desmosomes in them hold the fibers together as they pull, and gap junctions let ions pass so the fibers contract together.

follow.q: Which feature lets cardiac muscle fibers contract as one unit?
options: Gap junctions in the intercalated discs
Many nuclei spread along the edge of each fiber
Dense bodies anchoring the thin filaments
Long, unbranched fibers that run the length of the heart
follow.why: Gap junctions pass ions from fiber to fiber, so an action potential spreads through the whole network. Many peripheral nuclei belong to skeletal fibers, dense bodies to smooth muscle, and cardiac fibers are short and branched.

labels.name: Capillary
labels.fn: The smallest blood vessel, with a wall one cell thick. Heart muscle is threaded with capillaries because it works nonstop and depends on a steady oxygen supply for aerobic respiration.

labels.name: Desmosome
labels.fn: A spot weld in the intercalated disc that keeps neighboring cardiac muscle fibers from pulling apart when they contract.

labels.name: Gap junction
labels.fn: Channels in the intercalated disc that let ions flow from one cardiac muscle fiber to the next, so an action potential spreads and the fibers contract as a unit.

labels.name: Gap junction
labels.fn: Channels in the intercalated disc that let ions flow from one cardiac muscle fiber to the next, so an action potential spreads and the fibers contract as a unit.

labels.name: Nucleus
labels.fn: The nucleus of a cardiac muscle fiber. Most cardiac fibers have one, in the center of the fiber, unlike the many peripheral nuclei of a skeletal fiber.

labels.name: Cardiac muscle fiber
labels.fn: A single cardiac muscle fiber: striated, short and branched, usually with one central nucleus, and joined to its neighbors at intercalated discs.

labels.name: Relaxed muscle cell
labels.fn: A relaxed smooth muscle cell: spindle shaped, with one central nucleus and no striations, because its actin and myosin are not lined up in sarcomeres.

follow.q: Why does smooth muscle lack striations?
options: It has no actin or myosin at all
Its filaments are not arranged in sarcomeres
Its single nucleus hides the filaments from view
It has only thick filaments and no thin ones
follow.why: Smooth muscle has actin and myosin, but they run at angles between dense bodies instead of lining up in repeating sarcomeres, so there are no bands to see.

labels.name: Contracted muscle cell
labels.fn: A contracted smooth muscle cell. Its filaments pull the dense bodies together, so the whole cell shortens and bunches up, twisting like a corkscrew.

labels.name: Intermediate filaments
labels.fn: A network of intermediate filaments running between dense bodies across the smooth muscle cell. It transmits the pull of the thin filaments through the whole cell.

labels.name: Dense bodies
labels.fn: Protein anchors scattered through the smooth muscle cell and attached to the sarcolemma. Thin filaments are tethered to them, so they do the job Z discs do in skeletal muscle.

follow.q: In smooth muscle, which structures do the job that Z discs do in skeletal muscle?
follow.why: Thin filaments are anchored to dense bodies, just as they are to Z discs in a sarcomere. Intermediate filaments link the dense bodies, intercalated discs join cardiac fibers and T tubules carry signals inward.

sets.title: Muscles of the head and neck

labels.name: Epicranial aponeurosis
labels.fn: The flat sheet of tendon across the top of the skull that joins the frontal and occipital bellies of occipitofrontalis. The two bellies pull on it from either end.

labels.name: Occipitofrontalis (frontal belly)
labels.fn: The front belly of occipitofrontalis, over the forehead. Pulling from the epicranial aponeurosis, it raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead.

labels.name: Corrugator supercilii
labels.fn: A small muscle deep to the eyebrow, running from the frontal bone to the skin of the eyebrow. It draws the eyebrows down and together, the frown.

labels.name: Orbicularis oculi
labels.fn: The ring of muscle around each eye. Its circular fibers close the eyelid, gently in a blink or tightly in a squint.

follow.q: The fibers of orbicularis oculi run in a ring around the eye. What does that arrangement let the muscle do?
follow.why: A circular muscle narrows the opening it surrounds, so orbicularis oculi closes the eyelid. Raising the eyebrows and wrinkling the forehead are the frontal belly of occipitofrontalis, and the eyeball is turned by separate muscles inside the orbit.

labels.name: Occipitofrontalis (occipital belly)
labels.fn: The back belly of occipitofrontalis, over the back of the skull. It pulls the scalp and the epicranial aponeurosis backward.

labels.name: Orbicularis oris
labels.fn: The ring of muscle around the mouth, inserting on the skin of the lips. It closes and purses the lips, as in whistling or kissing.

labels.name: Buccinator
labels.fn: The flat muscle forming the wall of the cheek. It presses the cheek against the teeth, which keeps food between the teeth when you chew and lets you blow out air.

follow.q: A trumpet player blows hard with the cheeks held flat against the teeth. Which muscle holds the cheeks in?
follow.why: Buccinator forms the wall of the cheek and presses it against the teeth, which is also how it keeps food between the teeth. Masseter and temporalis close the jaw, and orbicularis oris purses the lips.

labels.name: Lateral pterygoid
labels.fn: A chewing muscle deep to the back part of the mandible, running roughly horizontally from the sphenoid bone to the neck of the mandible and the jaw joint. It pulls the mandible forward, opening the jaw, and moves it side to side for grinding.

labels.name: Temporalis
labels.fn: The fan-shaped chewing muscle over the temple. It runs from the temporal fossa, under the zygomatic arch, to the coronoid process of the mandible, and it closes the jaw and pulls it back.

labels.name: Medial pterygoid
labels.fn: A chewing muscle on the inner face of the back part of the mandible, from the sphenoid bone to the angle of the mandible. It closes the jaw with masseter and helps move it side to side.

labels.name: Masseter
labels.fn: The thick, strong chewing muscle over the angle of the jaw, from the zygomatic arch to the angle of the mandible. It is the prime mover for closing the jaw; you can feel it bulge when you clench your teeth.

follow.q: Which movement do masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid share?
follow.why: All three pull the mandible up toward the skull, closing the jaw for biting. The lateral pterygoid pulls the jaw forward and helps open it, and the infrahyoid muscles lower the hyoid bone.

labels.name: Geniohyoid
labels.fn: A suprahyoid muscle running from the inside of the chin (mandible) to the hyoid bone, just above mylohyoid. It pulls the hyoid bone up and forward.

labels.name: Digastric
labels.fn: A suprahyoid muscle with two bellies joined by a tendon that loops through a sling on the hyoid bone. It raises the hyoid bone and, with the hyoid held still, pulls the mandible down to open the mouth.

follow.q: When the infrahyoid muscles hold the hyoid bone still, what does contraction of digastric do?
options: Pulls the mandible down, opening the mouth
Pulls the mandible up, closing the jaw tightly
Turns the head to the opposite side
follow.why: With its lower attachment fixed, digastric pulls on the mandible, lowering it to open the mouth. Closing the jaw is the work of masseter and temporalis, and turning the head is sternocleidomastoid.

labels.name: Inferior edge of mandible
labels.fn: The lower border of the mandible, the jawbone. Several suprahyoid muscles attach along its inner surface.

labels.name: Mylohyoid
labels.fn: A flat suprahyoid muscle stretched between the two sides of the mandible, forming the muscular floor of the mouth. It raises the floor of the mouth and the hyoid bone.

labels.name: Styloglossus
labels.fn: A small muscle running from the styloid process of the temporal bone forward into the side of the tongue. It pulls the tongue up and back.

labels.name: Stylohyoid
labels.fn: A slender suprahyoid muscle from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the hyoid bone. It pulls the hyoid bone up and back.

labels.name: Hyoid bone
labels.fn: The U-shaped bone in the front of the neck, below the mandible, that touches no other bone. The suprahyoid muscles attach to it from above and the infrahyoid muscles from below.

labels.name: Thyrohyoid
labels.fn: A short infrahyoid muscle from the large cartilage at the front of the throat (the Adam's apple) up to the hyoid bone. It pulls the hyoid bone down, or pulls that cartilage up toward the hyoid.

labels.name: Omohyoid
labels.fn: A long, thin infrahyoid muscle with two bellies that runs from the scapula to the hyoid bone. It pulls the hyoid bone down.

labels.name: Sternohyoid
labels.fn: An infrahyoid strap muscle from the sternum and clavicle up to the hyoid bone. It pulls the hyoid bone down.

labels.name: Sternothyroid
labels.fn: An infrahyoid strap muscle deep to sternohyoid, from the sternum to the large cartilage at the front of the throat (the Adam's apple). It pulls that cartilage down.

labels.name: Right and left clavicles
labels.fn: The collarbones, the S-shaped bones running from the sternum to the scapula. The sternocleidomastoid and the infrahyoid strap muscles attach near their inner ends.

labels.name: Sternum
labels.fn: The breastbone, the flat bone in the front of the chest to which the ribs attach through cartilage. Neck and chest muscles anchor to it.

labels.name: Scapula
labels.fn: The shoulder blade, a flat triangular bone on the back of the rib cage. Many muscles of the neck, back and arm attach to it.

hints.why: A group heading printed over the list of suprahyoid muscles; it names the group the muscles below it belong to, so it is masked in the quiz.
A group heading printed over the list of infrahyoid muscles; it names the group the muscles below it belong to, so it is masked in the quiz.

labels.name: Suboccipital muscles
labels.fn: Small, deep muscles between the base of the skull and the first two cervical vertebrae. They tilt and turn the head in fine adjustments.

labels.name: Sternocleidomastoid
labels.fn: The long diagonal neck muscle from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process behind the ear. One side turns the head to the opposite side; both together flex the neck.

follow.q: The right sternocleidomastoid contracts on its own. Which way does the face turn?
follow.why: The muscle runs from the sternum and clavicle in front to the mastoid process behind the ear. Pulling the right mastoid down and forward turns the face to the left, the opposite side.

labels.name: Acromion process of scapula
labels.fn: The flat bony tip of the shoulder, where the scapula meets the clavicle. It is an attachment point for muscles that cross the top of the shoulder.

labels.name: 1st thoracic vertebrae
labels.fn: T1, the first thoracic vertebra, just below the seventh cervical vertebra at the base of the neck. Deep neck and back muscles attach to its processes.

labels.name: Scalenes
labels.fn: Three muscles (anterior, middle and posterior) on the side of the neck, from the cervical vertebrae to the first two ribs. They bend the neck to the side and raise the upper ribs in a deep breath.

labels.name: Sternocleidomastoid
labels.fn: The long diagonal neck muscle from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process behind the ear. One side turns the head to the opposite side; both together flex the neck.

labels.name: Splenius capitis
labels.fn: A deep back muscle of the neck, from the lower cervical and upper thoracic spinous processes to the mastoid process and skull. Both sides extend the head; one side turns the head to the same side.

labels.name: Splenius
labels.fn: The splenius muscles, a bandage-like sheet in the back of the neck (splenius capitis and splenius cervicis). They extend and turn the head and neck.

labels.name: Splenius cervicis
labels.fn: The lower part of the splenius group, from the upper thoracic spinous processes to the upper cervical transverse processes. It extends and turns the neck.

labels.name: Medial scalene
labels.fn: The middle scalene, the largest of the three scalenes, from the cervical transverse processes to the first rib. It bends the neck to the side and raises the first rib when you breathe hard.

labels.name: Anterior scalene
labels.fn: The front scalene, from the cervical transverse processes to the first rib. It bends the neck forward and to the side and raises the first rib in a deep breath.

labels.name: Clavicle
labels.fn: The collarbone, the S-shaped bone from the sternum to the acromion of the scapula. Neck, chest and shoulder muscles attach to it.

labels.name: Longissimus capitis
labels.fn: The top part of the longissimus column of erector spinae, reaching the mastoid process. It extends the head and turns it to the same side.

labels.name: Semispinalis capitis (joined with deep spinalis capitis)
labels.fn: A deep (transversospinales) back muscle running from the transverse processes up to the back of the skull. It extends the head and neck.

labels.name: Iliocostalis cervicis
labels.fn: The top part of the iliocostalis column, the outer column of erector spinae, from the upper ribs to the cervical vertebrae. It extends the neck and bends it to the side.

labels.name: Semispinalis cervicis
labels.fn: The neck part of semispinalis, spanning several vertebrae from transverse processes to spinous processes. It extends the neck and turns it to the opposite side.

labels.name: Iliocostalis thoracis
labels.fn: The middle part of the iliocostalis column, running between the ribs. It extends the back and bends it to the side.

labels.name: Longissimus thoracis
labels.fn: The main part of longissimus, the middle column of erector spinae, from the sacrum and lumbar vertebrae to the thoracic vertebrae and ribs. It extends the back and bends it to the side.

labels.name: Longissimus cervicis
labels.fn: The neck part of longissimus, from the upper thoracic to the cervical transverse processes. It extends the neck and bends it to the side.

labels.name: Iliocostalis lumborum
labels.fn: The lowest part of the iliocostalis column (the outer column of erector spinae), from the iliac crest and sacrum to the lower ribs. It extends the lower back and bends it to the side.

follow.q: Iliocostalis, longissimus and spinalis together form which group?
follow.why: The three columns running up either side of the spine are the erector spinae, which extend the back. The rotatores are small deep muscles, the scalenes are in the neck, and the suboccipital muscles lie under the skull.

labels.name: Spinalis thoracis
labels.fn: The chest part of spinalis, the column of erector spinae closest to the midline, joining spinous processes. It extends the back.

labels.name: Transverse processes of vertebrae
labels.fn: The bony projections sticking out sideways from each vertebra. Deep back muscles such as the rotatores and intertransversarii attach to them and use them as levers.

labels.name: Semispinalis thoracis
labels.fn: The chest part of semispinalis, from thoracic transverse processes to spinous processes several levels higher. It extends the back and turns it to the opposite side.

labels.name: Rotator brevis
labels.fn: One of the rotatores, tiny deep back muscles; this short one runs from a transverse process to the spinous process of the vertebra just above. They steady and turn the spine.

labels.name: Rotator longus
labels.fn: One of the rotatores; the long rotator skips one vertebra, from a transverse process to the spinous process two levels up. It helps steady and turn the spine.

labels.name: Multifidus
labels.fn: A deep back muscle made of many short bundles, each spanning a few vertebrae from transverse to spinous processes, thickest in the lower back. It stabilizes the vertebrae as the spine moves.

labels.name: Interspinales
labels.fn: Short muscles joining the spinous processes of neighboring vertebrae. They help extend the spine.

labels.name: Short rotator
labels.fn: A short rotator muscle (one of the rotatores), running from a transverse process to the vertebra just above. It steadies the spine and helps it turn.

labels.name: Intertransversarii
labels.fn: Short muscles between the transverse processes of neighboring vertebrae. They bend the spine to the side and steady it.

labels.name: External oblique
labels.fn: The outermost flat abdominal muscle, with fibers running down and forward from the lower ribs to the iliac crest and the linea alba. It compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk and turns it to the opposite side.

labels.name: Rectus sheath
labels.fn: The sleeve of tendon (the aponeuroses of the three flat abdominal muscles) that wraps around rectus abdominis. The sheaths of the two sides meet at the linea alba.

labels.name: Transversus abdominis
labels.fn: The deepest flat abdominal muscle, with fibers running horizontally around the abdomen like a belt. It compresses the abdomen and steadies the trunk.

follow.q: Which abdominal muscle has fibers running horizontally around the waist like a belt?
options: Quadratus lumborum in the back wall
follow.why: Transversus abdominis, the deepest layer, runs horizontally and compresses the abdomen. Rectus abdominis runs vertically, and the obliques run diagonally at right angles to each other.

labels.name: External oblique
labels.fn: The outermost flat abdominal muscle, with fibers running down and forward from the lower ribs to the iliac crest and the linea alba. It compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk and turns it to the opposite side.

follow.q: Why do the external and internal obliques have fibers at right angles to each other?
options: So that each one can move only a single rib at a time
Crossed layers make a stronger wall and turn the trunk both ways
So that neither of them can compress the abdomen at all
Because one is smooth muscle and the other one is skeletal
follow.why: Layers crossing at angles, like plywood, make a strong wall, and each oblique turns the trunk a different way, so working together they twist and flex it. Both are skeletal muscle and both compress the abdomen.

labels.name: Linea alba (of the rectus sheath)
labels.fn: The "white line", a band of tendon down the midline of the abdomen from the sternum to the pubis, where the aponeuroses of the flat abdominal muscles on each side meet.

labels.name: Rectus abdominis (enclosed within rectus sheath)
labels.fn: The vertical strap muscle on each side of the midline, from the pubis up to the lower ribs and sternum, divided by tendinous intersections into segments. It flexes the trunk and compresses the abdomen.

labels.name: Tendinous intersections (between the anterior segments of the rectus abdominis)
labels.fn: Bands of tendon that cross rectus abdominis and divide it into segments, giving the "six-pack" look in a lean person.

labels.name: Rectus abdominis
labels.fn: The vertical strap muscle on each side of the midline, from the pubis up to the lower ribs and sternum, divided by tendinous intersections into segments. It flexes the trunk and compresses the abdomen.

labels.name: Aponeurosis of internal oblique
labels.fn: The flat sheet of tendon that ends internal oblique toward the midline. It splits around rectus abdominis to help form the rectus sheath.

labels.name: Internal oblique
labels.fn: The middle flat abdominal muscle, fibers running up and forward, at right angles to external oblique. It compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk and turns it to the same side.

labels.name: Quadratus lumborum
labels.fn: A square muscle of the back wall of the abdomen, from the iliac crest to the 12th rib and the lumbar vertebrae. It bends the trunk to the side and holds the 12th rib down.

labels.name: Ilia of hip bones
labels.fn: The ilia, the broad upper parts of the two hip bones that form the flared sides of the pelvis. Their crests anchor the abdominal muscles.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone at the base of the spine, made of five fused vertebrae, that joins the two hip bones. Deep back muscles anchor to it.

labels.name: Central tendon of diaphragm
labels.fn: The flat, leaf-shaped sheet of tendon in the middle of the dome of the diaphragm, where all its muscle fibers insert. When the fibers contract they pull the central tendon down, flattening the dome.

labels.name: Sternum
labels.fn: The breastbone, the flat bone in the front of the chest to which the ribs attach through cartilage. Neck and chest muscles anchor to it.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle between the thoracic and abdominal cavities, from the lower ribs, sternum and lumbar vertebrae to the central tendon. It is the main muscle for breathing in at rest: contracting flattens the dome and enlarges the thoracic cavity.

follow.q: When the diaphragm contracts, what happens to the thoracic cavity?
options: It enlarges as the dome flattens
It shrinks as the dome rises into the chest
Its size does not change at all
It shrinks as the ribs are pulled down
follow.why: Contracting fibers pull the central tendon down, flattening the dome and making the thoracic cavity taller, which draws air in. Relaxing lets the dome rise again for a quiet breath out.

labels.name: 12th (floating) ribs
labels.fn: The 12th ribs, the lowest pair, called floating ribs because their front ends do not reach the sternum. Quadratus lumborum and the diaphragm attach near them.

labels.name: Left quadratus lumborum
labels.fn: The square muscle of the back wall of the abdomen, from the iliac crest to the 12th rib and lumbar vertebrae. It bends the trunk to the side and holds the 12th rib down in a breath.

labels.name: Vertebrae
labels.fn: The bones of the spine. The diaphragm anchors to the lumbar vertebrae through two tendinous legs.

labels.name: Clavicle
labels.fn: The collarbone, the S-shaped bone from the sternum to the acromion of the scapula. Neck, chest and shoulder muscles attach to it.

labels.name: Ribs
labels.fn: The curved bones of the rib cage. The intercostal muscles fill the spaces between neighboring ribs and move them in breathing.

labels.name: Innermost intercostal
labels.fn: The deepest layer of intercostal muscle, lying just inside the internal intercostals with fibers in the same direction. It helps the internal intercostals pull the ribs down in a forced breath out.

labels.name: Internal intercostal
labels.fn: The middle layer of intercostal muscle, fibers running down and back from one rib to the rib below, at right angles to the external intercostals. They pull the ribs down in a forced breath out.

labels.name: Sternum
labels.fn: The breastbone, the flat bone in the front of the chest to which the ribs attach through cartilage. Neck and chest muscles anchor to it.

labels.name: External intercostals
labels.fn: The outer layer of muscle between the ribs, fibers running down and forward from each rib to the one below. They raise the ribs to enlarge the chest when you breathe in.

labels.name: External intercostal
labels.fn: The outer intercostal layer, with fibers running down and forward from one rib to the next. It lifts the ribs to widen the chest when you breathe in.

follow.q: Which muscles lift the ribs when you breathe in?
follow.why: The external intercostals raise the ribs and widen the chest during a breath in. The internal and innermost intercostals, and the abdominal muscles, pull the ribs down in a forced breath out.

labels.name: Internal intercostal
labels.fn: The middle layer of intercostal muscle, fibers running down and back from one rib to the rib below, at right angles to the external intercostals. They pull the ribs down in a forced breath out.

labels.name: Pubic crest
labels.fn: The rough upper edge of the pubis at the front of the pelvis, where rectus abdominis attaches and the pelvic floor begins.

labels.name: Pubococcygeus
labels.fn: The front part of levator ani, running from the pubis back to the coccyx around the openings in the pelvic floor. It supports the pelvic organs and helps close those openings.

labels.name: Levator ani
labels.fn: The broad funnel of muscle that makes up most of the pelvic floor, formed by pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus. It supports the pelvic organs and resists the pressure pushed down on them when you cough or strain.

follow.q: A person coughs hard. Which muscle keeps the pressure from pushing the pelvic organs down?
follow.why: Levator ani forms most of the pelvic floor and tightens against the rise in abdominal pressure. Transversus abdominis and the diaphragm raise that pressure from above and around, and quadratus lumborum lies in the back wall.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone at the base of the spine, made of five fused vertebrae, that joins the two hip bones. Deep back muscles anchor to it.

labels.name: Iliococcygeus
labels.fn: The back part of levator ani, running from the side wall of the pelvis to the coccyx. It supports the pelvic organs.

labels.name: Iliac crests
labels.fn: The curved upper rims of the ilia, which you feel as the top of your hips. Abdominal and back muscles attach along them.

sets.title: Muscles of the shoulder and upper limb

labels.name: Deltoid (cut)
labels.fn: The deltoid, cut and folded back here to show the muscles beneath. It caps the shoulder and is the prime mover for abducting the arm.

labels.name: Coracoid process of scapula
labels.fn: The hook-like projection on the front of the scapula, below the clavicle. Pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps brachii attach to it.

labels.name: Subclavius
labels.fn: A small muscle under the clavicle, from the first rib to the clavicle. It pulls the clavicle down and forward and steadies it.

labels.name: Pectoralis major (cut)
labels.fn: Pectoralis major, cut here to show the deeper chest muscles. It flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

labels.name: Acromion process of scapula
labels.fn: The flat bony tip of the shoulder, where the scapula meets the clavicle. It is an attachment point for muscles that cross the top of the shoulder.

labels.name: Rhomboid minor
labels.fn: The upper of the two rhomboids, from the lower cervical spinous processes to the medial border of the scapula. It retracts the scapula toward the spine and rotates it downward.

labels.name: Scapula
labels.fn: The shoulder blade, a flat triangular bone on the back of the rib cage. Many muscles of the neck, back and arm attach to it.

labels.name: Pectoralis minor
labels.fn: A thin chest muscle beneath pectoralis major, from the 3rd to 5th ribs to the coracoid process. It pulls the scapula forward and down.

labels.name: Rhomboid major
labels.fn: The larger, lower rhomboid, from the upper thoracic spinous processes to the medial border of the scapula. It retracts the scapula and rotates it downward.

labels.name: Sternum
labels.fn: The breastbone, the flat bone in the front of the chest to which the ribs attach through cartilage. Neck and chest muscles anchor to it.

labels.name: Serratus anterior
labels.fn: The saw-toothed muscle on the side of the chest, from the upper eight or nine ribs to the medial border of the scapula. It pulls the scapula forward around the rib cage, as in a punch, and rotates it upward.

follow.q: A boxer throws a punch and the scapula slides forward around the rib cage. Which muscle is the prime mover?
follow.why: Serratus anterior pulls the scapula forward (protraction) around the ribs. The rhomboids and trapezius pull it back toward the spine, and latissimus dorsi moves the humerus.

labels.name: Deltoid
labels.fn: The thick, triangular muscle that caps the shoulder, from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. It is the prime mover for abducting the arm.

labels.name: Trapezius
labels.fn: The large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck, from the skull and the cervical and thoracic spinous processes to the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula. It elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula.

labels.name: Pectoralis major
labels.fn: The large fan-shaped chest muscle, from the clavicle, sternum and rib cartilages to the humerus. It flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

labels.name: Deltoid
labels.fn: The thick, triangular muscle that caps the shoulder, from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. It is the prime mover for abducting the arm.

labels.name: Latissimus dorsi
labels.fn: The broad, flat muscle of the lower back, from the lower thoracic and lumbar spinous processes and the iliac crest to the humerus. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

labels.name: Teres minor
labels.fn: A rotator cuff muscle along the lower border of the scapula, from the lateral border to the greater tubercle of the humerus. It laterally rotates the arm and holds the humeral head in its socket.

labels.name: Supraspinatus
labels.fn: The rotator cuff muscle above the spine of the scapula, in the supraspinous fossa, inserting on the greater tubercle. It starts abduction of the arm and helps hold the humeral head in the glenoid cavity.

labels.name: Deltoid (cut)
labels.fn: The deltoid, cut and folded back here to show the muscles beneath. It caps the shoulder and is the prime mover for abducting the arm.

labels.name: Spine of scapula
labels.fn: The raised ridge across the back of the scapula, ending in the acromion. It divides the supraspinous from the infraspinous fossa and anchors trapezius and the deltoid.

labels.name: Coracoid process of scapula
labels.fn: The hook-like projection on the front of the scapula, below the clavicle. Pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps brachii attach to it.

labels.name: Deltoid (cut)
labels.fn: The thick, triangular muscle that caps the shoulder, from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. It is the prime mover for abducting the arm.

labels.name: Infraspinatus
labels.fn: The rotator cuff muscle below the spine of the scapula, in the infraspinous fossa, inserting on the greater tubercle. It laterally rotates the arm and holds the humeral head in its socket.

labels.name: Pectoralis major (cut)
labels.fn: Pectoralis major, cut here to show the deeper chest muscles. It flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

labels.name: Humerus
labels.fn: The bone of the arm, from the shoulder to the elbow. Shoulder muscles insert on it and muscles that move the forearm arise from it.

labels.name: Subscapularis
labels.fn: The rotator cuff muscle on the front surface of the scapula (the subscapular fossa), inserting on the lesser tubercle of the humerus. It medially rotates the arm and holds the humeral head in its socket.

follow.q: Which of these muscles is NOT part of the rotator cuff?
follow.why: The rotator cuff is supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis, whose tendons wrap the humeral head. Teres major also runs from the scapula to the humerus but inserts on the front of the shaft and does not hold the joint together.

labels.name: Teres major
labels.fn: A thick muscle from the lower angle of the scapula to the front of the humerus, next to latissimus dorsi. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm. It is not part of the rotator cuff.

labels.name: Latissimus dorsi (near its origin)
labels.fn: The broad, flat muscle of the lower back, from the lower thoracic and lumbar spinous processes and the iliac crest to the humerus. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

labels.name: Teres major
labels.fn: A thick muscle from the lower angle of the scapula to the front of the humerus, next to latissimus dorsi. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm. It is not part of the rotator cuff.

labels.name: Triceps brachii: long head
labels.fn: The long head of triceps brachii, arising from the scapula just below the glenoid cavity. It extends the elbow and, because it crosses the shoulder, also helps extend the arm.

labels.name: Serratus anterior
labels.fn: The saw-toothed muscle on the side of the chest, from the upper eight or nine ribs to the medial border of the scapula. It pulls the scapula forward around the rib cage, as in a punch, and rotates it upward.

labels.name: Triceps brachii: lateral head
labels.fn: The lateral head of triceps brachii, arising from the back of the humerus. It extends the elbow.

labels.name: Biceps brachii (short head)
labels.fn: The short head of biceps brachii, arising from the coracoid process. The biceps flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm.

labels.name: Triceps brachii (lateral head)
labels.fn: The lateral head of triceps brachii, arising from the back of the humerus. It extends the elbow.

labels.name: Biceps brachii (long head)
labels.fn: The long head of biceps brachii, whose tendon arises above the glenoid cavity and runs through the groove on the humerus. The biceps flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm.

labels.name: Triceps brachii (long head)
labels.fn: The long head of triceps brachii, arising from the scapula just below the glenoid cavity. It extends the elbow and, because it crosses the shoulder, also helps extend the arm.

labels.name: Brachialis
labels.fn: The muscle beneath biceps brachii on the front of the arm, from the humerus to the ulna. It is the prime mover for flexing the elbow, whatever the forearm's position.

labels.name: Triceps brachii
labels.fn: The three-headed muscle on the back of the arm, from the scapula and humerus to the olecranon of the ulna. It is the prime mover for extending the elbow.

labels.name: Biceps brachii
labels.fn: The two-headed muscle on the front of the arm, from the scapula to the radius. It flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm, turning the palm up.

labels.name: Brachioradialis
labels.fn: The forearm muscle on the thumb side, from the lower humerus to the lower end of the radius. It flexes the elbow, working best with the forearm halfway between palm up and palm down.

follow.q: Biceps brachii, brachialis and brachioradialis all do which movement?
follow.why: All three cross the front of the elbow and flex it. Triceps brachii extends the elbow, pronator teres and pronator quadratus pronate, and the extensors on the back of the forearm extend the wrist.

labels.name: Extensor carpi radialis longus
labels.fn: A muscle on the thumb side of the back of the forearm, from the lateral humerus to the second metacarpal. It extends the wrist and abducts the hand.

labels.name: Extensor carpi radialis brevis
labels.fn: The shorter partner of extensor carpi radialis longus, from the lateral epicondyle to the third metacarpal. It extends the wrist and abducts the hand.

labels.name: Lateral epicondyle of humerus
labels.fn: The bony bump on the outer side of the lower humerus. Most muscles that extend the wrist and fingers arise from it, through a shared tendon.

labels.name: Pronator teres
labels.fn: A short muscle across the front of the upper forearm, from the medial epicondyle to the radius. It pronates the forearm (turns the palm down) and helps flex the elbow.

labels.name: Abductor pollicis longus
labels.fn: A deep muscle of the back of the forearm, from the radius and ulna to the base of the thumb's metacarpal. It abducts the thumb and helps abduct the hand.

labels.name: Flexor carpi radialis
labels.fn: A superficial muscle on the front of the forearm, from the medial epicondyle to the second and third metacarpals. It flexes the wrist and abducts the hand.

labels.name: Extensor pollicis brevis
labels.fn: A deep forearm muscle on the back of the forearm, from the radius to the thumb's first phalanx. It extends the thumb.

labels.name: Anconeus
labels.fn: A small triangular muscle behind the elbow, from the lateral epicondyle to the ulna. It helps triceps brachii extend the elbow.

labels.name: Extensor pollicis longus
labels.fn: A deep muscle of the back of the forearm, from the ulna to the tip of the thumb. It extends the thumb.

labels.name: Palmaris longus
labels.fn: A slender muscle on the front of the forearm with a long tendon to the palm; it is missing in some people. It helps flex the wrist.

labels.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
labels.fn: A muscle on the little-finger side of the back of the forearm, from the lateral epicondyle and ulna to the fifth metacarpal. It extends the wrist and adducts the hand.

labels.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
labels.fn: A superficial muscle on the little-finger side of the front of the forearm, from the medial epicondyle and ulna to the pisiform and fifth metacarpal. It flexes the wrist and adducts the hand.

labels.name: Extensor digitorum
labels.fn: The main extensor of the fingers, in the middle of the back of the forearm, from the lateral epicondyle to the four fingers. It extends the fingers and helps extend the wrist.

labels.name: Flexor digitorum superficialis
labels.fn: The middle-layer flexor of the front of the forearm, sending tendons to the middle phalanges of the four fingers. It flexes the fingers and the wrist.

labels.name: Extensor digiti minimi
labels.fn: A slender muscle beside extensor digitorum that extends the little finger.

labels.name: Lateral epicondyle of humerus
labels.fn: The bony bump on the outer side of the lower humerus. Most muscles that extend the wrist and fingers arise from it, through a shared tendon.

labels.name: Medial epicondyle of humerus
labels.fn: The bony bump on the inner side of the lower humerus. Most muscles that flex the wrist and fingers, and pronator teres, arise from it.

labels.name: Supinator
labels.fn: A deep muscle wrapped around the upper radius, from the lateral epicondyle and ulna. It supinates the forearm (turns the palm up).

labels.name: Flexor pollicis longus
labels.fn: A deep flexor of the front of the forearm, from the radius to the tip of the thumb. It flexes the thumb.

labels.name: Abductor pollicis longus
labels.fn: A deep muscle of the back of the forearm, from the radius and ulna to the base of the thumb's metacarpal. It abducts the thumb and helps abduct the hand.

labels.name: Brachialis (cut)
labels.fn: Brachialis, cut here to show the deep forearm. It runs from the humerus to the ulna and flexes the elbow.

labels.name: Medial epicondyle of humerus
labels.fn: The bony bump on the inner side of the lower humerus. Most muscles that flex the wrist and fingers, and pronator teres, arise from it.

labels.name: Pronator quadratus
labels.fn: A square muscle across the front of the lower forearm, from the ulna to the radius. It is the main pronator, turning the palm down.

follow.q: You turn a key to the left with your right hand, palm turning down. Which muscles do the turning?
options: Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris
follow.why: Turning the palm down is pronation, done by pronator quadratus and pronator teres. Supinator and biceps brachii turn the palm up, the carpi ulnaris muscles move the wrist, and brachialis and anconeus move the elbow.

labels.name: Extensor pollicis longus
labels.fn: A deep muscle of the back of the forearm, from the ulna to the tip of the thumb. It extends the thumb.

labels.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
labels.fn: The deepest finger flexor, from the ulna to the tips (distal phalanges) of the four fingers. It flexes the fingers, including the fingertip joints.

labels.name: Flexor digitorum profundus
labels.fn: The deepest finger flexor, from the ulna to the tips (distal phalanges) of the four fingers. It flexes the fingers, including the fingertip joints.

labels.name: Extensor pollicis brevis
labels.fn: A deep forearm muscle on the back of the forearm, from the radius to the thumb's first phalanx. It extends the thumb.

labels.name: Flexor retinaculum (cut)
labels.fn: A strong band across the front of the wrist, cut here, that holds the flexor tendons in place. It forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.

labels.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
labels.fn: A superficial muscle on the little-finger side of the front of the forearm, from the medial epicondyle and ulna to the pisiform and fifth metacarpal. It flexes the wrist and adducts the hand.

labels.name: Extensor indicis
labels.fn: A deep muscle on the back of the forearm, from the ulna to the index finger. It extends the index finger, as in pointing.

labels.name: Extensor retinaculum
labels.fn: A band across the back of the wrist that holds the extensor tendons against the bones so they do not bowstring when the wrist bends back.

labels.name: Opponens pollicis
labels.fn: A thenar muscle in the base of the thumb, from the carpals to the thumb's metacarpal. It pulls the thumb across the palm to touch the fingertips (opposition).

follow.q: Touching the tip of the thumb to the little fingertip uses which movement of the thumb?
follow.why: Bringing the thumb across the palm to meet a fingertip is opposition, done by opponens pollicis. Abduction and adduction move the thumb away from or toward the palm, and extension straightens it.

labels.name: Abductor digiti minimi
labels.fn: A hypothenar muscle along the little-finger edge of the palm. It abducts the little finger.

labels.name: Abductor pollicis brevis
labels.fn: A thenar muscle in the ball of the thumb, from the carpals to the thumb's first phalanx. It abducts the thumb, moving it away from the palm.

labels.name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis
labels.fn: A hypothenar muscle along the little-finger edge of the palm. It flexes the little finger.

labels.name: Pisometacarpal ligament
labels.fn: A ligament from the pisiform to the fifth metacarpal. It carries the pull of flexor carpi ulnaris on to the metacarpal.

labels.name: Flexor pollicis brevis
labels.fn: A thenar muscle in the ball of the thumb. It flexes the thumb.

labels.name: Opponens digiti minimi
labels.fn: A hypothenar muscle from the hamate to the fifth metacarpal. It draws the little finger toward the thumb, cupping the palm.

labels.name: Adductor pollicis
labels.fn: A fan-shaped muscle deep in the palm, from the metacarpals to the thumb. It adducts the thumb, pulling it toward the palm, as in gripping.

labels.name: Lumbricalis muscles
labels.fn: The lumbricals, four small worm-like muscles attached to the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus. They flex the knuckles while extending the finger joints beyond them.

labels.name: Palmar interossei muscles
labels.fn: Muscles between the metacarpals, on the palm side. They adduct the fingers, pulling them together toward the middle finger.

labels.name: Dorsal interossei muscles
labels.fn: Muscles between the metacarpals, on the back of the hand. They abduct the fingers, spreading them apart.

sets.title: Muscles of the hip and lower limb

labels.name: Quadratus lumborum
labels.fn: A square muscle of the back wall of the abdomen, from the iliac crest to the 12th rib and the lumbar vertebrae. It bends the trunk to the side and holds the 12th rib down.

labels.name: Psoas major
labels.fn: A long muscle from the lumbar vertebrae, across the front of the hip, to the lesser trochanter of the femur; with iliacus it forms iliopsoas. It is the main flexor of the hip.

labels.name: Iliacus
labels.fn: The muscle that fills the bowl of the ilium and joins psoas major to insert on the lesser trochanter of the femur. Together, as iliopsoas, they flex the hip.

labels.name: Pectineus
labels.fn: A short, flat muscle in the upper medial thigh, from the pubis to the femur. It adducts and flexes the hip.

labels.name: Crest of ilium
labels.fn: The iliac crest, the curved upper rim of the ilium. Abdominal, back and gluteal muscles attach along it.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone at the base of the spine, made of five fused vertebrae, that joins the two hip bones. Deep back muscles anchor to it.

labels.name: Adductor longus
labels.fn: A medial thigh muscle from the pubis to the middle of the femur. It adducts the thigh and helps flex it.

labels.name: Tensor fascia latae
