labels.fn: A small muscle on the side of the hip, from the iliac crest into the iliotibial tract. It flexes and abducts the thigh and tightens the iliotibial tract to steady the knee.

labels.name: Gracilis
labels.fn: A long, thin strap muscle on the inner thigh, from the pubis to the medial tibia. It adducts the thigh and helps flex the knee.

labels.name: Adductor magnus
labels.fn: The largest adductor, a big triangular muscle of the medial thigh from the pubis and ischium to the femur. It adducts the thigh; its back part helps extend the hip.

labels.name: Rectus femoris
labels.fn: The part of quadriceps femoris that runs straight down the front of the thigh from the ilium to the patella. It extends the knee and, because it crosses the hip, also flexes the hip.

follow.q: Why can rectus femoris flex the hip when the three vastus muscles cannot?
options: It is the largest part of quadriceps femoris
It crosses the hip as well as the knee
It inserts on the fibula below the knee
It arises from the shaft of the femur
follow.why: Rectus femoris arises from the ilium, so it crosses the hip joint as well as the knee, and it flexes the hip as well as extending the knee. The vasti arise from the femur and cross only the knee. Vastus lateralis, not rectus femoris, is the largest part.

labels.name: Sartorius
labels.fn: The longest muscle in the body, a strap crossing the thigh diagonally from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia. It flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the thigh and flexes the knee, as in sitting cross-legged.

labels.name: Vastus medialis
labels.fn: The part of quadriceps femoris on the inner front of the thigh, from the femur to the quadriceps tendon. It extends the knee.

labels.name: Vastus lateralis
labels.fn: The largest part of quadriceps femoris, on the outer front of the thigh. It extends the knee.

labels.name: Quadriceps tendon (or patellar tendon)
labels.fn: The tendon of quadriceps femoris, which holds the patella; below the patella it continues as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. It carries the pull that extends the knee.

labels.name: Patellar ligament
labels.fn: The band from the patella to the tibial tuberosity, the continuation of the quadriceps tendon. It carries quadriceps pull to the tibia, and tapping it tests the knee jerk.

labels.name: Gluteus medius (cut)
labels.fn: A thick, fan-shaped muscle on the side of the hip, partly under gluteus maximus, from the ilium to the greater trochanter. It abducts the thigh and holds the pelvis level when you stand on one leg.

labels.name: Crest of ilium
labels.fn: The iliac crest, the curved upper rim of the ilium. Abdominal, back and gluteal muscles attach along it.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone at the base of the spine, made of five fused vertebrae, that joins the two hip bones. Deep back muscles anchor to it.

labels.name: Iliac crest
labels.fn: The curved upper rim of the ilium, the top of your hip. Abdominal, back and gluteal muscles attach along it.

labels.name: Gluteus minimus
labels.fn: The smallest and deepest gluteal muscle, beneath gluteus medius, from the ilium to the greater trochanter. It abducts and medially rotates the thigh.

labels.name: Pectineus
labels.fn: A short, flat muscle in the upper medial thigh, from the pubis to the femur. It adducts and flexes the hip.

labels.name: Obturator internus
labels.fn: A deep lateral rotator of the hip, from the inner surface around the obturator foramen out to the greater trochanter. It laterally rotates the thigh.

labels.name: Pubis
labels.fn: The front part of the hip bone. The adductor muscles and pectineus arise from it.

labels.name: Piriformis
labels.fn: A pear-shaped deep hip muscle from the front of the sacrum to the greater trochanter. It laterally rotates the thigh.

follow.q: Piriformis, the gemelli, obturator internus and quadratus femoris share which action?
options: Adducting the thigh toward the midline
follow.why: These deep hip muscles all pass behind the hip to the greater trochanter and turn the thigh outward. The adductor group adducts, the hamstrings flex the knee, and quadriceps extends it.

labels.name: Obturator externus
labels.fn: A deep lateral rotator on the outer surface of the obturator foramen, reaching the femur. It laterally rotates the thigh.

labels.name: Superior gemellus
labels.fn: A small deep lateral rotator of the hip, from the ischial spine to the greater trochanter, just above obturator internus. It laterally rotates the thigh.

labels.name: Gluteus maximus (cut)
labels.fn: The largest and most superficial gluteal muscle, from the ilium, sacrum and coccyx to the femur and iliotibial tract. It is the main extensor of the hip, used in climbing stairs and rising from a chair.

labels.name: Inferior gemellus
labels.fn: A small deep lateral rotator from the ischial tuberosity to the greater trochanter, just below obturator internus. It laterally rotates the thigh.

labels.name: Adductor brevis
labels.fn: A short medial thigh muscle from the pubis to the upper femur, beneath adductor longus. It adducts the thigh.

labels.name: Adductor longus
labels.fn: A medial thigh muscle from the pubis to the middle of the femur. It adducts the thigh and helps flex it.

labels.name: Adductor group
labels.fn: The medial thigh muscles (adductor longus, brevis and magnus, with gracilis and pectineus). They pull the thigh toward the midline.

labels.name: Obturator externus
labels.fn: A deep lateral rotator on the outer surface of the obturator foramen, reaching the femur. It laterally rotates the thigh.

labels.name: Femur
labels.fn: The thigh bone, the longest bone in the body. Hip and thigh muscles attach along it.

labels.name: Adductor magnus
labels.fn: The largest adductor, a big triangular muscle of the medial thigh from the pubis and ischium to the femur. It adducts the thigh; its back part helps extend the hip.

labels.name: Gracilis
labels.fn: A long, thin strap muscle on the inner thigh, from the pubis to the medial tibia. It adducts the thigh and helps flex the knee.

labels.name: Quadratus femoris
labels.fn: A short, square deep hip muscle from the ischial tuberosity to the femur. It laterally rotates the thigh.

labels.name: Semimembranosus
labels.fn: The deepest hamstring on the back of the thigh, from the ischial tuberosity to the medial tibia. It extends the hip and flexes the knee.

labels.name: Biceps femoris
labels.fn: The lateral hamstring, with a long head from the ischial tuberosity and a short head from the femur, inserting on the fibula. It extends the hip and flexes the knee.

follow.q: Which muscles make up the hamstrings?
options: Vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and rectus femoris
follow.why: The hamstrings are biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus on the back of the thigh; they extend the hip and flex the knee. The vasti and rectus femoris are the quadriceps, and the gluteal group moves the hip.

labels.name: Semitendinosus
labels.fn: The medial hamstring with a long, cord-like tendon, from the ischial tuberosity to the medial tibia. It extends the hip and flexes the knee.

labels.name: Gastrocnemius (lateral head)
labels.fn: The two-headed calf muscle, arising from the femur above the knee and inserting on the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. It plantar flexes the foot and helps flex the knee.

labels.name: Tibialis anterior
labels.fn: The muscle along the front of the shin, from the tibia to the medial foot. It dorsiflexes and inverts the foot; weakness causes foot drop.

follow.q: A patient cannot lift the front of the foot and scuffs the toes when walking. Which muscle is most likely weak?
follow.why: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes the foot; when it is weak the foot drops. Soleus and gastrocnemius plantar flex the foot, and fibularis longus mainly everts it.

labels.name: Popliteus
labels.fn: A small muscle behind the knee, from the lateral femur to the tibia. It unlocks the fully extended knee by rotating the femur on the tibia.

labels.name: Gastrocnemius (medial head)
labels.fn: The two-headed calf muscle, arising from the femur above the knee and inserting on the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. It plantar flexes the foot and helps flex the knee.

labels.name: Fibularis longus
labels.fn: A muscle of the lateral leg, from the fibula; its tendon runs behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot. It everts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the arch.

labels.name: Soleus (cut)
labels.fn: The broad, flat calf muscle beneath gastrocnemius, from the tibia and fibula to the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. It plantar flexes the foot and keeps you from falling forward when you stand.

labels.name: Extensor digitorum longus
labels.fn: A muscle of the front of the leg, lateral to tibialis anterior, sending tendons to the four lateral toes. It extends the toes and dorsiflexes the foot.

labels.name: Fibularis longus
labels.fn: A muscle of the lateral leg, from the fibula; its tendon runs behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot. It everts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the arch.

labels.name: Plantaris
labels.fn: A small muscle behind the knee with a very long, thin tendon to the calcaneus. It weakly helps gastrocnemius.

labels.name: Fibularis brevis
labels.fn: The shorter lateral leg muscle, beneath fibularis longus, from the fibula to the fifth metatarsal. It everts the foot.

labels.name: Tibialis posterior
labels.fn: The deepest muscle of the back of the leg, from the tibia and fibula to the bones of the medial foot. It inverts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the arch.

labels.name: Extensor hallucis longus
labels.fn: A muscle of the front of the leg with a tendon to the big toe. It extends the big toe and dorsiflexes the foot.

labels.name: Soleus
labels.fn: The broad, flat calf muscle beneath gastrocnemius, from the tibia and fibula to the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. It plantar flexes the foot and keeps you from falling forward when you stand.

follow.q: Why does gastrocnemius plantar flex the foot best with the knee straight, while soleus works equally well with the knee bent?
options: Gastrocnemius crosses the knee; soleus does not
Soleus is one of the hamstring muscles
Gastrocnemius inserts on the tibia instead
Soleus has no tendon joining it to bone
follow.why: Gastrocnemius arises from the femur, so bending the knee slackens it; soleus arises below the knee from the tibia and fibula, so its length is not changed by the knee. Both insert on the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon.

labels.name: Flexor digitorum longus
labels.fn: A deep muscle of the back of the leg sending tendons under the foot to the four lateral toes. It flexes the toes.

labels.name: Fibularis tertius
labels.fn: A small muscle at the lower front of the leg, from the fibula to the fifth metatarsal. It dorsiflexes and everts the foot.

labels.name: Flexor hallucis longus
labels.fn: A deep muscle of the back of the leg with a tendon to the big toe. It flexes the big toe, giving the push-off in walking.

labels.name: Superior extensor retinaculum
labels.fn: A band across the front of the lower leg, just above the ankle, that holds the extensor tendons against the bones.

labels.name: Calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
labels.fn: The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, the thickest tendon in the body, joining gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus. It carries the calf pull that plantar flexes the foot.

labels.name: Fibularis brevis
labels.fn: The shorter lateral leg muscle, beneath fibularis longus, from the fibula to the fifth metatarsal. It everts the foot.

labels.name: Inferior extensor retinaculum
labels.fn: A Y-shaped band across the top of the ankle that holds the extensor tendons down as they turn onto the foot.

labels.name: Calcaneus (heel)
labels.fn: The heel bone, the largest tarsal. The calcaneal tendon inserts on it.

labels.name: Occipitofrontalis (frontal belly)
labels.fn: The front belly of occipitofrontalis, over the forehead. It raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead by pulling on the epicranial aponeurosis.

labels.name: Sternocleidomastoid
labels.fn: The long diagonal neck muscle from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process behind the ear. One side turns the head to the opposite side; both together flex the neck.

labels.name: Deltoid
labels.fn: The thick muscle that caps the shoulder and abducts the arm. It is the deltoid intramuscular injection site, used for small volumes such as most vaccines, placed in the thick middle part a few finger-widths below the acromion.

follow.q: Why is the deltoid site used for small volumes only, such as most vaccines?
options: The muscle is small, so only about 1 mL fits
The deltoid has almost no blood supply
The deltoid is made of smooth muscle
It is the thickest muscle in the whole body
follow.why: The deltoid is a fairly small muscle, so only small volumes (about 1 mL in adults) are given there. Larger volumes go into the ventrogluteal site (gluteus medius) or vastus lateralis. It is well supplied with blood, which is why drugs are absorbed from it.

labels.name: Trapezius
labels.fn: The large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck, from the skull and the cervical and thoracic spinous processes to the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula. It elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula.

labels.name: Pectoralis major
labels.fn: The large fan-shaped chest muscle, from the clavicle, sternum and rib cartilages to the humerus. It flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

labels.name: Pectoralis minor
labels.fn: A thin chest muscle beneath pectoralis major, from the 3rd to 5th ribs to the coracoid process. It pulls the scapula forward and down.

labels.name: Serratus anterior
labels.fn: The saw-toothed muscle on the side of the chest, from the upper eight or nine ribs to the medial border of the scapula. It pulls the scapula forward around the rib cage, as in a punch, and rotates it upward.

labels.name: Rectus abdominis
labels.fn: The vertical strap muscle on each side of the midline, from the pubis up to the lower ribs and sternum, divided by tendinous intersections into segments. It flexes the trunk and compresses the abdomen.

labels.name: Biceps brachii
labels.fn: The two-headed muscle on the front of the arm, from the scapula to the radius. It flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm, turning the palm up.

labels.name: Brachialis
labels.fn: The muscle beneath biceps brachii on the front of the arm, from the humerus to the ulna. It is the prime mover for flexing the elbow, whatever the forearm's position.

labels.name: Abdominal external oblique
labels.fn: The outermost flat abdominal muscle, fibers running down and forward from the lower ribs toward the midline. It compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk and turns it to the opposite side.

labels.name: Brachioradialis
labels.fn: The forearm muscle on the thumb side, from the lower humerus to the lower end of the radius. It flexes the elbow, working best with the forearm halfway between palm up and palm down.

labels.name: Pronator teres
labels.fn: A short muscle across the front of the upper forearm, from the medial epicondyle to the radius. It pronates the forearm (turns the palm down) and helps flex the elbow.

labels.name: Pectineus
labels.fn: A short, flat muscle in the upper medial thigh, from the pubis to the femur. It adducts and flexes the hip.

labels.name: Flexor carpi radialis
labels.fn: A superficial muscle on the front of the forearm, from the medial epicondyle to the second and third metacarpals. It flexes the wrist and abducts the hand.

labels.name: Adductor longus
labels.fn: A medial thigh muscle from the pubis to the middle of the femur. It adducts the thigh and helps flex it.

labels.name: Tensor fasciae latae
labels.fn: A small muscle on the side of the hip that pulls on the iliotibial tract. It flexes and abducts the thigh and steadies the knee.

labels.name: Sartorius
labels.fn: The longest muscle in the body, a strap crossing the thigh diagonally from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial tibia. It flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the thigh and flexes the knee, as in sitting cross-legged.

labels.name: Iliopsoas
labels.fn: Psoas major and iliacus together, from the lumbar vertebrae and the ilium to the lesser trochanter of the femur. It is the prime mover for flexing the hip.

labels.name: Rectus femoris
labels.fn: The part of quadriceps femoris that runs straight down the front of the thigh from the ilium to the patella. It extends the knee and, because it crosses the hip, also flexes the hip.

labels.name: Gracilis
labels.fn: A long, thin strap muscle on the inner thigh, from the pubis to the medial tibia. It adducts the thigh and helps flex the knee.

labels.name: Vastus lateralis
labels.fn: The largest part of quadriceps femoris, on the outer front of the thigh; it extends the knee. It is the vastus lateralis injection site, the preferred site in infants because it is thick and has no large vessels or nerves nearby.

follow.q: Which intramuscular site is preferred in infants?
follow.why: In infants vastus lateralis is the best-developed of these muscles and lies away from large nerves and vessels. The deltoid is too small in infants, and the gluteal muscles develop only after the child starts walking.

labels.name: Vastus medialis
labels.fn: The part of quadriceps femoris on the inner front of the thigh, from the femur to the quadriceps tendon. It extends the knee.

labels.name: Soleus and gastrocnemius
labels.fn: The two calf muscles that share the calcaneal tendon. Both plantar flex the foot, as in standing on tiptoe; gastrocnemius also flexes the knee.

labels.name: Fibularis longus
labels.fn: A muscle of the lateral leg, from the fibula; its tendon runs behind the lateral malleolus and under the foot. It everts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the arch.

labels.name: Tibialis anterior
labels.fn: The muscle along the front of the shin, from the tibia to the medial foot. It dorsiflexes and inverts the foot; weakness causes foot drop.

labels.name: Occipitofrontalis (occipital belly)
labels.fn: The back belly of occipitofrontalis, over the back of the skull. It pulls the scalp backward through the epicranial aponeurosis.

labels.name: Epicranial aponeurosis
labels.fn: The flat sheet of tendon across the top of the skull that joins the frontal and occipital bellies of occipitofrontalis. The two bellies pull on it from either end.

labels.name: Splenius capitis
labels.fn: A deep back muscle of the neck, from the lower cervical and upper thoracic spinous processes to the mastoid process and skull. Both sides extend the head; one side turns the head to the same side.

labels.name: Levator scapulae
labels.fn: A muscle from the upper cervical vertebrae down to the upper corner of the scapula. It elevates the scapula, as in a shrug, and bends the neck to the side.

labels.name: Rhomboids
labels.fn: Rhomboid major and minor, from the spinous processes to the medial border of the scapula. They retract the scapula toward the spine.

labels.name: Supraspinatus
labels.fn: The rotator cuff muscle above the spine of the scapula, in the supraspinous fossa, inserting on the greater tubercle. It starts abduction of the arm and helps hold the humeral head in the glenoid cavity.

labels.name: Trapezius
labels.fn: The large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck, from the skull and the cervical and thoracic spinous processes to the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula. It elevates, retracts and rotates the scapula.

labels.name: Teres minor
labels.fn: A rotator cuff muscle along the lower border of the scapula, from the lateral border to the greater tubercle of the humerus. It laterally rotates the arm and holds the humeral head in its socket.

labels.name: Deltoid
labels.fn: The thick, triangular muscle that caps the shoulder, from the clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula to the deltoid tuberosity of the humerus. It is the prime mover for abducting the arm.

labels.name: Infraspinatus
labels.fn: The rotator cuff muscle below the spine of the scapula, in the infraspinous fossa, inserting on the greater tubercle. It laterally rotates the arm and holds the humeral head in its socket.

labels.name: Latissimus dorsi
labels.fn: The broad, flat muscle of the lower back, from the lower thoracic and lumbar spinous processes and the iliac crest to the humerus. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

labels.name: Teres major
labels.fn: A thick muscle from the lower angle of the scapula to the front of the humerus, next to latissimus dorsi. It extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm. It is not part of the rotator cuff.

labels.name: Brachioradialis
labels.fn: The forearm muscle on the thumb side, from the lower humerus to the lower end of the radius. It flexes the elbow, working best with the forearm halfway between palm up and palm down.

labels.name: Triceps brachii
labels.fn: The three-headed muscle on the back of the arm, from the scapula and humerus to the olecranon of the ulna. It is the prime mover for extending the elbow.

labels.name: Extensor carpi radialis
labels.fn: The extensor carpi radialis muscles (longus and brevis) on the thumb side of the back of the forearm. They extend the wrist and abduct the hand.

labels.name: Serratus posterior inferior
labels.fn: A thin muscle from the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spinous processes to the lower four ribs. It pulls those ribs down and back.

labels.name: Extensor digitorum
labels.fn: The main extensor of the fingers, in the middle of the back of the forearm, from the lateral epicondyle to the four fingers. It extends the fingers and helps extend the wrist.

labels.name: Extensor carpi ulnaris
labels.fn: A muscle on the little-finger side of the back of the forearm, from the lateral epicondyle and ulna to the fifth metacarpal. It extends the wrist and adducts the hand.

labels.name: External oblique
labels.fn: The outermost flat abdominal muscle, with fibers running down and forward from the lower ribs to the iliac crest and the linea alba. It compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk and turns it to the opposite side.

labels.name: Flexor carpi ulnaris
labels.fn: A superficial muscle on the little-finger side of the front of the forearm, from the medial epicondyle and ulna to the pisiform and fifth metacarpal. It flexes the wrist and adducts the hand.

labels.name: Gluteus medius (dissected)
labels.fn: The fan-shaped muscle on the side of the hip that abducts the thigh and levels the pelvis. It is the target of the ventrogluteal injection site, located with the hand on the greater trochanter and the fingers toward the iliac crest.

follow.q: The ventrogluteal site is preferred over the dorsogluteal site. Why?
options: It is the only site that can take a vaccine
The dorsogluteal site lies over a large nerve and vessels
Gluteus maximus absorbs every drug far too fast to be safe
The ventrogluteal site is really part of the deltoid
follow.why: The dorsogluteal site on gluteus maximus lies close to a large nerve and major vessels, so an injection there risks injury. The ventrogluteal site targets gluteus medius, away from them.

labels.name: Gluteus minimus
labels.fn: The smallest and deepest gluteal muscle, beneath gluteus medius, from the ilium to the greater trochanter. It abducts and medially rotates the thigh.

labels.name: Gemellus muscles
labels.fn: The superior and inferior gemellus, small deep hip muscles on either side of obturator internus. They laterally rotate the thigh.

labels.name: Gluteus maximus (dissected)
labels.fn: The largest gluteal muscle, the main hip extensor. The old dorsogluteal injection site in its upper outer part is avoided now because a large nerve and vessels run beneath it; the ventrogluteal site into gluteus medius is used instead.

labels.name: Biceps femoris
labels.fn: The lateral hamstring, with a long head from the ischial tuberosity and a short head from the femur, inserting on the fibula. It extends the hip and flexes the knee.

labels.name: Semimembranosus
labels.fn: The deepest hamstring on the back of the thigh, from the ischial tuberosity to the medial tibia. It extends the hip and flexes the knee.

labels.name: Semitendinosus
labels.fn: The medial hamstring with a long, cord-like tendon, from the ischial tuberosity to the medial tibia. It extends the hip and flexes the knee.

labels.name: Gracilis
labels.fn: A long, thin strap muscle on the inner thigh, from the pubis to the medial tibia. It adducts the thigh and helps flex the knee.

labels.name: Peroneus longus
labels.fn: The older name for fibularis longus, a lateral leg muscle whose tendon passes under the foot. It everts and plantar flexes the foot.

labels.name: Gastrocnemius (dissected)
labels.fn: The two-headed calf muscle, arising from the femur above the knee and inserting on the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. It plantar flexes the foot and helps flex the knee.

labels.name: Tibialis posterior
labels.fn: The deepest muscle of the back of the leg, from the tibia and fibula to the bones of the medial foot. It inverts and plantar flexes the foot and supports the arch.

labels.name: Soleus
labels.fn: The broad, flat calf muscle beneath gastrocnemius, from the tibia and fibula to the calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon. It plantar flexes the foot and keeps you from falling forward when you stand.

labels.name: Cell body (soma)
labels.fn: The neuron's cell body, or soma. It holds the nucleus and the dark clumps of rough ER (Nissl bodies) that make the proteins for the whole neuron, and it receives signals along with the dendrites.

follow.q: Why is a neuron's cell body packed with so much rough ER?
options: It stores calcium to trigger the neuron's signals
It makes the myelin that wraps the neuron's axon
It breaks down worn-out organelles returned from the axon
It makes proteins for the whole neuron, axon included
follow.why: Almost all of a neuron's proteins are made in the soma and shipped down the axon by axonal transport, and the axon can hold hundreds of times more cytoplasm than the soma. That takes a lot of ribosome-studded rough ER, seen as Nissl bodies. Myelin is made by glial cells, not the neuron, and breaking down worn-out parts is the job of lysosomes.

labels.name: Axon
labels.fn: The single long process that carries action potentials away from the cell body. It leaves the soma at the axon hillock and ends in branched axon terminals; this one is wrapped in segments of myelin.

labels.name: Oligodendrocyte
labels.fn: A CNS glial cell with a few arms. Each arm wraps a segment of a different axon in layers of myelin, so one oligodendrocyte myelinates parts of many axons.

follow.q: How does an oligodendrocyte differ from a Schwann cell in the way it makes myelin?
options: It myelinates only axons in the PNS
It makes myelin from protein rather than from layers of membrane
It wraps segments of many different axons, one per arm
It wraps only one segment of one axon
follow.why: An oligodendrocyte, in the CNS, sends out several arms, and each arm wraps a segment of a different axon. A Schwann cell, in the PNS, wraps a single segment of a single axon. Both build myelin the same basic way, from many layers of their own plasma membrane.

labels.name: Cell membrane
labels.fn: The neuron's plasma membrane. Ion channels in it let the charge across the membrane change, and those changes, graded potentials and action potentials, are the neuron's signals.

labels.name: Dendrites
labels.fn: Short, tapering, heavily branched processes that receive signals from other neurons, often on tiny dendritic spines, and carry graded potentials toward the cell body.

follow.q: Which comparison between dendrites and the axon is correct?
options: Dendrites carry action potentials away from the soma; the axon carries graded potentials toward it
A neuron usually has many axons but a single dendrite
Dendrites are wrapped in myelin and the axon is bare
Dendrites carry graded potentials toward the soma; the axon carries action potentials away
follow.why: Signals come in on the dendrites as graded potentials and spread toward the soma; the single axon carries action potentials away from it. A neuron usually has many dendrites and one axon, and it is the axon, not the dendrites, that is often myelinated.

labels.name: Node of Ranvier
labels.fn: A tiny gap between two segments of myelin where the axon's membrane is bare. Voltage-gated sodium channels are packed densely at the nodes and sparse under the myelin.

follow.q: Along a myelinated axon, where are voltage-gated sodium channels most densely packed?
options: At the nodes of Ranvier, the bare gaps between segments
Under the middle of each myelin segment, where insulation is thickest
follow.why: The membrane under the myelin has few voltage-gated sodium channels, while the bare nodes of Ranvier between segments are packed with them. Dendrites carry graded potentials and are not where the axon's channels sit.

labels.name: Myelin sheath
labels.fn: Many tight layers of a glial cell's plasma membrane spiraled around an axon segment. Being mostly lipid, it insulates the axon, so action potentials travel much faster, and its fat makes white matter white.

labels.name: Synapse
labels.fn: Where an axon terminal meets the next neuron. The terminal releases neurotransmitter, which crosses a narrow gap and binds receptor proteins on the next cell.

labels.name: Bipolar neuron
labels.fn: A neuron with two processes, one axon and one dendrite, leaving opposite ends of the cell body. Bipolar neurons are rare, found only in a few sense organs: the eye, the smell-sensing lining of the nose and the inner parts of the ear.

follow.q: Where would you expect to find bipolar neurons?
options: Throughout the gray matter of the brain and spinal cord, where they integrate signals
In every ganglion beside the spinal cord
In a few sense organs: the eye, the nose and the inner parts of the ear
follow.why: Bipolar neurons are rare and sit in a few sense organs: the light-sensing layer of the eye, the smell-sensing lining of the nose and the inner parts of the ear. Spinal cord gray matter is full of multipolar neurons, and the ganglia beside the spinal cord hold the cell bodies of unipolar sensory neurons. Skeletal muscle holds no neuron cell bodies at all.

labels.name: Unipolar neuron
labels.fn: A neuron with one short process that splits like a T into two long branches: one runs out to a sensory receptor ending and the other into the CNS. Most sensory neurons are this type, with the cell body in a ganglion.

follow.q: A neuron's cell body sits in a ganglion beside the spinal cord, and its single process splits into two long branches. What is it most likely to be?
options: A bipolar neuron in a sense organ
follow.why: One process that splits in two makes it unipolar, and most unipolar neurons are sensory neurons whose cell bodies sit in ganglia outside the CNS. Interneurons and somatic motor neurons are multipolar with their cell bodies in the CNS, and bipolar neurons have two separate processes.

labels.name: Multipolar neuron
labels.fn: A neuron with one axon and two or more dendrites. It is by far the most common type: every motor neuron and nearly every interneuron in the CNS is multipolar.

labels.name: Microglial cell
labels.fn: A small CNS glial cell with fine, constantly moving processes. Microglia patrol the tissue and, where they find damage or infection, multiply and engulf dead cells, debris and microbes, acting as the CNS's resident defense cells.

follow.q: A small area of brain tissue is injured, leaving dead cells and debris. Which glial cells move in and engulf the debris?
follow.why: Microglia patrol the CNS and, when they detect damage, multiply, move to the spot and engulf dead cells and debris. Ependymal cells line fluid-filled cavities, oligodendrocytes make myelin, and satellite cells are PNS glia around cell bodies in ganglia.

labels.name: Astrocyte
labels.fn: A star-shaped CNS glial cell with many branching processes. Astrocytes take up excess potassium and neurotransmitter around neurons, wrap the brain's capillaries with their end-feet, store glycogen, and wall off injuries with a glial scar.

follow.q: During intense firing, potassium ions build up in the narrow spaces around neurons. Which glial cell takes up the excess?
options: Oligodendrocytes, which wrap segments of nearby axons in myelin
Ependymal cells, which line fluid-filled cavities
Astrocytes, which regulate the fluid around neurons
follow.why: Astrocytes take up the potassium that leaks out of firing neurons, and the neurotransmitter released at synapses, keeping the fluid around neurons within its normal range. Oligodendrocytes make myelin, microglia clear debris, and ependymal cells line the fluid-filled cavities.

labels.name: Ependymal cells
labels.fn: A single layer of cube- to column-shaped CNS glial cells lining the fluid-filled cavities inside the brain and the canal down the middle of the spinal cord. Many carry cilia whose beating helps keep that fluid moving.

labels.name: Oligodendrocytes
labels.fn: CNS glial cells with a few arms. Each arm flattens and wraps a segment of a different axon in myelin, so one oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of dozens of axons.

labels.name: Peripheral ganglionic neuron cell body (unipolar cell)
labels.fn: The round cell body of a sensory neuron, sitting in a ganglion outside the brain and spinal cord and wrapped by a layer of satellite cells. It is a unipolar cell: one short process leaves it and splits into a long axon that runs in from the body and one that runs on into the CNS, so signals can pass the cell body without going through it.

labels.name: Satellite cells
labels.fn: Flattened PNS glial cells covering the cell bodies of neurons in a ganglion. They support those neurons and regulate the fluid around them, much as astrocytes do in the CNS.

follow.q: Satellite cells in a ganglion do a job much like which CNS glial cell?
options: Astrocytes, which tend the fluid around neurons
Microglia, which engulf debris and dead cells
Ependymal cells, which line fluid-filled cavities
follow.why: Satellite cells cover neuron cell bodies in PNS ganglia and control the fluid around them, the same role astrocytes play around neurons in the CNS. In the PNS, myelin comes from Schwann cells, and there is no PNS match for ependymal cells.

labels.name: Schwann cells
labels.fn: PNS glial cells lined up along axons. Each one wraps a single segment of a single axon in myelin, or cradles several thin unmyelinated axons, and after an injury they guide the cut axon as it regrows.

follow.q: A PNS axon has 200 myelin segments along its length. How many Schwann cells made them?
options: About 20, since each cell wraps about ten segments
None; PNS myelin comes from oligodendrocytes
follow.why: Each Schwann cell wraps just one segment of one axon, so 200 segments need 200 Schwann cells. It is the oligodendrocyte, in the CNS, whose arms wrap segments of several axons, and oligodendrocytes do not myelinate PNS axons.

labels.name: Axon
labels.fn: The long process of the ganglion neuron, wrapped segment by segment by Schwann cells. It carries action potentials past the cell body, which sits off to one side, on into the CNS.

labels.name: Central sulcus
labels.fn: The deep groove running down the side of each hemisphere from the top. It separates the frontal lobe in front from the parietal lobe behind it.

follow.q: Which two lobes does the central sulcus separate?
follow.why: The central sulcus runs down from the top of the hemisphere with the frontal lobe in front of it and the parietal lobe behind it. The lateral sulcus sets off the temporal lobe, and the parieto-occipital sulcus separates the parietal and occipital lobes.

labels.name: Frontal lobe
labels.fn: The front lobe of each hemisphere, lying ahead of the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. It plans and starts voluntary movement and handles planning, judgment and personality.

follow.q: A tumor damages the cortex just in front of the central sulcus. Which lobe is it in?
follow.why: Everything in front of the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus is frontal lobe. The parietal lobe starts just behind the central sulcus, the temporal lobe lies below the lateral sulcus, and the occipital lobe is at the back.

labels.name: Parietal lobe
labels.fn: The lobe behind the central sulcus and in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus. It receives and interprets body sensations such as touch, pressure and the position of your limbs.

labels.name: Parieto-occipital sulcus
labels.fn: The groove toward the back of the hemisphere that marks the border between the parietal lobe and the occipital lobe. It is seen best on the brain's inner, midline surface.

labels.name: Lateral sulcus
labels.fn: The deep horizontal groove on the side of the hemisphere. It separates the temporal lobe below from the frontal and parietal lobes above.

labels.name: Occipital lobe
labels.fn: The lobe at the back of each hemisphere, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus. It receives and processes vision.

follow.q: A blow to the back of the head injures the occipital lobes. Which ability is most likely affected?
follow.why: The occipital lobe at the back of the brain processes vision. Hearing is handled in the temporal lobe, touch in the parietal lobe, and starting movement in the frontal lobe.

labels.name: Temporal lobe
labels.fn: The lobe on the side of the brain below the lateral sulcus, near your temple. It processes hearing and plays a large part in memory and understanding language.

labels.name: Cerebrum
labels.fn: The largest part of the brain: two folded hemispheres that sit on top of the brainstem. Its gray-matter surface handles conscious thought, sensation and voluntary movement.

labels.name: Corpus callosum
labels.fn: The broad band of white matter at the floor of the longitudinal fissure, shown as a dashed outline because it lies deep inside. Its axons connect the right and left hemispheres so the two sides can share information.

follow.q: What is the corpus callosum made of, and what does it do?
options: Gray matter that controls both sides of the body
A fluid-filled space that cushions the hemispheres
White matter that links the two hemispheres
Blood vessels that feed the cortex
follow.why: The corpus callosum is a thick band of axons (white matter) crossing between the hemispheres, which lets the two sides communicate. It contains no cell bodies of note, and it is neither a fluid space nor a set of blood vessels.

labels.name: Longitudinal fissure
labels.fn: The deep midline groove that divides the cerebrum into right and left hemispheres. The corpus callosum lies at the bottom of it.

labels.name: Right hemisphere
labels.fn: The right half of the cerebrum. For the most part it receives sensation from, and controls movement of, the left side of the body.

labels.name: Left hemisphere
labels.fn: The left half of the cerebrum. For the most part it receives sensation from, and controls movement of, the right side of the body.

follow.q: A stroke damages the left hemisphere's movement areas. Which side of the body is most likely to become weak?
options: Neither side, since the cerebellum controls movement
follow.why: Each hemisphere mainly controls the opposite side of the body, because the pathways cross over. Left hemisphere damage therefore weakens the right side. The cerebellum coordinates movement but does not start it.

labels.name: Cerebral cortex
labels.fn: The thin outer layer of gray matter covering the cerebrum, folded into gyri and sulci. Folding packs more cortex, and so more neurons, into the skull.

labels.name: Thalamus
labels.fn: The egg-shaped mass of gray matter in the middle of the brain, part of the diencephalon. It relays and filters almost all incoming sensory information on its way to the cerebral cortex.

follow.q: Signals for touch on your hand travel up toward the cortex. Where are they relayed just before reaching it?
follow.why: The thalamus is the relay station for incoming sensory signals on their way to the cerebral cortex. The hypothalamus runs homeostatic controls, the cerebellum coordinates movement, and the pons is a brainstem region that the signals pass through earlier.

labels.name: Hypothalamus
labels.fn: The small region of the diencephalon just below the thalamus. It controls body temperature, thirst, hunger, daily rhythms and the autonomic output, and it controls the pituitary gland hanging beneath it.

follow.q: A lesion in which region would most likely disturb body temperature control?
follow.why: The hypothalamus is the brain's control center for body temperature, thirst and hunger. The thalamus relays sensory signals, the occipital lobe handles vision, and the cerebellum coordinates movement.

labels.name: Pituitary gland
labels.fn: A pea-sized gland hanging from the underside of the hypothalamus on a short stalk. The hypothalamus tells it which of its hormones to release.

labels.name: Midbrain
labels.fn: The top part of the brainstem, just below the diencephalon. It carries pathways between the cerebrum and the rest of the brainstem and holds centers for visual and hearing reflexes.

labels.name: Pons
labels.fn: The bulging middle part of the brainstem, between the midbrain and the medulla. It relays signals between the cerebrum and the cerebellum and helps set the rhythm of breathing.

follow.q: Which list gives the brainstem parts from top to bottom?
follow.why: Just below the diencephalon comes the midbrain, then the bulging pons, then the medulla, which continues into the spinal cord. Any other order places a part on the wrong side of its neighbor.

labels.name: Medulla
labels.fn: The medulla oblongata, the lowest part of the brainstem, which continues into the spinal cord. It holds the vital centers that control heart rate, blood pressure and breathing.

follow.q: Why is an injury to the medulla oblongata so often fatal?
options: It processes what the eyes see
It holds the centers that control heartbeat, blood pressure and breathing
It is the only link between the two hemispheres
It plans the words you speak
follow.why: The medulla holds the vital centers for heart rate, blood pressure and breathing, so damage there can stop them. Vision, the link between the hemispheres and speech planning belong to other structures.

labels.name: Cingulate gyrus
labels.fn: The arched fold of cortex on the brain's inner surface, curving just above the corpus callosum. It is part of the limbic system and links emotion to attention and decision making.

labels.name: Hypothalamic nuclei
labels.fn: The clusters of neurons that make up the hypothalamus, below the thalamus. The limbic system connects to them, which is how emotions can change your heart rate, breathing and hormone release.

labels.name: Corpus callosum
labels.fn: The arched band of white matter above the thalamus, cut across in this midline view. Its axons connect the right and left hemispheres.

labels.name: Amygdala
labels.fn: An almond-shaped cluster of neurons deep in the temporal lobe, part of the limbic system. It attaches emotion, especially fear, to experiences and helps store emotional memories.

follow.q: Which limbic structure most directly attaches fear to a memory, such as the place where you were bitten by a dog?
follow.why: The amygdala tags experiences with emotion, especially fear. The hippocampus forms the memory of the event itself, the thalamus relays sensory signals, and the corpus callosum links the hemispheres.

labels.name: Thalamus
labels.fn: The paired egg-shaped mass at the center of the brain, ringed here by limbic structures. It relays sensory information to the cerebral cortex.

labels.name: Hippocampus
labels.fn: A curved ridge of cortex along the inner edge of the temporal lobe, part of the limbic system. It is needed to store new facts and experiences so they can be recalled later.

follow.q: After damage to both hippocampi, a patient remembers his childhood but cannot remember people he met this week. What is he unable to do?
options: Store new facts and events for later recall
follow.why: The hippocampus is needed to store new experiences so they can be recalled later, so without it new events are lost while events stored long ago remain. Fear depends on the amygdala and coordination on the cerebellum.

labels.name: Cerebellum
labels.fn: The "little brain" behind the brainstem, below the occipital lobes. It compares the movement you intend with the movement that happens and corrects it, which keeps movement smooth and balanced.

follow.q: A person walks with wide, staggering steps and overshoots when reaching for a cup, but has normal strength. Which region is most likely damaged?
follow.why: The cerebellum coordinates movement, so its damage causes clumsy, unsteady movement (ataxia) with normal strength. The occipital lobe handles vision, the hypothalamus homeostasis, and the corpus callosum links the hemispheres.

labels.name: Pons
labels.fn: The bulging front part of the brainstem, just in front of the cerebellum. It relays signals from the cerebrum to the cerebellum.

labels.name: Deep cerebellar white matter (arbor vitae)
labels.fn: The branching white matter deep inside the cerebellum, named the "tree of life" for its shape when cut. Its axons carry signals into and out of the cerebellar cortex that surrounds it.

labels.name: Inferior olive
labels.fn: An olive-shaped bulge on the front of the medulla oblongata. Its neurons send signals up to the cerebellum that help it learn and correct movements.

labels.name: Veins
labels.fn: Veins on the brain's surface that cross the subarachnoid space and the dura to drain blood from the brain into the large channel in the dura.

labels.name: Bone
labels.fn: The skull bone (cranium) that encloses the brain. The dura mater lies against its inner surface.

labels.name: Dura mater
labels.fn: The tough, thick outer layer of the meninges ("tough mother"), lying against the skull. It anchors the brain and encloses the large venous channels that drain it.

follow.q: List the meninges from the skull inward.
options: Pia mater, arachnoid mater, dura mater
Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
Arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater
Dura mater, pia mater, arachnoid mater
follow.why: The tough dura mater lies against the skull, the web-like arachnoid mater lies under it, and the thin pia mater clings to the brain surface. Any other order puts a layer on the wrong side of its neighbor.

labels.name: Arachnoid mater
labels.fn: The middle layer of the meninges, a thin sheet under the dura that sends web-like strands (trabeculae) down to the pia. The space beneath it holds cerebrospinal fluid.

labels.name: Subdural space
labels.fn: The potential space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater. Normally it holds almost nothing, but bleeding from torn veins can collect there.

follow.q: An older adult falls, tearing veins that cross from the brain to the dura. Where does the blood most likely collect?
options: Between the skull and the dura
Between the dura and the arachnoid
follow.why: Veins that cross the subdural space tear with a sudden jolt, and the blood collects between the dura and the arachnoid, a subdural bleed. Bleeding between the skull and dura is usually from an artery, and the ventricles and corpus callosum lie inside the brain.

labels.name: Subarachnoid space
labels.fn: The space between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater, crossed by arachnoid trabeculae and filled with cerebrospinal fluid that cushions the brain.

follow.q: A lumbar puncture samples cerebrospinal fluid. Which space does the fluid come from?
follow.why: Cerebrospinal fluid around the brain and spinal cord flows in the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and the pia, and a lumbar puncture needle enters it low in the back. The subdural and epidural spaces do not hold CSF, and the needle never reaches the ventricles.

labels.name: Pia mater
labels.fn: The thin, delicate innermost layer of the meninges ("tender mother"). It clings to the brain surface, following every gyrus and sulcus, and carries small blood vessels.

labels.name: Arachnoid trabeculae
labels.fn: Fine strands of the arachnoid mater that cross the subarachnoid space to the pia mater, giving the arachnoid its spider-web look and suspending the brain in the fluid.

labels.name: Longitudinal fissure
labels.fn: The deep midline groove between the two hemispheres. The dura dips down into it as a vertical fold.

labels.name: Cerebral cortex
labels.fn: The outer gray matter of the cerebrum, directly under the pia mater.

labels.name: Cerebral vein
labels.fn: A vein running in the subarachnoid space over the brain surface. Such veins drain blood from the cortex toward the channels in the dura.

labels.name: Arachnoid granulation
labels.fn: Knob-like outpouchings of the arachnoid mater that push into the venous channel in the dura. Cerebrospinal fluid passes through them from the subarachnoid space back into venous blood.

follow.q: Where does cerebrospinal fluid classically return to the venous blood?
follow.why: CSF drains from the subarachnoid space into venous blood through the arachnoid granulations. The choroid plexus makes CSF, and the interventricular foramen and median aperture are openings it flows through on the way. (Some CSF also drains along nerve sheaths and through vessels in the dura; how the load is split in people is still being worked out.)

labels.name: Subarachnoid space
labels.fn: The fluid-filled space between the arachnoid and pia mater, surrounding the whole brain and spinal cord. CSF leaving the fourth ventricle circulates here.

labels.name: Meningeal dura mater
labels.fn: The meningeal layer of the dura mater, the tough outer covering of the brain just inside the skull.

labels.name: Choroid plexus
labels.fn: Tufts of leaky capillaries covered by a layer of modified ependymal cells, one in each ventricle. The covering cells, sealed by tight junctions, secrete cerebrospinal fluid: they actively transport sodium into the ventricle, and other ions and water follow.

follow.q: A child is born with a narrowed cerebral aqueduct. The choroid plexus keeps making CSF. Which ventricles swell?
options: None; the CSF drains into the spinal cord
follow.why: CSF made upstream in the lateral and third ventricles cannot pass the blocked aqueduct, so those ventricles fill and enlarge (hydrocephalus). The fourth ventricle lies downstream of the block, so it stays small.

labels.name: Right lateral ventricle
labels.fn: The largest of the four ventricles, one in each hemisphere, shaped like a C. Its choroid plexus makes much of the cerebrospinal fluid.

labels.name: Interventricular foramen
labels.fn: The small opening through which each lateral ventricle drains its cerebrospinal fluid into the third ventricle.

labels.name: Third ventricle
labels.fn: The narrow midline ventricle between the two halves of the thalamus. It receives CSF from both lateral ventricles and passes it down the cerebral aqueduct.

labels.name: Cerebral aqueduct
labels.fn: The narrow channel through the midbrain that carries cerebrospinal fluid from the third ventricle down to the fourth ventricle. Its narrowness makes it a common site of blockage.

follow.q: Which structure connects the third ventricle to the fourth?
follow.why: The cerebral aqueduct runs through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle. The interventricular foramen links each lateral ventricle to the third, and the apertures let CSF out of the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.

labels.name: Median aperture
labels.fn: The single opening in the midline of the fourth ventricle's roof. CSF leaves the ventricles through it into the subarachnoid space.

labels.name: Lateral aperture
labels.fn: One of the two side openings of the fourth ventricle. Along with the median aperture, they are the only exits from the ventricles into the subarachnoid space.

labels.name: Fourth ventricle
labels.fn: The ventricle between the brainstem (pons and medulla) and the cerebellum. It receives CSF from the cerebral aqueduct and sends it out through the median and lateral apertures.

labels.name: Posterior median sulcus
labels.fn: The shallow groove running down the back midline of the spinal cord. It divides the white matter at the back into right and left halves.

labels.name: Posterior column
labels.fn: The white matter between the posterior median sulcus and the dorsal horn. Its tracts are ascending: they carry fine touch, vibration and the sense of limb position up to the brain.

labels.name: Dorsal horn
labels.fn: The narrow gray horn reaching toward the back. Sensory axons arriving through the dorsal root end here on interneurons and on neurons whose axons carry the signal up the cord.

labels.name: Lateral horn
labels.fn: A small gray bump between the dorsal and ventral horns, found only from about T1 to L2. It holds the cell bodies of the autonomic (sympathetic) motor neurons that control glands, smooth muscle and the heart.

follow.q: A section shows a small gray bump sticking out at each side, between the dorsal and ventral horns. Which part of the cord did the section come from?
follow.why: Lateral horns hold sympathetic motor neurons and exist only from about T1 to L2, so a section showing them comes from the thoracic or upper lumbar cord. Neck, sacral and coccygeal sections have dorsal and ventral horns but no lateral horn.

labels.name: Lateral column
labels.fn: The white matter at each side of the cord, between the dorsal and ventral horns. It carries ascending tracts (including those for pain and temperature) and descending tracts that control movement.

labels.name: Central canal
labels.fn: The tiny canal in the middle of the gray matter, running the length of the cord. It is lined by ependymal cells and holds cerebrospinal fluid, continuous with the fourth ventricle above.

labels.name: Ventral horn
labels.fn: The broad gray horn reaching toward the front. It holds the cell bodies of the motor neurons whose axons leave through the ventral root to the skeletal muscles.

follow.q: A virus destroys neurons in one region of the spinal cord's gray matter. The patient's muscles weaken and waste away, but touch and pain are still felt. Which region was destroyed?
follow.why: The ventral horn holds the cell bodies of the motor neurons to skeletal muscle, so losing them leaves muscles without signals while sensation, which enters through the dorsal root and dorsal horn, is spared. The dorsal horn, posterior column and dorsal root ganglion all handle incoming sensory signals.

labels.name: Anterior column
labels.fn: The white matter between the ventral horn and the anterior median fissure. It carries descending tracts that control movement and some ascending tracts.

labels.name: Anterior median fissure
labels.fn: The deep groove running down the front midline of the spinal cord. Because the groove at the front is deep and the one at the back is shallow, it tells you which way a section faces.

follow.q: You are handed an unlabeled spinal cord section. Which feature tells you which side is the front?
options: The deep midline groove, which is at the front
The central canal, which sits closer to the front
The shallow midline groove, which is at the front
The broad gray horns, which point toward the back
follow.why: The anterior median fissure is deep and the posterior median sulcus is shallow, so the deep groove marks the front. The broad ventral horns also point to the front, not the back, and the central canal sits in the middle of the gray matter.

labels.name: Dorsal root
labels.fn: The bundle of sensory axons entering the back of the cord. It carries signals from the skin, muscles and organs into the dorsal horn.

follow.q: A surgeon cuts the dorsal roots of several neighboring segments to relieve pain. What is the expected result in the region they supply?
options: Loss of feeling, with movement spared
Loss of both feeling and movement
No change, because the ventral roots take over
follow.why: The dorsal roots carry only sensory axons into the cord, so cutting them removes feeling from their region while the motor axons in the ventral roots still reach the muscles. (Neighboring roots overlap, so cutting just one dulls feeling rather than removing it.) Paralysis would follow damage to the ventral roots, and they carry no sensory signals to take over.

labels.name: Dorsal root ganglion
labels.fn: The swelling on the dorsal root just outside the cord. It holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons whose axons run in the dorsal root.

follow.q: Where are the cell bodies of the sensory neurons that bring touch signals from your hand into the spinal cord?
follow.why: Sensory neuron cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglion, outside the cord. The ventral horn holds motor neurons, the lateral horn holds autonomic motor neurons, and the central canal is a fluid-filled channel with no neurons in it.

labels.name: Ventral root
labels.fn: The bundle of motor axons leaving the front of the cord from ventral horn neurons. Just beyond the ganglion it joins the dorsal root, so the nerve they form carries both sensory and motor axons.

labels.name: Cervical plexus
labels.fn: The network formed by the ventral rami of C1 to C4 in the neck. Its branches supply skin and some muscles of the neck, and it gives rise to the phrenic nerve.

labels.name: Brachial plexus
labels.fn: The network formed by the ventral rami of C5 to T1. Its fibers mix and regroup on the way to the armpit and leave as the nerves of the shoulder and upper limb, including the axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves.

follow.q: Which spinal nerves form the brachial plexus?
follow.why: The brachial plexus comes from the ventral rami of C5 to T1 and supplies the upper limb. C1 to C4 form the cervical plexus, L1 to L4 the lumbar plexus and L4 to S4 the sacral plexus.

labels.name: Phrenic nerve
labels.fn: A nerve from the cervical plexus, mainly C3 to C5, that runs down through the chest to the diaphragm. It is the only motor nerve to the diaphragm, so every breath depends on it.

follow.q: Cutting the spinal cord at C2 stops a patient's breathing, but cutting it at C7 does not. Why?
options: The phrenic nerve leaves the cord at C3 to C5
The brachial plexus drives the diaphragm
The ulnar nerve moves the diaphragm
The diaphragm needs no nerve signals
follow.why: The phrenic nerve, the diaphragm's only motor supply, leaves the cord at C3 to C5. An injury at C2 cuts the brain off from those segments, while one at C7 leaves them connected. The brachial plexus supplies the upper limb, the ulnar nerve supplies the hand, and the diaphragm is skeletal muscle that contracts only when its nerve fires.

labels.name: Axillary nerve
labels.fn: A brachial plexus branch that wraps behind the upper end of the humerus. It moves the deltoid, which lifts the arm out to the side, and carries feeling from the skin over the shoulder.

labels.name: Median nerve
labels.fn: A brachial plexus nerve that runs down the middle of the arm and forearm and through the wrist into the palm. It moves most of the muscles that bend the wrist and fingers and the muscles of the thumb, and carries feeling from the thumb side of the palm.

labels.name: Radial nerve
labels.fn: The largest branch of the brachial plexus. It winds around the back of the humerus and supplies the muscles that straighten the elbow, wrist and fingers, plus skin on the back of the arm and hand.

follow.q: A break through the middle of the humerus leaves a patient unable to lift the wrist and fingers (wrist drop). Which nerve was most likely injured?
follow.why: The radial nerve winds around the back of the middle of the humerus and supplies the muscles that straighten the wrist and fingers, so a break there can stretch or cut it. The median and ulnar nerves mostly bend the wrist and fingers, and the axillary nerve supplies the shoulder.

labels.name: Ulnar nerve
labels.fn: A brachial plexus nerve that passes behind the inner bump of the elbow (the "funny bone") into the hand. It supplies most of the small muscles of the hand and the skin on the little finger side.

labels.name: Lumbar plexus
labels.fn: The network formed by the ventral rami of L1 to L4. Its main branches, the femoral and obturator nerves, supply the front and inner thigh.

labels.name: Femoral nerve
labels.fn: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus. It enters the front of the thigh, moves the quadriceps, which straighten the knee, and carries feeling from the front of the thigh.

labels.name: Obturator nerve
labels.fn: A lumbar plexus nerve that leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen. It moves the muscles that pull the thigh inward and carries feeling from the skin of the inner thigh.

labels.name: Sacral plexus
labels.fn: The network formed by the ventral rami of L4 to S4. It supplies the buttock, the back of the thigh, all the muscles below the knee and most of the skin there, mainly through the sciatic nerve.

labels.name: Common fibular nerve
labels.fn: The branch of the sciatic nerve that wraps around the top of the fibula just below the knee, where it lies close to the skin. It moves the muscles that lift the foot and toes, so damage there causes foot drop.

labels.name: Sciatic nerve
labels.fn: The largest nerve in the body, from the sacral plexus (L4 to S3). It runs down the back of the thigh, moves the hamstrings, and above the knee splits into the tibial and common fibular nerves.

follow.q: An injection placed too low and too close to the middle of the buttock can injure which nerve, weakening the back of the thigh and everything below the knee?
follow.why: The sciatic nerve passes through the lower inner part of the buttock and supplies the hamstrings and all the muscles below the knee. Injections avoid the buttock and use the ventrogluteal site on the side of the hip instead. The femoral and obturator nerves supply the front and inner thigh, and the phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm.

labels.name: Tibial nerve
labels.fn: The branch of the sciatic nerve that continues down the back of the leg. It moves the calf muscles that point the foot and the muscles of the sole, and carries feeling from the sole.

labels.name: C5 dermatome
labels.fn: The C5 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve C5. Its standard landmark is the skin over the outer side of the upper arm.

labels.name: C6 dermatome
labels.fn: The C6 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve C6. Its standard landmark is the thumb. Across the hand, C6 is the thumb, C7 the middle finger and C8 the little finger.

follow.q: A patient has numbness of the thumb only. Which spinal nerve root is most likely involved?
follow.why: The thumb lies in the C6 dermatome. C8 covers the little finger side of the hand, T1 the inner forearm, and L5 the top of the foot.

labels.name: C7 dermatome
labels.fn: The C7 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve C7. Its standard landmark is the middle finger.

labels.name: C8 dermatome
labels.fn: The C8 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve C8. Its standard landmark is the little finger.

labels.name: T4 dermatome
labels.fn: The T4 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve T4. Its standard landmark is the chest at the level of the nipples. The thoracic dermatomes run as horizontal bands around the trunk.

labels.name: T10 dermatome
labels.fn: The T10 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve T10. Its standard landmark is the navel.

follow.q: After an injury to the spinal cord, a patient has lost feeling from the level of the navel down. At about which segment is the injury?
follow.why: The navel is the T10 landmark, so feeling lost from the navel down points to a cord injury at about T10. T4 is the nipple line, L1 the groin, and C8 the little finger.

labels.name: L1 dermatome
labels.fn: The L1 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve L1. Its standard landmark is the groin.

labels.name: L4 dermatome
labels.fn: The L4 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve L4. Its standard landmark is the inner side of the leg just below the knee.

labels.name: L5 dermatome
labels.fn: The L5 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve L5. Its standard landmark is the top of the foot and the big toe.

follow.q: Pressure on one nerve root in the lower back causes numbness on the top of the foot and the big toe. Which root is affected?
follow.why: The top of the foot and the big toe form the L5 dermatome. S1 covers the outer edge of the foot and the little toe, L1 the groin, and C7 the middle finger.

labels.name: S1 dermatome
labels.fn: The S1 dermatome: the strip of skin whose sensation reaches the spinal cord through the dorsal root of spinal nerve S1. Its standard landmark is the outer edge of the foot and the little toe.

sets.title: Cranial nerves on the inferior brain

labels.name: Olfactory nerve I
labels.fn: Cranial nerve I, purely sensory. Its fibers run from the lining high in the roof of the nose up into the skull to the underside of the frontal lobe and carry the sense of smell.

labels.name: Oculomotor nerve III
labels.fn: Cranial nerve III, a motor nerve from the midbrain. It moves most of the muscles that turn the eye, raises the upper eyelid, and through parasympathetic fibers makes the pupil smaller.

follow.q: A patient's right eye rests turned down and out, the right upper eyelid droops and the right pupil is wide. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
follow.why: The oculomotor nerve moves most eye muscles, lifts the eyelid and narrows the pupil, so losing it leaves the eye pulled down and out by the two muscles it does not supply, a drooping lid and a wide pupil. The trochlear and abducens nerves each move one eye muscle and do not touch the lid or pupil, and the facial nerve closes the eye rather than opening it.

labels.name: Optic nerve II
labels.fn: Cranial nerve II, purely sensory. It carries vision from each eye back into the brain; the two optic nerves meet beneath the brain, where some of their fibers cross to the other side.

labels.name: Trochlear nerve IV
labels.fn: Cranial nerve IV, the smallest cranial nerve and the only one leaving the back of the brainstem (the midbrain). It moves the one eye muscle that turns the eye down and slightly out. Its downward pull is strongest when the eye points toward the nose, so you test it by looking down and in.

labels.name: Trigeminal nerve V
labels.fn: Cranial nerve V, a mixed nerve from the pons. Its three branches carry touch, pain and temperature from the face, the front of the scalp, the mouth and the inside of the nose, and its motor fibers work the chewing muscles.

follow.q: Which cranial nerve carries touch and pain from the skin of the face?
follow.why: The trigeminal nerve is the main sensory nerve of the face. The facial nerve, despite its name, mainly moves the face, the hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue, and the vagus nerve serves the throat and the organs of the chest and abdomen.

labels.name: Abducens nerve VI
labels.fn: Cranial nerve VI, a motor nerve that leaves where the pons meets the medulla. It moves the one eye muscle that turns the eye outward.

labels.name: Facial nerve VII
labels.fn: Cranial nerve VII, a mixed nerve from the lower pons. It moves the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue, and drives tear and saliva secretion.

follow.q: A patient cannot close her left eye or smile on the left, and food tastes dull on the front of the left side of her tongue. Which nerve is affected?
follow.why: The facial nerve moves the muscles of facial expression, including the one that closes the eye, and carries taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue, so one lesion explains both. The trigeminal nerve carries touch from the face and works the chewing muscles, the glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from the back of the tongue, and the hypoglossal nerve moves the tongue.

labels.name: Vestibulocochlear nerve VIII
labels.fn: Cranial nerve VIII, a sensory nerve from the ear that enters where the pons meets the medulla. One part carries hearing and the other carries balance: the position and movement of the head.

labels.name: Glossopharyngeal nerve IX
labels.fn: Cranial nerve IX, a mixed nerve from the medulla. It carries taste and touch from the back third of the tongue and the throat, helps you swallow, and drives saliva secretion from the gland in front of the ear.

labels.name: Hypoglossal nerve XII
labels.fn: Cranial nerve XII, a motor nerve from the medulla that moves the tongue. When one side is damaged, the stuck-out tongue points toward the injured side.

labels.name: Vagus nerve X
labels.fn: Cranial nerve X, the "wandering" nerve from the medulla. It is the main parasympathetic nerve to the heart, the lungs and most of the gut, and it moves the muscles of the throat and voice box.

follow.q: Which cranial nerve carries most of the parasympathetic signals that slow the heart and speed digestion?
follow.why: The vagus nerve wanders from the medulla through the neck into the chest and abdomen and carries most of the body's parasympathetic output to the heart, lungs and gut. The glossopharyngeal and oculomotor nerves carry parasympathetic fibers only to glands and eye structures in the head, and the accessory nerve is purely motor to two neck muscles.

labels.name: Accessory nerve XI
labels.fn: Cranial nerve XI, a motor nerve whose rootlets come from the upper cervical spinal cord and rise through the foramen magnum into the skull before leaving it again. It moves the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, which turn the head and shrug the shoulders.

labels.name: Eyebrow
labels.fn: A ridge of short, thick hairs over the brow. It sheds sweat and falling particles to the side, away from the eye.

labels.name: Orbicularis oculi muscle
labels.fn: The ring of skeletal muscle inside the eyelids and around the orbit. It closes the eye, gently when you blink and tightly when you squeeze the eyes shut.

labels.name: Levator palpebrae superioris muscle
labels.fn: A thin muscle that runs from the back of the orbit into the upper eyelid. It raises the upper eyelid to open the eye.

follow.q: A patient cannot fully raise the right upper eyelid, but can still squeeze both eyes shut. Which muscle is most likely weak?
options: Orbicularis oculi, the ring muscle around the eye
Superior rectus, which turns the eye upward
Inferior oblique, which turns the eye up
follow.why: The levator palpebrae superioris lifts the upper eyelid, so its weakness leaves the lid drooping. The orbicularis oculi closes the eye, and it still works because the eyes squeeze shut. The superior rectus and inferior oblique move the eyeball, not the lid.

labels.name: Palpebral conjunctiva
labels.fn: The part of the conjunctiva that lines the inner surface of the eyelids. It folds back onto the eyeball as the conjunctiva that covers the white of the eye.

labels.name: Eyelashes
labels.fn: Rows of stiff hairs along the eyelid margins. Touching them sets off a blink, which keeps particles off the surface of the eye.

labels.name: Cornea
labels.fn: The clear, curved front of the fibrous tunic, continuous with the sclera. It has no blood vessels and does most of the eye's bending (refraction) of incoming light.

labels.name: Conjunctiva
labels.fn: A thin mucous membrane covering the white of the eye and lining the eyelids. It stops at the edge of the cornea and keeps the eye's surface moist.

follow.q: In conjunctivitis ("pink eye") the conjunctiva is inflamed. Which part of the eye's surface stays clear, because the conjunctiva does not cover it?
follow.why: The conjunctiva covers the white of the eye and lines the eyelids, but it stops at the edge of the cornea. Its tiny blood vessels swell in conjunctivitis and turn the white and the lid linings red, while the cornea, which has no blood vessels, stays clear.

labels.name: Superior oblique muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle whose tendon loops through the trochlea before attaching to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye down, most strongly when the eye is turned in, and rotates its top inward.

labels.name: Trochlea
labels.fn: A small loop of cartilage ("pulley") at the upper inner corner of the orbit. The superior oblique tendon passes through it and changes direction toward the eyeball.

labels.name: Superior oblique tendon
labels.fn: The tendon of the superior oblique muscle. It passes through the trochlea, turns back and attaches to the top of the eyeball, so the muscle pulls from the front of the orbit.

follow.q: Why does the superior oblique pull the front of the eyeball down, even though the muscle itself lies along the top of the orbit?
options: It attaches to the lower surface of the eyeball
It starts from the floor of the orbit, below the eye
Its tendon turns through the trochlea at the front
It only works together with the inferior rectus muscle
follow.why: The tendon runs forward to the trochlea, turns back through it and attaches to the top of the eyeball behind its center. The pull therefore comes from the front inner corner of the orbit, which pulls the front of the eye down. The muscle attaches to the top of the eyeball and starts at the back of the orbit, not the floor.

labels.name: Superior rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye upward.

labels.name: Lateral rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the outer side of the eyeball. It turns the eye outward, away from the nose; the abducens nerve (VI) supplies it.

follow.q: A patient's left eye cannot turn outward, away from the nose. Which muscle, and which nerve, is most likely affected?
follow.why: The lateral rectus is the only muscle that turns the eye outward, and the abducens nerve supplies it alone. The medial rectus turns the eye inward, the superior oblique turns it down, most strongly when it is turned in, and the inferior rectus turns it down.

labels.name: Common tendinous ring
labels.fn: A ring of tendon at the back of the orbit around the optic nerve. The four rectus muscles all start from it.

labels.name: Inferior rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the bottom of the eyeball. It turns the eye downward.

labels.name: Inferior oblique muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the floor of the orbit under the eyeball to its outer side. It turns the eye up, most strongly when the eye is turned in, and rotates its top outward.

labels.name: Superior rectus
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye upward.

labels.name: Trochlea
labels.fn: A small loop of cartilage ("pulley") at the upper inner corner of the orbit. The superior oblique tendon passes through it and changes direction toward the eyeball.

labels.name: Superior oblique
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle whose tendon loops through the trochlea before attaching to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye down, most strongly when the eye is turned in, and rotates its top inward.

labels.name: Lateral rectus
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the outer side of the eyeball. It turns the eye outward, away from the nose; the abducens nerve (VI) supplies it.

labels.name: Medial rectus
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the side of the eyeball nearest the nose. It turns the eye inward, toward the nose.

labels.name: Inferior oblique
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the floor of the orbit under the eyeball to its outer side. It turns the eye up, most strongly when the eye is turned in, and rotates its top outward.

labels.name: Inferior rectus
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the bottom of the eyeball. It turns the eye downward.

labels.name: Posterior cavity (vitreous chamber)
labels.fn: The large space behind the lens, filled with the clear, jelly-like vitreous humor. The vitreous holds the eyeball's shape and presses the retina flat against the choroid.

labels.name: Superior rectus muscle
labels.fn: An extrinsic eye muscle that runs from the common tendinous ring to the top of the eyeball. It turns the eye upward.

labels.name: Scleral venous sinus (canal of Schlemm)
labels.fn: A ring-shaped channel where the sclera meets the cornea. Aqueous humor drains into it and back into the blood; if drainage fails, pressure in the eye rises (glaucoma).

follow.q: The scleral venous sinus becomes blocked. What happens inside the eye?
options: Vitreous humor drains away and the eyeball softens
The lens stiffens and can no longer change its shape
The pupil stays wide open because the iris is squeezed
Aqueous humor builds up and pressure in the eye rises
follow.why: The ciliary processes keep making aqueous humor, which normally drains through the scleral venous sinus. If it cannot drain, the fluid builds up and pressure rises (glaucoma), which can damage the optic nerve. The vitreous humor is not drained this way, and lens shape and pupil size depend on muscles.

labels.name: Sclera
labels.fn: The tough, white outer coat of the eyeball (fibrous tunic). It protects the eye, keeps its shape and gives the extrinsic eye muscles an attachment.

labels.name: Suspensory ligaments
labels.fn: Fine fibers (zonule fibers) that run from the ciliary body to the edge of the lens and hold it in place. Their pull on the lens sets how round it is.

labels.name: Choroid
labels.fn: The dark, blood-rich layer of the vascular tunic between the sclera and the retina. It feeds the outer retina and absorbs stray light.

labels.name: Lens
labels.fn: A clear, flexible disc behind the iris, held by the suspensory ligaments. It changes shape to fine-tune focus for near and far objects (accommodation).

labels.name: Cornea
labels.fn: The clear, curved front of the fibrous tunic, continuous with the sclera. It has no blood vessels and does most of the eye's bending (refraction) of incoming light.

labels.name: Retina
labels.fn: The inner, neural tunic of the eyeball. It holds the rods and cones that turn light into electrical signals, and the neurons that send those signals out through the optic nerve.

labels.name: Iris
labels.fn: The colored ring of the vascular tunic in front of the lens. Its two sets of smooth muscle change the size of the pupil and so control how much light enters.

labels.name: Pupil
labels.fn: The opening at the center of the iris. Light passes through it to the lens; it narrows in bright light and widens in dim light.

labels.name: Fovea centralis
labels.fn: A small pit in the center of the retina, packed with cones and without rods. It gives the sharpest, most detailed color vision.

labels.name: Anterior cavity (contains aqueous humor)
