labels.fn: A blind-ended tube of endothelium threaded among the blood capillaries. Fluid, protein and cells that have left the blood enter it between loosely overlapping endothelial cells.

labels.name: Tissue cells
labels.fn: The cells of the tissue, bathed by interstitial fluid. They trade nutrients and wastes with the blood through that fluid.

labels.name: Collagen fiber
labels.fn: A collagen fiber of the surrounding connective tissue. Fine anchoring filaments tie lymphatic capillaries to fibers like this, so when the tissue swells they pull the capillaries open.

labels.name: Arteriole
labels.fn: The small artery that feeds the capillary bed. Fluid filters out of the blood capillaries it supplies, and the lymphatic capillaries collect what is not taken back.

labels.name: Interstitial fluid
labels.fn: The fluid between the cells, filtered out of the blood capillaries. When its pressure is higher than the pressure inside a lymphatic capillary, it pushes the endothelial flaps inward and flows in.

labels.name: Venule
labels.fn: The small vein that drains the capillary bed. The blood capillaries take back only part of the fluid that filtered out; the rest returns to the blood through the lymphatic vessels.

labels.name: Lymph (interstitial fluid)
labels.fn: Interstitial fluid is called lymph once it enters a lymphatic vessel. The fluid itself does not change at that moment: water, small solutes, some protein, and cells.

labels.name: Tissue fluid
labels.fn: Another name for interstitial fluid: the fluid filtered from the blood capillaries that bathes the cells until lymphatic capillaries collect it.

labels.name: Lymphatic vessel
labels.fn: A collecting vessel formed as lymphatic capillaries join. Its one-way valves and the smooth muscle in its wall move lymph toward the lymph nodes and on to the veins.

labels.name: Endothelial “flaps”
labels.fn: The loosely overlapping edges of neighboring endothelial cells. Higher pressure outside pushes them inward so fluid enters; higher pressure inside presses them shut, so lymph cannot leak back out.

follow.q: The pressure inside a lymphatic capillary rises above the pressure of the interstitial fluid around it. What do the endothelial flaps do?
options: They press shut and hold the lymph in
They open wider and lymph flows back out
They contract and pump lymph forward
They let water out but hold protein in
follow.why: The flaps are loosely overlapping cell edges that act as one-way inlets. Higher pressure outside pushes them inward so fluid enters; higher pressure inside presses them against the cell they overlap, so lymph cannot leak back out. They do not contract (smooth muscle in the collecting vessels pumps lymph), and the gaps are wide enough for protein, so they do not sort water from protein.

labels.name: Lymph vessel endothelial cells
labels.fn: The flat endothelial cells that make up the lymphatic capillary wall. They overlap loosely instead of sealing together, leaving gaps wide enough for protein, cells and bacteria.

labels.name: Backflow prevention valve
labels.fn: A one-way valve inside the lymphatic vessel. Lymph moving toward the heart pushes it open and backflow closes it, so each squeeze of the vessel moves lymph forward.

labels.name: Right lymphatic duct
labels.fn: The short duct serving the right arm, the right side of the chest and the right side of the head and neck. It empties where the right internal jugular vein meets the right subclavian vein.

labels.name: Right internal jugular vein
labels.fn: The deep vein draining the right side of the head and neck. The right lymphatic duct empties into the angle where it joins the right subclavian vein.

labels.name: Left internal jugular vein
labels.fn: The deep vein draining the left side of the head and neck. The thoracic duct empties into its junction with the left subclavian vein.

labels.name: Thoracic duct drains into subclavian vein
labels.fn: The end of the thoracic duct, the largest lymphatic vessel, where it pours lymph into the blood at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins.

labels.name: Right subclavian vein
labels.fn: The vein draining the right arm. Lymph from the right lymphatic duct enters the blood where it joins the right internal jugular vein.

labels.name: Left subclavian vein
labels.fn: The vein draining the left arm. Where it meets the left internal jugular vein, the thoracic duct empties lymph into the blood.

labels.name: Thoracic duct
labels.fn: The larger of the two lymphatic ducts. It runs up in front of the spine through the chest and drains about three quarters of the body: both legs, the abdomen and pelvis, and the left side of the upper body.

follow.q: A splinter wound in your left foot becomes infected. Through which vessel does lymph from the foot finally reach the blood?
options: A vein in the foot, straight from the lymphatic capillaries
follow.why: Lymph from the left leg passes through nodes behind the knee and in the groin, joins the lumbar trunk and the cisterna chyli, and climbs the thoracic duct, which empties at the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins. The right lymphatic duct drains only the right upper body. Lymphatic capillaries do not open into veins in the tissues, and the spleen filters blood, not lymph.

labels.name: Cisterna chyli of thoracic duct
labels.fn: The sac at the start of the thoracic duct, in the upper abdomen in front of the first two lumbar vertebrae. It receives lymph from the legs, pelvis and gut through the lumbar and intestinal trunks.

labels.name: Drained by right lymphatic duct
labels.fn: The region whose lymph returns through the right lymphatic duct: the right arm, the right side of the chest and the right side of the head and neck, about a quarter of the body.

labels.name: Drained by thoracic duct
labels.fn: The region whose lymph returns through the thoracic duct: both legs, the abdomen and pelvis, the left arm, and the left side of the chest, head and neck, about three quarters of the body.

labels.name: Afferent lymphatic vessel
labels.fn: One of several vessels that bring lymph into the node, entering all over its curved surface. Valves in them stop backflow.

labels.name: Capsule
labels.fn: The layer of dense connective tissue around the node. It sends trabeculae inward as partitions.

labels.name: Subcapsular sinus
labels.fn: The narrow space just under the capsule where lymph from the afferent vessels first pours in. From here it trickles through sinuses lined with macrophages.

labels.name: Lymphoid nodule
labels.fn: A round cluster of lymphocytes in the outer cortex, also called a follicle. Its lymphocytes belong to the line that can turn into antibody-releasing cells.

labels.name: Germinal center
labels.fn: The paler middle of a lymphoid nodule. It forms when the nodule's lymphocytes meet the antigen they recognize, and they multiply rapidly there.

follow.q: A lymph node under your jaw swells during a sore throat. Which change inside the node best explains the swelling?
options: Its lymphocytes multiply in germinal centers
Red blood cells pile up in its sinuses
Its efferent vessel widens so lymph drains faster
follow.why: When the lymphocytes of a nodule meet the antigen they recognize, they multiply rapidly in a germinal center, and more lymphocytes are held in the node, so it swells. Fat does not fill the capsule, red blood cells are filtered by the spleen rather than lymph nodes, and faster drainage would shrink a node.

labels.name: Cortex
labels.fn: The outer region of the node, just inside the capsule and subcapsular sinus. It holds the lymphoid nodules.

labels.name: Paracortex
labels.fn: The deep cortex, between the nodules and the medulla. It holds mostly the thymus-matured line of lymphocytes, which enter the node from the blood through high endothelial venules.

labels.name: Medulla
labels.fn: The inner region nearest the hilum: cords of lymphocytes and macrophages, with medullary sinuses between them that carry lymph toward the efferent vessel.

labels.name: Trabecula
labels.fn: A partition of connective tissue running inward from the capsule. Trabeculae support the node and divide it into compartments.

labels.name: Efferent lymphatic vessel
labels.fn: The vessel that carries lymph out at the hilum. There are fewer efferent than afferent vessels, which slows lymph in the node and gives macrophages time to clear it.

follow.q: Why does lymph move slowly through a lymph node?
options: More vessels bring lymph in than carry it out
The capsule squeezes the lymph back upstream
The node has no sinuses for lymph to flow through
The efferent vessel is wider than the afferent ones
follow.why: Several afferent vessels enter, but only one or two efferent vessels leave, and the maze of sinuses has a wide total cross section, so lymph lingers and macrophages have time to clear it. The capsule does not pump lymph, the node is full of sinuses, and a single wide outlet would speed flow, not slow it.

labels.name: Hilum
labels.fn: The indented side of the node, where the efferent lymphatic vessel leaves and the node's artery and vein enter and leave.

labels.name: Artery
labels.fn: The node's artery, entering at the hilum. It feeds blood capillaries inside the node, which take back a good share of the lymph's water.

labels.name: Vein
labels.fn: The node's vein, leaving at the hilum. Lymphocytes leave the blood and enter the node through its small venules, the high endothelial venules of the paracortex.

labels.name: Splenic artery
labels.fn: The artery that brings blood to the spleen, entering at its hilum. The spleen filters this blood; it receives no lymph.

labels.name: Splenic vein
labels.fn: The vein that carries blood away from the spleen at its hilum, after the red pulp has filtered it.

labels.name: Hilum
labels.fn: The indented side of the spleen, where the splenic artery enters and the splenic vein leaves. Unlike a lymph node, the spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels arriving here.

follow.q: Which structure does a lymph node have that the spleen lacks?
follow.why: The spleen filters blood, so nothing brings lymph into it: it has no afferent lymphatic vessels. Both organs have a connective tissue capsule, trabeculae running inward from it, and a hilum where vessels enter and leave.

labels.name: Capsule
labels.fn: The thin connective tissue covering of the spleen. It sends trabeculae inward.

labels.name: Trabecula
labels.fn: A connective tissue partition running inward from the capsule. It supports the soft tissue of the spleen and carries blood vessels into it.

labels.name: White pulp
labels.fn: Pale islands of lymphoid tissue wrapped around the central arteries, arranged much like a lymph node's cortex and paracortex. Here lymphocytes meet antigens carried in the blood.

labels.name: Central artery
labels.fn: The small artery at the core of each island of white pulp. Its blood passes the lymphocytes of the white pulp before flowing on into the red pulp.

labels.name: Red pulp
labels.fn: The dark red tissue that fills about three quarters of the spleen: blood in spongy cords of reticular tissue. Its macrophages remove old and damaged red blood cells, platelets and bacteria.

follow.q: Where in the spleen are old, stiff red blood cells trapped and destroyed?
follow.why: In the red pulp, blood must squeeze from the cords through narrow slits into the venous sinuses; stiff old red cells get stuck and macrophages engulf them. The white pulp is lymphoid tissue where lymphocytes meet antigens, the central artery only carries blood in, and the capsule is a covering.

labels.name: Venous sinus
labels.fn: A wide, leaky channel in the red pulp. Blood must squeeze through narrow slits in its wall; an old, stiff red blood cell gets stuck, and a macrophage engulfs it.

labels.name: Root
labels.fn: The top of the external nose, where it meets the forehead between the eyes.

labels.name: Bridge
labels.fn: The upper, bony part of the nose's ridge, just below the root. The nasal bones form it.

labels.name: Dorsum nasi
labels.fn: The ridge of the external nose, running from the root down to the tip.

labels.name: Ala
labels.fn: The flared wing on each side of the nose. Cartilage stiffens it, and it forms the outer wall of a nostril.

labels.name: Apex
labels.fn: The tip of the external nose.

labels.name: Philtrum
labels.fn: The vertical groove between the bottom of the nose and the upper lip. It is a landmark of the face, not part of the airway.

labels.name: Frontal bone
labels.fn: The forehead bone. Its lower edge meets the nasal bones at the root of the nose.

labels.name: Nasal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of small bones that form the bony bridge of the nose.

labels.name: Maxillary bone
labels.fn: The upper jaw bone. Its upward process sits beside the nasal bone and frames the side of the nasal opening.

labels.name: Septal cartilage
labels.fn: The plate of hyaline cartilage that forms the front of the nasal septum, the wall between the left and right sides of the nasal cavity. Along the top of the nose it spreads into a wing on each side that shapes the side of the nose, and this line points to that wing.

follow.q: The septal cartilage forms part of which structure?
follow.why: The septal cartilage is the front of the nasal septum, the midline wall that splits the nasal cavity into left and right halves. The conchae are shelves on the side walls, the ala is supported by the alar cartilage, and the frontal sinus is a space in the frontal bone.

labels.name: Major alar cartilage
labels.fn: The curved cartilage that shapes the tip of the nose and the ala on each side, holding the nostril open.

labels.name: Septal cartilage
labels.fn: The plate of hyaline cartilage that forms the front of the nasal septum, the wall between the left and right sides of the nasal cavity.

labels.name: Sphenoidal sinus
labels.fn: An air-filled space in the sphenoid bone, behind and above the nasal cavity. Like the other paranasal sinuses, it is lined with mucous membrane and drains into the nasal cavity.

labels.name: Frontal sinus
labels.fn: An air-filled space in the frontal bone above the eyes. It drains into the nasal cavity; the sinuses make the skull lighter and add mucus and moisture to the air.

labels.name: Ethmoid bone
labels.fn: The skull bone between the eye sockets. Its thin, perforated roof plate forms the top of the nasal cavity, and the nerve fibers for smell pass up through its holes.

labels.name: Olfactory epithelium
labels.fn: The patch of epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity that holds the sensory receptors for smell.

labels.name: Nasal meatuses (superior, middle, and inferior)
labels.fn: The grooves of air space under each nasal concha. Air flowing through these narrow channels touches a large area of warm, moist lining.

labels.name: Nasal conchae
labels.fn: The three curled shelves (superior, middle and inferior) on each side wall of the nasal cavity. They make inhaled air swirl against the warm, moist mucous membrane, which warms, humidifies and cleans it.

follow.q: What do the nasal conchae do to the air you breathe in?
options: Close off the nasal cavity whenever you swallow
Hold the sensory receptors that detect smells
Make it swirl so the lining can warm and clean it
Vibrate to make the sound of the voice
follow.why: The curled conchae break the airstream into turbulent flow, so more air touches the warm, moist, mucus-covered lining, which warms it, adds water and traps particles. The sensory receptors for smell sit in the olfactory epithelium in the roof, and the voice comes from the vocal folds.

labels.name: Pharyngeal tonsil
labels.fn: Lymphoid tissue on the back wall of the nasopharynx, also called the adenoid. It traps microbes carried in with the air; when it swells in a child it can block breathing through the nose.

follow.q: A child's pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) is badly swollen. Which is it most likely to block?
follow.why: The pharyngeal tonsil sits in the nasopharynx, the air-only passage behind the nasal cavity. A swollen one blocks air coming from the nose, so the child breathes through the mouth. Food and mouth breathing use the oropharynx below it, and the glottis is in the larynx.

labels.name: Nasal vestibule
labels.fn: The skin-lined entrance just inside each nostril. Its coarse hairs filter large particles out of incoming air.

labels.name: Opening of auditory tube
labels.fn: Where the auditory tube opens into the nasopharynx. The tube links the middle ear to the throat, so air pressure on both sides of the eardrum can equalize.

labels.name: Nostril
labels.fn: One of the two openings of the nose (the nares), through which air enters the nasal cavity.

labels.name: Nasopharynx
labels.fn: The upper part of the pharynx, behind the nasal cavity. Only air passes through it, and its ciliated lining sweeps mucus down toward the throat.

labels.name: Tongue
labels.fn: The muscular organ on the floor of the mouth. It belongs to the digestive system, but its back forms the front wall of the oropharynx.

labels.name: Palatine tonsil
labels.fn: Lymphoid tissue in each side wall of the oropharynx. It samples microbes entering through the mouth.

labels.name: Lingual tonsil
labels.fn: Lymphoid tissue at the back of the tongue, in the front wall of the oropharynx.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. When you swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds down over its opening, steering food and drink toward the esophagus.

follow.q: What does the epiglottis do each time you swallow?
options: Rises to seal the nasal cavity from the throat
Folds down over the entrance to the larynx
Vibrates to make a swallowing sound
follow.why: As the larynx is pulled up during a swallow, the epiglottis tips down over its entrance, so food slides past into the esophagus instead of the airway. It does not seal the nose, make sound or work the auditory tube.

labels.name: Oropharynx
labels.fn: The middle part of the pharynx, behind the mouth. Both air and food pass through it, so it is lined with stratified squamous epithelium that stands up to rubbing.

follow.q: Why is the oropharynx lined with stratified squamous epithelium instead of a ciliated lining like the nasopharynx?
options: Oxygen must diffuse across it quickly into the blood
Swallowed food would wear a thin lining away
It makes the mucus that traps dust
It never comes into contact with air
follow.why: Food passes through the oropharynx, and many layers of flat cells can lose their surface cells to friction and still protect the tissue beneath. Gas exchange does not happen in the pharynx, the mucus comes from goblet cells and glands, and air passes through the oropharynx on every breath.

labels.name: Hyoid bone
labels.fn: The U-shaped bone in the upper neck that does not join any other bone. The larynx hangs from it, and tongue and neck muscles attach to it.

labels.name: Laryngopharynx
labels.fn: The lowest part of the pharynx, behind the larynx. It leads forward into the larynx for air and back into the esophagus for food.

labels.name: Vestibular fold
labels.fn: The upper pair of folds in the larynx, also called the false vocal cords. They do not make the voice; they help close the larynx to protect the airway.

labels.name: Thyroid cartilage
labels.fn: The largest cartilage of the larynx, a shield of hyaline cartilage in the front of the neck. Its front ridge is the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple).

labels.name: Vocal fold
labels.fn: The lower pair of folds in the larynx, the true vocal cords. Air pushed out between them makes them vibrate, which produces the voice.

labels.name: Cricoid cartilage
labels.fn: The ring of hyaline cartilage at the bottom of the larynx, the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway. The trachea begins just below it.

labels.name: Nasal cavity
labels.fn: The air space inside the nose, divided into left and right by the nasal septum. Its mucous membrane warms, moistens and cleans the air you breathe in.

labels.name: Tongue
labels.fn: The muscular organ on the floor of the mouth. It belongs to the digestive system, but its back forms the front wall of the oropharynx.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx that folds down over the laryngeal opening during a swallow.

labels.name: Larynx (voice box)
labels.fn: The voice box: a short tube of cartilages, ligaments and membranes between the laryngopharynx and the trachea. It keeps the airway open, guards it during swallowing and makes the voice.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: The muscular tube behind the trachea that carries swallowed food from the laryngopharynx to the stomach. It is part of the digestive tract, not the airway.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe, which carries air from the larynx down into the chest. It lies in front of the esophagus.

labels.name: Nasopharynx
labels.fn: The upper part of the pharynx (green here), behind the nasal cavity. Only air passes through it.

labels.name: Oropharynx
labels.fn: The middle part of the pharynx (teal here), behind the mouth. Air and food both pass through it.

labels.name: Laryngopharynx
labels.fn: The lowest part of the pharynx (purple here), behind the larynx. It opens into both the larynx and the esophagus.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. It folds down over the laryngeal opening when you swallow.

labels.name: Body of hyoid bone
labels.fn: The front, central part of the U-shaped hyoid bone. The larynx hangs from it by the thyrohyoid membrane.

labels.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
labels.fn: The sheet of connective tissue joining the top of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. It suspends the larynx from the hyoid.

labels.name: Thyroid cartilage
labels.fn: The largest cartilage of the larynx: two plates of hyaline cartilage joined in front like a shield. It protects the vocal folds, which attach to its inner surface.

labels.name: Laryngeal prominence
labels.fn: The ridge at the front of the thyroid cartilage where its two plates meet, known as the Adam's apple. It is usually larger in adult men.

labels.name: Cricothyroid ligament
labels.fn: The band of connective tissue between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below. It lies just under the skin, below the vocal folds.

follow.q: Something is stuck at the vocal folds and the person cannot breathe. Where can an emergency airway be opened through the front of the neck, below the blockage?
follow.why: The cricothyroid ligament lies just under the skin between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, below the level of the vocal folds, so an opening there bypasses a blockage at the glottis. The thyrohyoid membrane is above the vocal folds, the laryngeal prominence is solid cartilage, and the epiglottis is at the top of the larynx.

labels.name: Cricoid cartilage
labels.fn: The ring of hyaline cartilage at the base of the larynx. It is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, and the trachea hangs from it.

follow.q: What sets the cricoid cartilage apart from the other cartilages of the airway?
options: It vibrates to produce the sound of the voice
It is the airway's only complete ring
It is made of elastic cartilage so it can fold
It hangs directly from the body of the hyoid bone
follow.why: The cricoid is a full ring, like a signet ring with its wide part at the back, so it holds the lower larynx open all the way around. The vocal folds make the voice, the epiglottis is the elastic cartilage, and the thyroid cartilage is the one that hangs from the hyoid bone.

labels.name: Cricotracheal ligament
labels.fn: The ligament that joins the bottom of the cricoid cartilage to the top of the trachea.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. It folds down over the laryngeal opening when you swallow.

labels.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
labels.fn: The sheet of connective tissue joining the top of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. It suspends the larynx from the hyoid.

labels.name: Body of hyoid bone
labels.fn: The front, central part of the U-shaped hyoid bone. The larynx hangs from it by the thyrohyoid membrane.

labels.name: Fatty pad
labels.fn: A pad of fat in front of the epiglottis, between it and the hyoid bone and thyrohyoid membrane. It gives the epiglottis a soft cushion to move against.

labels.name: Cuneiform cartilage
labels.fn: A small rod of elastic cartilage in the fold of tissue that runs from each arytenoid cartilage up to the epiglottis. It stiffens that fold.

labels.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
labels.fn: The sheet of connective tissue joining the top of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. It suspends the larynx from the hyoid.

labels.name: Corniculate cartilage
labels.fn: A small horn-shaped cartilage perched on top of each arytenoid cartilage.

labels.name: Vestibular fold
labels.fn: The upper pair of folds in the larynx, the false vocal cords. They do not make the voice; they help close off the larynx.

labels.name: Arytenoid cartilage
labels.fn: One of a pair of small pyramid-shaped cartilages sitting on the back of the cricoid cartilage. The vocal folds attach to them, and muscles that swivel them open and close the gap between the folds.

follow.q: Small muscles pivot the arytenoid cartilages. What does that change?
options: The tension and spacing of the vocal folds
How far the nasal conchae stick out into the air
Where the hyoid bone sits in the neck
Whether the auditory tube is open
follow.why: The back ends of the vocal folds attach to the arytenoid cartilages, so rotating or sliding them spreads the folds apart for breathing, brings them together for speech, and changes how tight they are, which changes the pitch. The conchae, hyoid and auditory tube are not moved by these muscles.

labels.name: Vocal fold
labels.fn: The lower pair of folds in the larynx, the true vocal cords. Air pushed between them makes them vibrate and produce sound.

follow.q: You take a breath, hold it and bear down to lift something heavy. What closes the airway?
options: The vocal folds close the glottis
The epiglottis rises to seal the nose
follow.why: Muscles pull the vocal folds together so the glottis, the opening between them, is shut and air is held in the chest. The epiglottis covers the larynx during swallowing and never seals the nose, and the cricoid and thyroid cartilages are rigid.

labels.name: Thyroid cartilage
labels.fn: The largest cartilage of the larynx: two plates of hyaline cartilage joined in front like a shield. It protects the vocal folds, which attach to its inner surface.

labels.name: Cricoid cartilage
labels.fn: The ring of hyaline cartilage at the base of the larynx. It is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, and the trachea hangs from it.

labels.name: Cricothyroid ligament
labels.fn: The band of connective tissue between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below. It lies just under the skin, below the vocal folds.

labels.name: Cricotracheal ligament
labels.fn: The ligament that joins the bottom of the cricoid cartilage to the top of the trachea.

labels.name: Pyriform fossa
labels.fn: A pocket of the laryngopharynx on each side of the larynx. Swallowed food and drink run through these pockets around the larynx on the way to the esophagus, and a fish bone can catch here.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: The entrance to the esophagus, behind the larynx. Swallowed food goes here, not into the airway.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe, seen here through the open glottis below the vocal folds.

labels.name: True vocal cord
labels.fn: The true vocal cord (vocal fold): the pale band on each side of the glottis. Air passing between the two cords makes them vibrate, producing the voice. They look pearly white because a thick stratified squamous lining covers a vocal ligament with few blood vessels.

follow.q: What makes the true vocal cords produce a sound?
options: Nerve signals alone, with the glottis shut
The epiglottis striking them as it folds down
Air breathed out making them vibrate
The tongue pressing on them from above
follow.why: Sound comes from air pushed up from the lungs between the nearly closed cords, which sets them vibrating. Muscles set their tension and spacing, but without airflow there is no sound. The epiglottis and tongue do not make them vibrate.

labels.name: Vestibular fold
labels.fn: The false vocal cord on each side, above the true vocal cord. It does not make the voice; it helps close off the larynx.

labels.name: Glottis
labels.fn: The vocal folds together with the opening between them. Widening it lets air through; closing it stops air, as when you hold your breath or build up pressure for a cough.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The epiglottis seen from above, at the front of the laryngeal opening. It folds back over the opening during swallowing.

labels.name: Tongue
labels.fn: The back of the tongue, which forms the front wall of the oropharynx.

labels.name: Nasal cavity
labels.fn: The air space inside the nose, where inhaled air is warmed, moistened and cleaned.

labels.name: Nostril
labels.fn: One of the two openings of the nose (the nares), where air enters the nasal cavity.

labels.name: Pharynx
labels.fn: The throat: a muscular tube, shared by air and food, that runs from behind the nasal cavity down to the larynx and the esophagus.

labels.name: Larynx
labels.fn: The voice box, between the pharynx and the trachea. It keeps the airway open, guards it during swallowing and makes the voice.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe: a tube held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that carries air from the larynx into the chest, where it splits into the two main bronchi.

labels.name: Right main bronchus
labels.fn: The first branch of the trachea to the right lung. It is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left main bronchus.

follow.q: A child breathes in a peanut. It most often lodges in the right main bronchus. Why?
options: It is wider and more vertical than the left
It has more cartilage rings, which catch objects
It is longer than the left main bronchus
The heart presses the left one shut
follow.why: The right main bronchus is wider and continues almost straight down from the trachea, so an object falling down the airway tends to follow it. The left bronchus angles off more sharply to pass beside the heart, but the heart does not close it, and cartilage rings do not catch objects.

labels.name: Left main bronchus
labels.fn: The first branch of the trachea to the left lung. It is longer, narrower and more horizontal than the right, because it runs out beside the heart.

labels.name: Right lung
labels.fn: The right lung, which has three lobes and is larger than the left.

labels.name: Left lung
labels.fn: The left lung, which has two lobes and a notch where the heart sits, so it is smaller than the right.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle under the lungs that separates the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities. When it contracts it flattens, making the chest cavity larger and drawing air in.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe: a tube held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that carries air from the larynx into the chest, where it splits into the two main bronchi.

labels.name: Superior lobe
labels.fn: The upper lobe of the left lung, separated from its inferior lobe by the oblique fissure.

labels.name: Superior lobe
labels.fn: The upper lobe of the right lung, separated from the middle lobe by the horizontal fissure.

labels.name: Main (primary) bronchus
labels.fn: A main (primary) bronchus: one of the two first branches of the trachea. Each enters its lung at the hilum.

labels.name: Lobar (secondary) bronchus
labels.fn: A lobar (secondary) bronchus: a branch of a main bronchus that supplies one lobe. The right lung has three and the left has two.

follow.q: Which airway supplies one whole lobe of a lung?
follow.why: Each main bronchus serves a whole lung and splits into lobar bronchi, one per lobe. Each lobar bronchus then splits into segmental bronchi, one per segment of the lobe, and the branching continues down to the terminal bronchioles.

labels.name: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus
labels.fn: A segmental (tertiary) bronchus: a branch of a lobar bronchus that supplies one segment of a lobe. Each segment has its own airway and blood supply.

labels.name: Middle lobe
labels.fn: The middle lobe, found only in the right lung, between its superior and inferior lobes.

follow.q: How many lobes does each lung have?
follow.why: The right lung has superior, middle and inferior lobes. The left has only superior and inferior lobes, because the heart takes up room on the left side.

labels.name: Cardiac notch
labels.fn: The indentation in the front edge of the left lung that makes room for the heart.

labels.name: Inferior lobe
labels.fn: The lower lobe of the right lung, resting on the diaphragm below the oblique fissure.

labels.name: Inferior lobe
labels.fn: The lower lobe of the left lung, resting on the diaphragm below the oblique fissure.

labels.name: Right lung
labels.fn: The right lung, which has three lobes and is larger than the left.

labels.name: Left lung
labels.fn: The left lung, which has two lobes and a notch where the heart sits, so it is smaller than the right.

labels.name: Intercostal muscle
labels.fn: The muscle between two neighboring ribs, part of the chest wall. The intercostal muscles move the ribs when you breathe.

labels.name: Lung
labels.fn: The surface of the lung, covered by the visceral pleura. Inside, the lung is spongy, filled with branching airways and tiny air sacs.

labels.name: Lung
labels.fn: The left lung, wrapped in its pleural sac. It is soft and spongy, filled with branching airways and tiny air sacs.

labels.name: Pleural sac
labels.fn: The pleura around one lung: a closed sac of serous membrane with two layers, one on the lung and one on the chest wall, and the pleural cavity between them.

labels.name: Parietal pleura
labels.fn: The outer layer of the pleura. It lines the inside of the chest wall, the top of the diaphragm and the side of the mediastinum.

labels.name: Intercostal muscles
labels.fn: The muscle between two neighboring ribs, part of the chest wall. The intercostal muscles move the ribs when you breathe.

labels.name: Visceral pleura
labels.fn: The inner layer of the pleura, stuck to the surface of the lung and dipping into its fissures.

labels.name: Pleural cavity
labels.fn: The thin space between the parietal and visceral pleura. A film of pleural fluid in it lets the layers slide and holds the lung against the chest wall.

follow.q: What does the pleural cavity of a healthy person contain?
options: Air that fills the lungs with each breath
A thin film of pleural fluid
Nothing at all, since the layers are fused
follow.why: The two pleural layers are separated only by a thin film of serous fluid. It lets them glide over each other and makes them cling together, so the lung follows the chest wall. Air in this space is abnormal, and blood stays inside vessels.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle under the lungs that separates the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities. When it contracts it flattens, making the chest cavity larger and drawing air in.

labels.name: Chest wall (rib cage, sternum, thoracic vertebrae, connective tissue, intercostal muscles)
labels.fn: Everything that encloses the thoracic cavity: the rib cage, sternum, thoracic vertebrae, connective tissue and intercostal muscles. The pleura links the lungs to it, so the lungs follow its movements.

labels.name: Terminal bronchiole
labels.fn: The last airway of the conducting zone. Its wall has no alveoli, so it only carries air.

labels.name: Smooth muscle
labels.fn: Bands of smooth muscle that wrap the bronchioles. Contracting narrows the airway and relaxing widens it, which changes how easily air flows.

follow.q: The smooth muscle around a bronchiole contracts. What happens to air flow through that bronchiole?
options: It rises, because the airway widens
It falls, because the airway narrows
It stays the same, since cartilage holds it open
follow.why: Contraction squeezes the bronchiole to a smaller radius, and a narrower tube resists flow much more, so less air gets through. Bronchioles have no cartilage to hold them open, which is why their smooth muscle controls their size.

labels.name: Deoxygenated blood from pulmonary artery
accept: deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery
labels.fn: A branch of the pulmonary artery bringing oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the capillaries around the alveoli.

follow.q: The blood reaching the alveolar capillaries from the pulmonary artery is:
options: Oxygen-rich, from the aorta through the bronchial arteries
follow.why: The pulmonary circuit starts at the right ventricle, which pumps oxygen-poor blood returning from the body into the pulmonary trunk and arteries. The left ventricle and aorta carry oxygen-rich blood to the body, and the left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

labels.name: Oxygenated blood to pulmonary vein
accept: oxygenated blood to the pulmonary vein
labels.fn: A vessel carrying oxygen-rich blood away from the alveolar capillaries toward the pulmonary veins, which return it to the left atrium.

labels.name: Respiratory bronchiole
labels.fn: The first airway of the respiratory zone: a bronchiole with a few alveoli budding from its wall, so gases start to move between air and blood here.

follow.q: Where does the respiratory zone begin?
follow.why: The respiratory zone starts where alveoli first appear, in the walls of the respiratory bronchioles. Everything above that, down to and including the terminal bronchioles, is conducting zone that only moves air.

labels.name: Alveolus
labels.fn: A tiny air sac whose wall is mostly very thin type I alveolar cells, wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across this thin wall.

follow.q: What makes the wall of an alveolus suited to moving gases between air and blood?
options: It is lined with a thick layer of mucus
It is stiffened by plates of cartilage
It is wrapped in bands of smooth muscle
follow.why: Diffusion is fast only over short distances, and the alveolar wall is a single layer of very flat cells pressed against capillaries. Mucus, cartilage or muscle in the way would thicken the barrier and slow diffusion.

labels.name: Alveolar sac
labels.fn: A cluster of alveoli at the end of an alveolar duct, like a bunch of grapes.

labels.name: Capillaries
labels.fn: The dense net of capillaries around the alveoli, where the blood picks up oxygen and gives up carbon dioxide.

labels.name: Alveolar duct
labels.fn: A short passage off a respiratory bronchiole whose wall is made almost entirely of alveoli. It leads to the alveolar sacs.

labels.name: Alveolar pores
labels.fn: Small openings in the walls between neighboring alveoli. They let air pass from one alveolus to the next, which evens out pressure and gives air a way around a blocked airway.

labels.name: Mouth
labels.fn: The entry to the tract. Teeth and tongue break food up and mix it with saliva, which starts the digestion of starch.

labels.name: Tongue
labels.fn: A muscular organ on the floor of the mouth. It moves food between the teeth, mixes it with saliva and pushes it back toward the throat to be swallowed.

labels.name: Pharynx
labels.fn: The throat: a muscular passage shared by food and air. When you swallow, its muscles push food down into the esophagus.

follow.q: Which of these tubes carries both food and air?
follow.why: The pharynx (throat) is the shared passage behind the nose and mouth: air passes through it to the larynx, and food passes through it to the esophagus. The esophagus carries only food, the trachea only air, and the large intestine only food residue.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: A muscular tube behind the trachea that carries swallowed food from the pharynx to the stomach by peristalsis. It absorbs nothing.

labels.name: Liver
labels.fn: The largest internal organ, under the right side of the diaphragm. An accessory organ: food never passes through it, but it makes bile, which it sends to the small intestine through ducts.

follow.q: Food does not pass through the liver, yet it is part of the digestive system. Why?
options: It stores swallowed food between meals
It makes bile for the small intestine
It squeezes the stomach during mixing
It absorbs water from the colon
follow.why: The liver is an accessory organ: it makes bile and sends it through ducts into the small intestine, where bile helps break fat into small droplets. Food itself travels only through the alimentary canal. The stomach, not the liver, holds food, and the colon absorbs its own water.

labels.name: Stomach
labels.fn: A J-shaped muscular sac below the diaphragm on the left. It stores a meal, churns it with acid and enzymes, and releases it a little at a time into the small intestine.

labels.name: Gallbladder
labels.fn: A small sac under the liver that stores and concentrates bile, then squeezes it into the small intestine after a fatty meal. An accessory organ.

labels.name: Spleen
labels.fn: A lymphatic organ that filters blood and removes old red blood cells. It sits beside the stomach but is not part of the digestive system; the figure shows it only for position.

follow.q: Which labeled organ in this view belongs to a different organ system?
follow.why: The spleen is a lymphatic organ that filters blood. The pancreas and gallbladder are accessory digestive organs that send secretions into the small intestine, and the esophagus is part of the alimentary canal.

labels.name: Pancreas
labels.fn: A long gland behind the stomach. As an accessory digestive organ it sends digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the small intestine through a duct; its islets also release insulin and glucagon into the blood.

labels.name: Appendix
labels.fn: A narrow, closed-ended tube hanging from the first part of the large intestine. It holds lymphatic tissue; food does not pass through it.

labels.name: Anus
labels.fn: The opening at the end of the tract, closed by sphincter muscles, through which feces leave the body (defecation).

hints.why: A group heading over the labels below it, not one structure: masked in the quiz because it names the group they belong to.
A group heading over the labels below it, not one structure: masked in the quiz because it names the group they belong to.

labels.name: Spinal cord
labels.fn: The spinal cord inside the vertebral canal, at the back of this cross section. It marks posterior, so you can orient the section.

labels.name: Vertebra
labels.fn: The bony vertebra at the back of the section. The organs pressed against the back wall behind the peritoneum lie beside it.

labels.name: Kidney
labels.fn: A kidney lying against the back wall, behind the parietal peritoneum. Organs in this position are retroperitoneal: they sit outside the peritoneal cavity.

labels.name: Kidney
labels.fn: The other kidney, also against the back wall behind the parietal peritoneum, so it is retroperitoneal.

follow.q: The kidneys lie behind the parietal peritoneum, against the back wall. What is this position called?
follow.why: Retroperitoneal means behind the peritoneum: the organ is covered by parietal peritoneum on its front only and is not hung in the cavity by a mesentery. Intraperitoneal organs, such as the stomach, are wrapped in visceral peritoneum and suspended by mesenteries.

labels.name: Spleen
labels.fn: The spleen on the left, wrapped in peritoneum. A lymphatic organ, shown here for position only.

labels.name: Pancreas
labels.fn: The pancreas lying across the back wall behind the stomach. Most of it is retroperitoneal: parietal peritoneum covers only its front.

labels.name: Small intestine
labels.fn: Coils of small intestine, hung from the back wall by a mesentery, a double fold of peritoneum that carries its vessels and nerves.

labels.name: Liver
labels.fn: The liver on the right, covered almost entirely by visceral peritoneum.

labels.name: Large intestine
labels.fn: A segment of large intestine cut across. Some parts of the colon are held against the back wall; others hang on a mesentery.

labels.name: Gallbladder
labels.fn: The gallbladder tucked under the liver, which stores bile.

labels.name: Large intestine
labels.fn: Another segment of large intestine, seen in cross section near the liver.

labels.name: Stomach
labels.fn: The stomach, wrapped in visceral peritoneum and suspended in the peritoneal cavity, so it can move and stretch as it fills.

labels.name: Small intestine
labels.fn: Another loop of small intestine, wrapped in visceral peritoneum and suspended in the peritoneal cavity.

labels.name: Visceral peritoneum
labels.fn: The inner layer of the peritoneum, fused to the surface of the organs. On the digestive tube it forms the serosa.

labels.name: Peritoneal cavity
labels.fn: The thin space between the parietal and visceral peritoneum. It holds only a little serous fluid, which lets the organs slide without friction.

follow.q: What normally fills the peritoneal cavity?
options: A thin film of serous fluid
follow.why: The peritoneal cavity is a potential space holding only a thin film of serous fluid that lets the visceral and parietal layers slide over each other. Food stays inside the lumen of the tract, and blood stays inside vessels.

labels.name: Parietal peritoneum
labels.fn: The outer layer of the peritoneum, lining the inside of the abdominal wall. It is continuous with the visceral layer through the mesenteries.

labels.name: Vein
labels.fn: A vein in the mesentery carrying blood away from the gut wall.

labels.name: Submucosal plexus (plexus of Meissner)
labels.fn: A network of enteric neurons in the submucosa. It mainly controls secretion by the glands and blood flow in the mucosa.

follow.q: Which nerve network mainly controls secretion and blood flow in the lining of the gut?
follow.why: The submucosal plexus lies just under the mucosa and mainly regulates gland secretion and local blood flow. The myenteric plexus, between the muscle layers, mainly controls motility. The vagus nerve can adjust both plexuses, but the gut wall runs these jobs through its own networks.

labels.name: Mesentery
labels.fn: A double fold of peritoneum that hangs the tube from the back wall and carries its blood vessels, lymphatic vessels and nerves.

labels.name: Artery
labels.fn: An artery in the mesentery bringing blood to the gut wall. Its branches run through the submucosa.

labels.name: Glands in submucosa
labels.fn: Glands in the submucosa (found only in some regions) whose ducts pass up through the mucosa to release mucus into the lumen.

labels.name: Nerve
labels.fn: A nerve in the mesentery linking the gut wall with the brain and spinal cord (the autonomic nervous system).

labels.name: Submucosa
labels.fn: The layer of dense connective tissue under the mucosa. It carries the larger blood and lymphatic vessels and the submucosal plexus.

follow.q: Which layer of the GI wall carries the larger blood vessels and a nerve plexus, just under the lining?
follow.why: The submucosa is connective tissue that holds the larger blood and lymphatic vessels and the submucosal plexus. The mucosa is the lining itself, the muscularis is the smooth muscle, and the serosa is the outer serous covering.

labels.name: Gland in mucosa
labels.fn: A gland in the mucosa that opens straight into the lumen and adds mucus or digestive secretions.

labels.name: Duct of gland outside tract
accept: duct of gland outside the tract
labels.fn: The duct of a gland that lies outside the tube wall, such as the liver or pancreas, carrying its secretion into the lumen.

labels.name: Myenteric plexus
labels.fn: A network of enteric neurons between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers. It mainly controls motility: the strength and rhythm of contractions.

follow.q: The myenteric plexus lies between the two muscle layers. What does it mainly control?
options: Blood clotting in the gut wall
follow.why: Sitting between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers, the myenteric plexus coordinates their contractions, so it mainly controls motility such as peristalsis and segmentation. Secretion and local blood flow are the submucosal plexus's main job.

labels.name: Lymphatic tissue
labels.fn: Clusters of lymphocytes in the mucosa (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) that guard against microbes arriving with food.

labels.name: Serosa
labels.fn: The outer layer of the wall in the abdomen: visceral peritoneum, a thin serous membrane of areolar connective tissue covered by a simple squamous epithelium.

labels.name: Lumen
labels.fn: The hollow center of the tube, where food moves and is digested. It is outside the body in the sense that nothing is absorbed until it crosses the mucosa.

labels.name: Areolar connective tissue
labels.fn: The loose connective tissue layer of the serosa, under its epithelium.

labels.name: Epithelium
labels.fn: The simple squamous epithelium on the outer surface of the serosa. It releases serous fluid so the organ slides smoothly against its neighbors.

labels.name: Mucosa
labels.fn: The innermost layer, lining the lumen: an epithelium, the lamina propria under it and a thin band of smooth muscle, the muscularis mucosae. It secretes, absorbs and protects.

follow.q: Which layer of the GI wall is in direct contact with food?
follow.why: The mucosa lines the lumen, so its epithelium touches food and does the secreting and absorbing. The submucosa and muscularis lie deeper, and the serosa covers the outside.

labels.name: Muscularis
labels.fn: The muscularis externa: smooth muscle in an inner circular and an outer longitudinal layer. Their contractions mix food and push it along.

labels.name: Epithelium
labels.fn: The epithelium lining the lumen. It is stratified squamous where food is rough (mouth, esophagus, anus) and simple columnar where the tract secretes and absorbs.

labels.name: Circular muscle
labels.fn: The inner layer of the muscularis, with fibers running around the tube. When it contracts it squeezes the tube narrower.

follow.q: Which muscle layer narrows the tube when it contracts, squeezing food ahead of it?
follow.why: Circular fibers run around the tube, so their contraction makes it narrower; a ring of contraction moving along is what pushes food in peristalsis. Longitudinal fibers shorten the tube, and the muscularis mucosae only moves the lining.

labels.name: Lamina propria
labels.fn: Areolar connective tissue under the mucosal epithelium, with capillaries and lymphatic vessels that take up absorbed nutrients, and lymphatic tissue.

labels.name: Longitudinal muscle
labels.fn: The outer layer of the muscularis, with fibers running along the tube. When it contracts it shortens the tube.

labels.name: Muscularis mucosae
labels.fn: A thin layer of smooth muscle at the bottom of the mucosa. It moves the lining in small folds, which helps mix and increases contact with the contents.

labels.name: Enamel
labels.fn: The hardest substance in the body, a mineral cap over the dentin of the crown. It has no living cells, so it cannot repair itself.

follow.q: Why can damaged enamel not grow back?
options: It has no living cells left
follow.why: The cells that make enamel are lost when the tooth erupts, so mature enamel is a nonliving mineral with no cells to repair it. Dentin, underneath, is made by cells that line the pulp cavity and can add more throughout life.

labels.name: Crown
labels.fn: The part of the tooth above the gum line, covered with enamel.

labels.name: Dentin
labels.fn: The bone-like tissue that makes up most of the tooth, under the enamel of the crown and the cementum of the root. It surrounds the pulp cavity.

follow.q: Which tissue forms the bulk of a tooth?
follow.why: Dentin, a mineralized tissue like bone, makes up most of the tooth. Enamel is only the outer cap of the crown, cementum is a thin layer over the root, and pulp is the soft tissue in the center.

labels.name: Gingiva (gum)
labels.fn: The gum: mucosa that surrounds the neck of the tooth and covers the bone of the socket.

labels.name: Neck
labels.fn: The narrow part of the tooth at the gum line, between the crown and the root.

labels.name: Pulp cavity (contains blood vessels and nerves)
labels.fn: The space in the center of the tooth filled with pulp: connective tissue with blood vessels and nerves that keep the dentin alive.

labels.name: Cementum
labels.fn: A thin bone-like layer over the dentin of the root. Fibers of the periodontal ligament anchor into it.

labels.name: Periodontal ligament
labels.fn: Dense connective tissue fibers that run from the cementum to the bone of the socket, holding the tooth in place and cushioning bite forces.

follow.q: What holds a tooth in its socket?
follow.why: The periodontal ligament is a sheet of collagen fibers running from the cementum of the root into the bone of the socket. It anchors the tooth and absorbs the force of biting. The gum only surrounds the neck.

labels.name: Root
labels.fn: The part of the tooth embedded in the jaw bone, below the gum and covered with cementum.

labels.name: Root canal
labels.fn: The narrow channel of the pulp cavity running down through the root, carrying blood vessels and nerves in and out at its tip.

labels.name: Bone
labels.fn: The jaw bone forming the socket (alveolus) that holds the root.

labels.name: Central incisor (7–8 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent upper tooth: a central incisor, one of the two front teeth in the middle of the arch, with a chisel edge that cuts. It usually erupts at 7–8 years.

labels.name: Lateral incisor (8–9 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent upper tooth: a lateral incisor, beside the central incisor, with a chisel edge that cuts. It usually erupts at 8–9 years.

labels.name: Cuspid or canine (11–12 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent upper tooth: a canine (cuspid), the pointed tooth at the corner of the arch that tears food. It usually erupts at 11–12 years.

labels.name: First premolar or bicuspid (9–10 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent upper tooth: the first premolar (bicuspid), with two cusps for crushing. It usually erupts at 9–10 years.

labels.name: Second premolar or bicuspid (10–12 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent upper tooth: the second premolar (bicuspid), with two cusps for crushing. It usually erupts at 10–12 years.

labels.name: First molar (6–7 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent upper tooth: the first molar, a broad back tooth with several cusps that grinds food. It usually erupts at 6–7 years.

follow.q: Which permanent tooth usually erupts first, at about 6 years?
follow.why: The first permanent molars erupt at about 6–7 years, behind the baby teeth, before any baby tooth is lost; that is why they are called the six-year molars. The permanent central incisors follow at 7–8 years, the canines at 9–12, and the third molars last, if at all.

labels.name: Second molar (12–13 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent upper tooth: the second molar, a broad grinding tooth. It usually erupts at 12–13 years.

labels.name: Third molar or wisdom tooth
labels.fn: A permanent upper tooth: the third molar (wisdom tooth), the last grinding tooth, often erupting in the late teens or not at all.

labels.name: Central incisor (8–12 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) upper tooth: central incisor, one of the two front teeth in the middle of the arch, with a chisel edge that cuts. It usually erupts at 8–12 months.

labels.name: Lateral incisor (12–24 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) upper tooth: lateral incisor, beside the central incisor, with a chisel edge that cuts. It usually erupts at 12–24 months.

labels.name: Cuspid or canine (16–24 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) upper tooth: canine (cuspid), the pointed tooth at the corner of the arch that tears food. It usually erupts at 16–24 months.

labels.name: First molar (12–16 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) upper tooth: first molar, a broad back tooth with several cusps that grinds food. It usually erupts at 12–16 months.

labels.name: Second molar (24–32 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) upper tooth: second molar, a broad grinding tooth. It usually erupts at 24–32 months.

follow.q: Which kind of tooth is found in the permanent set but not in the deciduous set?
follow.why: The 20 deciduous teeth are incisors, canines and molars. The permanent premolars erupt in the places of the deciduous molars, and three permanent molars on each side are added behind them, giving 32 teeth.

labels.name: Second molar (24–32 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) lower tooth: second molar, a broad grinding tooth. It usually erupts at 24–32 months.

labels.name: First molar (12–16 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) lower tooth: first molar, a broad back tooth with several cusps that grinds food. It usually erupts at 12–16 months.

labels.name: Cuspid or canine (16–24 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) lower tooth: canine (cuspid), the pointed tooth at the corner of the arch that tears food. It usually erupts at 16–24 months.

labels.name: Lateral incisor (12–15 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) lower tooth: lateral incisor, beside the central incisor, with a chisel edge that cuts. It usually erupts at 12–15 months.

labels.name: Central incisor (6–8 mo)
labels.fn: A deciduous (baby) lower tooth: central incisor, one of the two front teeth in the middle of the arch, with a chisel edge that cuts. It usually erupts at 6–8 months.

follow.q: How many deciduous (baby) teeth does a child have?
follow.why: The deciduous set has 20 teeth: in each quarter of the mouth two incisors, one canine and two molars. The permanent set has 32, adding premolars and a third molar in each quarter.

labels.name: Third molar or wisdom tooth
labels.fn: A permanent lower tooth: the third molar (wisdom tooth), the last grinding tooth, often erupting in the late teens or not at all.

labels.name: Second molar (11–13 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent lower tooth: the second molar, a broad grinding tooth. It usually erupts at 11–13 years.

labels.name: First molar (6–7 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent lower tooth: the first molar, a broad back tooth with several cusps that grinds food. It usually erupts at 6–7 years.

labels.name: Second premolar or bicuspid (11–12 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent lower tooth: the second premolar (bicuspid), with two cusps for crushing. It usually erupts at 11–12 years.

labels.name: First premolar or bicuspid (9–10 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent lower tooth: the first premolar (bicuspid), with two cusps for crushing. It usually erupts at 9–10 years.

labels.name: Cuspid or canine (9–10 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent lower tooth: a canine (cuspid), the pointed tooth at the corner of the arch that tears food. It usually erupts at 9–10 years.

labels.name: Lateral incisor (7–8 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent lower tooth: a lateral incisor, beside the central incisor, with a chisel edge that cuts. It usually erupts at 7–8 years.

labels.name: Central incisor (7–8 yr)
labels.fn: A permanent lower tooth: a central incisor, one of the two front teeth in the middle of the arch, with a chisel edge that cuts. It usually erupts at 7–8 years.

labels.name: Superior lip
labels.fn: The upper lip: skeletal muscle covered by skin outside and mucosa inside. The lips close the mouth and keep food in during chewing.

labels.name: Superior labial frenulum
labels.fn: A fold of mucosa in the midline joining the inside of the upper lip to the gum.

labels.name: Gingivae (gums)
labels.fn: The gums: mucosa over dense connective tissue that surrounds the necks of the upper teeth and covers the bone that holds them.

labels.name: Palatoglossal arch
labels.fn: The front fold running from the soft palate down to the side of the tongue. It marks the edge between the mouth and the throat.

labels.name: Fauces
labels.fn: The opening from the mouth into the throat (oropharynx), framed by the two arches on each side.

labels.name: Hard palate
labels.fn: The front, bony part of the roof of the mouth. The tongue presses food against it during chewing.

labels.name: Palatopharyngeal arch
labels.fn: The back fold running from the soft palate down the side wall of the pharynx. The palatine tonsil sits between it and the palatoglossal arch.

labels.name: Soft palate
labels.fn: The back, muscular part of the roof of the mouth. It rises during swallowing to close off the nasal cavity.

follow.q: During swallowing, what keeps food from going up into the nasal cavity?
options: The tongue presses against the hard palate
The soft palate and uvula rise
follow.why: The soft palate and uvula lift and seal off the nasopharynx when you swallow, so the bolus cannot enter the nasal cavity. The epiglottis covers the larynx instead, the hard palate is fixed bone, and the lower esophageal sphincter works at the stomach end.

labels.name: Uvula
labels.fn: The small tag hanging from the back edge of the soft palate. It rises with the soft palate during swallowing.

labels.name: Palatine tonsil
labels.fn: A mass of lymphatic tissue between the two arches on each side of the fauces. It samples microbes that enter through the mouth.

labels.name: Cheek
labels.fn: The side wall of the mouth, with the buccinator muscle inside. It keeps food between the teeth during chewing.

labels.name: Molars
labels.fn: The broad back teeth. Their wide, bumpy surfaces crush and grind food.

labels.name: Tongue (underside)
labels.fn: The underside of the tongue, raised to show the lingual frenulum and the floor of the mouth.

labels.name: Lingual frenulum
labels.fn: A fold of mucosa joining the underside of the tongue to the floor of the mouth. It limits how far the tongue can move backward.

labels.name: Opening duct of submandibular gland
labels.fn: Where the duct of the submandibular gland opens, on each side of the lingual frenulum under the tongue, releasing saliva.

labels.name: Premolars
labels.fn: The teeth between the canines and the molars, with two cusps (bicuspids). They crush and grind.

labels.name: Cuspid (canine)
labels.fn: The pointed tooth at the corner of the dental arch. It tears food.

labels.name: Gingivae (gums)
labels.fn: The gums of the lower jaw, which grip the necks of the lower teeth.

labels.name: Incisors
labels.fn: The flat, chisel-edged front teeth. They cut and bite off pieces of food.

follow.q: Which teeth cut and bite off pieces of food?
follow.why: Incisors have a thin chisel edge that cuts. Canines tear, and premolars and molars (including the wisdom teeth, the third molars) have broad cusped surfaces that crush and grind.

labels.name: Inferior labial frenulum
labels.fn: A fold of mucosa in the midline joining the inside of the lower lip to the gum.

labels.name: Oral vestibule
labels.fn: The space between the lips and cheeks outside and the teeth and gums inside.

labels.name: Inferior lip
labels.fn: The lower lip, which with the upper lip closes the mouth during chewing.

labels.name: Cardia
labels.fn: The small region around the opening from the esophagus, where food enters the stomach.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: The esophagus, bringing swallowed food into the stomach through the cardia.

labels.name: Muscularis externa
labels.fn: The stomach's muscle coat. Unlike the rest of the tract it has three layers (longitudinal, circular and an inner oblique layer), which lets it churn food.

follow.q: How does the stomach's muscularis externa differ from that of the rest of the tract?
options: It has an extra oblique layer
It lies inside the mucosa, under the epithelium
follow.why: Most of the tract has an inner circular and an outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle. The stomach adds a third, innermost oblique layer, so it can twist and churn food into chyme, not just push it along.

labels.name: Fundus
labels.fn: The dome-shaped part that rises above the level of the cardia, under the left side of the diaphragm. It often holds swallowed air.

labels.name: Longitudinal layer
labels.fn: The outer layer of the stomach's muscularis externa, with fibers running along the stomach.

labels.name: Circular layer
labels.fn: The middle layer of the stomach's muscularis, with fibers running around it. It thickens at the pylorus to form the pyloric sphincter.

labels.name: Oblique layer
labels.fn: The innermost muscle layer, found only in the stomach. It helps twist and churn the contents.

labels.name: Serosa
labels.fn: The outer covering of the stomach, the visceral peritoneum.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The large main part of the stomach, between the fundus and the pyloric region.

labels.name: Lesser curvature
labels.fn: The short, concave right border of the stomach.

labels.name: Pyloric sphincter (valve) at pylorus
labels.fn: A thick ring of circular smooth muscle at the pylorus. It lets chyme leave the stomach in small squirts and keeps it from flowing back.

follow.q: What controls how fast chyme leaves the stomach for the small intestine?
follow.why: The pyloric sphincter at the stomach's outlet opens only a little with each mixing wave, so chyme leaves in small squirts. The lower esophageal sphincter guards the entrance, and the fundus and rugae are parts of the stomach wall, not valves.

labels.name: Lumen
labels.fn: The space inside the stomach, where food is mixed with gastric juice into chyme.

labels.name: Rugae of mucosa
labels.fn: Folds of the mucosa and submucosa in an empty stomach. They flatten out as the stomach fills, letting it hold a large meal.

follow.q: What is the main job of the rugae?
options: They push food into the esophagus
follow.why: Rugae are folds that flatten as the stomach fills, so the stomach can expand a great deal without much rise in pressure. Acid comes from parietal cells in the gastric glands, and the stomach absorbs very few nutrients.

labels.name: Pyloric canal
labels.fn: The narrow passage at the end of the stomach, leading to the pyloric sphincter.

labels.name: Greater curvature
labels.fn: The long, convex left border of the stomach.

labels.name: Pyloric antrum
labels.fn: The wider funnel-shaped region of the stomach before the pyloric canal, where mixing waves are strongest.

labels.name: Parietal cell
labels.fn: A cell in the gastric glands that secretes hydrochloric acid, using proton pumps, and intrinsic factor.

follow.q: A drug blocks the proton pumps of parietal cells. What happens to the stomach contents?
follow.why: Parietal cells make hydrochloric acid by pumping hydrogen ions into the lumen with proton pumps. Blocking the pumps cuts acid output, so the pH of the stomach contents rises (less acidic). Chief cells still release pepsinogen, and mucous cells still make mucus.

labels.name: Surface epithelium
labels.fn: Simple columnar epithelium of mucous cells lining the stomach. It secretes a thick, alkaline mucus that protects the lining from acid and pepsin.

labels.name: Gastric pit
labels.fn: A small opening in the surface lining into which several gastric glands empty their secretions.

labels.name: Mucosa
labels.fn: The stomach's lining: surface epithelium with gastric pits and glands, the lamina propria and the muscularis mucosae.

labels.name: Gastric gland
labels.fn: A tubular gland opening into a gastric pit, with parietal, chief, mucous neck and enteroendocrine cells. Together they make gastric juice.

labels.name: Lamina propria
labels.fn: Loose connective tissue between the gastric glands, carrying capillaries.

labels.name: Chief cell
labels.fn: A cell deep in the gastric glands that secretes pepsinogen, the inactive precursor that acid converts to the protein-digesting enzyme pepsin.

follow.q: Chief cells release pepsinogen, not active pepsin. Why does that matter?
options: It cannot digest the cells that store it
Pepsinogen is absorbed straight into the blood for use elsewhere
Pepsin works only in the mouth
follow.why: Pepsinogen is a zymogen, an inactive precursor. Only in the acid of the lumen does it cut itself into active pepsin, so the enzyme cannot digest the proteins of the chief cells that store it. Pepsin digests protein, not fat, and works in the acid of the stomach.

labels.name: Muscularis mucosae
labels.fn: A thin layer of smooth muscle at the base of the mucosa, which helps squeeze secretions out of the glands.

labels.name: Submucosa
labels.fn: Connective tissue under the mucosa, carrying larger blood vessels and the submucosal plexus.

labels.name: Oblique layer
labels.fn: The innermost of the stomach's three muscle layers, found only in the stomach.

labels.name: Circular layer
labels.fn: The middle muscle layer, with fibers running around the stomach.

labels.name: Muscularis externa
labels.fn: The stomach's three layers of smooth muscle (oblique, circular and longitudinal), which churn food into chyme.

labels.name: Enteroendocrine cell
labels.fn: A hormone-releasing cell in the gastric glands. G cells, for example, release gastrin into the blood, which stimulates acid secretion.

labels.name: Longitudinal layer
labels.fn: The outer muscle layer, with fibers running along the stomach.

labels.name: Serosa
labels.fn: The outer covering of the stomach, the visceral peritoneum.

labels.name: Central vein
labels.fn: The vein at the center of each lobule, seen here as the dark point where the lines of cells meet.

labels.name: Connective tissue
labels.fn: Thin connective tissue partitions between the lobules, carrying the portal triads at the corners.

labels.name: Lobules
labels.fn: The six-sided units that make up the liver, each built of plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, with portal triads at the corners.

follow.q: What sits at the corners of a liver lobule?
follow.why: Each corner of the lobule carries a portal triad: a portal venule, a hepatic arteriole and a bile duct. The central vein sits at the center of the lobule, not at its corners.

labels.name: Central vein
labels.fn: The vein at the center of the lobule. It collects blood that has run through the sinusoids and carries it toward the hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava.

follow.q: Blood leaves a liver lobule through which vessel?
follow.why: Blood enters at the corners of the lobule from portal venules and hepatic arterioles, mixes in the sinusoids and drains inward to the central vein, which leads to the hepatic veins. The bile duct carries bile, not blood.

labels.name: Sinusoids
labels.fn: Leaky capillaries between the plates of hepatocytes. Mixed blood from the portal venules and arterioles flows through them toward the central vein, and the hepatocytes exchange materials with it.

follow.q: Blood in the liver sinusoids is a mix of which two sources?
options: Hepatic portal vein and hepatic artery
Hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava
follow.why: Portal venules bring nutrient-rich blood from the gut and hepatic arterioles bring oxygen-rich blood; both empty into the sinusoids and mix. The central vein and hepatic veins are the way out, and the ducts carry bile.

labels.name: Plates of hepatocytes
labels.fn: Sheets of hepatocytes, the liver's working cells, radiating from the central vein. They process nutrients from the blood and make bile.

labels.name: Portal venule
accept: branch of the hepatic portal vein
labels.fn: A branch of the hepatic portal vein at the corner of the lobule, bringing nutrient-rich blood from the stomach and intestines into the sinusoids.

labels.name: Portal arteriole
labels.fn: A branch of the hepatic artery at the corner of the lobule, bringing oxygen-rich blood into the sinusoids.

labels.name: Bile duct
labels.fn: A small duct at the corner of the lobule that collects bile from the bile canaliculi. Bile flows outward, the opposite direction to the blood.

follow.q: Bile and blood move in which directions through a liver lobule?
options: Both flow toward the central vein
Opposite ways: blood inward, bile outward
Both flow outward to the corners of the lobule
Bile flows into the sinusoids with the blood
follow.why: Blood runs from the corners through the sinusoids to the central vein. Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi between them, and bile flows the other way, out to the bile ducts in the portal triads.

labels.name: From portal vein
labels.fn: Blood arriving from the hepatic portal vein, which drains the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas, reaches the lobule through the portal venules.

labels.name: Left hepatic duct
labels.fn: The duct draining bile from the left side of the liver. It joins the right hepatic duct.

labels.name: Right hepatic duct
labels.fn: The duct draining bile from the right side of the liver. It joins the left hepatic duct to form the common hepatic duct.

labels.name: Cystic duct
labels.fn: The duct of the gallbladder. Bile flows in through it to be stored and out through it when the gallbladder contracts.

follow.q: A gallstone lodges in the cystic duct. Which flow is blocked?
options: Bile from the liver to the duodenum
Bile into and out of the gallbladder
Pancreatic juice flowing to the duodenum
follow.why: The cystic duct joins only the gallbladder to the bile ducts, so a stone there traps bile in or out of the gallbladder. Bile from the liver can still reach the duodenum through the common hepatic and common bile ducts, and the pancreatic duct is separate.

labels.name: Gallbladder
labels.fn: A muscular sac under the liver that stores bile and concentrates it by absorbing water. CCK makes it contract after a fatty meal.

labels.name: Body
labels.fn: The main part of the gallbladder, between the fundus and the neck.

labels.name: Fundus
labels.fn: The rounded end of the gallbladder, which projects below the edge of the liver.

labels.name: Neck
labels.fn: The narrow part of the gallbladder that leads into the cystic duct.

labels.name: Common hepatic duct
labels.fn: The duct formed by the right and left hepatic ducts. It carries bile from the liver and joins the cystic duct.

labels.name: Common bile duct
labels.fn: The duct formed by the common hepatic and cystic ducts. It carries bile down to the duodenum, joining the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

labels.name: Liver
labels.fn: The underside of the liver, where the gallbladder sits.

labels.name: Right lobe
labels.fn: The large right lobe of the liver.

labels.name: Quadrate lobe
labels.fn: A small lobe on the underside of the liver, beside the gallbladder.

labels.name: Left lobe
labels.fn: The smaller left lobe of the liver, separated from the right lobe in front by the falciform ligament.

labels.name: Caudate lobe
labels.fn: A small lobe on the back and underside of the liver, near the inferior vena cava.

labels.name: Spleen
labels.fn: A lymphatic organ beside the tail of the pancreas; it is not a digestive organ. Its vein drains into the hepatic portal vein.

labels.name: Gallbladder
labels.fn: The gallbladder, which stores and concentrates bile between meals.

labels.name: Right hepatic duct
labels.fn: The duct draining bile from the right side of the liver.

labels.name: Pancreas
labels.fn: A gland behind the stomach whose acinar cells make pancreatic juice (enzymes and bicarbonate) for the duodenum; its islets release hormones into the blood.

labels.name: Cystic duct
labels.fn: The duct of the gallbladder, joining the common hepatic duct.

labels.name: Common hepatic duct
labels.fn: The duct formed where the right and left hepatic ducts meet.

labels.name: Pancreatic duct
labels.fn: The main pancreatic duct, running the length of the pancreas and carrying pancreatic juice to the duodenum.

follow.q: The common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct usually join where?
options: In the neck of the gallbladder, beside the cystic duct
In the wall of the stomach
follow.why: The two ducts usually meet at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens into the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla under the control of the hepatopancreatic sphincter. That is why a stone at the ampulla can block both bile and pancreatic juice.

labels.name: Common bile duct
labels.fn: The duct carrying bile from the joined common hepatic and cystic ducts to the duodenum.

follow.q: A gallstone blocks the common bile duct. What happens to bile reaching the duodenum?
options: It stays the same, because the cystic duct takes over
It is replaced by pancreatic juice
follow.why: All bile headed for the duodenum, from the liver and from the gallbladder, passes through the common bile duct, so a stone there cuts the supply and fat is poorly emulsified. The cystic duct only connects the gallbladder, upstream of the block.

labels.name: Left hepatic duct
labels.fn: The duct draining bile from the left side of the liver.

hints.why: A group heading over the labels below it, not one structure: masked in the quiz because it names the group they belong to.

labels.name: Cortical blood vessels
labels.fn: The cortical radiate arteries and veins: small branches that run straight out from the arcuate vessels through the cortex toward the surface of the kidney, carrying blood to and from the cortex.

labels.name: Arcuate blood vessels
labels.fn: The arcuate arteries and veins, which arch over the base of each pyramid at the border between the cortex and the medulla.

follow.q: Where do the arcuate arteries run?
options: Along the border between the cortex and the medulla, over the pyramid bases
Along the outer surface of the renal capsule
Through the renal columns toward the papillae
follow.why: Arcuate means "bowed". These arteries arch over the base of each pyramid at the corticomedullary border and give off the cortical radiate arteries. The interlobar arteries are the ones that run in the renal columns.

labels.name: Interlobar blood vessels
labels.fn: The interlobar arteries and veins, which run outward through the renal columns between the pyramids, linking the segmental vessels with the arcuate vessels.

labels.name: Minor calyx
labels.fn: A small cup that fits around the papilla of one pyramid and catches the urine that drips from it. Several minor calyces join to form a major calyx.

follow.q: What drains directly into a minor calyx?
options: The papilla of a renal pyramid
follow.why: Urine leaves each pyramid through the openings at its papilla, and the papilla sits inside a minor calyx. Minor calyces then drain into major calyces, which drain into the renal pelvis. Renal columns are cortical tissue, not a drainage channel.

labels.name: Major calyx
labels.fn: A larger cup formed where two or three minor calyces meet. The major calyces (usually two or three per kidney) empty into the renal pelvis.

labels.name: Renal vein
labels.fn: The large vein that carries blood out of the kidney through the hilum to the inferior vena cava. It lies in front of the renal artery at the hilum.

labels.name: Renal pelvis
labels.fn: The funnel inside the renal sinus formed where the major calyces join. It collects all the urine the kidney makes and narrows into the ureter as it leaves the hilum.

follow.q: The renal pelvis narrows to become which structure?
follow.why: The funnel-shaped renal pelvis collects urine from the major calyces and continues out of the hilum as the ureter, which carries urine down to the bladder. The urethra drains the bladder, not the kidney.

labels.name: Renal nerve
labels.fn: Nerves that enter the kidney at the hilum with the renal artery. They carry mainly sympathetic fibers, which can narrow the kidney’s blood vessels.

labels.name: Renal hilum
