labels.fn: The notch on the concave medial border of the kidney, where the renal artery, renal vein, nerves, lymph vessels and the ureter enter or leave.

follow.q: Which structure leaves the kidney at the hilum?
follow.why: The hilum is the kidney’s doorway on its medial side: the renal artery and nerves enter, and the renal vein, lymph vessels and ureter leave. The adrenal gland sits on top of the kidney, and the renal columns lie inside it.

labels.name: Pyramid
labels.fn: A cone-shaped, striped region of the renal medulla. Its stripes are bundles of fine tubes that carry forming urine toward its tip, the papilla. Each kidney has about 8 to 18 pyramids.

follow.q: Which way does the base of a renal pyramid face?
options: Toward the renal cortex, at the outer edge of the medulla
Toward the renal columns on either side
follow.why: Each pyramid’s broad base lies against the cortex and its tip, the papilla, points inward toward a minor calyx and the renal pelvis. Renal columns lie along its sides, not at its base.

labels.name: Renal artery
labels.fn: The branch of the abdominal aorta that brings blood to the kidney. It enters at the hilum and divides into segmental arteries. The kidneys take about a fifth of the heart’s output at rest.

labels.name: Papilla
labels.fn: The rounded tip of a renal pyramid, pointing into a minor calyx. Urine drains out through tiny openings on its surface.

labels.name: Medulla
labels.fn: The inner region of the kidney, made of the renal pyramids. It lies deep to the cortex and around the renal sinus.

labels.name: Renal column
labels.fn: An extension of the cortex that reaches inward between two pyramids. The interlobar arteries and veins run through it.

follow.q: A renal column is made of tissue like that of which region?
follow.why: Renal columns are inward extensions of the cortex that separate neighboring pyramids, so they look and work like cortex. The pyramids between them are the medulla.

labels.name: Ureter
labels.fn: The muscular tube that carries urine from the renal pelvis down to the urinary bladder, moving it along by waves of smooth muscle contraction (peristalsis).

labels.name: Cortex
labels.fn: The outer, grainy region of the kidney just under the capsule. It surrounds the pyramids and sends renal columns between them.

labels.name: Capsule
labels.fn: The renal capsule: a thin, tough layer of dense connective tissue that covers the kidney’s surface and helps keep its shape.

labels.name: Cortical radiate artery
labels.fn: Small arteries that branch off the arcuate arteries and run straight out through the cortex toward the surface. They feed the smallest arterial branches in the cortex.

labels.name: Arcuate artery
labels.fn: An artery that arches over the base of a pyramid at the border of the cortex and the medulla. It comes from an interlobar artery and gives off the cortical radiate arteries.

follow.q: Which vessel comes right after the arcuate artery on blood’s path through the kidney?
follow.why: The arterial route is renal, segmental, interlobar, arcuate and then cortical radiate arteries. The interlobar and segmental arteries come before the arcuate artery, and the renal vein is on the way out.

labels.name: Interlobar artery
labels.fn: An artery that runs outward through a renal column, between two pyramids, from a segmental artery to the arcuate arteries.

labels.name: Segmental artery
labels.fn: One of the first branches of the renal artery inside the renal sinus. Each supplies one segment of the kidney and divides into interlobar arteries.

follow.q: A segmental artery branches directly from which vessel?
follow.why: The renal artery divides into segmental arteries near the hilum, and each segmental artery divides into interlobar arteries. The aorta gives off the renal artery itself.

labels.name: Renal artery
labels.fn: The branch of the abdominal aorta that carries blood into the kidney at the hilum, where it divides into segmental arteries.

labels.name: Cortical radiate vein
labels.fn: A small vein that runs inward through the cortex, collecting blood from the cortex and draining it into an arcuate vein.

labels.name: Arcuate vein
labels.fn: A vein that arches along the border of the cortex and the medulla, collecting blood from the cortical radiate veins and draining into an interlobar vein.

labels.name: Interlobar vein
labels.fn: A vein that runs through a renal column between two pyramids, carrying blood from the arcuate veins toward the renal vein.

labels.name: Renal vein
labels.fn: The vein that carries blood out of the kidney at the hilum to the inferior vena cava. The kidney has no segmental veins; interlobar veins join to form it.

labels.name: Glomerular capsule
labels.fn: The double-walled cup (Bowman’s capsule) around the glomerulus. Its inner layer of podocytes covers the capillaries, and the space inside collects the fluid filtered from the blood and passes it into the proximal convoluted tubule.

follow.q: Fluid filtered out of the glomerulus first enters which space?
options: The lumen of the collecting duct
The space inside the glomerular capsule
follow.why: Filtered fluid crosses the capillary wall and the podocyte layer into the capsular space of the glomerular capsule, and from there flows into the proximal convoluted tubule. The collecting duct and renal pelvis come much later.

labels.name: Efferent arteriole
labels.fn: The arteriole that carries blood out of the glomerulus. In most nephrons it is narrower than the afferent arteriole, which helps keep pressure high in the glomerulus, and it leads into the peritubular capillaries (and, in juxtamedullary nephrons, the vasa recta).

labels.name: Afferent arteriole
labels.fn: The arteriole that brings blood from a cortical radiate artery into the glomerulus. Narrowing or widening it changes the blood flow and pressure in the glomerulus.

follow.q: Compared with the efferent arteriole, the afferent arteriole is usually
options: narrower, so blood leaves the glomerulus faster than it enters
wider, which helps keep pressure in the glomerulus high
the same width, because the two are one vessel
a vein rather than an arteriole
follow.why: Blood enters through the wider afferent arteriole and leaves through the narrower efferent arteriole, so pressure in the glomerular capillaries stays high. Both are arterioles; the glomerulus lies between them.

labels.name: Proximal convoluted tubule
labels.fn: The first, coiled part of the renal tubule, leaving the glomerular capsule in the cortex. Its cells have a brush border and many mitochondria, and it takes back most of the filtered water and solutes.

follow.q: Which part of the renal tubule receives fluid straight from the glomerular capsule?
options: The ascending limb of the nephron loop
follow.why: The order is glomerular capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, nephron loop (descending then ascending limb), distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct.

labels.name: Cortical radiate artery
labels.fn: An artery that runs out through the cortex and gives off the afferent arterioles, one to each glomerulus.

labels.name: Venule
labels.fn: A small vein that collects blood from the peritubular capillaries and drains it into a cortical radiate vein.

labels.name: Cortical radiate vein
labels.fn: A vein in the cortex that collects blood from the venules draining the peritubular capillaries and carries it toward the arcuate veins.

labels.name: Loop of the nephron
labels.fn: The hairpin part of the renal tubule (loop of Henle). Its descending limb dips into the medulla and its ascending limb climbs back to the cortex.

follow.q: Where does the nephron loop run?
options: It stays within the renal capsule
Down into the medulla and back up to the cortex
follow.why: The loop starts in the cortex, its descending limb runs down into the medulla, and its ascending limb returns to the cortex, where it becomes the distal convoluted tubule. Long loops belong to juxtamedullary nephrons.

labels.name: Peritubular capillary network
labels.fn: The capillary bed fed by the efferent arteriole that wraps around the tubules. It takes back the water and solutes the tubules return and drains into venules.

labels.name: Peritubular capillaries
labels.fn: The second capillary bed of the nephron, fed by the efferent arteriole. It wraps around the tubules in the cortex and takes back the water and solutes the tubules return to the blood.

follow.q: What feeds the peritubular capillaries?
follow.why: The efferent arteriole leaves the glomerulus and breaks up into the peritubular capillaries, so blood passes through two capillary beds in a row. The afferent arteriole feeds the glomerulus instead.

labels.name: Efferent arteriole
labels.fn: The arteriole that carries blood out of the glomerulus. It leads into a second capillary bed, the peritubular capillaries or the vasa recta.

follow.q: Blood leaving the glomerulus flows next into which vessel?
follow.why: Blood enters the glomerulus through the afferent arteriole and leaves through the efferent arteriole, which leads into the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta. Only after those capillaries does blood reach the veins.

labels.name: Glomerulus
labels.fn: A ball of fenestrated capillaries inside the glomerular capsule, where fluid is pressed out of the blood into the capsule, the first step of urine formation.

labels.name: Afferent arteriole
labels.fn: The small artery that carries blood from a cortical radiate artery into a glomerulus. Its width sets how much blood enters the glomerulus.

labels.name: Cortical radiate artery
labels.fn: Small arteries that branch off the arcuate arteries and run straight out through the cortex toward the surface. They feed the smallest arterial branches in the cortex.

labels.name: Arcuate artery
labels.fn: An artery that arches over the base of a pyramid at the border of the cortex and the medulla. It comes from an interlobar artery and gives off the cortical radiate arteries.

follow.q: Which vessel comes right after the arcuate artery on blood’s path through the kidney?
follow.why: The arterial route is renal, segmental, interlobar, arcuate and then cortical radiate arteries. The interlobar and segmental arteries come before the arcuate artery, and the renal vein is on the way out.

labels.name: Interlobar artery
labels.fn: An artery that runs outward through a renal column, between two pyramids, from a segmental artery to the arcuate arteries.

labels.name: Segmental artery
labels.fn: One of the first branches of the renal artery inside the renal sinus. Each supplies one segment of the kidney and divides into interlobar arteries.

follow.q: A segmental artery branches directly from which vessel?
follow.why: The renal artery divides into segmental arteries near the hilum, and each segmental artery divides into interlobar arteries. The aorta gives off the renal artery itself.

labels.name: Renal artery
labels.fn: The branch of the abdominal aorta that carries blood into the kidney at the hilum, where it divides into segmental arteries.

labels.name: Cortical radiate vein
labels.fn: A small vein that runs inward through the cortex, collecting blood from the cortex and draining it into an arcuate vein.

labels.name: Arcuate vein
labels.fn: A vein that arches along the border of the cortex and the medulla, collecting blood from the cortical radiate veins and draining into an interlobar vein.

labels.name: Interlobar vein
labels.fn: A vein that runs through a renal column between two pyramids, carrying blood from the arcuate veins toward the renal vein.

labels.name: Renal vein
labels.fn: The vein that carries blood out of the kidney at the hilum to the inferior vena cava. The kidney has no segmental veins; interlobar veins join to form it.

labels.name: T10
labels.fn: The 10th thoracic vertebra. It lies above the kidneys, level with the lower ribs.

labels.name: T11
labels.fn: The 11th thoracic vertebra. The upper pole of the left kidney reaches about this level.

labels.name: T12
labels.fn: The 12th (last) thoracic vertebra, the one the 12th ribs attach to. The kidneys start at about this level.

follow.q: Between which vertebral levels do the kidneys lie?
follow.why: The kidneys lie against the back wall of the abdomen from about T12 to L3, partly covered by the 11th and 12th ribs. The right kidney sits a little lower than the left because the liver lies above it.

labels.name: L1
labels.fn: The 1st lumbar vertebra. The renal hilum sits near this level.

labels.name: L2
labels.fn: The 2nd lumbar vertebra. It lies beside the middle of the kidneys.

labels.name: L3
labels.fn: The 3rd lumbar vertebra. The lower poles of the kidneys reach about this level.

labels.name: L4
labels.fn: The 4th lumbar vertebra. It lies below the kidneys, beside the ureters on their way down.

labels.name: L5
labels.fn: The 5th (last) lumbar vertebra. It sits on the sacrum, below the kidneys.

labels.name: Liver
labels.fn: The large organ in the upper right abdomen. It lies above the right kidney and pushes it a little lower than the left.

follow.q: Why does the right kidney usually sit a little lower than the left?
options: The heart lies on the right
follow.why: The liver takes up the upper right abdomen, so the right kidney sits slightly lower. The spleen is on the left, above the left kidney.

labels.name: Kidney
labels.fn: One of two bean-shaped organs that lie behind the peritoneum (retroperitoneal) on either side of the spine. The kidneys filter the blood and make urine.

labels.name: 12th rib
labels.fn: The lowest rib, a floating rib. It crosses the back of the upper part of each kidney, so a blow to the lower ribs from behind can injure a kidney.

labels.name: Ureter
labels.fn: The tube that carries urine from each kidney down to the bladder, running beside the spine and in front of the lower vertebrae.

labels.name: Ureter
labels.fn: The tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. It enters the back of the bladder at a slant, so a filling bladder presses it shut and urine cannot flow back.

labels.name: Urinary bladder
labels.fn: The hollow, muscular organ behind the pubic bone that stores urine. Its smooth muscle wall (the detrusor) and stretchy lining let it fill, and the detrusor contracts to empty it.

labels.name: Pubic bone
labels.fn: The front part of the hip bone. The urinary bladder sits just behind the two pubic bones and the joint between them.

labels.name: Urethra
labels.fn: The tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside. In females it is short, about 4 cm, and opens in front of the vaginal opening.

follow.q: Why do females get bladder infections more often than males?
options: Their urethra is much shorter, so bacteria reach the bladder more easily
follow.why: The female urethra is about 4 cm long and opens close to the anus, so bacteria have a short path to the bladder. The male urethra is about 20 cm long.

labels.name: Rectum
labels.fn: The last straight part of the large intestine, lying behind the urinary bladder in the pelvis.

labels.name: Anus
labels.fn: The opening at the end of the digestive tract, behind the urethral opening.

labels.name: Urinary bladder
labels.fn: The hollow, muscular organ behind the pubic bone that stores urine. Its smooth muscle wall (the detrusor) and stretchy lining let it fill, and the detrusor contracts to empty it.

labels.name: Ureter
labels.fn: The tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder. It enters the back of the bladder at a slant, so a filling bladder presses it shut and urine cannot flow back.

labels.name: Pubic bone
labels.fn: The front part of the hip bone. The urinary bladder sits just behind the two pubic bones and the joint between them.

labels.name: Urethra
labels.fn: The tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside. In males it is about 20 cm long and runs the length of the external genitals.

follow.q: About how long is the male urethra?
follow.why: The male urethra runs about 20 cm from the bladder to its opening at the tip of the external genitals. The female urethra is about 4 cm long.

labels.name: Rectum
labels.fn: The last straight part of the large intestine, lying behind the urinary bladder in the pelvis.

labels.name: Anus
labels.fn: The opening at the end of the digestive tract, behind the urethral opening.

labels.name: Sacrum
labels.fn: The triangular bone at the base of the spine. The sacral spinal nerves that control the bladder (S2 to S4) leave through it.

labels.name: Urinary bladder
labels.fn: The muscular sac that stores urine. Parasympathetic nerves from the sacral cord make its detrusor muscle contract during urination.

labels.name: Pubic bone
labels.fn: The front part of the hip bone. The urinary bladder sits just behind the two pubic bones and the joint between them.

labels.name: Sphincter
labels.fn: The external urethral sphincter: a ring of skeletal muscle around the urethra that you control on purpose. It stays shut until you decide to urinate.

follow.q: What kind of muscle forms the external urethral sphincter?
follow.why: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle, driven by the pudendal nerve, so you can hold urine on purpose. The internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck is smooth muscle and works without your control.

labels.name: Pudendal nerve
labels.fn: A somatic nerve from the sacral spinal cord (S2 to S4). Its motor fibers keep the external urethral sphincter contracted until you choose to urinate.

follow.q: Which nerve keeps the external urethral sphincter closed?
follow.why: The pudendal nerve carries somatic motor fibers from S2 to S4 to the external urethral sphincter. When you decide to urinate, its firing falls and the sphincter relaxes.

labels.name: Anus
labels.fn: The opening at the end of the digestive tract, behind the urethral opening.

labels.name: Penis
labels.fn: The male organ of copulation and the outlet for both urine and semen. Its shaft holds three columns of erectile tissue around the spongy urethra.

labels.name: Corona
labels.fn: The raised rim at the base of the glans, where the glans meets the shaft of the penis.

labels.name: Glans penis
labels.fn: The enlarged, cap-shaped tip of the penis, formed by the widened end of the corpus spongiosum. It is rich in sensory nerve endings, and the external urethral opening sits at its tip.

labels.name: Prepuce (foreskin)
labels.fn: The loose fold of skin that covers the glans of an uncircumcised penis. Circumcision removes it.

labels.name: Scrotum
labels.fn: The skin-covered sac that hangs outside the body cavity and holds the testes. It keeps them a few degrees cooler than the core of the body, which sperm production needs.

labels.name: Prostate gland
labels.fn: A walnut-sized gland wrapped around the urethra just below the urinary bladder. It adds a thin, milky fluid, about a third of the volume of semen.

labels.name: Ductus (vas) deferens
labels.fn: The muscular duct that carries sperm from the tail of the epididymis up through the spermatic cord and inguinal canal, over the bladder, to the ejaculatory duct. Cutting it (vasectomy) keeps sperm out of the semen.

follow.q: A vasectomy keeps sperm out of the semen. Which structure does it cut?
follow.why: A vasectomy cuts and ties the ductus deferens on each side, in the scrotum where it is easy to reach, so sperm from the epididymis can no longer reach the ejaculatory duct. The epididymis sits on the testis, and the ejaculatory ducts and urethra lie deep in the pelvis and also carry the glands' fluids, which still make up almost all of the semen.

labels.name: Suspensory ligament of penis
labels.fn: A band of connective tissue that anchors the root of the penis to the front of the pubic symphysis.

labels.name: Ampulla of ductus deferens
labels.fn: The widened last part of the ductus deferens, behind the bladder, where it joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct.

labels.name: Urinary bladder
labels.fn: The muscular sac that stores urine. In males the prostate lies just below it and the seminal vesicles lie behind it.

labels.name: Pubic symphysis
labels.fn: The cartilage joint that joins the two pubic bones at the front of the pelvis. The root of the penis is anchored in front of it.

labels.name: Seminal vesicle
labels.fn: One of a pair of glands behind the bladder. It makes most of the volume of semen, a thick fluid rich in the sugar fructose that fuels the sperm.

follow.q: Which glands make most of the volume of semen?
follow.why: The seminal vesicles supply roughly two thirds of the volume of semen, a thick fluid rich in fructose. The prostate adds most of the rest, the bulbourethral glands add only a few drops of mucus before ejaculation, and the sperm from the testes make up a tiny fraction of the volume.

labels.name: Ejaculatory duct
labels.fn: A short duct formed where the ampulla of the ductus deferens joins the duct of the seminal vesicle. It runs through the prostate and empties into the prostatic urethra.

labels.name: Prostatic urethra
labels.fn: The first part of the male urethra, running through the prostate. The ejaculatory ducts and the ducts of the prostate open into it.

labels.name: Deep muscles of perineum
labels.fn: The layer of skeletal muscle in the pelvic floor that the membranous urethra passes through. It includes the external urethral sphincter, which lets you hold urine by choice.

labels.name: Bulbourethral gland
labels.fn: A pea-sized gland beside the membranous urethra. Just before ejaculation it releases clear mucus that lubricates the urethra and neutralizes traces of acidic urine.

labels.name: Muscles of perineum surrounding anus
labels.fn: Skeletal muscle of the pelvic floor that rings the anus. It forms the external anal sphincter, which keeps the anus closed until you choose to open it.

labels.name: Corpus cavernosum
labels.fn: One of the two paired columns of erectile tissue along the top of the penis. When they fill with blood the penis becomes stiff.

labels.name: Membranous urethra
labels.fn: The short middle part of the male urethra, passing through the deep muscles of the perineum between the prostate and the penis.

labels.name: Spongy urethra
labels.fn: The longest part of the male urethra, running through the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral opening. It carries both urine and semen.

labels.name: Testis
labels.fn: One of the paired male gonads, inside the scrotum. Its coiled seminiferous tubules make sperm, and the cells between the tubules make testosterone.

labels.name: Epididymis
labels.fn: A single, tightly coiled tube about 6 m long lying along the back of the testis. Sperm mature and are stored here, gaining the ability to swim.

follow.q: Where do sperm gain the ability to swim and wait until ejaculation?
follow.why: Sperm leave the testis unable to swim and mature over about two weeks in the epididymis, which also stores them. The seminal vesicles and prostate are glands that add fluid, not storage sites, and the ejaculatory duct is only a short passage through the prostate.

labels.name: Scrotum
labels.fn: The skin-covered sac that hangs outside the body cavity and holds the testes. It keeps them a few degrees cooler than the core of the body, which sperm production needs.

labels.name: Corpus spongiosum
labels.fn: The single column of erectile tissue along the underside of the penis. It surrounds the spongy urethra and widens at the tip into the glans. It stays softer during erection, so the urethra stays open.

labels.name: External urethral opening
labels.fn: The opening at the tip of the glans penis through which urine and semen leave the body.

labels.name: Spermatic cord
labels.fn: The bundle running between the abdomen and each testis: the ductus deferens, testicular artery, veins, nerves and lymphatic vessels, wrapped in connective tissue and the cremaster muscle.

labels.name: Cremaster muscle
labels.fn: Skeletal muscle in the spermatic cord that wraps the testis. It contracts in the cold, pulling the testis up toward the warm body, and relaxes to lower it again.

follow.q: A man steps into a cold pool. What do his cremaster muscles do?
options: Relax, letting the testes hang lower
Contract, pushing sperm into the ductus deferens
Relax, so more blood reaches the testes
follow.why: Cold makes the cremaster muscles contract and pull the testes up against the warm body, which holds their temperature steady. They relax again in the warmth, letting the testes hang lower to lose heat. They do not move sperm along the ducts, and the change is about heat, not blood flow.

labels.name: Tunica vaginalis
labels.fn: The outer, double-layered serous sac around the front and sides of the testis, with a film of fluid between its layers.

labels.name: Efferent ductule
labels.fn: One of about a dozen small ducts that carry sperm from the rete testis into the head of the epididymis.

labels.name: Head of epididymis
labels.fn: The top part of the epididymis, where the efferent ductules bring sperm in from the testis.

labels.name: Body of epididymis
labels.fn: The middle part of the epididymis, running down the back of the testis, where sperm keep maturing.

labels.name: Seminiferous tubule lobules
labels.fn: The wedge-shaped compartments of the testis, about 250 of them, each holding one to four tightly coiled seminiferous tubules, where sperm are made.

labels.name: Ductus deferens
labels.fn: The muscular duct that carries sperm from the tail of the epididymis up through the spermatic cord and inguinal canal, over the bladder, to the ejaculatory duct.

labels.name: Septa (tunica albuginea)
labels.fn: Thin walls that run inward from the tunica albuginea and divide the testis into lobules. The printed "(tunica albuginea)" names the capsule they grow from.

labels.name: Rete testis
labels.fn: A network of channels at the back of the testis that collects sperm from the straight tubules and passes them to the efferent ductules.

follow.q: Put the route right: sperm leave the seminiferous tubules and pass through which structure just before the efferent ductules?
follow.why: The order is seminiferous tubule, straight tubule, rete testis, efferent ductules, then the head, body and tail of the epididymis, the ductus deferens and the ejaculatory duct. The rete testis is the network at the back of the testis that feeds the efferent ductules; the others all come later on the route.

labels.name: Tunica albuginea
labels.fn: The tough, white capsule of dense connective tissue directly around the testis. It sends septa inward that divide the testis into lobules.

labels.name: Straight tubule
labels.fn: The short, straight end of a seminiferous tubule that carries sperm into the rete testis.

labels.name: Tail of epididymis
labels.fn: The lowest part of the epididymis, where mature sperm are stored before the tube continues as the ductus deferens.

labels.name: Raphe
labels.fn: The visible midline ridge of the scrotal skin. It marks where the scrotal septum lies inside.

labels.name: Scrotal septum
labels.fn: The wall of connective tissue and smooth muscle that divides the scrotum into two compartments, one for each testis.

labels.name: Cremaster muscles
labels.fn: Skeletal muscle in the spermatic cord that wraps the testis. It contracts in the cold, pulling the testis up toward the warm body, and relaxes to lower it again.

labels.name: Dartos muscles
labels.fn: A layer of smooth muscle just under the scrotal skin. It contracts in the cold, wrinkling the skin and drawing the scrotum closer to the body to hold in heat.

labels.name: Plexus of testicular veins
labels.fn: The tangle of veins around the testicular artery in the spermatic cord (the pampiniform plexus). Cooler blood coming back from the testis takes heat from the arterial blood going in, which helps keep the testis cool.

labels.name: Ductus deferens
labels.fn: The muscular duct that carries sperm from the tail of the epididymis up through the spermatic cord and inguinal canal, over the bladder, to the ejaculatory duct.

labels.name: Spermatic cord
labels.fn: The bundle running between the abdomen and each testis: the ductus deferens, testicular artery, veins, nerves and lymphatic vessels, wrapped in connective tissue and the cremaster muscle.

labels.name: Testicular artery
labels.fn: The artery that supplies each testis. It branches from the abdominal aorta just below the renal arteries and runs down in the spermatic cord.

labels.name: Autonomic nerve
labels.fn: A nerve in the spermatic cord carrying autonomic fibers to the testis and its blood vessels.

labels.name: Lymphatic vessel
labels.fn: A vessel in the spermatic cord that drains lymph from the testis up to lymph nodes in the abdomen.

labels.name: Testis
labels.fn: One of the paired male gonads, inside the scrotum. Its coiled seminiferous tubules make sperm, and the cells between the tubules make testosterone.

labels.name: Epididymis
labels.fn: A single, tightly coiled tube about 6 m long lying along the back of the testis. Sperm mature and are stored here, gaining the ability to swim.

labels.name: Penile venules (uncompressed)
labels.fn: Small veins that drain blood out of the erectile tissue. In the relaxed penis they stay open, so blood leaves as fast as it arrives; during erection the swollen tissue presses them flat.

labels.name: Deep dorsal vein
accept: deep dorsal vein of the penis
labels.fn: The vein along the top of the penis, between the corpora cavernosa, that drains blood from the erectile tissue.

labels.name: Corpora cavernosa
labels.fn: The two columns of erectile tissue along the top of the penis. During erection their spaces fill with blood and they do most of the stiffening.

labels.name: Cavernosal arteries
labels.fn: An artery running down the center of each corpus cavernosum. When parasympathetic signals relax its smooth muscle, it widens and floods the erectile tissue with blood.

follow.q: What starts an erection?
options: Skeletal muscle in the shaft contracts
The corpus spongiosum fills with air
follow.why: Parasympathetic signals relax the smooth muscle of the cavernosal arteries, so they widen and blood pours into the erectile tissue. The swelling tissue then squeezes the venules and veins that drain it, trapping blood. A wider vein would let blood out faster, and the shaft has no skeletal muscle doing the stiffening.

labels.name: Spongy urethra
labels.fn: The longest part of the male urethra, running through the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral opening. It carries both urine and semen.

labels.name: Prepuce
labels.fn: The loose fold of skin that covers the glans of an uncircumcised penis. Circumcision removes it.

labels.name: Corpus spongiosum
labels.fn: The single column of erectile tissue along the underside of the penis. It surrounds the spongy urethra and widens at the tip into the glans. It stays softer during erection, so the urethra stays open.

follow.q: Which column of erectile tissue surrounds the urethra?
follow.why: The single corpus spongiosum runs along the underside of the penis around the spongy urethra and widens into the glans. The paired corpora cavernosa lie above it, the tunica albuginea is the tough covering around the columns, and the deep dorsal vein runs along the top.

labels.name: Uterus
labels.fn: The hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ in the pelvis between the bladder and the rectum. Its thick smooth-muscle wall (myometrium) and inner lining (endometrium) hold and nourish a developing baby.

labels.name: Ovary
labels.fn: One of the paired female gonads, beside the uterus. It holds the oocytes, each in a follicle, and makes estrogen and progesterone.

labels.name: Cervix
labels.fn: The narrow lower end of the uterus that projects into the top of the vagina. Its canal links the cavity of the uterus with the vagina.

follow.q: Which part of the uterus projects into the top of the vagina?
follow.why: The cervix is the narrow lower end of the uterus, and it pokes into the top of the vagina with its canal opening there. The fundus is the rounded top above the tubes, the body is the main middle part, and the broad ligament is a sheet of peritoneum, not part of the uterus.

labels.name: Rectum
labels.fn: The last straight part of the large intestine, lying behind the vagina and uterus.

labels.name: Vagina
labels.fn: The muscular tube, about 10 cm long, from the cervix to the outside. It receives the penis, lets menstrual flow out and forms the birth canal.

labels.name: Anus
labels.fn: The opening at the end of the digestive tract, behind the vaginal opening.

labels.name: Bladder
labels.fn: The muscular sac that stores urine. It lies in front of the uterus and above the front wall of the vagina.

labels.name: Pubic symphysis
labels.fn: The cartilage joint that joins the two pubic bones at the front of the pelvis. The mons pubis lies over it.

labels.name: Mons pubis
labels.fn: The rounded pad of fat and hair-bearing skin over the pubic symphysis.

labels.name: Urethra
labels.fn: The short tube, about 4 cm long, that carries urine from the bladder to its opening just in front of the vaginal opening. In females it carries only urine.

follow.q: Why are bladder infections more common in females than in males?
options: The female bladder wall has no smooth muscle layer
The female urethra also carries menstrual flow out
Its urethra is short and opens near the anus
Females have no sphincters around the urethra
follow.why: The female urethra is only about 4 cm long and opens in the vestibule, not far from the anus, so bacteria reach the bladder easily. The bladder wall is muscular in both sexes, menstrual flow leaves through the vagina, not the urethra, and both sexes have urethral sphincters.

labels.name: Clitoris
labels.fn: A small erectile organ at the front of the vulva, where the labia minora meet. Like the penis, it has erectile tissue and many sensory nerve endings.

labels.name: Labia minora
labels.fn: The thin inner folds of hairless skin on either side of the vestibule, around the urethral and vaginal openings. They meet at the front to form the hood over the clitoris.

labels.name: Labia majora
labels.fn: The outer pair of fat-filled, hair-bearing skin folds that enclose and protect the rest of the vulva.

labels.name: Ovary
labels.fn: One of the paired female gonads, beside the uterus. It holds the oocytes, each in a follicle, and makes estrogen and progesterone.

labels.name: Fimbriae
labels.fn: The finger-like fringes at the open end of each uterine tube. They drape over the ovary and sweep a released oocyte into the tube.

follow.q: What do the fimbriae do?
options: Anchor the ovary to the side of the uterus
Sweep an oocyte into the tube
follow.why: The fimbriae are the fringed, moving ends of the uterine tube; they sweep over the ovary and draw a released oocyte into the tube. The ovarian ligament anchors the ovary, the greater vestibular glands moisten the vestibule, and the ovary itself makes the hormones.

labels.name: Ovarian ligament
labels.fn: A cord of connective tissue that ties each ovary to the side of the uterus.

labels.name: Uterus
labels.fn: The hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ in the pelvis between the bladder and the rectum. Its thick smooth-muscle wall (myometrium) and inner lining (endometrium) hold and nourish a developing baby.

labels.name: Broad ligament
labels.fn: A wide double fold of peritoneum draped over the uterus, uterine tubes and ovaries, anchoring them to the side walls of the pelvis.

labels.name: Uterine tube (oviduct)
labels.fn: The tube, about 10 cm long, that runs from beside each ovary to the top of the uterus. Its cilia and smooth muscle move an oocyte along toward the uterus, and it is where sperm usually meet the oocyte.

labels.name: Cervix
labels.fn: The narrow lower end of the uterus that projects into the top of the vagina. Its canal links the cavity of the uterus with the vagina.

labels.name: Labia minora
labels.fn: The thin inner folds of hairless skin on either side of the vestibule, around the urethral and vaginal openings. They meet at the front to form the hood over the clitoris.

labels.name: Vagina
labels.fn: The muscular tube, about 10 cm long, from the cervix to the outside. It receives the penis, lets menstrual flow out and forms the birth canal.

labels.name: Labia majora
labels.fn: The outer pair of fat-filled, hair-bearing skin folds that enclose and protect the rest of the vulva.

labels.name: Prepuce
labels.fn: The fold of skin, formed where the labia minora meet at the front, that covers the glans of the clitoris.

labels.name: Glans clitoris
labels.fn: The exposed tip of the clitoris, packed with sensory nerve endings.

labels.name: Labia minora
labels.fn: The thin inner folds of hairless skin on either side of the vestibule, around the urethral and vaginal openings. They meet at the front to form the hood over the clitoris.

labels.name: Corpus cavernosum
labels.fn: One of the paired columns of erectile tissue that form the body of the clitoris. Like the corpora cavernosa of the penis, they fill with blood during sexual arousal.

labels.name: Bulb of vestibule
labels.fn: A mass of erectile tissue on each side of the vaginal opening, under the labia. It fills with blood during sexual arousal.

labels.name: Urethral opening
labels.fn: The opening of the urethra, between the clitoris and the vaginal opening.

labels.name: Labia majora
labels.fn: The outer pair of fat-filled, hair-bearing skin folds that enclose and protect the rest of the vulva.

labels.name: Vaginal opening
labels.fn: The opening of the vagina into the vestibule, just behind the urethral opening.

labels.name: Opening of right Bartholin's gland
labels.fn: Where the duct of a greater vestibular (Bartholin's) gland opens, beside the vaginal opening.

labels.name: Anus
labels.fn: The opening at the end of the digestive tract, behind the vaginal opening.

labels.name: Bartholin's glands
labels.fn: A pair of pea-sized glands beside and behind the vaginal opening (the greater vestibular glands). During sexual arousal they release mucus that moistens the vestibule.

follow.q: A blocked duct makes a painful swelling beside the vaginal opening. Which glands are involved?
follow.why: The greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands sit beside the vaginal opening, and a blocked duct makes a cyst there. The paraurethral glands are tiny glands beside the urethral opening, areolar glands are in the breast, and the bulbourethral glands are the male counterpart of the greater vestibular glands.

labels.name: Areolar glands
labels.fn: Small glands on the surface of the areola. Their oily secretion protects the skin of the nipple and areola.

labels.name: Fat tissue
labels.fn: Adipose tissue that fills the spaces between the lobes and gives the breast most of its size.

labels.name: Alveoli
labels.fn: Small sacs lined with milk-making cells and wrapped in contractile cells that squeeze the milk out. Clusters of alveoli form lobules.

follow.q: Where in the breast is milk made?
follow.why: Milk is made by the cells lining the alveoli. The lactiferous ducts carry it to the nipple, the lactiferous sinuses are widened parts of those ducts where it collects, and the areolar glands make an oily secretion for the skin, not milk.

labels.name: Lactiferous ducts
labels.fn: Ducts that carry milk from the lobes of the mammary gland to openings on the nipple.

labels.name: Areola
labels.fn: The ring of pigmented skin around the nipple.

labels.name: Lobule (contains alveoli)
labels.fn: A cluster of milk-making alveoli that drains into a duct. Several lobules make up each lobe of the mammary gland.

labels.name: Suspensory ligament
labels.fn: Bands of connective tissue running from the skin through the breast to the tissue over the chest muscles. They support the breast.

labels.name: Lactiferous sinuses
labels.fn: Widened parts of the lactiferous ducts just behind the nipple, where milk collects.

labels.name: Nipple
labels.fn: The raised tip of the breast, where the lactiferous ducts open to the surface.

labels.name: Acrosome
labels.fn: A cap-like sac over the front of the sperm head, filled with enzymes that let the sperm digest a path through the layers around an oocyte.

follow.q: What does the acrosome hold?
follow.why: The acrosome is a sac of enzymes over the front of the head that the sperm uses to digest its way through the layers around an oocyte. The mitochondria are in the midpiece, the nucleus is under the acrosome in the head, and microtubules form the core of the tail.

labels.name: Plasma membrane
labels.fn: The membrane that encloses the whole sperm cell, head to tail.

labels.name: Nucleus
labels.fn: The nucleus in the sperm head, holding a haploid set of 23 chromosomes packed very tightly.

labels.name: Mitochondria
labels.fn: Mitochondria wound in a spiral around the midpiece. They make the ATP that powers the beating tail.

labels.name: Centriole
labels.fn: A centriole at the base of the head, from which the core of the tail grows.

labels.name: Flagellum
labels.fn: The whip-like tail, one long flagellum whose beating drives the sperm forward.

labels.name: Axial filament
labels.fn: The core of microtubules running the length of the tail. Motor proteins slide the microtubules past each other, which bends the flagellum.

labels.name: Head
labels.fn: The front part of the sperm, holding the nucleus under the acrosome.

labels.name: Mid-piece
labels.fn: The short section behind the head, packed with mitochondria that supply ATP for swimming.

follow.q: Which part of a sperm holds the mitochondria that power its tail?
follow.why: The mitochondria are wound around the midpiece, right where the tail starts, so the ATP they make is close to the beating flagellum. The head holds the nucleus, the acrosome holds enzymes, and the end piece is the thin tip of the tail.

labels.name: Tail
labels.fn: The long main part of the flagellum, which beats to push the sperm forward.

labels.name: End piece
labels.fn: The thin last stretch of the tail, where the flagellum ends.

labels.name: GnRH
labels.fn: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone, released by the hypothalamus into the portal vessels. It stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH.

labels.name: FSH release
labels.fn: Follicle-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary. In males it acts on Sertoli cells to support sperm production.

labels.name: LH release
labels.fn: Luteinizing hormone from the anterior pituitary. In males it stimulates the Leydig cells to make testosterone.

follow.q: A drug blocks LH from acting in the testis. Which output falls first?
follow.why: LH acts on the Leydig cells, so blocking it cuts testosterone production first. With less testosterone feeding back, GnRH and FSH release rise rather than fall, and inhibin comes from Sertoli cells, which respond mainly to FSH.

labels.name: Leydig (interstitial) cells
labels.fn: Cells in the tissue between the seminiferous tubules. LH stimulates them to make testosterone.

labels.name: Interstitial space
labels.fn: The tissue between the seminiferous tubules, holding the Leydig cells and blood vessels.

labels.name: Seminiferous tubule
labels.fn: One of the coiled tubules of the testis where sperm are made. Its wall holds germ cells at every stage, supported by Sertoli cells.

labels.name: Sertoli cell
labels.fn: A tall supporting cell in the wall of the seminiferous tubule. Driven by FSH and testosterone, it nurtures developing sperm, forms the blood-testis barrier, makes androgen-binding protein and releases inhibin.

follow.q: Which cells does FSH act on to support sperm production?
follow.why: FSH binds to Sertoli cells, which then nurture the developing sperm and release inhibin and androgen-binding protein. Leydig cells respond to LH, the spermatogonia are nursed by the Sertoli cells rather than acted on directly, and the pituitary makes FSH rather than responding to it.

labels.name: Inhibin release
labels.fn: Inhibin, a hormone released by Sertoli cells. It feeds back on the anterior pituitary to lower FSH release.

labels.name: Androgen-binding protein (ABP) release
labels.fn: A protein Sertoli cells secrete into the tubule. It binds testosterone and keeps its concentration high around the developing sperm.

labels.name: Testosterone release
labels.fn: Testosterone from the Leydig cells. It drives sperm production and feeds back to lower GnRH and LH release.

labels.name: Trophoblast
labels.fn: The outer layer of cells of the blastocyst. It attaches to the endometrium and invades it during implantation, and later forms the embryo's share of the chorion; none of it becomes part of the embryo's body.

labels.name: Inner cell mass
labels.fn: The cluster of cells inside the blastocyst, pressed against one side of the cavity. It gives rise to the embryo itself, along with the amnion and yolk sac.

follow.q: Which part of the blastocyst goes on to form the embryo's body?
follow.why: The inner cell mass becomes the embryonic disc, and every tissue of the body comes from it. The trophoblast forms the embryo's share of the chorion, the blastocoel is only a fluid-filled space, and the zona pellucida is the oocyte's glycoprotein coat, shed before implantation.

labels.name: Blastocoel
labels.fn: The fluid-filled cavity inside the blastocyst, enclosed by the trophoblast, with the inner cell mass at one side.

labels.name: Eight-cell stage
labels.fn: The embryo after three cleavage divisions, about day 3. Each division makes more, smaller cells (blastomeres), so the embryo stays about the size of the original oocyte.

follow.q: During cleavage the zygote divides again and again. What happens to the embryo's overall size?
options: It roughly doubles with each division
It stays about the same size
It shrinks to half with each division
It grows only after the morula forms
follow.why: Cleavage divides the cytoplasm of the zygote into more and more cells without a growth phase between divisions, so the cells get smaller while the whole embryo stays about the size of the oocyte, still held inside the zona pellucida. It does not double or shrink, and real growth starts only once the embryo implants and takes in nutrients.

labels.name: Morula (16 cells)
labels.fn: A solid ball of about 16 cells (morula = little mulberry), reached around day 3 to 4 as the embryo nears the uterus.

labels.name: Blastocyst (70–100 cells)
labels.fn: The hollow ball of about 70 to 100 cells that forms by about day 5: an outer trophoblast, an inner cell mass and a fluid-filled blastocoel. It hatches from the zona pellucida and implants in the endometrium.

follow.q: Where does the blastocyst normally implant?
options: In the wall of the uterine tube
In the endometrium of the uterus
On the surface of the ovary
In the lining of the cervix
follow.why: The blastocyst reaches the uterus around day 5, hatches from the zona pellucida and burrows into the endometrium, usually high on the back wall. The uterine tube is where fertilization and cleavage happen, not implantation; the ovary only releases the oocyte, and the cervix is below the normal site.

labels.name: Four-cell stage
labels.fn: The embryo after two cleavage divisions, about day 2, still inside the zona pellucida and moving down the uterine tube.

labels.name: Two-cell stage
labels.fn: The embryo after the first cleavage division, about 30 hours after fertilization. Cleavage splits the cells without growth, so the two cells together are no bigger than the zygote.

labels.name: Fertilized Oocyte
labels.fn: The oocyte just after a sperm has entered it. Once the sperm and oocyte nuclei combine, it is the zygote, the first cell of the new individual. Fertilization normally happens in the ampulla of the uterine tube.

labels.name: Unfertilized Oocyte
labels.fn: The secondary oocyte released at ovulation, still wrapped in its zona pellucida and corona radiata. It survives only about a day unless a sperm fertilizes it.

labels.name: Endometrium
labels.fn: The inner lining of the uterus. Its glands and blood vessels nourish the implanting embryo, and the trophoblast digests its way into it.

labels.name: Blastocyst cavity
labels.fn: The fluid-filled cavity of the blastocyst (the blastocoel). During the second week, hypoblast cells spread over its inner surface to line the yolk sac.

labels.name: Hypoblast
labels.fn: The lower layer of the two-layered embryonic disc, facing the blastocyst cavity. Its cells help form the yolk sac, and most of them are replaced by endoderm during gastrulation.

labels.name: Epiblast
labels.fn: The upper layer of the embryonic disc, facing the amniotic cavity. During gastrulation its cells form all three germ layers, so every tissue of the body comes from it.

follow.q: During gastrulation, which layer of the embryonic disc gives rise to all three germ layers?
follow.why: Epiblast cells move through the primitive streak to form endoderm and mesoderm, and the ones that stay behind become ectoderm. The hypoblast is mostly pushed aside by the new endoderm, and the two trophoblast layers form the chorion, not the embryo.

labels.name: Embryonic disc
labels.fn: The flat, two-layered plate, epiblast over hypoblast, that the inner cell mass becomes in the second week. The embryo's whole body forms from it.

labels.name: Amnion
labels.fn: The thin membrane that grows from the epiblast and encloses the amniotic cavity. Its fluid cushions the embryo and lets it move and grow evenly.

labels.name: Amniotic cavity
labels.fn: The fluid-filled space above the epiblast, enclosed by the amnion. It enlarges until it surrounds the whole embryo.

labels.name: Trophoblast
labels.fn: The outer layer of cells of the blastocyst. It attaches to the endometrium and invades it during implantation, and later forms the embryo's share of the chorion; none of it becomes part of the embryo's body.

labels.name: Cytotrophoblast
labels.fn: The inner layer of the trophoblast, made of separate cells that keep dividing and feed new cells into the syncytiotrophoblast above them.

labels.name: Syncytiotrophoblast
labels.fn: The outer, invading layer of the trophoblast: cells fused into one mass of cytoplasm with many nuclei and no cell boundaries. It digests the endometrium to bury the embryo and secretes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone.

follow.q: Which layer secretes hCG, the hormone that a pregnancy test detects?
follow.why: The syncytiotrophoblast, the invading outer layer of the trophoblast, makes hCG from about the time of implantation. hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive and making progesterone. The hypoblast and epiblast form the embryonic disc, and the amnion encloses the amniotic fluid; none of them secretes hCG.

labels.name: Reestablished uterine mucosa
labels.fn: The surface lining of the endometrium, grown back over the spot where the blastocyst burrowed in. By about day 12 the embryo lies completely buried in the uterine wall.

labels.name: Endometrium
labels.fn: The inner lining of the uterus. Its glands and blood vessels nourish the implanting embryo, and the trophoblast digests its way into it.

labels.name: Hypoblast
labels.fn: The lower layer of the two-layered embryonic disc, facing the blastocyst cavity. Its cells help form the yolk sac, and most of them are replaced by endoderm during gastrulation.

labels.name: Trophoblast
labels.fn: The outer layer of cells of the blastocyst. It attaches to the endometrium and invades it during implantation, and later forms the embryo's share of the chorion; none of it becomes part of the embryo's body.

labels.name: Epiblast
labels.fn: The upper layer of the embryonic disc, facing the amniotic cavity. During gastrulation its cells form all three germ layers, so every tissue of the body comes from it.

labels.name: Amniotic cavity
labels.fn: The fluid-filled space above the epiblast, enclosed by the amnion. It enlarges until it surrounds the whole embryo.

labels.name: Reestablished uterine mucosa
labels.fn: The surface lining of the endometrium, grown back over the spot where the blastocyst burrowed in. By about day 12 the embryo lies completely buried in the uterine wall.

labels.name: Endometrium
labels.fn: The inner lining of the uterus. Its glands and blood vessels nourish the implanting embryo, and the trophoblast digests its way into it.

labels.name: Endoderm
labels.fn: The innermost germ layer, formed when epiblast cells moving through the primitive streak push the hypoblast aside. It forms the lining of the digestive tract and airways, and glands such as the liver and pancreas.

labels.name: Mesoderm
labels.fn: The middle germ layer, formed from epiblast cells that move through the primitive streak and spread between the other two layers. It forms muscle, bone and connective tissue, the heart, blood vessels and blood, and the kidneys.

labels.name: Amniotic cavity
labels.fn: The fluid-filled space above the epiblast, enclosed by the amnion. It enlarges until it surrounds the whole embryo.

labels.name: Trophoblast
labels.fn: The outer layer of cells of the blastocyst. It attaches to the endometrium and invades it during implantation, and later forms the embryo's share of the chorion; none of it becomes part of the embryo's body.

labels.name: Ectoderm
labels.fn: The outer germ layer, formed from the epiblast cells that stay in place. It forms the epidermis, hair and nails and the whole nervous system.

labels.name: Primitive streak
labels.fn: A groove along the midline of the epiblast that appears at the start of week 3 and marks the embryo's head-to-tail axis. Epiblast cells move in through it to form endoderm and mesoderm (gastrulation).

follow.q: Epiblast cells move in through the primitive streak. Which germ layer forms from the epiblast cells that stay behind?
follow.why: The cells that stay on the surface of the epiblast become ectoderm. The first cells to move through the streak displace the hypoblast and become endoderm, and the next ones spread between the layers as mesoderm. The hypoblast is an older layer that the new endoderm replaces.

labels.name: Maternal blood supply in intervillous space
labels.fn: Maternal blood from the uterine arteries pools in the intervillous space around the chorionic villi. Oxygen and nutrients diffuse from it into the fetal capillaries inside the villi; the two bloods do not mix.

labels.name: Uterine artery and vein
labels.fn: The mother's vessels in the uterine wall. Branches of the uterine arteries (spiral arteries) open into the intervillous space, and uterine veins drain the used blood back into her circulation.

labels.name: Chorionic villi
labels.fn: Finger-like projections of the chorion, each holding fetal capillaries, that hang in the pool of maternal blood. Their large surface is where the fetus takes up oxygen and nutrients and gives off carbon dioxide and wastes.

follow.q: In the placenta, how do oxygen and nutrients get from the mother's blood into the fetus's blood?
options: Maternal and fetal blood mix in the intervillous space
They cross the thin villus wall into fetal capillaries
Maternal red blood cells carry them into fetal vessels
The umbilical arteries bring them from the uterine arteries
follow.why: Maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi, and oxygen and nutrients move down their gradients across the thin villus wall into the fetal capillaries inside. The two bloods stay separate, maternal red blood cells do not cross, and the umbilical arteries carry fetal blood to the placenta, not maternal blood.

labels.name: Placenta
labels.fn: The disc-shaped organ built from the chorion (the fetal side) and the endometrium (the mother's side). It exchanges gases, nutrients and wastes between mother and fetus without mixing their blood, and it makes hormones that maintain the pregnancy.

labels.name: Yolk sac
labels.fn: A small membrane sac hanging from the embryo's belly side. In humans it holds no real yolk; early on it makes the first blood cells, and part of it is taken into the gut. It shrinks away before birth.

labels.name: Amniotic fluid
labels.fn: The fluid inside the amnion. It cushions the fetus, keeps its temperature steady, lets it move freely to build muscle and bone, and is swallowed and drawn into the airways as the gut and lungs develop.

labels.name: Uterus
labels.fn: The muscular organ in which the embryo and fetus develop. Its thick smooth-muscle wall, the myometrium, stretches as the fetus grows.

labels.name: Uterus
labels.fn: The muscular organ in which the embryo and fetus develop. Its thick smooth-muscle wall, the myometrium, stretches as the fetus grows.

labels.name: Chorion
labels.fn: The outermost membrane around the embryo, formed from the trophoblast and a layer of mesoderm. Its villi on the side facing the uterine wall form the fetal part of the placenta.

labels.name: Umbilical cord
labels.fn: The cord joining the fetus to the placenta. It carries two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein in a protective jelly.

follow.q: How many blood vessels does a normal umbilical cord contain?
follow.why: A normal cord has two umbilical arteries, carrying oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta, and one umbilical vein, carrying oxygen-rich blood back to the fetus. A cord with only one artery is a recognized variant that prompts a closer look at the fetus.

labels.name: Amnion
labels.fn: The thin inner membrane that holds the amniotic fluid around the fetus. It fuses with the chorion as the amniotic cavity grows.

labels.name: Umbilical vein
labels.fn: The single vessel in the cord that carries oxygen-rich, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus. It is called a vein because it carries blood toward the fetal heart, not because of its oxygen.

follow.q: The figure colors the umbilical vein blue. What kind of blood does it actually carry?
options: Oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta
Oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus
Maternal blood from the uterine veins
Oxygen-poor blood from the placenta to the fetus
follow.why: The umbilical vein carries blood that has just picked up oxygen in the placenta toward the fetal heart; the figure uses blue only because it is a vein. The umbilical arteries carry the oxygen-poor blood from the fetus to the placenta, and maternal blood never enters the cord.

labels.name: Umbilical artery
labels.fn: The paired vessels in the cord that carry oxygen-poor blood and wastes from the fetus to the placenta. They branch from the fetus's internal iliac arteries.

labels.name: Placenta
labels.fn: The disc-shaped organ built from the chorion (the fetal side) and the endometrium (the mother's side). It exchanges gases, nutrients and wastes between mother and fetus without mixing their blood, and it makes hormones that maintain the pregnancy.

labels.name: Aorta
labels.fn: The main artery leaving the left ventricle. In the fetus it also receives blood from the pulmonary trunk through the ductus arteriosus, just beyond the arch.

labels.name: Ductus arteriosus
labels.fn: A short fetal vessel joining the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Because the lungs' vessels strongly resist flow before birth, most blood from the right ventricle takes this shortcut past the lungs.

follow.q: Before birth, why does most blood in the pulmonary trunk pass through the ductus arteriosus instead of into the lungs?
options: The fluid-filled lungs' vessels resist flow strongly
Aortic pressure is lower than pulmonary pressure after birth
The pulmonary valve stays shut until the first breath
The lungs already finished their gas exchange
follow.why: Before birth the lungs are collapsed and full of fluid, and their arterioles are constricted by the low oxygen, so resistance in the pulmonary circuit is high. Blood follows the easier path through the ductus arteriosus into the aorta. The pulmonary valve opens with every beat, the lungs do no gas exchange before birth, and pressure after birth does not explain flow before it.

labels.name: Pulmonary trunk
labels.fn: The artery leaving the right ventricle. In the fetus most of its blood bypasses the fluid-filled lungs through the ductus arteriosus and goes into the aorta.

labels.name: Foramen ovale
labels.fn: An opening in the wall between the atria, covered by a flap of the septum primum that lets blood pass only from right to left. It sends the oxygen-rich blood arriving in the inferior vena cava straight to the left side of the heart, bypassing the lungs.

follow.q: Which way does blood flow through the foramen ovale before birth?
options: From the left atrium to the right atrium
From the right atrium to the left atrium
From the right ventricle to the left ventricle
From the left ventricle to the right ventricle
follow.why: Before birth, pressure in the right atrium is higher than in the left, because little blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium. Blood pushes the flap open and passes from right to left. The foramen ovale is between the atria, not the ventricles, and its flap blocks flow in the other direction.

labels.name: Ductus venosus
labels.fn: A fetal vessel in the liver that carries much of the oxygen-rich blood of the umbilical vein straight into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver's capillaries.

labels.name: Aorta
labels.fn: The descending aorta, carrying mixed blood to the lower body. The umbilical arteries branch from its internal iliac branches to take blood back to the placenta.

labels.name: Inferior vena cava
labels.fn: The large vein returning blood from the lower body to the right atrium. In the fetus it also carries the oxygen-rich blood from the ductus venosus, so its blood is the best oxygenated to reach the heart.

labels.name: Umbilical arteries
labels.fn: The paired vessels in the cord that carry oxygen-poor blood and wastes from the fetus to the placenta. They branch from the fetus's internal iliac arteries.

labels.name: Umbilical vein
labels.fn: The single vessel in the cord that carries oxygen-rich, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus. It is called a vein because it carries blood toward the fetal heart, not because of its oxygen.

labels.name: Placenta
labels.fn: The disc-shaped organ built from the chorion (the fetal side) and the endometrium (the mother's side). It exchanges gases, nutrients and wastes between mother and fetus without mixing their blood, and it makes hormones that maintain the pregnancy.

labels.name: Bladder
labels.fn: The fetal urinary bladder. The fetal kidneys make urine from about week 10, and that urine becomes much of the amniotic fluid.

os-1-13.alt: Two views of a standing woman with paired arrows. In the side view a vertical arrow runs from cranial at the head to caudal at the lower back, and a horizontal arrow runs from posterior (dorsal) at the back to anterior (ventral) at the front. In the front view, superior is at the top of the page and inferior at the bottom, right and left are marked on her own sides, an arrow runs from the midline outward to lateral, and arrows along the left arm and right leg run from proximal near the trunk to distal at the hand and foot.

os-1-14.alt: A woman standing in anatomical position, seen from the front and slightly to one side, crossed by four flat panels. A vertical panel running front to back divides her into right and left parts (the sagittal plane). A vertical panel running side to side divides her into front and back parts (the frontal, or coronal, plane). A horizontal panel at hip level divides her into upper and lower parts (the transverse plane). A slanted panel through the lower legs is an oblique plane.

os-1-15.alt: Side and front views of the body with the cavities shaded. The cranial cavity inside the skull holds the brain, and a narrow canal runs down from it through the backbone; together they form the dorsal body cavity. In the chest, the two lung spaces sit on either side of a central space whose lower part surrounds the heart. A dome-shaped diaphragm lies below the chest. Below it, the large abdominal cavity continues into the funnel-shaped pelvic cavity; chest, abdominal and pelvic spaces together form the ventral body cavity.

os-1-17.alt: Left: the heart enclosed in a two-layered sac. The inner layer lies on the heart's surface, the outer layer forms the outside of the sac, and a thin space lies between them. Right: the same arrangement modeled by a fist pushed into a soft, partly filled balloon. The balloon wall touching the fist matches the inner layer, the far wall matches the outer layer, and the air inside matches the space between them.

os-1-12.alt: Front and back views of a person standing in anatomical position, with the surface divided into named regions: head, face, eyes, cheeks, ears, chin, neck, chest, armpit, arm, bend of the elbow, forearm, wrist, palm, fingers, abdomen, navel, hip, groin, pubic area, thigh, front of the knee, leg, ankle and foot on the front; head, neck, shoulder, back, arm, back of the elbow, lower back, sacrum, forearm, hand, buttock, thigh, back of the knee, calf, heel and sole on the back.

os-1-16.alt: Two front views of the abdomen showing the organs behind the wall. On the left, two vertical and two horizontal lines divide it into nine regions: right hypochondriac, epigastric and left hypochondriac across the top; right lumbar, umbilical and left lumbar across the middle; right iliac, hypogastric and left iliac across the bottom. On the right, one vertical and one horizontal line crossing at the navel divide it into four quadrants: right upper, left upper, right lower and left lower. The dome of the diaphragm is outlined at the top.

os-3-4.alt: A section of plasma membrane: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins spanning it or sitting on its surfaces, cholesterol tucked between the phospholipids, and sugar chains attached to some proteins and lipids on the outer face.

os-3-13.alt: A cutaway drawing of a generalized human cell showing the plasma membrane, the nucleus, and the internal structures of the cytoplasm, including the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosomes, peroxisomes, ribosomes and a pair of centrioles.

os-3-15.alt: The Golgi apparatus drawn as a stack of flattened, curved membrane sacs, with small vesicles arriving on the side facing the endoplasmic reticulum and budding off the far side, beside an electron micrograph of the same stacked sacs.

os-3-17.alt: A peroxisome drawn as a small round sac bounded by a single membrane, with a dense, crystal-like core of enzymes inside.

os-3-18.alt: The three kinds of cytoskeleton fiber side by side: a hollow microtubule built from paired protein subunits, a thin microfilament made of two twisted strands of actin, and a rope-like intermediate filament made of many coiled protein strands.

os-4-5.alt: Close-up drawings of the membranes of two neighboring cells joined in different ways: a tight junction, where strands of protein stitch the two membranes together; a gap junction, where paired protein tubes connect the two cells' interiors; and anchoring junctions, including a desmosome with dense plaques on each side linked across the gap by adhesion proteins and anchored inside to rope-like filaments.

os-3-19.alt: Cutaway drawing of a cell nucleus. A double-layered nuclear envelope, studded with pores, surrounds the nucleus. Threads of chromatin fill the inside, and a dense, darker nucleolus sits within them. Flattened sacs of rough endoplasmic reticulum, dotted with ribosomes, curve around the outside of the envelope and connect to it.

os-3-22.alt: Levels of DNA packing, from a compact X-shaped chromosome down to its chromatin fiber, then to beads of DNA wrapped around histone proteins (nucleosomes), then to the bare double helix, and finally to the helix drawn flat as a ladder.

os-3-32.alt: A row of drawings, each with a short list of events underneath and a fluorescence micrograph below, showing a cell passing through the stages of mitosis and then cytokinesis: chromosomes condense, line up across the middle, separate to opposite ends, and two new nuclei form as the cell pinches in two.

os-4-6.alt: A grid of drawings of epithelial sheets sitting on a basement membrane. Rows are squamous (flat), cuboidal (cube-shaped) and columnar (tall) cells; columns are simple (one layer) and stratified (many layers). A separate panel shows pseudostratified columnar epithelium: one layer of cells of different heights, nuclei at different levels, cilia on top.

os-10-22.alt: A small outline of the heart with a box on its wall, enlarged into a drawing of branching, striped cardiac muscle fibers beside a capillary. Each fiber has a central nucleus, and wavy intercalated discs join the fibers end to end. A further enlargement of one disc shows desmosomes holding the two membranes together and gap junctions bridging them.

os-12-8.alt: Drawing of a single neuron. An irregular cell body holding a nucleus sends out several short, branching dendrites. One long axon leaves the cell body and is wrapped in evenly spaced segments of insulating covering; a glial cell reaches out with two arms to form two of the segments. The axon ends in many branches whose tips meet the dendrites of the next neuron. At the upper left, the axon of another neuron ends on this neuron's dendrites.

os-4-9.alt: A table of drawings of exocrine glands sunk into a surface epithelium. Each drawing shows surface cells, duct cells lining a pit, and secretory cells at its bottom. The simple glands have one unbranched duct; the compound glands have a branching duct. The secretory parts are tube-shaped (tubular), end in round sacs (alveolar, or acinar), or mix both (tubuloalveolar).

os-4-10.alt: Three drawings of a row of gland cells on a basement membrane, each with a nucleus below and a Golgi apparatus budding secretory vesicles above. Merocrine: vesicles fuse with the top of the cell and release their contents while the cell stays whole. Apocrine: the top of the cell, packed with vesicles, pinches off. Holocrine: the cell fills with product and the whole cell becomes the secretion.

os-4-4.alt: Front view of a woman's body with text boxes pointing to four kinds of membrane: the lining of the mouth and airway, the linings around the lungs and the abdominal organs, the skin of the hand, and the inside of the knee joint.

os-19-2.alt: Front view of an opened chest with the ribs cut away. The heart sits in the middle of the chest between the two lungs, resting on the dome of the diaphragm, with its pointed tip angled down and to the left. A dashed line marks the cut edge of the sac around the heart. A small side view shows the heart behind the sternum and in front of the esophagus and vertebral column.

os-19-5.alt: A small drawing of the heart with a box on its outer wall, enlarged into a slice showing the layers from inside to outside: a thin inner lining, a thick band of muscle, a thin outer covering, a narrow fluid-filled space, a thin membrane, and a tough outer fibrous layer.

os-19-6.alt: Two drawings of the outside of the heart. The front view shows the four chambers from the surface, the ear-shaped flaps of the upper chambers, the large vessels leaving the top, and surface vessels running in fat-filled grooves toward the tip. The back view shows the veins entering the upper chambers and the surface vessels on the back of the heart.

os-19-9.alt: A front view of the heart cut open in a frontal plane. It shows the two upper and two lower chambers, the wall between the lower chambers, the valves between upper and lower chambers held by thin cords to small muscles on the lower chamber walls, the valves at the exits to the two large arteries, the large veins entering, and the thick muscular wall of the lower left chamber.

os-19-12.alt: The heart seen from above with the upper chambers and large vessels removed, so all four valves are visible in one plane. Two large valves sit at the back, one with three flaps on the right side and one with two flaps on the left. Two smaller round valves with three half-moon flaps each sit in front of them.

os-19-4.alt: Two drawings of the circulation. Above, the heart with its large vessels: vessels carrying oxygen-poor blood shown in blue and vessels carrying oxygen-rich blood shown in red. Below, a loop diagram: the right side of the heart sends blood through a small loop to the capillaries of the lungs and back to the left side, which sends it through a larger loop to the capillaries of the body and back to the right side.

os-19-15.alt: Front and back views of the heart showing its own blood vessels. Red arteries branch from the base of the aorta: one runs down the front groove toward the tip, one curves around the left side in the groove between upper and lower chambers, and one runs around the right side and down the back. Blue veins run beside them and gather into a wide vein in the groove on the back of the heart that empties into the right upper chamber.

os-19-18.alt: The heart cut open in a frontal plane, seen from the front, with its conduction pathway drawn as yellow lines. A small node sits high in the wall of the right upper chamber near where the large vein from above enters. Three pathways run from it down through the right upper chamber to a second node low in the wall between the upper chambers, and a band crosses to the left upper chamber. From the second node a single bundle runs into the wall between the lower chambers, splits into right and left branches that run down toward the tip, and then fans out as fine fibers up the walls of both lower chambers.

os-20-4.alt: Three curved wedges of vessel wall side by side, each with its inner, middle and outer layers bracketed. The elastic artery has a thick middle layer packed with wavy dark elastic fibers. The muscular artery has a thick middle layer of smooth muscle, a wavy inner elastic line, and small vessels in its outer layer. The arteriole has a thin wall with only a few large smooth muscle cells in its middle layer.

os-20-5.alt: Three short capillary tubes cut open at one end. The first has an unbroken wall of endothelial cells wrapped in a complete basement membrane, with narrow clefts between cells. The second has a similar wall dotted with small pores through the cells. The third has large gaps between cells and a basement membrane with holes in it.

os-20-7.alt: Wedges of wall from three veins with their layers bracketed. The large vein has a thick outer layer containing small vessels, nerves and some smooth muscle, over a thin middle layer. The medium vein has a thin middle layer and paired flaps projecting into the lumen, shown closed, with a side view of the flaps. The venule has a very thin wall of lining cells and a trace of muscle.

os-20-24.alt: A front view of a standing woman with her main arteries drawn in red. The aorta rises from the heart, arches, and runs down the back of the trunk, giving branches to the head, both arms, the abdominal organs and the kidneys, then splits in the pelvis into two branches that run down each leg to the foot. The arm arteries divide at the elbow into two forearm branches that meet in arches in the palm.

os-20-25.alt: The aorta on its own. It rises from the aortic valve, where two small arteries leave for the heart muscle, curves up and over to the left, and runs straight down. Three branches leave the top of the curve: one short trunk on the right that splits in two, then separate branches to the left side of the neck and the left arm.

os-20-27.alt: The underside of the brain with its arteries in red. Two arteries run up the underside of the brainstem and join into one midline artery. That artery splits at its top end, and short connecting arteries link it to the two arteries arriving at the front, closing a ring of arteries around the base of the brain.

os-20-28.alt: The aorta running down the back of the chest and abdomen in front of the spine, with the ribs, diaphragm and kidneys in place. Small branches leave it in the chest for the chest wall and organs. It passes through an opening in the diaphragm, gives off a short trunk that splits three ways, single branches to the gut, paired branches to the kidneys and to the reproductive glands, and splits into two large branches in the pelvis.

os-20-11.alt: An outline drawing of a standing woman with black dots at the places where a pulse can be felt: the temple, the jaw, the side of the neck, the inner arm above the elbow, the thumb side of the wrist, the groin, the back of the knee, behind the inner ankle and on the top of the foot.

os-20-35.alt: A front view of a standing woman with her main veins drawn in blue. Veins from the head, neck and arms join into two large trunks that meet in one large vein entering the top of the heart. Veins from the legs, pelvis, kidneys and liver join a second large vein that runs up the back of the abdomen to the bottom of the heart. Superficial veins run up the inner and outer sides of each arm, and a long vein runs up the inner side of each leg.

os-20-37.alt: A side view of the head and neck showing the veins. Wide venous channels run inside the skull, along the top midline and around the back and base of the skull, and drain into a large deep vein running down the neck beside the airway. A smaller vein runs down the outside of the neck, and veins from the face and scalp join both. The neck veins end in a vein running under the collarbone.

os-20-38.alt: The veins of the right arm, front view, with deep veins shown darker than superficial ones. Deep veins run beside the forearm and arm bones. A superficial vein runs up the thumb side, another up the little-finger side, and a short vein crosses the front of the elbow to link them. All drain into a vein in the armpit and then one under the collarbone.

os-20-41.alt: The veins of the lower limb in front and back views. Deep veins run beside the leg and thigh bones and join into one vein behind the knee and one in the thigh, which passes into the pelvis. A long superficial vein runs from the inner ankle up the inner side of the leg to the groin, and a shorter one runs up the back of the calf to the back of the knee. A venous arch crosses the top of the foot.

os-20-43.alt: The abdominal organs with the veins that drain the gut. Veins from the stomach, pancreas, spleen and intestines gather into three main veins that join behind the pancreas into a single large vein running up into the liver.

os-22-3.alt: Three drawings of the nose. A front view and a side view of a face name the parts of the outer nose from the root between the eyes down the ridge to the tip and the flared wings beside each nostril. A third drawing shows the framework beneath: the nasal and upper jaw bones at the top and plates of cartilage, including the septal cartilage, forming the lower nose.

os-22-4.alt: A midline cut through the head and neck seen from the side. The nasal cavity with three curled shelves on its side wall sits above the roof of the mouth, with the sinuses of the frontal and sphenoid bones around it. Behind the nose, mouth and voice box the throat is divided into upper, middle and lower parts. The voice box below shows the leaf-shaped flap at its top, its two pairs of folds, and the large shield-shaped cartilage and ring-shaped cartilage in its wall, with the hyoid bone above.

os-22-6.alt: A side view outline of the head and neck with the throat shaded in three colors: the upper part behind the nasal cavity, the middle part behind the mouth and the lower part behind the voice box, continuing down as the esophagus behind the trachea.

os-22-7.alt: The voice box from the front and from the right side.
